- Older data (late 2022): Meta's VR headset platform had about 200,000 monthly active users against a 500,000 target. [L1092.109]
- VR 3D shopping was therefore not a planning factor for online stores in the coming few years. [L1092.109]

### Tools

- PayHip is a platform for selling digital products such as PDFs. [L1216.027]
- Setup: add the product, set up checkout, and customize the store design. It then generates a simple sales link. [L1216.027]
- Its checkout is a one-page checkout. [L1216.027]

### Applying dropshipping methods to other online businesses

- Human psychology and platform mechanics carry over from dropshipping to other online businesses. [L1251.048]
- Only the objective changes. For example, a lead-generation campaign books sales calls instead of making a direct product sale. [L1251.048]

### Direct mail

- Direct mail sells very different products with the same method, because buyer reactions stay the same across products. A seller who understands those reactions can apply one approach to any new offer. [L1369.001]
- Direct mail reaches buyers quickly and at low cost in good and bad markets. It shows early whether a product sells, so a campaign can still run within the selling season. [L1369.002]
- This only works for products with real merit and enough people who want them or can be made to want them. [L1369.002]
- Management can check every claim before a direct mail piece goes out, which makes written promises easier to control than a salesman's spoken pitch. [L1369.003]
- Small mailings let a seller test an idea cheaply before committing to a large budget. [L1369.003]
- Direct mail can prepare a sales team's prospects before a visit, so salespeople meet buyers who already know the offer. [L1369.004]
- The same letter technique can help a business sell to its own staff and partners. [L1369.004]

### AI-first dropshipping

- An AI-first dropshipping system is designed for speed and leaner operations across product research, store build and ad creative. This is why its milestones are set aggressively. [L1452.013]
- The old approach of guessing, testing blindly, or spending weeks building a store is replaced by AI-supported work that speeds up each stage. The goal is faster decisions and less wasted effort. [L1459.002]
- AI dropshipping can be organized into five areas where AI tools add leverage: [L1459.020]
  - product research [L1459.020]
  - store creation [L1459.020]
  - creatives and content [L1459.020]
  - customer experience [L1459.020]
  - data-based decisions [L1459.020]
- Each area is a place where manual work or guesswork can be replaced by tools. [L1459.020]

### Membership, coaching and community

- Business 100k Club membership is available only after crossing $100,000 in cumulative sales with a Source A store. [L0805.060]
- Coaching call schedule (older, 2022): the first Wednesday of each month at 2 PM Eastern Time. [L0969.100]
- Replays and transcripts of the calls are published on the fastbusinessforum.com forum after each call (older, 2022). [L0969.101]
- Case (March 2020): a coaching call document contains only administrative metadata: the coach's name, a recording date of 4 March 2020, and a link to a Source A retreat held in Portugal in 2020. It has no spoken content, rules, figures or procedures that could be extracted as know-how. [L0980.001]
- Case (September 2018): a founder's coaching call lists only three external resources as links from the session: a search engine domination course, a retreat ticket sale, and a new podcast on the eCommerce lifestyle. The transcript has no further figures, metrics or procedures. [L1273.001]

### High-ticket dropshipping course: scope and audience

- Older advice (2021-22): the growth phase applies to an existing business. The build phase applies only to someone starting a new business, so a store already running should focus on growth content. [L1456.034]
- The course is aimed at people who already run a high-ticket dropshipping business, not at beginners. Learners still in the launch stage are told to start with the build-phase material. [L1495.001]
- Older advice (2021-22): the program targets stores trading for anywhere from a few months to several years. A store at either end of that range can use the grow-phase material. A store still being set up should begin with the build phase. [L1495.012]
- Sources differ on the entry point, and both apply in their own case. The course is framed for existing owners [L1495.001]. A beginner only needs to focus on the Build phase at the start [L1496.005]. Existing owners use the course directly, and beginners start with Build. [L1495.001, L1496.005]
- Training is meant to stay useful well after launch, including one or two years into a running business. A beginner can leave advanced material until the business has grown. [L1496.011]

### High-ticket dropshipping course: structure

- The course is split into a build phase, which covers setting up and launching the business, and a grow phase, which covers scaling traffic and conversion. An existing business owner can skip the build-phase modules. [L1495.002]
- The Build phase covers building and launching the business. The Grow phase covers marketing and outsourcing after launch. [L1496.005]
- Older (2021-22): the high-ticket dropshipping process is described as a sequence of five steps: build the business, then launch it, then grow it. The build phase is the first stage. The unit names only build, launch and grow, so the other two steps are not named in this source. [L1490.003]
- Older (2021-22): in the members area, the Build phase modules appear first, at the top of the page below the welcome video, under a heading called Build Phase. The course has about six Build phase modules, which must be completed in numbered order. [L1496.006]
- The growth stage consists of about ten modules, each tackling a single dimension of marketing for high-ticket dropshipping. That count keeps rising over time. Named modules: conversion rate optimization, backlink acquisition, content marketing, search engine optimization (SEO), pay-per-click advertising, email marketing and retargeting. [L1495.004]
- There is no fixed order for working through the grow-phase modules. Start with the weakest area of the business, or with a traffic channel not yet tested. [L1495.005]

### High-ticket dropshipping course: working through the Build phase

Older advice (2021-22). [L1496.007]

1. Join the private members-only Facebook group. [L1496.007]
2. Open Module 1 in the Build phase. [L1496.007]
3. Watch one lesson per day and complete its action item. [L1496.007]
4. Move to the next module only after finishing the current one, following the numbered order. [L1496.007]
5. Attend the coaching calls. [L1496.007]
6. When stuck, use the support channels: Facebook group search first, then email. [L1496.007]


# 2. Niche and product research

## Choosing a Business Model and Setting Research Goals

### Definitions: Niche, Product and Market

- A niche is an industry, product category or product type, such as outdoor lights or solar streetlights, not one specific product. Each category can be researched separately, and a first dropshipping store should be built around a niche [L0585.002, L0963.111].
- Market selection means deciding three linked things: the market you sell in, the customers you serve and the products you sell. These decisions shape the rest of the business (older, 2021-22) [L1059.001].
- Market selection is important but is not the single factor that decides success in high-ticket dropshipping. Store setup, supplier relationships and marketing matter just as much (older, 2021-22) [L1059.003].
- When using a broad category as the search term, you only need enough products within it that meet the price, shipping, supplier and competition needs, not every product in the category. A specific product type can be used instead (older, 2021-22) [L1329.008].
- Focusing on a whole niche rather than a single product tends to produce more repeat business, because customers notice a brand that knows its category and product quality. Research the niche first, then build the brand around it [L1251.005].
- Dropshipping lets you experiment with products and niches without large inventory commitments. Gather customer feedback, then pivot product offerings or focus on the niches showing the most potential, and optimize based on what customers actually want [L0007.025].
- Without holding inventory, a dropshipper can test any product available from supply sources such as AliExpress or Alibaba, and can test any niche, since no stock is tied to one product [L0760.010].

### Why Niche Selection Comes First

- Niche selection is the foundation of a profitable dropshipping business and the first step in building a semi-automated store. Selecting the wrong niche causes business failure even when every other aspect of the operation is executed correctly [L0010.001, L0591.006].
- Niche selection deserves the most careful work before other store setup, because a poor niche choice undermines everything built on top of it [L0585.003].
- Validate thoroughly before launch rather than rushing the decision [L0009.003].
- Validate niche ideas on objective, measurable criteria rather than gut feeling or assumptions. This removes guesswork and increases the probability of long-term success [L0043.001].
- Market research is the foundation for everything that follows. Skipping it or treating it lightly leads to stores built around weak niches that cannot succeed [L0043.004].
- A niche that makes sales is not automatically a good choice. Launching without proper research can bring revenue while the business becomes unsustainable (mistake) [L0585.004].
- Testing removes weak niches before time is spent on them, so many failing niches are a good sign [L0451.008].
- A brainstormed list of niche ideas does not show which niches will work. Each idea has to pass a series of market research tests before it is worth pursuing [L1057.001].

### Business Models: High-Ticket, Low-Ticket and Trend Products

| Model | Price point | Order logic | Customer service load | Sources |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High-ticket (definition) | Single unit about USD 150 to 200 or more [L0660.012] | Higher percentage profit per sale, so far fewer orders are needed for the same revenue as a business selling USD 20 to 100 items (older, 2021-22) [L0994.002] | Varies by product: custom luxury items at several thousand USD need more calls, follow-up and support [L1277.018] (older, 2020); around USD 2,000 products with many suppliers need fewer customer contacts [L1281.025] (older, 2022) | [L0660.012, L0994.002, L1277.018, L1281.025] |
| Market-average high-ticket | Average market price of USD 800 or more, examples USD 1,000 to 6,000 (older, 2021-22) [L0771.014] | Built around a market, not a single product [L1059.001] | Depends on product type [L1277.018, L0766.001] | [L0771.014, L1059.001] |
| Low-ticket (definition) | Products up to about USD 80 to 90, mostly leather jackets [L0660.012] | Low margin per sale, much harder to run this way (older, 2021-22) [L0994.002] | Not recommended for cheap products by the author [L1346.005] | [L0660.012, L0994.002, L1346.005] |
| Trend / viral (pump and dump) | Target low to moderate ticket, roughly USD 30 to 50 [L1211.007] | Impulse purchases; novelty drives demand [L1211.006] | Not specified in source | [L1211.006, L1211.007] |

### High-Ticket Products

- High-ticket is defined as a product with a single-unit price of about USD 150 to 200 or more. The example store sold low-ticket products up to about USD 80 to 90, mostly leather jackets [L0660.012].
- High-ticket dropshipping focuses on higher-priced physical products, such as lighting, that fit the store model. These products were sourced and sold to customers directly, with no need to hold inventory (older, 2021-22) [L1014.017].
- The research process for high-ticket dropshipping is specific because it aims to find a market with a high probability of success. Generic product research is not enough for this model (older, 2021-22) [L1058.004].
- Higher-priced products around USD 2,000 are a good fit for a first store with many suppliers, because ads reveal the winners and fewer customers need to be contacted. Choose products that meet the criteria, not cheap items that cannot carry ad spend (older, 2022) [L1281.025].
- High-ticket products such as custom luxury items at several thousand USD need more phone calls, follow-up and support before and after the sale. Enter this segment only if you are ready to provide that level of service (older, 2020) [L1277.018].
- High-end or luxury products can still sell but need more work. They suit a seller willing to handle more customer contact, not one who wants a low-touch business [L0766.001].
- Between a high-demand niche and a high-price niche, both can work. High search volume gives more opportunity, while high-price niches with fewer orders often earn the most profit per order (older, 2019) [L1275.009].

### Low-Ticket and Trend Products

- The author does not recommend low-ticket dropshipping of cheap products. If a store is built that way anyway, competitor listings can still be a source of marketing ideas, although this does not always work [L1346.005].
- Good pump-and-dump products usually have viral potential that works well on TikTok and Instagram Reels. They should be eye-catching or emotionally triggering, with a clear wow factor [L1211.005].
- Good pump-and-dump products are usually gadgety or gimmicky. Their appeal is the novelty of the item, not an established need or a lasting use case [L1211.006].
- Target a low to moderate ticket price, roughly USD 30 to 50. Lower prices make impulse purchases easier [L1211.007].
- Beginners should avoid supplement, beauty and pet niches. The hit rate is low, and large brands spend six or even seven figures on ads, which a small seller without large cash flow cannot outspend [L1175.004].

### Service Resale and Local Services

- When starting out, a dropshipping operator can resell a service they do not perform themselves, such as Invisalign. The operator runs ads for it and receives payment per lead or as a monthly fee, which multiplies income without building a separate product business [L0440.016].
- Local service niches with high ticket value, such as dentists offering Invisalign or veneers, are attractive because a single converted patient can be worth about USD 3,000 to 5,000 [L0440.017].

### B2B Niches

- B2B niches can be as profitable as B2C niches, and the store setup changes little between them. Do not reject a good B2B niche only for its audience (older, 2020) [L0664.047].
- When targeting B2B niches, include a phone number on the site, because businesses typically require phone contact before purchasing. Also prepare for bulk orders and more intensive customer service demands [L0031.002].

### Physical Products, Lead Value and Private Label

- Physical-product niches are not a fit for this business model unless they serve lead value optimization, such as promoting affiliate products to existing physical-product customers [L0835.142].
- Private labeling (own brand, produced by a current supplier) is a later stage for established stores with profits and data. It is more work, takes more time and often more money than dropshipping [L0971.016].
- Some niches and product types, such as jewelry, are hard to turn into a real brand. Decide early whether a product is a quick private-label flip or a product with long-term brand potential [L1469.016].

### Service Resale and Effort per Revenue

- Niche and product selection should aim for products that need little effort for big results: little time on phone calls and email handling, and no need to list thousands of products. Building a business still takes real work, but the goal is to minimize effort per unit of revenue [L1518.002].
- Some industries should be avoided by default because they are too time- and resource-intensive for the money they return, not because no profit is possible. This is a judgment about upside relative to workload [L0766.002].
- Whether a niche is good depends on the seller's goals and the effort they want to put in [L0766.001].
- Niche choice is a judgment about upside relative to workload, so compare the profit of each niche with the amount of time and support it requires [L0585.006].

### Criteria for Choosing a Niche

- Select a niche with high sales volume, minimal customer service requirements and high profit per transaction [L0009.001].
- Optimal niches support semi-automated operations with minimal post-sale customer support, which reduces operational overhead and workload [L0009.004].
- Review each potential niche against a fixed set of criteria before entering it, comparing profit with the amount of time and support it requires [L0585.006].
- For every researched niche, identify the price points, calculate the profit margins and track search demand to confirm that enough people are actively looking for the product [L1057.003].
- Run a brand loyalty test and a dropship-friendly test on each niche before choosing it. Both filter out niches unsuited to a dropshipping store [L1057.005].
- A niche must be dropship friendly, have enough demand, have acceptable competition and be evergreen, meaning it sells year round (older, 2021) [L0671.023].
- A niche must pass these criteria: dropship friendly, enough demand, acceptable competition and evergreen (older, 2021) [L0671.023].

#### Six Yes/No Market Criteria (Source B, older, 2021-22)

Run every candidate niche through six yes/no criteria. A niche that answers yes to all six is the strongest choice. The lesson's example with five yes answers and one maybe was still viable but weaker [L0458.029].

Validate each market idea by answering six questions. A viable market gets a yes on every question [L0771.014]:

1. Is the average product price right? The average should be 800 USD or more, with examples of 1,000 to 6,000 USD [L0771.014].
2. Can you identify local suppliers and brands? Aim for at least 10 potential brands or suppliers in total across the product types of the market [L0771.014].
3. Is the competition right? Count competitors per individual product, not in total; 5 to 15 per product is the target [L0771.014].
4. Is there recurring sales potential? Find other products or accessories the same customer can buy over time [L0771.014].
5. Are enough people searching? The main keyword should have at least 10,000 monthly searches in the US, or at least 5,000 in a smaller country [L0771.014].
6. Is the market an enthusiast market? Customers buy because they want to, not because they must [L0771.014].

An enthusiast market is one where people buy products because they want to, not because they have to. Answer it yes or no per idea. A minority of buyers needing the product for work does not disqualify a market if most buyers are hobbyists (older, 2021-22) [L1329.007].

#### Four Checks Before Committing (Source A 2021, older)

Before committing to a niche:

1. Check the price point [L0671.162].
2. Check the number of available suppliers [L0671.162].
3. Check the competition on the first page of Google Shopping results [L0671.162].
4. Confirm the niche is dropship friendly, has enough demand, acceptable competition, and sells year round (evergreen) [L0671.162].

### Passion, Interest and Personal Fit

- Judge a niche by the quality of its opportunity, not by how much you personally enjoy it. The same amount of work produces very different results depending on whether the opportunity is strong or weak [L0924.002].
- Do the market research before committing to a niche, because research reveals opportunity quality while enthusiasm does not. A niche that looks attractive on passion alone may score poorly once researched [L0924.004].
- Choosing a niche to fund personal interests such as travel is a valid reason, as long as the niche still passes the opportunity research [L0924.005].
- If you are passionate about a product that meets all the niche criteria, choose it, because you will face a smaller learning curve [L0769.018].
- Shortlist ideas you feel at least some personal interest in, because you will talk to customers and work with suppliers in that market for years. You do not need to be fully passionate, but an idea you actively dislike should not be pursued (older, 2021-22) [L1329.004].
- Choose a category you are genuinely interested in, because daily interest makes the extra work feel less like work. In a saturated market like clothing, the reality is harder than it appears, and paid advertising is needed to get noticed among many competitors [L1438.011].
- Choose a clothing niche or style that you can connect with emotionally and already know well, because this makes the brand easier to build and talk about [L0779.006].
- Stronger niches are built around strong identity or passion, such as sports clubs, music fan bases, religion, or pride in a home country or heritage. Buyers spend money to show belonging [L1131.039].
- Passionate niches with a specific target audience tend to outperform random product designs, because buyers respond to designs that clearly speak to their identity or interest. Broad themes like religion or astrology can reach large audiences, but only if the design is specific and emotionally strong [L1184.002].
- Competitive niches with strong brand-building potential include fashion, baby, jewellery, makeup, beauty, cosmetics, outdoors and gym. Choose a niche with these kinds of demand before picking individual products [L1251.004].
- In the beginning, test multiple niches to find ones that are both interesting to the seller and profitable. Products that sell to women, such as fashion and jewelry, tended to work for this seller, while products for men did not [L0678.032].
- An existing business or hobby can give you a competitive advantage. If the niche meets the criteria, follow the same validation process and use what you already have, such as existing supplier relationships (older, 2019) [L1002.014].

### Who Does the Research

- Niche selection and market research should be done by the business owner rather than delegated to a virtual assistant, even for low-capital online businesses. The owner must know the numbers and prove the business works before investing. The same logic applies to larger physical retail investments, such as a store with a USD 10,000 monthly lease and a USD 300,000 build-out (older, 2022) [L0429.022].
- Choosing a niche is the foundation of the whole business, so do the research yourself even if it takes longer. Paying someone else to pick it is not recommended (older, 2019) [L1002.013].
- Doing product research yourself rather than hiring freelancers is recommended. In the example, a freelancer who made video ads for the speaker produced outdated, low-quality work [L0690.013].

### Research Time Limits

- A niche search for a product should take about three to four hours of brainstorming and research and should never run longer than one week. Beyond that point, the extra time adds delay without adding much information [L1083.001].
- A niche should be selectable within a matter of hours when a structured process is followed. A niche search that runs for years indicates the process is being done without a clear method or time limit [L0555.004].
- Do not spend months searching for the perfect niche. Once a niche meets all criteria, commit to it and build, then research more niches later (older, 2020) [L1111.008].
- The goal of early research is to find one viable market quickly and keep momentum, not to do hundreds of hours of research. Enough research to find a viable idea that appeals to you is the target (older, 2021-22) [L1329.005].

### How Many Ideas and Niches to Research

- Start niche research with a brainstormed list of at least 50 niche ideas before running any validation tests [L1057.002].
- Do not research every brainstormed idea in depth. Brainstorming only gets ideas onto paper, and researching 40 ideas in detail can take weeks and delay launching the business (older, 2021-22) [L1329.002].
- Shortlisting and first market research with the tracker:
  1. Pick five ideas from the list that appeal most to you at face value [L1329.003].
  2. Research only these five ideas against the market criteria: enthusiast market (Y/N), average price, shipping (Y/N), and later suppliers, competition, recurring revenue and traffic volume [L1329.003].
  3. If one of the five meets the criteria, choose it and stop researching the others [L1329.003].
  4. If none of the five meet the criteria, select the next batch of three to five ideas and research them the same way until a viable idea is found [L1329.003].
  
  (older, 2021-22) [L1329.003]
- Testing several products over the budget gives a fair result, while quitting after a few small tests usually does not [L0690.042].

### Research Sequence and Definition of the Business

- Choose the market in sequence (older, 2021-22) [L1058.002]:
  1. Research products, customers and competition through a set of exercises [L1058.002].
  2. Identify candidate markets [L1058.002].
  3. Select one market and build the business around it. Do not start building the store before the selection is made [L1058.002].
- Define the business in this order before contacting suppliers [L1438.009]:
  1. Decide which product type you want to release [L1438.009].
  2. Define what is needed to make that product (materials, production requirements) [L1438.009].
  3. Define the audience you will sell to [L1438.009].
  
  Narrowing these decisions first avoids repeated back-and-forth with suppliers, which is costly and slow [L1438.009].

### Test Budgets

- Commit to a total product-testing budget in advance, roughly USD 5,000 to 6,000 in the speaker example, before deciding the model does not work [L0690.042].
- Do not spend much money on product research tools in the beginning. Use free or cheap methods and put the budget into running ads, since the winners often come from low-cost sources [L1184.004].
- A niche often earns far less than first expected, for example USD 15,000 to 25,000 per month instead of USD 100,000. A profitable store at that level should still be kept running and used to fund the next store (older, 2019) [L1086.008].

### Where Sources Disagree

- **High-ticket threshold.** Source C defines high-ticket as a single unit of about USD 150 to 200 or more [L0660.012]. Source B's market test requires an average market price of USD 800 or more (older, 2021-22) [L0771.014]. Source A suggests around USD 2,000 for a first store (older, 2022) [L1281.025]. The 150 to 200 figure applies to the product price, the 800 figure to the market average, and the 2,000 figure to a first-store recommendation [L0660.012, L0771.014, L1281.025].
- **Low-ticket ceiling.** Source C places low-ticket at up to about USD 80 to 90 [L0660.012]. Source B describes low-ticket as items of USD 20 to 100 (older, 2021-22) [L0994.002]. Viral pump-and-dump products target USD 30 to 50 [L1211.007]. Use the range that matches the model you are testing.
- **Customer contact load.** Custom luxury items at several thousand USD need more calls and follow-up [L1277.018] (older, 2020), and luxury products need more customer contact [L0766.001]. Products around USD 2,000 with many suppliers need fewer contacts because ads reveal the winners [L1281.025] (older, 2022). The difference depends on whether the product is custom or off the shelf and sold through ads.
- **Physical products.** Source A states physical-product niches are not a fit for this business model unless they serve lead value optimization [L0835.142]. Source B's high-ticket model uses higher-priced physical products that fit the store model (older, 2021-22) [L1014.017]. Follow L0835.142 for lead value work and L1014.017 for high-ticket physical dropshipping. The sources do not reconcile these further.
- **Research depth.** Brainstorm at least 50 ideas [L1057.002], but do not research every idea in depth (older, 2021-22) [L1329.002]. Brainstorm broadly and research narrowly.
- **Competition check.** Source B counts 5 to 15 competitors per individual product (older, 2021-22) [L0771.014]. Source A checks the first page of Google Shopping results before committing (older, 2021) [L0671.162]. Use both checks.

## Brainstorming Niche Ideas

### Targets and Minimum Counts

- Write at least 10 ideas yourself before using any AI tool, then expand the list with AI to 50 or more. [L0010.002, L0024.001, L0159.001, L0591.001]
- If fewer than 10 manual ideas exist, pause and brainstorm more before going on. [L0024.001, L1179.022]
- The 10-idea minimum gives the AI enough context and keeps its suggestions from being purely generic, without your market intuition. [L0159.003]
- Your manual brainstorm captures market intuition and unique angles, while AI finds systematic variations that meet your explicit criteria. [L0159.011]

| Target | Rule | Source ids |
|---|---|---|
| Manual minimum | At least 10 self-written ideas before AI | L0010.002, L0024.001, L0159.001, L0159.003, L0591.001, L1179.022 |
| Working list | At least 50 niche ideas on the worksheet before narrowing | L0010.002, L0034.001, L0451.014, L0532.005, L0585.007, L1056.001 |
| Final count | At least 50; any count above 50 is acceptable | L0024.007 |
| Market-idea count (older, 2021-2022) | At least 20 market ideas before assessing them | L0458.014, L0771.013, L0996.008, L0996.010 |
| Testing stage (older, 2020) | Start with about 50 ideas; do not refill the list to 50 as ideas are eliminated, because it should shrink toward the strongest ones | L0961.041 |
| Screening stage (2025) | Screen about 50 ideas for the criteria spreadsheet; there is no need to work through 500 | L1116.045 |
| Expansion target | Expand toward roughly 50 candidates with AI-assisted brainstorming | L1179.022 |

- Brainstorm size matters before testing: reach at least 50 niche ideas on the worksheet. [L0451.014]
- Do not narrow down to one niche for the first store until the list holds at least 50 niche ideas. [L0532.005]
- Niche research should end with a list of at least 50 different niches that could be very profitable, from which the best are chosen to run. [L0585.007]
- The first module has one measurable goal: a list of 50 niche ideas, at least 10 of them personally brainstormed and the remaining 40 generated by AI. [L0591.001]
- Module 1 is complete only when the list reaches at least 50 niches. The task cannot be skipped, because the list is the foundation for scoring, validation and elimination in Module 2. [L0024.008, L0034.001]
- Collect at least 50 niche ideas in the worksheet before moving on. Each idea is tested in the next research stage, which selects the best candidate for the first store. [L1056.001]
- A longer niche list gives more chances to find a winner, so add categories that could sell at higher prices and have not yet been considered. [L1179.014]

### Principles of the Brainstorm

- The brainstorm only collects candidates; you do not need to be sure any idea is the best one. Profitability is checked later, where weak ideas are set aside. [L1082.002]
- Brainstorming produces candidates only, and every candidate must then be validated. [L0468.022, older 2020]
- Brainstorm many ideas before choosing, because most will be weak and only one to three will fit you. Discarding weak ideas is a normal part of the process. [L1040.001, older 2021-2022]
- Generate ideas freely without filtering them against criteria during brainstorming, because filtering early kills ideas before they are developed. The goal of this stage is volume. [L0996.009, older 2021-2022]
- Add any idea that might work, even if it seems unlikely; strict filtering happens later in market research against defined criteria. [L1056.017]
- Sources differ on timing. One view says the research criteria must be set before brainstorming, because a list of a hundred niche ideas can still be all bad if you do not know what to look for. [L0506.002] The other says do not filter while generating; filtering comes after. [L0996.009, L1056.017] Apply both: know your criteria first, and apply them only after the list is written.
- Brainstorming is a habit. Opportunities for product ideas are everywhere once you look for them, and the idea list grows faster with practice. [L1082.013]
- Aim for a long idea list now, because the later action tasks ask for many ideas. Keep all ideas in one spreadsheet so they are ready for research. [L1082.014]
- Record product types rather than single brands or models, for example electric mountain bikes, car rims or chandeliers. Product types are broader and easier to research. [L1082.015]
- A market idea can be a product type or a market defined by its audience or interest. Both forms are valid, and you can use whichever is clearer to you. [L0996.011]
- A product-type idea names one specific item, such as a gear category like wetsuits or dive equipment. An audience-type idea names the interest group and leaves the product range open, such as scuba divers who buy a range of diving gear. [L0996.012]
- Narrow a broad category, such as home furniture, into specific product types, such as sofas, dining room tables, patio furniture or hammocks, before researching niches. [L0359.009]

### Price Thresholds

| Stage | Threshold | When it applies | Source ids |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brainstorm from your environment and purchases | Physical products above $200 | Writing down ideas from your home, office, gym, credit card statements and daily life | L0012.007, L0029.001, L0029.002, L1082.003 |
| AI research prompt (criteria) | Average sale price of $500 or more | Full research prompts and the expensive-products prompt used to generate a qualified list | L0159.002, L1067.001, L1067.002 |
| Sub-niche expansion example | $500 or more | Rug types for upper-middle-class buyers; small area rugs under $100 to $200 are left out | L1517.011 |

- Focus the brainstorm on physical products that cost more than $200. Earlier lessons set this threshold, and it applies to your own spending history too. [L1082.003]
- Review your personal purchase history and bank statements, noting products you have spent over $200 on. These are established niches with proven demand from someone who understands the market firsthand. [L0029.001]
- People who make large purchases have validated niche demand with their own spending, so ask family and friends what they bought online for over $200. [L0029.002]
- Price is the only selection criterion at the first brainstorm stage: disregard personal passion and interests. [L0012.007]
- High-ticket examples: people who keep fish need aquariums and fish-keeping products that can sell for thousands of dollars, and coffee lovers buy high-end espresso machines priced from $1,000 to $6,000. [L0458.016, older 2021-2022]
- Avoid low-cost hobby lists, because cheap hobbies point to low-priced products, which does not fit a high-ticket model. [L0996.024, older 2021-2022]
- The model targets high-ticket items, so every source should be screened for products that could sell at high ticket prices. [L0996.016, older 2021-2022]

### Step 1: Set Up the Worksheet

- Open the Source A X Research Worksheet in Google Drive or Excel. [L0012.009]
- Fill in Column A only on the Niche Research Worksheet tab. [L0012.009]
- Use Google Sheets, Microsoft Excel or Apple Numbers. The app does not matter. [L1056.002]
- Write every idea into column A of the niche research worksheet. [L1082.004]
- In a market research tracker, work only in the Market Idea column. [L0996.008, older 2021-2022]
- The market research tracker starts with a long list of candidate niches, such as Auto Accessories, 4x4 Accessories, Fishing, Hunting Accessories, Boating, Caravans/RVs, Home Storage, Woodworking, Model Trains and Above Ground Pools. Each niche is tested against the same supplier threshold before any niche is chosen. [L1484.017, older 2021-2022]

**Worksheet procedure (keep in order)**

1. Open the Source A X Research Worksheet in Google Drive or Excel. [L0012.009]
2. Add as many high-ticket niche ideas as come to mind, focusing on $200+ products. [L0012.009, L0012.007]
3. Use simple observations from your home, office, gym or daily life for inspiration. [L0012.009]
4. Fill in Column A only on the Niche Research Worksheet tab. [L0012.009]
5. Mark this lesson complete. [L0012.009]
6. Move to the next lesson to continue building your niche list. [L0012.009]

**Build procedure (keep in order)**

1. Open the niche research worksheet in Google Sheets, Microsoft Excel or Apple Numbers. The app does not matter. [L1056.002]
2. Fill the first column with the ideas from the earlier brainstorming. [L1056.002]
3. Use the earlier brainstorming techniques first. They should reach 50 ideas on their own. [L1056.002]
4. If the list is still under 50, add ideas from the resources below. [L1056.002]
5. Do not filter yet. Collect candidates and leave testing for later. [L1056.002]

### Step 2: Personal Environment and Purchase History

**Brainstorm order (keep in order)**

1. Look around your home and your workplace and write down physical products you see or own, keeping the $200 threshold in mind. [L1082.004]
2. Open your credit card statements, find past purchases over $200, and add every physical product to your list. [L1082.004]
3. Ask close friends and family which products they have bought, then ask a wider group, for example with a Facebook post to your connections. [L1082.004]
4. Go through your hobbies: note products advertised in magazines and blogs, products mentioned or advertised in podcasts, product-type questions in Facebook groups about your hobbies, sidebar ads and product reviews on blogs you follow. [L1082.004]
5. Observe products in everyday places such as work, the gym, the shopping mall and the doctor's office, and add anything that could become a product idea. [L1082.004]
6. Write every idea into column A of the niche research worksheet. [L1082.004]

**Examples from everyday surroundings**

- Everyday places are full of product ideas. At a doctor's office these include reception desks, medical chairs, examination lights, medical tools such as scalpels and lobby chairs. At a gym they include weight machines and cardio machines. [L1082.010]
- Ideas can come from whatever is in front of you. Examples are a chandelier in your home, a built-in wine refrigerator in your kitchen, or car rims on a car next to you in traffic. Each goes straight onto the list. [L1082.012]
- A single living room contains more than 17 product categories that can be niches: chandeliers, wall lighting, table lamps, crown molding, wallpaper, coffee tables, sofas, fireplaces, mirrors, vases, bookshelves, dining tables, dining chairs and wood flooring. Look around for product types. [L0988.009, L1082.011]
- Items to list from one living room photo include chandeliers, wall lighting, crown molding, lamps, sofas, coffee tables, wood flooring, dining tables and chairs, fireplaces, mirrors and bookshelves. [L1082.011, L0988.009]
- Product ideas can come from everyday observation, such as outdoor items, pools, fire pits, garden structures and large smokers seen around a home or on a walk. (older, 2020) [L0967.003]
- Niche ideas can come from everyday objects around you, such as furniture in your living room. Test each idea against the validation criteria before you commit to it. (older, 2019) [L1275.005]
- Niche ideas can come from everyday observation, such as background products in movies or shows. Test each idea against the normal validation criteria before committing. (older, 2021) [L0853.042]
- Everyday personal needs, such as children's play equipment, can suggest niche ideas that are worth checking against price and shipping criteria. [L1179.018]

**Principles for personal sources**

- Hobbies are a source of product inspiration, not a requirement. You do not have to build a business around a hobby you are passionate about to use it for niche ideas. [L1082.008]
- Record product types rather than single brands when you note an item from your surroundings. [L1082.015]

### Step 3: Asking Family, Friends and Your Network

- Ask family and friends what products they have purchased online where they spent over $200, since people who make large purchases have validated niche demand with their own spending. [L0029.002]
- Use this message as a direct message to people you know, or as a post to your own connections. [L0029.003, L1082.005]

**Message template (L0029.003)**

```
I'm researching which products would be viable to sell through online channels. Have you made any online purchases exceeding $200? If so, I'd appreciate it if you'd share which specific products those were. Feel free to reach out if you'd like to know the reasoning behind my data collection-I'm happy to explain.
```

[L0029.003]

**Facebook and direct message template (L1082.005)**

```
Hi, I am researching which physical products people buy online, and I would really appreciate your help. If you have ever spent more than $200 while shopping online, could you send me a message with the names of the products you bought? Thank you in advance.
P.S. If you are curious what the information is for, send me a message and I will explain.

Use this as a Facebook post to your own connections or as a direct message to people you know. Replies usually name products people are willing to pay a lot for, which makes the post a good source for your niche list.
```

[L1082.005]

### Step 4: Hobbies, Interests and Magazines

**Hobby brainstorm procedure (keep in order)**

1. List things people do, love or are passionate about, such as hobbies, sports and interests, and not things they only have to do. [L0771.013, older 2021-2022]
2. Use Google searches for lists of hobbies, activities and interests, and check books and specialist magazines for more ideas. [L0771.013, older 2021-2022]
3. Write the ideas into a spreadsheet or on paper, aiming for about 20 ideas. [L0771.013, older 2021-2022]
4. Do not evaluate them yet; the brainstorm is only the list that is researched next. [L0771.013, older 2021-2022]

**Market-idea procedure (keep in order)**

1. Open the research tracker and work only in the Market Idea column. [L0996.008, older 2021-2022]
2. Write down ideas without judging them against any criteria. [L0996.008, older 2021-2022]
3. Each idea can be a product you could sell, a customer group you could serve, or an interest you could serve with products. [L0996.008, older 2021-2022]
4. If you are stuck, take ideas from outside sources such as online searches, marketplace categories, magazines, library books, or hobby lists. [L0996.008, older 2021-2022]
5. Keep adding ideas until you have at least 20 market ideas. [L0996.008, older 2021-2022]
6. Only then move on to assessing the ideas against the other criteria. [L0996.008, older 2021-2022]

**Interest-group procedure (keep in order)** (older, 2021-2022)

1. Brainstorm at least 20 market ideas, using paper or a spreadsheet, based on hobbies and interests you, your friends and family, Google hobby lists, and books or magazines. [L0458.014]
2. For each interest group, list the high-ticket products its members would need or want to buy. [L0458.014]
3. Run each idea through the six market criteria using Google Shopping and a keyword tool. [L0458.014]
4. Mark each criterion yes, no or maybe in your tracker. [L0458.014]
5. Prioritise ideas with yes on all six criteria; keep the others on the list in case they are needed. [L0458.014]

**Google hobby-list procedure (keep in order)** (older, 2021-2022)

1. Search for 'list of hobbies' in Google. [L0996.021]
2. Open one of the hobby lists that appear in the results. [L0996.021]
3. Go through the listed hobbies one by one. [L0996.021]
4. For each hobby, ask whether participants buy equipment or products, and if so, write that product or the hobby as a market idea. [L0996.021]
5. Move on to the next hobby until you have enough ideas. [L0996.021]

**Hobby sources and examples**

- Products that people buy for their own hobbies, see on special interest TV shows, or that friends and family use are good starting points. People who already buy expensive products for a pastime are a strong signal for a high-ticket market. [L0996.017, older 2021-2022]
- Special interest magazines are useful because their advertisers are typically companies selling products for that interest. Flipping through a magazine's ads shows which product types are sold to that audience. [L0996.018, older 2021-2022]
- Ads in a hobby magazine or blog for a new type of product can be added to the list directly. A mountain biker who sees ads for electric mountain bikes in biking magazines or forums would add electric mountain bikes as an idea. [L1082.009]
- One hobby list was described as containing 549 hand-picked hobby ideas, which gives a large pool to screen. This is one example of how a single search can deliver hundreds of candidate interests. [L0996.022, older 2021-2022]
- A Google search for a list of hobbies returns Wikipedia's list, a compiled list of about 549 hand-picked hobby ideas, and hobby category sites such as Discover a Hobby. Together these give a large pool of candidate interests from a single search. [L0996.032, older 2021-2022]
- Hobby lists can be used from any country, because the hobbies are not tied to one region. A hobby that is popular locally but not in the target market should still be recorded and checked later. [L0996.033, older 2021-2022]
- Not every hobby contains products worth selling. Hobbies that require equipment, supplies or specialised gear are promising, while hobbies that involve only giving advice or performing a skill often have no products to sell. [L0996.023, older 2021-2022]
- Beekeeping implies equipment purchases, and commercial t-shirt pressing may involve expensive machinery, so both are worth recording. A handyman trade or giving advice typically has few products, so those are weaker candidates. Interior design usually involves many relatively high-priced home products. [L0996.025, older 2021-2022]
- An activity such as horse riding can be recorded as a market idea, or a specific expensive product linked to it, such as horse saddles, can be recorded instead. Product ideas that look expensive can be written down now and researched later. [L0996.026, older 2021-2022]
- On a Sports & Outdoors hobby page, bodybuilding, cardio workouts, cycling, golf, horse riding and camping are examples of hobbies that involve purchasable gear. Each can be recorded as a market idea or narrowed to a specific product such as horse saddles. [L0996.034, older 2021-2022]
- Water hobbies such as kayaking and canoeing are worth recording because quality kayaks and canoes tend to be expensive. Water sports is a broader alternative label that can be used instead. [L0996.035, older 2021-2022]
- Crafts such as engraving and car detailing should be screened even though the craft itself is not a product. The tools and consumables used in these crafts can be the products to research. [L0996.036, older 2021-2022]
- A list of over 1,000 hobbies can be scanned for niche ideas. Not every hobby is a niche or a product category, so look for the ones that stand out. [L1056.018]
- Hobby-based expansion procedure:
  1. Copy a hobby from the list. [L1056.019]
  2. If the hobby is unfamiliar, ask ChatGPT to define it first. [L1056.019]
  3. Paste the hobby into the prompt 'Please list examples of expensive products in the [niche] niche' or the equivalent wording. [L1056.019]
  4. Read the products and filter them using the same rules as for broad categories. [L1056.019]
  5. Add the remaining products to the niche worksheet. [L1056.019]
- Aquascaping, the craft of arranging aquatic plants, rocks and driftwood in an aquarium, produced these product ideas: rimless and Starfire glass tanks, ADA Solar Series lighting, Kessel freshwater LED lights, aquarium filtration systems, CO2 systems and substrates. [L1056.020]

**Hobby filters and sub-niches**

- Passionate sub-niches such as travel can perform well on Facebook. Before entering one, check whether large players already dominate it and how big the market is. (Source C) [L0895.037]

### Step 5: Pitch-a-Niche and Reflection Exercises

**Pitch-a-niche (keep in order)**

1. Write down every niche you think is a good fit for dropshipping. [L0831.015]
2. For each niche, write down the reasons behind your choice. The purpose is to bring out the underlying 'what for' motives that drive the choice. [L0831.015]

**Timed first-reaction brainstorm (keep in order)**

1. Set a two-minute timer. [L1513.027]
2. Write down as many possible niches as you can in that time. [L1513.027]
3. Note the first thoughts that come up, such as worthiness, fear or excitement. These thoughts reveal the programming that will influence later decisions. [L1513.027]

**Timing rule**

- Complete the first brainstorm within 15-20 minutes. [L0012.007]

### Step 6: AI-Assisted Expansion

**Expansion procedure (keep in order)**

1. Brainstorm and list at least 10 niche ideas manually on your niche research worksheet (10 is the minimum threshold; more is acceptable). [L0159.001]
2. Open ChatGPT (free) or Gemini. [L0159.001]
3. Copy the provided AI prompt for high-ticket niche expansion. [L0159.001]
4. Paste the complete prompt into your AI tool. [L0159.001]
5. Delete the placeholder line "paste your list here". [L0159.001]
6. Return to your niche research worksheet. [L0159.001]
7. Select all existing brainstormed niche ideas from your list. [L0159.001]
8. Copy them. [L0159.001]
9. Return to ChatGPT. [L0159.001]
10. Under the section "Existing niches (Do not repeat):", paste your complete list. [L0159.001]
11. Send the prompt to the AI and wait for results. [L0159.001]
12. Click the copy icon to copy the full generated list. [L0159.001]
13. Return to your research worksheet. [L0159.001]
14. Position cursor in the row below your lowest existing niche number. [L0159.001]
15. Paste the AI-generated ideas. [L0159.001]
16. Delete any duplicate text that copied along with the niche names. [L0159.001]
17. Delete extra rows to clean up formatting. [L0159.001]
18. Resize columns to match your existing column widths and formatting. [L0159.001]
19. Verify numbering is sequential and complete. [L0159.001]
20. Mark the action task complete when finished. [L0159.001]

**Shorter expansion procedure (keep in order)**

1. Open the Niche Research Worksheet (Google Drive or Excel) and confirm it contains at least 10 manually brainstormed niches. [L0024.005]
2. Copy the AI prompt provided under this lesson and paste it into ChatGPT, Gemini, or your chosen AI tool. [L0024.005]
3. Paste your existing niche list into the "Existing Niches, Do Not Repeat" section of the prompt, replacing the placeholder text. [L0024.005]
4. Run the prompt in the AI tool and wait for it to generate 50+ new niche ideas. [L0024.005]
5. Copy the AI-generated list. [L0024.005]
6. Return to your worksheet and paste the new ideas into Column A, below your existing niches. [L0024.005]
7. Remove any extra lines of copied prompt text and adjust formatting (row height, font) to match your existing list. [L0024.005]
8. Verify your final niche list contains at least 50 ideas. [L0024.005]
9. Mark this lesson complete and proceed to Module 2. [L0024.005]

**Rules for the AI step**

- Paste your complete existing niche list into the "Existing Niches, Do Not Repeat" section of the AI prompt to prevent the tool from suggesting ideas you have already brainstormed. [L0024.006]
- Use the AI prompt to generate at least 50 additional niche ideas beyond your manual list. This quantity ensures a comprehensive pool of candidates to evaluate in market research. [L0159.004]
- Note the difference in counting: L0159.004 asks for at least 50 additional AI ideas beyond the manual list, while L0591.001 and L0024.007 count the final list as at least 50 with the AI supplying the remaining 40 in the module 1 goal. Use whichever matches your plan, and make sure the final list reaches at least 50. [L0159.004, L0591.001, L0024.007]
- Expansion example: 17 manually brainstormed niche ideas plus the AI prompt generated 51 additional ideas that met all criteria, for a total research list of 68 niches qualified for supplier research and demand validation. [L0159.013]
- Use ChatGPT (free tier available) or Gemini. Both tools process the same prompt structure and produce equivalent results for niche expansion. [L0159.012]
- Any AI chat tool such as ChatGPT or Gemini can suggest narrower sub-niches and higher-price variants of a broad niche. Its output is a list of ideas to test, not a verified demand source. [L1517.013]
- AI niche ideas must be checked against every research criterion before use, because the tool can return niches that break the rules, such as consumables or custom-only products. [L1067.003]
- ChatGPT draws on training data from a very large part of the internet, and for brainstorming it often produces ideas that a person would not reach through manual research alone. [L1056.012]

**Expansion prompts**

Expensive-products prompt (short form):

```
Please list expensive products in the [EDIT] niche.
```

[L0034.003]

Broad-category expansion prompt:

```
Please list examples of expensive products in the [niche] niche. Replace [niche] with the broad category or niche you want to expand. Only list physical products, not services. Skip products dominated by a few big brands, and name the product type instead of a brand.
```

[L1056.013]

High-ticket expansion prompt (full text):

```
I'm building a list of at least 50 product categories for e-commerce dropshipping where typical prices exceed $500, buyers are affluent with low vendor loyalty, items are physical goods shipped directly, regulatory burden is minimal, niches avoid luxury or collector markets, and excluded are consumables, personalization-dependent products, made-to-order-only items, and low-ticket accessories unless paired with high-ticket inventory-avoiding duplication with an existing category list.
```

[L0159.002]

Full research prompt with CSV output:

```
I'm looking into premium product categories for a web shop that sells online.

Formatting rule: deliver the output as a comma-separated, CSV-like table without any markdown styling, with commas only as column separators. The header row must read: Niche,Estimated average sale price (USD),Target buyer,Why buyers choose on features or price. Every idea gets its own row. Inside any field, swap commas for semicolons. Add no text before or after the table.

Research criteria:
- Produce at least 50 more niche concepts that:
  - reach an average sale price of $500 or higher
  - attract upper-middle-class or wealthy shoppers
  - show weak brand loyalty, so buyers decide based on features or price
  - involve physical goods that get shipped
  - sit outside heavy regulation (no firearms, medical devices, and the like)
  - are neither luxury fashion nor driven by collecting
- Steer clear of:
  - consumables such as coffee pods, vitamins, or pet food
  - products that are only personalized or made to order
  - low-priced accessories, unless they come bundled with high-priced products

Niches already covered (don't repeat these):
[PASTE YOUR LIST HERE]
```

[L1067.001]

Procedure for the full research prompt (keep in order):

1. Copy the complete niche research prompt, including the output format and all research requirements. [L1067.002]
2. Paste it into ChatGPT or another AI writing tool. [L1067.002]
3. Replace the placeholder [PASTE YOUR LIST HERE] with your current niche list so the tool does not repeat those niches. [L1067.002]
4. Check that the returned list contains at least 50 niches, each on its own line in comma-separated format. [L1067.002]
5. Review each niche against the criteria: average sale price of $500 or more, affluent buyers, low brand loyalty, shipped physical product, not highly regulated, not luxury fashion or collectible, not a consumable, not custom-only. [L1067.002]
6. Remove any niche that fails a criterion or duplicates your existing list before further research. [L1067.002]

Rug sub-niche prompt:

```
What types of rugs typically sell for $500 or more? Focus on rug types that appeal to upper middle class buyers, and leave out small area rugs that sell for less than $100 to $200. List the rug categories and the materials they are made from.
```

[L1517.011]

**Filtering AI and expansion results**

Procedure for filtering ChatGPT results (keep in order):

1. Paste the broad category into the prompt and run it. [L1056.014]
2. Read through the returned products. [L1056.014]
3. Remove entries dominated by a few big brands, such as well-known skincare brands or luxury perfume houses. [L1056.014]
4. Remove services, such as professional cosmetic procedures. Keep the products used to deliver those services, such as the equipment or supplies. [L1056.014]
5. Turn single-brand items into generic product types. For example, change a specific brand of bike to fitness bikes or exercise bikes. [L1056.014]
6. Keep plausible ideas such as home gym systems, high-end hair tools and home spa treatments. [L1056.014]
7. Add the remaining items to the niche worksheet. [L1056.014]

- Some ChatGPT results are too advanced to start with, such as surgical robots. Advanced ideas such as advanced prosthetics can still be added at the brainstorming stage. They are checked later in research. [L1056.016]
- The expensive-products prompt on health and fitness returned high-end treadmills and ellipticals, branded exercise bikes, smart fitness tech, home gym systems and personal trainers. Personal trainers are a service and are dropped, while generic items such as exercise bikes and home gym systems go on the list. Branded items are turned into product types before they are added. [L1056.027]
- Broad categories such as health, fitness and personal care are too wide to be a niche. Look for the specific sub-niche before adding a listing to the list. If the listing gives no detail, the broad label should not be added as is. [L1056.010]
- Narrow broad categories into specific product types before testing them. [L0359.009]

### Sold Stores, Listings and Marketplaces

**Business brokerage and sold-store research**

- Business brokerage websites list online businesses for sale, showing asking price, business age and net profit. Browsing their online and technology section reveals which products real stores sell. Use these sites for idea research only, not for buying a store. [L1056.004]
- The online and technology section of one brokerage site listed 1,368 businesses for sale at the time of recording. [L1056.006]
- A two-year-old Shopify store selling premium wall paneling was listed for almost $1.5 million and made about $600,000 net profit per year. Premium wall paneling is therefore a niche to add to the list. [L1056.005]
- A current e-commerce listing for LED lighting was shown with $362,000 in sales per month. Listings for active stores with high monthly sales are useful for finding product categories. [L1056.008]
- Empire Flippers is a marketplace for selling online businesses, and its e-commerce section shows stores for sale with details. Use the listings for research: look up what the store sells and which products it carries. A store listed for almost $3 million selling health, fitness, personal care and medical products is one example. [L1056.009]
- Sold-store and listing research can include content sites rather than pure e-commerce stores. A content-driven site that sells gear still shows product categories, such as fishing, camping and hiking equipment, that are worth adding to the list. [L1056.026]

**FE International procedure (keep in order)**

1. Open the section that shows businesses already sold. [L1056.007]
2. Select the category e-commerce. [L1056.007]
3. Note the names of the sold e-commerce companies. [L1056.007]
4. Google each company name to see which products it sells. [L1056.007]
5. Add the product types to the niche list. Not every sold store will be a winner. [L1056.007]

**Marketplaces and category pages**

- Wayfair.com is useful for browsing subcategories when brainstorming potential niches. Navigate its category structure to spark ideas for specific sub-niches within broader categories. (older, 2022) [L0272.010]
- Brainstorm niche ideas from any source, including eBay's main collection page or Wayfair categories. Brainstorming only produces candidates, and each must then be validated. (older, 2020) [L0468.022]
- For inspiration, look at Kickstarter for trending products with high prices, then search for other brands that make the same kind of product. This helps with brainstorming niches. (older, 2020) [L0551.010]
- Brainstorming tools in the research list:
  - 500 High-Ticket Niche Ideas: downloadable PDF of pre-researched expensive product categories. [L0034.002]
  - Biz Buy Sell: online business marketplace to identify established niches. [L0034.002]
  - FE International: business sales platform showing profitable existing businesses. [L0034.002]
  - Empire Flippers: online business listings to find successful niche examples. [L0034.002]
  - 1000+ Hobbies: database of hobbies and interests to spark niche ideas. [L0034.002]
  - ChatGPT: AI assistant for generating product lists when combined with a specific niche. [L0034.002]
- A 237-product idea list is linked under lesson 1.0 of module one as a starting point for finding a product. It downloads as a PDF from the lesson notes. (2023) [L0964.013]
- Use a niche list from brokerages and marketplaces for research only. Do not treat any listing as proof of demand. [L1056.004, L1517.013]

**Warnings for pre-made and public sources**

- Do not start niche brainstorming by searching online for best dropshipping products or products to sell this year. Those searches mostly surface middlemen suppliers and make it very hard to find something that works. Generate ideas from your own purchases, surroundings and daily life instead. [L1082.001]
- Ready-made lists of top-selling products or niches are shared with thousands of people, so the top items are usually too competitive. Do not start from such a list; generate your own market ideas. (older, 2021-2022) [L0458.013]
- Do not rely on pre-made lists of approved niches. When many people pick the same few markets, competition rises and those markets stop being profitable for everyone. Find market ideas through your own research. (older, 2021-2022) [L0996.013]
- In dropshipping communities, asking other sellers for their winning niche is considered taboo. Generate niche candidates from your own research instead. [L1513.029]

### Stalled Brainstorming and Outside Sources

- When brainstorming stalls, use outside sources to find ideas, such as internet searches on passions and hobbies, marketplace category browsing, special interest magazines, library books, and hobby lists. (older, 2021-2022) [L0996.016]
- When a category produces a promising product, use that category name as a new search term in other sources, such as Google, magazines or libraries. A single category can lead to a broader or more refined market idea. (older, 2021-2022) [L0996.030]
- Stuck-brainstorm procedure (older, 2019):
  1. Go through a list of hobbies and mark the ideas that stand out. [L1002.007]
  2. Run each marked idea through the niche verification tool. [L1002.007]
  3. If an idea passes all checks, start building the store right away instead of delaying. [L1002.007]
- Note on the 2019 procedure: it moves straight to building the store once an idea passes its checks. Current guidance requires at least 50 niche ideas before narrowing to one niche for the first store. [L1002.007, L0532.005, L0591.001]

### Narrowing and Filtering the List

**Quick checks (keep in order)**

1. Brainstorm a broad initial list of niches. [L0766.023]
2. Filter the list using the quick checks: electronics, emotional attachment, strict deadlines, personalized items that must be seen or felt, and seasonality. [L0766.023]
3. Verify the remaining niches against size, price and target demographic before committing. [L0766.023]

**Connection, passion and market size**

- Do not limit yourself to one niche at the start. If you have a personal connection to a niche, start there; otherwise choose by problem and market size. Sub-niches can be built later within the same problem area. (Source C) [L0871.006]
- Pick a niche by listing the brands you would like to resemble and studying the customer base they already attract. If your brand differs clearly from those brands, build your own audience instead of copying theirs. (Source C) [L1438.010]
- Passion is set aside at the first brainstorm stage, where price is the only criterion. [L0012.007]
- Conflict: the first brainstorm disregards passion and interests [L0012.007], while the Source C approach starts from a personal connection when one exists [L0871.006]. Use the price-first list for the initial 50, and apply the personal-connection rule when choosing where to begin among the survivors.

**Other filters**

- Hobbies that require equipment, supplies or specialised gear are promising; hobbies that only involve advice or skill are weak candidates. [L0996.023, older 2021-2022]
- Do not start with a single niche: scoring, validation and elimination happen in Module 2. [L0024.008, L0034.001]

### Common Mistakes

- Sources warn against starting from a short list of pre-approved niches, against broad labels, and against cheap hobbies. [L0458.013, L0996.013, L1056.010, L0996.024]
- A list of a hundred niche ideas can still be all bad if the research criteria are not set before brainstorming. [L0506.002]
- Avoid searching for best dropshipping products or products to sell this year at the brainstorm stage. [L1082.001]
- Do not request winning niches from other sellers; generate candidates from your own research. [L1513.029]

## Setting Up the Research Worksheets and Trackers

### Where the worksheets live and how to set them up

- The Niche Research Worksheet is the central spreadsheet for niche selection. It is available as a Google Sheets template or as a downloadable Excel file, and it works in Microsoft Excel or Apple Numbers as well [L0591.002, L0010.003].
- The worksheet is a free spreadsheet that stores the niche idea list. The Google Sheets version opens as a copy in your own account, is editable, and can be used from a phone or computer. The downloadable Excel version works with Microsoft Excel, Apple Numbers and other spreadsheet software [L1082.006].
- Google Drive is the preferred free option. Alternatively, download the template as an Excel file and open it locally in Microsoft Excel or Apple Numbers [L0591.004].
- To get an editable copy of the Niche Research Worksheet in Google Drive [L0591.003]:
  1. Open the Google Drive link of the template (named 'Source A X research').
  2. Click 'File'.
  3. Click 'Make a copy'.
  4. Rename the copy as desired and keep it in your own Google Drive.
- Make one editable copy and keep using that same copy for the whole program. Each later module adds more columns and sheets to the same file, so it should not be recreated for each module [L0591.009].
- The niche research worksheet is a spreadsheet-style list of candidate niches that is revised as your understanding of prices, margins and shipping improves [L1179.016].
- The worksheet collects product ideas for the niche, with the product ideas listed in column A. It can be kept as a Google Drive file or downloaded as a local file [L0474.010].
- To set up the Source D Product Research Sheet [L0038.003]:
  1. Open the Google Sheets template provided.
  2. Click File (top left).
  3. Click Make a Copy.
  4. Save it to your Google Drive.
  5. Begin adding your product research data.
- Use File > Make a copy (top left) to get your own editable version of the product research sheet, then add one row per product candidate [L0354.022].

### Niche research worksheet: columns and layout

- Keep one row per candidate niche so that all candidates can be compared side by side on the same criteria before you choose one [L0540.002].
- The niche research worksheet has these columns, in this order [L0540.001, L0542.001, L0543.001]:

| Niche | Average Price | Average Profit | Demographic | Brand Loyalty | Seasonal | Demand | DS Friendly | Est. Suppliers |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| [candidate niche] | [average price] | [average profit] | [target demographic] | [brand loyalty level] | [seasonal or not] | [demand level] | [dropship friendly or not] | [estimated number of suppliers] |

- Worksheet layout for niche grading, with the optional Grade column inserted as column B [L1081.026]:

| Column | Content | Source |
|---|---|---|
| B | Grade (optional) | Research tool letter grade |
| C | Average price, formatted as currency without decimals | Research tool |
| D | Average profit = average price x 0.25 | Formula |
| E | Demographic: pass if box is green | Research tool |
| F | Brand loyalty: pass if box is green | Research tool |
| G | Seasonality: pass if 4 out of 4 | Research tool |
| H | Demand: average monthly searches | Research tool |
| I | DS friendly (filled later) | Later step |
| J | Estimated suppliers (filled later) | Later step |

- The earlier data-source table uses the same columns with a different format. Column entries are listed below, with the Data Source and How to Fill columns [L0045.002]:

| Column | Data Source | How to Fill | Entry Value |
|--------|-------------|-------------|-------------|
| Grade | Source A Research Tool results | Copy the grade directly from tool | Tool's assigned grade |
| Average Price | Source A Research Tool results | Copy price and format as currency | Price amount (e.g., $49.99) |
| Average Profit | Calculate from Average Price | Formula: =Average Price * 0.25 | Calculated value (25% of price) |
| Demographic | Source A Research Tool results | Enter "Pass" if box is green | "Pass" or blank |
| Brand Loyalty | Source A Research Tool results | Enter "Pass" if box is green | "Pass" or blank |
| Seasonality | Source A Research Tool results | Enter "Pass" if shows 4 out of 4 seasons | "Pass" or blank |
| Demand | Source A Research Tool results | Copy average monthly search volume | Search volume number (e.g., 15000) |

- Average profit formula: =Average Price * 0.25. It calculates net profit assuming a 25% net profit margin on the average product price. For example, if the average price is $100, the calculated net profit is $25 per sale [L0045.003].
- Average price format: the earlier layout copies the price and formats it as currency, with cents shown (e.g., $49.99) [L0045.002]. The later layout formats it as currency and removes the decimals [L1081.002, L1081.026]. The value is the same in both; use one format per sheet.
- Demand is the average monthly search volume shown by the tool (example: 15000) [L0045.002, L1081.002].
- Demographic, Brand Loyalty and Seasonality take "Pass" (or "pass") when the tool's box is green or, for seasonality, when it shows 4 out of 4 seasons. Otherwise leave the cell blank [L0045.002, L1081.002].
- The Demographic column records the demographics test result for each niche, so you can track which niches pass and which need a pivot [L0457.014].
- Insert an optional Grade column: click the column B header, right-click, choose "Insert one column left", and name it "Grade." The column is not required but helps with comparison [L0045.001, L1081.003].
- The columns depend on each other: Seasonality, Demand and Average Price must be filled in before the Average Profit column is calculated [L1150.007].
- Columns I (DS friendly) and J (estimated suppliers) stay empty while grading niches. They are filled in later, after columns B to H are complete [L1081.023].
- Fill in the Estimated Suppliers column with the number of suppliers counted in the niche's master supplier list (see the master supplier section) [L1079.003].
- Fill the DS Friendly column with Yes or No and the Estimated Suppliers column with a number [L0459.016].
- Complete one full research worksheet per niche, containing all collected data. The worksheet is the basis for choosing which niche to launch the first store with [L1057.007].
- Fill in every empty column of the niche research worksheet, together with the future competitors and master suppliers sheets, before choosing the first niche. The goal is to pick one niche for the first store based on complete competitor and supplier data [L0584.002].
- The niche research can be split into three sheets: one for niche research, one for future competitors, and one for master suppliers. Each sheet tracks a different layer of the research, from the market candidates to the competitors and the suppliers behind them [L0584.001].

### Phase 1: brainstorming with column A only

- In the first phase, populate only Column A on the 'Niche Research Worksheet' sheet to list niche candidates. Defer analysis of other columns, such as average price, profit, demographic and brand loyalty, until later phases, once you have refined your list [L0010.004].
- In the first module, only column A of the first sheet ('niche research worksheet') is filled in. Other columns such as average price, profit, demographics and brand loyalty are covered in later modules, and the other sheets are not needed yet [L0591.005].
- During brainstorming, column A receives the raw idea list. The other columns hold research steps from the next module and can be ignored at this stage [L1082.007].
- Expand the list until it contains at least 10 candidate niches [L1179.015].
- Research all 50 or more brainstormed niches in the test round, filling in the demand, seasonality and average price columns for each, before continuing [L0451.010].

### Early price pass before data

Use this pass before the research tool data is complete. It is based on rough intuition, not on data [L1179.015].

1. Open the niche research worksheet.
2. For each niche, estimate its likely selling price using rough intuition.
3. Remove or deprioritize niches whose price is too low for bulky or heavy items.
4. Split broad niches into higher-priced subtypes.
5. Add new niches in higher-ticket categories, especially large or heavy products.
6. Flag niches with unclear pricing so they can be checked with real data later.
7. Keep expanding the list until it contains at least 10 candidate niches.

- When a $200 average-price filter is applied, a niche that falls below $200 is moved to the bottom of the list and no longer counts as a candidate. In one worksheet, tripods were the only niche under $200, and the other niches stayed on the candidate list [L1150.013].

### Getting the data from the research tool

- The Source A research tool is a custom tool for Source A members. It evaluates and validates niches using real data instead of assumptions [L0043.002].
- The tool gives members unlimited searches. Enter a niche keyword and click search. It returns grade, average price, demographic, brand loyalty, seasonality and monthly demand data from linked data sources, which saves many hours of manual research [L1081.001].
- The research tool at the source's own site requires login. It replaces the earlier research tools by combining their functions in one place. Select the target country before searching (the example uses the US) [L1075.001].
- Searches for niches that were not researched before can take 10 to 15 seconds. Previously researched niches usually return within a few seconds. The tool allows unlimited searches [L1075.008].
- Workflow in the research tool [L1075.002]:
  1. Log in to the research tool at the source's own site
  2. Select the target country.
  3. Enter the niche to research and click search.
  4. Read the demand test result (monthly search volume).
  5. Read the evergreen test box: green passes, red fails.
  6. Read the price analysis result.
  7. Refresh the page before starting a new search.
- Opening a niche's full data in the research tool shows the exact reasons it failed each test. This is optional and useful for understanding a weak niche, but it is not needed to choose the top 5 niches from the worksheet [L1081.025].
- The Source A Research Software is a research tool for finding and evaluating drop shipping products [L1096.003].
- A niche screen can check several criteria for each candidate niche: demand, whether sales hold up across all four seasons, average price point, the target buyer demographic, and brand loyalty. Scoring every niche on the same checks makes it easier to compare a long list of candidates side by side [L1097.046].

Procedure for grading each niche in the worksheet [L0045.001]:

1. Open your Niche Research Worksheet from Module 1.
2. Optionally add a Grade column by clicking on Column B, right-clicking, selecting "Insert one column left," and naming it "Grade."
3. For each niche on your list, copy the niche name from your worksheet.
4. Paste the niche name into the Source A Research Tool.
5. Click Search in the tool.
6. Review the tool's results for this niche.
7. Fill the Grade column with the grade shown in the research tool.
8. Fill the Average Price column with the average price shown by the tool and format it as currency.
9. Calculate Average Profit using the formula =Average Price * 0.25 to represent 25% net profit margin.
10. For the Demographic column, enter "Pass" if the box is green in the tool.
11. For the Brand Loyalty column, enter "Pass" if the box is green in the tool.
12. For the Seasonality column, enter "Pass" if the tool shows 4 out of 4 seasons.
13. For the Demand column, enter the average monthly search volume shown in the tool.
14. Repeat steps 3-13 for all niches on your list (typically takes 30 minutes or less).
15. Sort the Demand column from A to Z (lowest to highest).
16. Highlight all niches with under 10,000 monthly searches.
17. Change the text color of highlighted niches to red.
18. Sort the Seasonality column and mark all failures (fewer than 4 seasons) in red.
19. Sort the Average Profit column from Z to A (highest to lowest).
20. Move all low-profit or red-marked niches to the bottom of your list.
21. Focus your analysis on the black (non-red) entries at the top of your list.
22. From the top candidates, narrow your selection down to exactly five niches that meet all top niche criteria.
23. Highlight your top five niches in green for clarity.
24. Keep your top five candidates at the top of your worksheet.
25. Keep all eliminated niches on your sheet for reference when planning future stores.

- Compact version of the same grading work [L1081.002]:
  1. Copy the niche keyword from your list (for example Persian rugs).
  2. Paste it into the research tool and click search.
  3. Enter the letter grade the tool gives the niche (for example A or A-).
  4. Enter the average price from the tool, format the cell as currency, and remove the decimals.
  5. Enter the average profit using the 25% formula (average price x 0.25).
  6. Enter 'pass' for the demographic test if its box is green.
  7. Enter 'pass' for the brand loyalty test if its box is green.
  8. Enter 'pass' for the seasonality test if it shows 4 out of 4.
  9. Enter the average monthly searches for the keyword as the demand.
  10. Drag the profit formula down the column to fill the other niches.
- Time per batch: repeating the grading steps for all niches typically takes 30 minutes or less [L0045.001]. The worksheet is completed in roughly 28 to 30 minutes per batch of niches, so plan 30 to 35 minutes for a full worksheet [L1081.004].

### Grading with traffic lights and colours

- Traffic light grading [L0490.017, older, 2021-22]:
