  - Green means approved.
  - Red means rejected because of a strikeout. Red niches are removed from the active shortlist.
  - Orange or yellow means maybe, for borderline cases.
- Market research tracker colour coding [L0490.018, older, 2021-22]:
  - Green for approved.
  - Red for not approved (a line through the row also works).
  - Orange or yellow for maybe.
- Source A's colour scheme for the worksheet [L0045.001, L0459.016, L0451.007]:
  - Demand under 10,000 monthly searches: red text.
  - Seasonality failures (fewer than 4 seasons): red.
  - Average profit sort: highest at top, low-profit or red-marked niches at the bottom.
  - Top five niches: green.
  - Mark a niche green when it passes on DS Friendly or estimated suppliers, and red when it fails [L0459.016].
  - Failing niches are marked red text and moved to the bottom, not deleted [L0451.007].
- In the evergreen test of the research tool, a green box passes and a red box fails [L1075.002].
- Black (non-red) entries at the top of the list are the focus of the analysis [L0045.001].

### Top five, the shortlist and the rule for failed niches

- Narrow the top candidates to exactly five niches that meet all top niche criteria. Highlight them in green and keep them at the top of the worksheet [L0045.001].
- Keep the red losers and their data on the sheet below the top 5 instead of deleting them. The data can be reused when researching a second, third or later store, so the research does not have to be repeated [L1081.016].
- Keep all eliminated or rejected niches on your worksheet rather than deleting them. These niches may be relevant for different business models or future store planning when market conditions change [L0045.007].
- Keep all eliminated niches on your sheet for reference when planning future stores [L0045.001].
- Keep passing niches (winners) at the top of the list and move failing niches (losers) to the bottom in red text instead of deleting them, so the record can be reused for future stores [L0451.007].
- Fill in the demand, seasonality and average price columns for failing niches as well as passing ones, so the worksheet keeps a complete record for future store research. Mark failing niches in red and move them to the bottom of the list rather than deleting them [L0451.017].
- Expected outcome of the test round: research all 50 or more brainstormed niches, fill in the demand, seasonality and average price columns for each, move losers to the bottom in red and keep winners on top before continuing [L0451.010].

### Future competitor sheets

- Create a separate competitor sheet for each niche that still passes all earlier tests [L0891.002]:
  1. Right-click the template sheet and click Duplicate.
  2. Click and hold the copy, then drag it to the left so it sits next to the template.
  3. Right-click the copy, click Rename, and name it '[niche name] future competitors', for example 'chandelier future competitors'.
  4. Repeat for every other niche that is still on the top of the list.
- Research future competitors in the worksheet by navigating to the tab labeled "Niche Future Competitors." For each niche you research, right-click this tab, click Duplicate, and rename the copy with your niche name (e.g., "Outdoor Kitchens, Future Competitors") [L0051.003].
- The future competitors sheet is part of your Niche Sheet from Module 1 [L0061.001]. To populate it [L0061.004]:
  1. Open your Niche Sheet from Module 1.
  2. Navigate to the [Niche] Future Competitors sheet.
  3. Populate with competitor URLs, store names, traffic ranks from SimilarWeb, and niches each competitor sells.
- Competitor sheet columns [L0051.004, L0540.003, L0542.002]:

| Column | Purpose |
|---|---|
| URL / Store URL | Website address of the competitor store |
| Store Name | Name of the competitor website |
| Traffic Rank | Country-specific rank from SimilarWeb in your target country |
| Niches Sold | Other product categories the store sells in (informs future niche expansion and multi-store planning) |

- The future competitor tracking sheet records each store that sells in the chosen niche, with its traffic rank and the other niches it sells, to monitor who may enter the market [L0542.002].
- The competitor table is the same as in the earlier version, with columns URL, Store Name, Traffic Rank and Niches Sold [L0540.003].
- Column layout of the niche future competitors sheet. Every competitor needs all four columns [L0891.003]:

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| A | URL |
| B | Store Name |
| C | Traffic Rank |
| D | Niches Sold |

- Column C (Traffic Rank) is filled in only after the URLs and niches are listed [L0891.003].
- Take the competitor URLs from the store research done in the previous step, which came from the first page of Google results and the Google Shopping sidebar. Copy each store's URL into column A and type a short store name in column B [L0891.004].
- In column D, list every product niche or category the store sells, not only the niche you are researching. Check the store's category menu to find them, for example office furniture, kitchen furniture, living room furniture, bedroom furniture and lighting [L0891.005].
- Example: one multi-category furniture store had over 1,850 chandeliers in its lighting category, so lighting was listed next to its furniture categories in column D. A store with bathroom lights, ceiling fans and other lighting types was logged with ceiling fans and lighting fixtures [L0891.006].
- A competitor list is complete only when columns A, B, C and D are filled in for every competitor. Only then should the lesson be marked as finished [L0891.017].
- Once a product is chosen, list three to five competitor stores selling it in the product research sheet before building any site. If a product has fewer competitors, record what exists and report the gap instead of skipping the step. Many products will still have three to five competitors [L0897.001].

- Build a product testing sheet in this order [L1162.003]:
  1. Make your own copy of the shared template.
  2. Enter the product name in the first field.
  3. Paste the ad link, taken from the Facebook Ad Library or an ad-analysis tool, for inspiration.
  4. Paste the competitor's store link to study what they do and what you can improve.
  5. Paste the AliExpress link so you can source the product from CJ or your current supplier.
  6. Mark engagement as high or low and competition as high, medium or low, then note your findings.
  7. Mark market size as small, medium or large.
  8. Make the go/no-go decision (test or not).
  9. Enter COGS (cost of goods sold, i.e. what it costs to fulfil one order with your supplier).
  10. Enter your selling price and the competitor's selling price.
  11. Calculate the breakeven ROAS using the calculator linked at the top right of the sheet, entering COGS and selling price.
  12. Write the reason for your product choice in the mentor notes field.
  13. Send the list to your mentor so they can comment on each product.

## Quick Disqualifiers and Bad Niche Traits

### Fast Filter: Physical, Shippable Products Only

- Sell only physical products that can be shipped. Digital goods, services and location-dependent items do not work in a dropshipping model. [L0024.004, L0159.007]
- Exclude services. Products used to perform a service are still acceptable. [L1056.015]
- Exclude consumables, personalization-only products, made-to-order-only goods, collectibles, and low-ticket accessories or add-ons, unless they are bundled into high-value core inventory. These fail because the model needs strong margins and repeat orders, which they do not provide. [L0024.004, L0159.010]
- Exclude luxury fashion and collectible-driven categories. These markets are dominated by established brands, or they need scarcity and brand prestige that a new store cannot build. [L0159.009]
- Avoid niches dominated by a few large brands, because a new store cannot compete there. [L1056.015]
- Avoid niches that generate no sales or problematic orders, require extensive customer service, or have low profit margins. [L0009.002]
- Avoid product categories you do not understand well, such as some feminine-care products, unless you can get expert input on use cases and quality. Unknown categories make it hard to judge demand and product claims. [L0372.015]
- Avoid AliExpress-style stores with no real brand, few barriers, and products that change every month. Buyers see little value in them, and the broker stopped listing them about a year before the talk because they were hard to sell. [L0554.018]
- Successful niches tend to have diverse styling and customization options, and customers accept lead times because the uniqueness justifies the wait. [L0028.001]
- Good niches have many styles and variations that buyers cannot easily find offline, and buyers are willing to wait a couple of weeks. Thousands of niches fit this profile. [L0766.022]

### Mentor Boundaries

- Personal rule of the mentor: he does not test health products with creams or chemicals, and he avoids fashion unless the exact return and shipping policies are known. Use the same kind of boundary to avoid high-chargeback and high-refund niches. [L0335.031]

### Customer Service and Return Load

- Niches that are not dropship-friendly or are customer-service intensive generate many calls, emails, complaints, returns and negative reviews. Their profit can be outweighed by the support workload. [L0585.005]
- Before choosing a niche, assess two factors outside the usual checklist: (1) how much customer service is needed before and after the sale, and (2) the likely return rate, found by searching supplier names for reviews on other stores about quality, damages and inconsistency. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0249.007]
- Study the niche as a buyer would: search the product, watch unboxing and review videos, and read competitor reviews. Avoid niches where customers repeatedly complain or are confused, and niches with high return rates such as electronics, apparel and personal items. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0801.008]
- Avoid niches where customers must see or touch the product before buying, such as most electronics, clothing, mattresses, comforters and bed sheets. Avoid these even if they meet other criteria. (Older advice, 2020.) [L0852.020]
- Avoid products that require strict deadlines, carry strong emotional significance, or need physical inspection before purchase. These generate excessive customer service issues and returns. [L0028.002]
- Avoid niches with strong personal preferences (mattresses, bedsheets), products that require installation (backyard playsets), or items easily damaged in shipping. These generate high return rates and customer service burden. [L0031.003]
- Niches with higher than average return rates include apparel, personal items such as bed sheets and mattresses, items buyers need to see and touch, luxury goods aimed at wealthy buyers, and most electronics. (Older advice, 2019.) [L0663.042]
- Apparel and other categories with high return rates should be avoided. A 28% return rate in apparel is cited as too high, because money goes out almost as fast as it comes in. (Older advice, 2019.) [L0663.005]

#### Community Check for Post-Sale Support (Procedure)

To estimate how much post-sale support a product niche will need, check the community research before choosing it:

1. Open Reddit and search for a community about the niche you are considering.
2. Read the questions people ask in that community.
3. If many questions are repetitive and other users have to help because the product is hard to figure out, expect a high level of post-sale support. [L0626.005]

### Electronics and Technical Products

#### Default Rule and Its Exceptions

- As a general rule, do not sell electronics in dropshipping. Electronics often confuse buyers, can be damaged in transit, and a single defect, such as a burnt-out part, creates a service exchange. Exceptions exist. [L0766.006]
- Avoid electronics as a default. They bring customer service issues and are often dominated by a few large players. Exception: buyers who are hobbyists and enjoy assembling and figuring out the product, such as 3D printer buyers. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0469.016]
- Electronics create continuous support problems because of technical complexity, which leads to returns and customer dissatisfaction. [L0028.006]
- Electronics niches are usually dominated by a few large brands. This is one main reason to avoid selling most consumer electronics in a dropship store. [L0626.001]
- Avoid consumer electronics such as televisions, stereos, digital cameras and drones. These markets are dominated by big brands, and the products are complex, need heavy support, and are more likely to break in shipping or arrive non-functional. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L0994.022]
- Avoid electronics such as VR headsets, game consoles and monitors when possible. They are brand-loyal and create frequent post-purchase questions and back-and-forth communication. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0968.090]
- Electronics and products with many buttons or features usually bring more customer service requests. Beginners should generally avoid them, but the niche can still be profitable if you enjoy it and expect the extra support work. (Older advice, 2018.) [L1274.016]
- Avoid products with many moving parts, such as juicers. They tend to generate more customer service calls and returns. Electronics with a high return risk should be avoided in general. (Older advice, 2019.) [L1069.032]
- Electronic products are a poor first test for a beginner, even when competitors run some ads for them. They usually need more explanation and trust than simple items. Start with a product that a single image ad can sell. [L1316.047]
- For a first business, avoid complex electronic products. They often need more technical support, have a higher chance of failure, and customers may not know how to use them. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L0994.025]
- Electronics can cause problems in dropshipping, including customs fines, seizure at the border, or a product that does not work on arrival. Whether this matters depends on the target countries, so a non-electronic product is the safer default. [L1220.011]

#### Technical Products After the Sale

- Technical electronics that need learning or setup can still be profitable, but expect more post-sale support. Simple electronics carry much less of this risk. [L0626.002]
- Technical niches are acceptable if customers mainly ask pre-sale questions. Avoid niches where products need technical knowledge after the sale, such as many electronics. (Source 2025.) [L0472.058]
- A technical product such as a supercharger or turbocharger requires customer service that can handle installation questions. Enter such a niche only if you have the knowledge or are ready to learn it. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0963.110]
- High-end espresso machines and in-home coffee bars count as a bad niche by default. They are electronic, have many points where things can break or be set up wrongly, and generate a lot of customer service work. A seller could still take them on if willing to invest the extra time. [L0766.007]
- Avoid large appliance categories such as refrigerators. Strong brand loyalty, buyers who need very specific sizes, and dominance by a few big players mean offline and online retailers can offer better prices than a dropshipper. [L0766.016]
- Avoid white goods such as fridges, washing machines, dryers and dishwashers. The market is dominated by very large brands, and these are needs before they are wants. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L0994.023]

### Fashion, Apparel and Sizing

#### General Avoidance

- Avoid apparel and other categories with high return rates. (Older advice, 2019.) [L0663.005]
- Avoid clothing niches and similar personal products such as fashion items. Their return rates are very high, and returns and customer service are costly. (Source 2024.) [L1115.020]
- Avoid apparel, meaning clothing, jackets, shirts and shoes, because it is dominated by well-known brands. The exception is apparel made only for one specific activity by specialist brands, such as mountain climbing gear, which can be viable. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L0994.024]
- Apparel is a poor fit for dropshipping not only because of low price points. Fit and feel often differ from customer expectations, which produces high return rates that a small dropshipping business cannot absorb. [L0769.009]
- Fashion and body-related categories (clothing, jewelry, shoes, fitness items, cosmetics) made up over 50% of one supplier's products, because dropshipping stock is hard when there are many colors, variants and sizes. Successful products tend to be simple and usable by anyone. [L0780.002]
- Fashion products are not recommended for beginners, because sizing is a major issue and returns are hard to handle. [L0708.013]

#### Sizing

- Fashion is not recommended for beginners because sizing is a major issue, and Chinese sizes differ from Western sizes. One-size items such as beanies, and shoes, can reduce this problem. [L0693.011]
- Avoid products that depend on sizing, because size problems create returns and return shipping costs. One-size or oversized clothing carries less risk. [L1431.008]
- Footwear, especially winter boots, carries sizing risk, and wrong sizes lead to returns that hurt margins. Leave shoes out of early tests unless clear size guidance can be provided. [L1185.013]
- Do not trust the size chart a supplier gives for footwear, especially when selling to the US or Australia. Ask the supplier for the length in centimeters of each size and recalculate the sizes for the target market. [L0661.013]

#### Fashion Subcategories

- Fast-fashion products are not recommended as a starting niche. Other fashion niches are considered better. [L0577.036]
- For fashion targeting older women, look for one-size products aimed at women over 35 to avoid sizing issues and returns. A one-size fashion product with many active ads is a strong test candidate. [L1316.026]
- Some product categories like shapewear and skin-revealing products have become saturated on TikTok and are harder to run on Facebook when skin is shown. Avoid these categories unless the ad account has a good standing and an advertising history. [L0638.029]
- Swimwear products face sizing issues, since a customer who buys a product that does not fit is a common return cause. Facebook and TikTok ads may restrict images that show too much skin. Use lifestyle imagery or product-only images instead of models in revealing swimwear. [L0678.033]

### Personal, Sensory and Fit-Dependent Products

- Products that pass the pricing test and the brand loyalty test can still be disqualified if they are highly personal, such as mattresses or high-quality bed sheets priced around $500. Customers return such items when they do not feel as expected. [L0769.008]
- Products with high personal sensory fit, such as mattresses or premium bed sheets, are poor niches even at high prices. Customers often return them because the feel differs from what they expected from online photos and descriptions. [L0769.022]
- Bedding products have naturally high return rates because customers require hands-on evaluation of comfort, materials and fit before purchase. [L0028.007]
- Items that are highly personal or need physical evaluation are excluded even when they meet other criteria. [L0852.020]

### Installation, Assembly and Bulky Items

#### Assembly and Post-Sale Support

- Products that need heavy assembly lead to more post-sale support, such as missing screws, damaged parts and replacement requests. These can usually be solved by asking the supplier to send replacement parts. (Older advice, 2020.) [L0961.047]
- Niches with products that require installation or technical explanation mean more direct customer contact for a solo operator. Reduce this by adding everything customers ask before ordering to the product pages, and updating them as inquiries come in. (Source 2023.) [L0964.007]

#### Installation-Heavy Products

- Installation-heavy products add delivery and assembly complexity, which is hard for a first store. If you pursue them, partner with a nationwide installer recommended by the supplier. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0247.014]
- Installation-heavy products, such as backyard swing sets, are a bad niche if you want to avoid heavy customer service. If you sell them, the product page must clearly show how the item arrives, what the finished product looks like, how long installation takes, and whether the customer should hire an installer. [L0769.010]
- For a niche where products need installation, either sell them with a note that the customer must hire a licensed electrician or other installer, or offer installation as a service by contracting local installers and earning a referral margin. (Source 2023.) [L0964.008]
- For niches that need installation, such as fireplaces, check how the top future competitors handle installation on the product pages of brands you are authorized to sell. Copy their approach, such as a note recommending a local contractor or an add-on installation service. (Source 2024.) [L0965.019]

#### Bulky Products

- For bulky products such as generators, first identify which type is being sold, since small units and whole-home units need different support. Then check what delivery and installation support competitors offer and copy that level. (Source 2024.) [L1285.016]
- Check for long backorders or supply delays before committing. During 2020 and 2021, home fitness equipment faced delivery waits of roughly 30 to 90 days. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0247.013]
- Avoid niches where items are easily damaged in shipping. [L0031.003]

#### Quote-Based Installation Items

- Items that need a fit check or professional installation, such as stairlifts, walk-in bathtubs, residential elevators, ceiling lift systems and pool lifts, add a consultation step to the sale. They suit a quote-based or sales-call process rather than a plain checkout. [L0546.006]

### Health, Medical, Regulated and Consumable Products

#### Regulation

- Exclude highly regulated product categories. Regulatory compliance creates licensing, approval or safety testing barriers that new stores cannot manage or afford. [L0159.008]
- Include only physical products that can be shipped. Exclude highly regulated products. [L0024.004]
- A heavily regulated niche can be an opportunity because fewer competitors will invest the work, but it does not guarantee success. The decision depends on how big the opportunity looks and whether you will invest the time. (Older advice, 2018.) [L0466.052]
- If the only approved supplier's products are accessories priced under about 200 dollars, running ads is not worth it. (Older advice, 2018.) [L0466.053]
- Regulated medical devices, such as CPAP machines, oxygen concentrators, digital stethoscopes and hyperbaric chambers, may need registration or a prescription in some markets. Check their regulatory status before using health or treatment terms on product pages or in ads. [L0546.021]
- A niche may be restricted for Google Ads even though it is dropship-friendly. When a niche verification returns a restriction, check the specific extra requirements (such as digital agreements) before concluding the niche is unusable. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0665.005]

#### Health Products and Claims

- Avoid products that touch the skin or make weight loss claims, because quality problems create chargebacks and disputes. For electronic gadgets, request supplier quality inspections and check each component. [L1218.028]
- Avoid chemical products and products that touch skin or hair unless you know the ingredients and are sure of the quality through the supplier. Without that certainty, these products can be harmful. [L0708.012]
- Avoid glass and other fragile products for beginners. Consider them only if the supplier guarantees quality or you can test a sample yourself. [L0708.011]

#### Insurance

- Avoid niches where the top competitors bill health insurance. Niches where competitors take out-of-pocket payment are acceptable. (Older advice, 2020.) [L1111.011]
- For niches with health or medical products, check whether insurance covers the product or whether shoppers pay out of pocket before committing. Look at how current sellers handle insurance, such as whether they list accepted insurers, because that changes the sales process and payment flow. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0803.095]

#### Medical Supplies

- A medical supplies niche usually requires working through distributors, because suppliers rarely sell directly to retailers. This made it a poor fit for a typical drop-shipping store. (Older advice, 2018.) [L1085.027]

#### Consumables and Supplements

- Supplement products generally do not fit the model, because the typical price point is below the roughly 200 dollars or more per item that is wanted. (Older advice, 2022.) [L1113.008]
- Views do not guarantee sales for consumable products. People hesitate to buy products related to eating or drinking. In the cited example, 15 million views produced only about 25 sales. [L1429.039]

### Seasonal, Date-Bound and Fad Products

#### Seasonal Products

- Seasonal products fail in dropshipping because their time-critical nature drives customer service burden. People buy them for specific deadlines. [L0028.005]
- Avoid seasonal products such as artificial Christmas trees for a first store, even when the market looks large. Buyers order only a few weeks before the holiday, so any delay, backorder or lost parcel becomes an urgent customer service problem. [L0766.004]
- Christmas tree lights are the worst niche. The products are cheap, can be bought locally, have little brand variation, and are extremely seasonal. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0854.100]
- Seasonal products such as outdoor Christmas decorations are neither clearly good nor bad, but seasonality makes them not good by default. A seller might add them once they already run several stores. [L0766.018]

#### Date-Bound Products

- Avoid products tied to a fixed calendar date, such as Christmas items, because the selling window can close before scaling is complete. Products without a fixed end date are preferred. Date-bound ones can be kept on a separate list for later. [L1185.003]

#### Fad Products

- Avoid fad niches, such as products that are popular for only a short period. Their value falls quickly once the trend passes. [L0554.017]

### Fringe, Adult and Restricted-Platform Products

- Adults-only products have fewer payment processors willing to work with them and fewer traffic sources available for advertising. This limits how many people can find your website. [L0769.015]
- Avoid unusual or very fringe product types. Most standard product types can be advertised almost anywhere, while niche products face restricted ad platforms and limited traffic. [L0769.016]
- Products that get repeatedly removed for dangerous content, such as some lighter products, carry a takedown risk. Check whether a product category is being taken down before investing in testing it. [L0706.040]
- Borderline products on the edge of restricted categories can sometimes work. Judge them carefully and check the platform rules for advertising and selling before you commit. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L0994.027]

### Ad Platform, Policy and Shipping Checks

#### Google Ads Policy Procedure

1. Before building a store in a niche, search Google Ads policy together with the niche name.
2. If competitors advertise the product, Google usually requires an extra policy agreement or certification. Complete it before running ads. (Source 2023.) [L0970.027]

- Some niches face repeated ad disapprovals, such as medical niches. Contact Google Ads support with the full history of approvals and disapprovals, and ask what to change so the disapprovals stop. (Source 2023.) [L0970.028]

#### Shipping Restrictions

- Check for item-specific shipping restrictions, such as for flammable goods, and ask suppliers about state-level shipping limits for large items. Brands already sold by large retailers have usually addressed these restrictions. (Source 2023.) [L0970.029]
- Judge shipping from product listings by visual size and common sense, for example whether the item would fit into a standard parcel or a small room. Check the weight limits for your country only when an item looks very large or heavy. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1329.025]

### Needs Versus Wants and Shortlisting

- Separate needs from wants. Basic household items people must have, such as basic lighting or a fridge, are poor choices. Wants can work, such as a crystal chandelier bought for status or interior design, or a surfboard, even if the product fails another criterion. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L0994.021]
- When shortlisting, answer the quick yes/no criteria, such as enthusiast market and shipping, before the slower price check. This removes weak ideas early and saves research time. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1329.020]
- A market where most buyers buy for hobby or enjoyment still passes the enthusiast check, even if a small share of buyers need the product for work. Count the majority of buyers, not the exceptions. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1329.024]

#### Further details

- Avoid baby strollers and cribs for dropshipping. Suppliers offer traditional stores better pricing and place them in a different MAP tier, which leaves an online seller little room. [L0356.006]

- Urns and memorial products have a big online market because they can be personalized with prayers or sayings and come in many styles. They are still a bad niche for dropshipping because the delivery is time-critical and the buyer is in a sensitive situation. [L0766.010]

- Bad niches share four traits: electronics, very high customer expectations with strict deadlines, strong emotional attachment, and personalized items that the buyer must see, feel or touch before purchase. Avoiding these reduces customer service burden and responsibility. [L0766.021]

## Price Point, Margin and Shipping Economics

### Minimum Price: The $200 Floor

- Products in a store should average at least $200, and this minimum has been used since the program began, so do not sell items priced below it (2025). [L0667.070]
- High-ticket products start at $200 or higher (2025). [L0278.001]
- Focus only on categories where most products are priced at $200 or more, so each sale leaves enough profit for a sustainable model. [L0012.001]
- Only consider products priced above $200, ideally higher, because lower-priced items usually leave too little profit to cover ads and fees (2020). [L0961.089]
- The minimum product price to sell is about $200. Within a niche, carve out a higher tier rather than selling cheap versions, for example studio lighting sets at $400 or more instead of $100 sets (2021). [L0801.010]
- Do not list products under $200 unless they are add-ons or accessories, because low-priced products rarely produce enough margin to justify ad spend (2025). [L0837.015]
- Sort a supplier's catalog by price and list only products above the set threshold. Products under $200 are usually not worth listing because their margins are too low (2024). [L0965.021]
- Core products should cost at least $200, and ideally more. The lesson's stores average above $1,000. Products below $200 can still be sold, but they should not be the products that paid traffic is bought for. [L1147.009]
- Cheap, very common products such as phone cases look easy to sell but face huge competition and many variations, so they usually earn little per order. Easy-looking demand is not a reason to choose a product. [L1147.011]
- Inexpensive items such as decorative pillows, ornaments and regular pillows are almost never a good niche for dropshipping. [L0766.019]
- Avoid the cheapest commodity segment of a niche (example: basic ceiling fans at $20 to $60) and focus on the premium segment (example: $300 and up). The premium segment has large demand and enough margin, and cheap items are not worth the time (2018). [L1085.025]
- Minimum price for a niche product is about $200, with no maximum. Higher-priced products are acceptable if supplier quality and pricing are right (2018). [L1109.012]
- Minimum price used as a filter is $200 or more. This floor must be combined with the target demographic and not used on its own. [L1518.012]
- A niche passes the price point test only when its average selling price is above $200. Niches below $200 move to the bottom of the research list. [L1150.001]
- The average price point of a niche's products should be at least $200. A niche with a lower average fails the price check even when demand and seasonality pass. [L0451.009, L0451.013]
- Half or more of the first-page search results for a product should be priced above $200. [L1092.030] (older: 2022)
- If all candidate products in a list are under $100, look for higher-priced products within the niche, or niche up to a broader category that contains a higher price range (2019). [L1110.020]
- Products with an average retail price under about $200 are not recommended, even with search volume above 200,000, because the margin cannot cover shipping, fees, fixed costs and ad spend (2020). The lesson framed this as a room-for-profit issue, not a niche problem. [L0358.020]
- For small, light products shipped with standard parcel carriers such as UPS or FedEx, a selling price of at least about $200 is the minimum threshold. [L1179.010]

**Conflicting thresholds for niche ideas (when each applies):**
- For generating niche ideas, the average sale price must be $500 or higher to qualify as viable for dropshipping. [L0024.002]
- For a niche to count as high-ticket, target an average product price of $500 or more. This attracts affluent buyers with more purchasing power and creates viable margins. [L0159.005]
- The $200 floor remains the price check applied to a listed niche. [L0451.009, L0451.013, L1150.001]

### Average Price: What to Measure and How

- Calculate average prices from new products only, excluding used items. Leave out shipping costs when shipping is not included in the listed price. [L1279.009]
- Ignore auctions and auction-based prices. Include only products at fixed prices that are new and currently for sale; eBay fixed-price new sales count. (2024) [L0276.069]
- Use the products on the first page of Google Shopping results for the niche term, since these are the most popular products and their prices give a usable average. [L0941.009]
- Use the first page of Google Shopping results. A few cheap, lower-quality competitors are acceptable because you sell the better, higher-priced products (2021). [L0469.012]
- Look at paid results first and weigh them more heavily than organic results, though organic prices also help. [L0671.029, L0671.168] (older: 2021, identical text)
- Organic first-page results should show an average of at least $200. There is no maximum price, but very high average order values bring more phone orders (2024). [L0806.002]
- Do not filter Google Shopping results by a price floor such as $200 when estimating a niche's average price. Default results show the most popular products, and a price filter distorts demand research (2021). [L0853.020]
- Find average prices from the default search results, not from price filters, because filters change which products appear as the most popular ones (2021). [L1112.066]
- Do not apply a price filter such as "over 500" when researching on Google Shopping. It changes which products show as most popular. Keep the unfiltered first page for research (2021). [L1279.010]
- When one product type spans a huge price range (example: sofas from $200 to $20,000), do not mix price segments. Change the search term (example: leather sofa or three-seater sofa) instead of using the sidebar price filter (2024). [L0806.006]
- When a niche has many products with very wide price ranges, add a qualifying keyword to the search to narrow results to the desired range rather than relying on sidebar price filters (2023). [L0855.092]
- Price variation inside a niche is normal. Sofas may range from about $100 to $20,000, so keep the selected items in the range where the brand and product mix is strongest (2020). [L0967.006]
- When a category has two price tiers, such as standard $1,500 sofas and $30,000 custom Italian leather sofas, pick one tier for the store. Choose the lower tier for simpler customer service, or the higher tier if you accept more service work (2021). [L0469.019]
- Estimate prices from several retailer sites and categories, not from a single product page. A rough estimate that reflects the range you see is enough for the decision. [L1329.015]
- Judge a niche by the typical average price across several retailers and categories, not by a single product. Individual products can sit above or below the target. [L1329.021]
- To find retailers for price research, use the sponsored ads and scroll down the main Google results for more store sites. One website does not show the full price range of a niche. [L1329.022]
- Keep a few high-priced outlier competitors in the average if their products still fit the niche. Deluxe versions that cost much more do not disqualify a niche (2023). [L0970.020]
- Include outliers only when they are relevant products you would list. If an outlier is a pricing error, exclude it. [L1283.066]
- Exclude price outliers that are obvious data errors, such as a $23,746 dresser caused by a misplaced decimal or a multiplication bug. Real products with genuine prices stay in the average (2021). [L0834.005]
- A supplier's shipping cost from offshore sources can distort average price. Fix this by refining the keyword, not by adding shipping to the average. [L1283.067]
- Products priced well above the calculated range can still be sold in the store, and suppliers offering higher-priced items raise profit margin. The average price remains the main pass criterion for a niche. [L1150.006]
- Average prices are estimated from what you see. Exact calculation is not needed at this stage. [L1329.009]
- Price research for a broad niche: 1) search the main keyword and look at the most popular products on the first page of Google results; 2) if you plan to sell only a subtype, price research that subtype; 3) if you plan to sell all types, average the prices across them (2021). [L0968.088]

#### Procedure: Average price from Google Shopping (Source A, 2020, older)

1. Search Google for the main keyword a potential customer would use for the product. [L0358.018]
2. Look at the first page of the Google Shopping results. [L0358.018]
3. Calculate the average price across those results. This average approximates what most buyers are willing to spend, because top results reflect the most popular products. [L0358.018]

#### Procedure: Source B's Shopping-tab check (2021-22, older)

1. Open Google, search the product type, and click the Shopping tab. [L0458.017]
2. Read the listed prices and scroll through the results pages. [L0458.017]
3. Use the price filter with the ranges Up to $500, $500 to $1,000, $1,000 to $3,000 and Over $3,000 to see how many listings sit in the high-ticket range. [L0458.017]
4. Calculate the average price of the listings and check it is at least $800. The lesson's generator example averaged about $1,000 or more. [L0458.017]
5. Mark the price criterion as yes only if the high-ticket range is well covered. [L0458.017]

#### Procedure: Estimating average price with Google Shopping (Source B, 2021-22, older)

1. Search the broad market idea or a specific product type in Google. [L1329.009]
2. Make sure results come from your target selling country. If you live elsewhere, use a VPN and set the location to that country. [L1329.009]
3. Review the Google Shopping ads (product image, title, price), which appear at the top or side of results, and open the Shopping tab for a dedicated page. [L1329.009]
4. Use the Shopping filters to narrow prices to your target range. [L1329.009]
5. Note the products that fall within your target price range, and note the product types you see (for example drawers or turbos) for later research. [L1329.009]
6. Open retailer websites from the ads and shopping results, browse their categories, and note products above and below your target range. [L1329.009]
7. Skip low-ticket categories that do not fit your price target. [L1329.009]
8. Estimate one average price per idea from the prices you saw. Exact calculation is not needed. [L1329.009]
9. Repeat for each of the five ideas. This takes about 10 to 20 minutes for all five. [L1329.009]

#### Procedure: Price test for a high-ticket product (Source A, 2022, older)

1. Search the product name on Google Shopping. [L1281.021]
2. Check the price spread of the results. [L1281.021]
3. Pass the product only if at least half of the results are priced at $200 or more. Products with mostly $20 to $50 results fail, even if they sell. [L1281.021]

#### Price filter brackets (conflicting sources, when each applies)

- Source B's Shopping-tab check uses the brackets Up to $500, $500 to $1,000, $1,000 to $3,000 and Over $3,000 to check the high-ticket range. [L0458.017]
- Source B's general price check uses the Shopping preset brackets Up to $100, $100 to $250, $250 to $600 and Over $600 to see whether results reach the target range. [L1329.011, L1329.019]
- On the Shopping results page, the Product rating filter's "4 and up" option narrows listings to better-rated products. [L1329.019]

#### Tool-based price analysis (Source A, no year)

- Before automated research tools, average prices were gathered manually: search the niche keyword on Google, open the Shopping tab and read the listed prices. [L1150.002]
- The research tool's average uses the interquartile range, a statistical method that removes outliers such as very expensive items and accessories in keyword searches. The displayed range is therefore narrower than the full set of prices found. [L1150.003]
- Example: chandeliers had an average of $305.49 from 33 products, with a range of $44.48 to $999 after outliers were removed. Raw listings such as $1,800, $2,730, $4,400 and $4,999 were excluded. [L1150.004]
- Judging a niche by individual high or low listings instead of the filtered average gives a misleading picture. Accessories and extreme outliers distort the impression of what a niche sells for. [L1150.005]
- The price panel at the bottom of the research tool's results shows three figures: the average price, the number of products the average is based on, and the price range after outliers are removed. For example, chandeliers showed an average of $305.49 from 33 products, with a range of $44.48 to $999. [L1150.015]
- The price analysis in the research tool checks a niche's average price against the price-point criteria taught in the Blueprint testing module. [L1075.007]
- AI tools such as ChatGPT often give pricing data that does not match live Google Shopping prices. Verify a few products manually before using AI for pricing, and drop a niche that fails at the rough filter stage (2024). [L0471.053]
- To estimate a product's selling price, check what similar items sell for on eBay and in Google Shopping results. Use those observed prices as the planning sale price before running margin calculations, for example a cheap phone case at about $10 and a paddleboard at about $1,000. [L1147.025]
- Judge a Shopping price against local retail as a ceiling check. Example: a vacuum canister sourced from AliExpress was priced around 37 pounds (about 45 dollars) in UK retail, compared with 20 to 40 dollars on Amazon. [L1186.043]

### Shipping: Size, Weight and COGS

- Profitability is determined by the relationship between COGS and shipping costs, not by product size or weight. [L0015.001]
- Disqualifying products during niche research based only on size or weight, without analyzing COGS and shipping, is a mistake. [L0015.002]
- Size and weight alone do not disqualify a niche. The decisive question is whether the sale price leaves enough net profit after COGS and shipping. Disqualify a product when the margin left over is too small. [L1180.009]
- Large and heavy products should not be ruled out automatically. Viability depends on the arithmetic of selling price, COGS and shipping, plus common sense about whether the seller can afford the shipping. [L1180.001]
- Most products in a category cost roughly the same to ship, so a fixed shipping burden hits low-priced items much harder than high-priced ones. The selling price decides whether a niche can absorb shipping. [L1179.008]
- For large and heavy products, shipping costs remain similar across price points. A $500 item and a $1,500 item may cost nearly the same to ship, making the higher-priced version far more profitable. [L0016.004]
- A low-priced bulky or heavy product can lose its entire gross margin to shipping, leaving zero net profit. Avoid such niches even if the product sells well. [L1179.009]
- Avoid niches dominated by inexpensive, large or heavy products, because shipping eliminates profit margins and leaves minimal or zero net earnings. [L0016.008]
- Heavy or bulky products are workable only when the selling price is above $1,000. Below that level, shipping costs on large, heavy items eat the profit (2019). [L0663.002]
- Do not sell large, heavy, inexpensive items. Shipping makes them unprofitable unless the retail price leaves a large spread over wholesale (2022). [L0969.022]
- Heavy or bulky products need a higher price point than standard items, because freight costs require a wider spread between wholesale and MAP to cover free shipping (2022). [L1092.031]
- Heavy or bulky items are better when their selling price is high enough to absorb shipping. Higher-priced items carry heavy freight better, and free shipping is possible only if the price covers the shipping cost. [L1285.014]
- The shipping problem comes mainly from products whose price leaves too little room between MAP and wholesale, not from size or weight alone. Large or heavy products can work if the price is high enough to cover shipping and ads. [L0359.013]
- Product options (variants) and product weight are generally not reasons to drop a niche. Heavy products are a problem only when prices are too low to cover shipping. [L0551.011]
- Products that are difficult to ship, such as large or heavy items, should not automatically be rejected. Shipping is harder than parcel shipping but can be learned quickly, while high customer service load is a stronger reason for caution (2020). [L0967.007]
- Heavy and bulky items have fewer sellers because many avoid freight shipping, so competition is often lower. Their shipping costs must be built into margin math before choosing them (2020). [L1111.013]
- Before listing a heavy B2B product, compare the item price with the wholesale cost and the shipping cost to check whether it leaves a healthy profit after free shipping (2021). [L0671.285]
- Before choosing a heavy or bulky product, calculate the shipping cost. A single item can cost hundreds of dollars to ship across the country. Avoid products whose shipping cost would be more than half of a low selling price (2020). [L0551.009]
- Shipping of around $2,500 on a $20,000 order is a sign that a supplier should not be listed if the customer saves that amount by ordering direct (2023). [L0964.016]
- Keep only the products that stay at least as profitable after shipping (2023). [L0964.016]
- Check the shipping feasibility of a product before testing. Liquids or large packages can be a problem, and shipping cost can kill the margin. [L1176.011]
- Bulky, heavy or installation-dependent items such as sinks, cabinets, lifts, saunas, pools, hot tubs, sheds and tiny homes raise shipping, handling and return costs. Weigh these costs before picking them. [L0546.005]
- Heavy commercial and industrial items such as Commercial Ranges and Ovens, Walk-in Refrigerators and Freezers, Forklifts, Car Lifts and Industrial Sewing Machines are often too heavy for standard parcel shipping. Plan freight or pallet delivery and a quote-based sale for them rather than a general checkout. [L0546.022]
- Bulky seasonal products such as barbecue grills can be considered for dropshipping if shipping costs are manageable. Timing the launch with the season, such as barbecue season, is a sensible way to leverage demand. [L0660.011]
- Products should weigh no more than 2 kg. Products of about 3 kg or more are very hard to ship and should be avoided (Source C). [L0708.010]
- Lightweight products with high perceived value, such as jewelry, keep shipping cost low relative to the selling price. Their low unit weight and room for custom boxes or private branding make them easier to scale. [L0780.038]
- If a bulky or heavy product fails at a low price point, check whether a higher-quality supplier version of the same type sells at a price high enough to absorb the shipping. Moving up the quality tier can turn an unprofitable item into a profitable one without changing the category. [L1180.015]
- Large and heavy products are harder to manage but not impossible to sell. Household furniture such as a table is acceptable, while items at the scale of a car are too big and too heavy (2021-22, older). [L0994.004, L0994.005]
- Shipping is a yes-or-no check based on common sense: are the products very large or very heavy? Detailed logistics are not needed at this stage. (2021-22, older) [L1329.016]
- Shipping limits to check (2021-22, older): in Australia, products over 100 kg are difficult to ship and may fail the shipping check. In the US, products weighing hundreds of pounds may be a problem. Products too large to fit in a small room of a home are too big to ship. [L1329.017]
- Examples of shippable high-ticket products (2021-22, older): canopies for pickup trucks at about $3,000 are not small but are not very large or heavy, so they pass. Airbag suspension kits at about $825 to over $1,000 come in boxes that can be sent by post, so they clearly pass. [L1329.018]
- Products must be small enough to ship comfortably. Very large or heavy items, such as big machines shipped from overseas, count against a niche in the shipping check (2021-22, older). [L0490.011]
- Avoid products that are too big or too heavy, because shipping them becomes difficult and costly for you and your supplier (2021-22, older). [L0994.004]
- Big or heavy products are only worth considering if their retail price is $3,000 or more. Below that, the shipping burden usually outweighs the margin (2021-22, older). [L0994.006]
- Sources differ on the threshold for bulky or heavy products: one mention says 300, while the summary checklist sets 3,000. Use 3,000 as the working threshold and treat anything below as a likely shipping problem (2021-22, older). [L0994.030]
- Check product size, weight and shipping cost against expected profit before going further with a niche. Shipping can make an attractive product unprofitable (2021). [L0247.006]
- Bulky and heavy items may be a niche to consider, but the seller should judge whether a sale is worth the freight. [L0551.009]
- Shipping problems come mainly from prices, and high-ticket items absorb freight. [L0359.013]

#### Heavy items and expensive versions within a niche

- Large and heavy products with a low sale price are generally not profitable with free shipping. If shipping eats the margin, sell only the more expensive products within the niche, for example fabric sofas instead of futons (2022, older). [L0665.006]
- Within one category, subtypes can differ widely in price. A futon is a low-priced sofa, while a three-seater fabric sofa averages about $1,500. A generic rug can be a cheap entryway mat, while Persian rugs sit well above $500. Narrow the niche to the subtype whose price can absorb shipping. [L1179.021]
- Avoid niches where all products are large and heavy and the selling price is around $600 or less, because there is typically no room for profit. A niche confirmed above this level can be pursued. [L1180.012]
- A product from a high-end segment, such as a $3,500 desk where a profit of $1,750 covers shipping, can be profitable where a cheaper heavy item cannot (2022). [L0969.021]

#### Shipping and freight arithmetic

| Rule | Formula or example | Source ids |
|---|---|---|
| Break-even when COGS is about 50% of price and shipping is paid from margin | Price = 2 × average shipping cost; below that, net profit is negative. Derived from the lesson's figures, not stated directly. | L1179.019 |
| Price needed for 30% net margin with free shipping, COGS at 50% | Price = S ÷ 0.20 (about 5 × S). At $250 average shipping, about $1,250. Derived from the lesson's figures. | L1179.020 |
| Shipping vs. low selling price | Avoid products whose shipping would be more than half of a low selling price. | L0551.009 |
| Items around $200-$300 | Shipping should not take roughly half of the selling price. | L1285.015 |
| Folding table at $500, COGS $250, shipping about $250 | Gross margin $250; net profit about $0; no room for operating costs. | L0016.006 |
| High-end dining table at $1,500, COGS $750, same shipping about $250 | Gross margin $750; net profit about $500 (33% net margin). | L0016.007 |

#### Procedure: Niche refinement with price and margin analysis (no year)

1. Open your niche research worksheet. [L0016.010]
2. Review each niche and refine it using the price and margin analysis. [L0016.010]
3. Expand niche categories where higher-ticket product versions exist. [L0016.010]
4. Add new niches that meet high-ticket (above $1,000) and profitability criteria. [L0016.010]
5. Spend 15 to 20 minutes on this refinement exercise. [L0016.010]
6. Complete the worksheet and proceed to detailed shipping cost validation. [L0016.010]

#### Procedure: Freight estimate before a supplier is found (Source A, 2022, older)

1. Enter a likely supplier warehouse zip code on freightcenter.com (Calculate freight rates). [L0665.007]
2. Enter a test zip code in a region such as Florida, California or New York. [L0665.007]
3. Enter the package dimensions and weight. [L0665.007]
4. Click View my rates to see rough shipping costs to different locations. [L0665.007]

### Margin Targets and Gross Margin Rules

- Target a net profit margin of approximately 30% on each sale. Some niches allow 25%, while others sustain higher margins, but 30% is the benchmark. [L0016.002]
- COGS from suppliers averages approximately 50% of the retail sale price. [L0016.001]
- A niche with a few brands ranking for the main keyword is viable if margins meet a 20% threshold and suppliers allow you to sell it (2020, older). [L0664.046]
- For a niche with 20 to 25% margins including shipping and an average product price around $1,500 to $2,000, first try to move to better pricing tiers with suppliers, and grow free organic traffic (product feed optimization, SEO) so ad costs do not eat the margin (2024). [L0805.038]
- Focus on gross margin percentage rather than margin dollars. High-ticket products still need enough percentage to pay for the more hands-on and expensive sales process (2019, older). [L1068.021]
- Example (2019, older): a $4,000 sale at a 20% margin gives $800 per sale, which is strong because more margin can absorb ad and discount costs. A $5,000 item with only $250 margin is not worth selling. [L1068.022]
- Example (2019, older): brands showing a 20 to 25% margin before ads and shipping can fall to 10 to 15% once a $100 shipping cost is included. A margin that thin is too small for paid traffic. [L1068.023]
- In furniture (2019, older), a $200 futon has so much shipping cost that little margin is left, while a $5,000 leather sofa leaves room for margin and shipping. Avoid low-priced bulky items where shipping absorbs the profit. [L1068.020]
- Procedure for low-margin brands in a niche (2019, older):
  1. Run Google Shopping product listing ads only for brands with healthy margins. [L1068.024]
  2. Upload low-margin products to the site but exclude them from Google Ads campaigns. [L1068.024]
  3. Let Facebook remarketing follow visitors who viewed those product pages. [L1068.024]
  4. Keep these brands for brand recognition, a larger catalog and organic sales, and do not buy cold traffic for them. [L1068.024]
- Only pursue products that can reach a gross profit margin of at least 3x the purchase price, with a minimum profit of $20 per product (Source C). [L0895.002]
- Technology gadgets can be sold at 3x to 6x their cost, and categories with high perceived value such as beauty, health, wellness and tech gadgets make it easier to set a high price (Source C). [L0638.024]
- A product with a sourcing cost around $40 and a selling price around $70 to $80 was judged a mid-range ticket item with a workable $30 gross margin. A price point near $100 was seen as a downside (Source C). [L0530.007]
- A low sourcing cost is not enough on its own. The selling price should sit where perceived value clearly exceeds the price, because an item that looks expensive for its value can kill the sale (Source C). [L0530.008]
- Price the product so that it still earns money after paying to acquire a customer. If the margin does not cover paid acquisition, every sale loses money. [L0790.010]
- Price tier decides how much profit each sale brings. A product priced around $300 with $60 to $70 net profit can work, and higher-ticket items add profit faster but may bring more service work (2021). [L0801.009]
- Higher-priced products in the $300 to $600 range can generate far more profit per sale than cheap products, so a store does not need $1,000 or more products to make Google Shopping work. Every ad dollar should go toward products that return the target ROAS when they sell (2020 and no-year). [L0748.007]
- Products selling well in this model typically retail for $20 to $40 and cost $10 to $20 through CJ dropshipping (Source C). [L0562.016]
- Check a product's real profitability by comparing competitor prices and margins. A product with high margins should be matched to the minimum price, not undercut (2021). [L0962.092]
- When two products have the same shipping cost, choose the more expensive one to protect the margin. Shipping is a fixed cost per item size, so higher prices keep the margin higher (2021). [L0962.088]
- Higher-priced products are where the real money is in this model, even though cheap products feel less risky. The perceived risk of large orders is usually greater than the real risk, and fraud protection tools cover most of it (2020). [L0551.008]
- Higher-priced products are a reasonable starting point when all other research criteria are equal, because expensive items give more revenue per order. [L0941.012]
- Higher-priced products are generally easier to make profitable than cheap ones, unless the product is a luxury good with different buying behavior (2018). [L1085.026]
- A product with about a 20% wholesale-to-MAP margin is not workable for paid ads. True margins only become visible after suppliers are set up and approved (2023). [L0970.026]
- Each niche is not a fixed margin. Margins depend on each supplier and product. After approval, compare each brand's wholesale price with MAP to see the real profit per product (2020). [L1277.015]
- Within a niche with a wide price range, check whether low-priced items can produce a real margin. If they cannot, drop them, because a niche with very cheap items may not pay for the work (2020). [L1277.016]
- Price high-ticket items above about $79 for a high-ticket store. One store sold items between $350 and $700 with about 250 units sold in one month (Source C). [L1440.051]
- Products priced around $25 fall into an impulse-buy range, where many shoppers buy spontaneously. Price points in this range are easier to sell cold to new audiences (Source C). [L1251.003]
- Products in a store should be evaluated by sourcing cost and ability to price. An AliExpress bottle opener costing about $5 with shipping is a very cheap product, which makes it attractive to test (Source C). [L0656.013]

### MAP and Non-MAP Suppliers

- The gap between wholesale and MAP differs per supplier and per product, and no tool reveals it in advance. The actual margin only becomes known during the approval phase, when price sheets arrive (2023). [L0804.021]
- In a niche where one of 20 suppliers had MAP, margins were 7 to 15%. Without MAP, margins can vary widely, so compare prices before committing (2022). [L0963.105]
- A margin seen from only a few supplier conversations is not evidence that every supplier in the niche offers the same terms. Contact more suppliers before judging a niche's margins (2025). [L0966.015]
- For a niche with many brands but unfamiliar products, check that the wholesale price is well below the selling price before committing. Products selling direct at a lower price on the supplier's own site are a red flag (2020). [L0551.075]
- Search the exact product name in Google Shopping as a shopper would. If you are the only seller shown, a higher price plus a discount code can work. If competitors list it cheaper, shrink the discount or remove it (2025). [L0966.016]
- A niche with many suppliers and a high-priced outlier is best handled by including outliers only when they are relevant products you would list. If one is a pricing error, exclude it (2023). [L1283.066]
- A supplier's shipping cost from offshore sources can distort average price. Refine the keyword rather than adding shipping to the average (2023). [L1283.067]

#### Procedure: Evaluating a non-MAP supplier (Source A, 2021, older)

1. Get the supplier's price list. [L0671.158]
2. Search Google Shopping for several of its products. [L0671.158]
3. Check whether anyone already advertises those products and at what markup. [L0671.158]
4. If competitors mark them up only 10% or 15%, do not list them. This is a no-go. [L0671.158]
5. If there is little competition, become the main seller for those products. If competitors sell them at healthy margins, list them too. [L0671.158]

#### Step: Large non-MAP supplier catalogs (no year)

- For a non-MAP supplier with a large price list (example: 100 SKUs), search each product name individually on Google Shopping and record the average competitor price for each one. Plan the time for this, because the research is done product by product. [L1051.015]

### Phone-Sale and Customer-Service Thresholds

- To avoid phone sales, focus on niches where the average product price is under $2,000. [L0050.003]
- If the business cannot handle phone calls, keep niches at product prices of $2,000 or less. Higher-priced niches (for example $2,000 and up) are only worth testing if phone sales are part of the model. [L0459.002]
- Target average order values of about $2,000 to $3,000 only if you are willing to handle phone calls and extra emails. If you want less customer service work, stay in the normal price range (2020 and no-year). [L0359.016]
- A niche with high technical complexity or a price point around $2,000 or more requires extra pre-sale and post-sale customer service. Such a niche is viable if the business can offer that service at first and outsource it later (2024). [L0836.019]
- Average order value in the $500 to $1,000 range is generally the sweet spot. It leaves enough margin per order and needs the least free selling and customer interaction. Higher averages (about $1,200 to $2,000) still work but bring more pre-sale calls and emails (2021). [L0834.011]
- Average prices above the $200 to $800 range can still work, but they bring more pre-sale and post-sale questions. Plan support capacity before choosing high-ticket products (2021). [L1279.016]
- A niche should show an average of at least $200 across organic first-page results. There is no maximum, but very high average order values bring more phone orders (2024). [L0806.002]
- To reach $2,000 profit per sale, the average order value must be between $6,000 and $7,000 (2025). [L0278.002]
- When targeting $2,000 profit per sale, eliminate all products under $6,000 during price research in Module 2 (2025). [L0278.003]
- For upper-middle-class customers, target product prices between $1,500 and $3,000 (2025). [L0278.021]
- Choosing a product only because it meets a minimum price, without checking shipping, can lead to a loss. Free shipping must still leave profit after actual shipping cost is subtracted. [L1180.010]
- A $200 futon earns much less per sale than a $2,000 product, but its buyers often still need support and return handling. Weigh profit per order against the workload each order creates before choosing a price point. [L1517.018]
- When choosing a first niche from several that pass testing, pick the one with the highest average order value, ideally at least $1,000 (2024). [L1115.018]
- Premium appliances priced around $10,000 for some models can have very good margins, but the volume is low. Plan the operation for fewer, more valuable orders. [L1472.060]

### Impulse, Cold Traffic and Buyer Price Points

- Very expensive products are hard to sell to cold traffic, because buyers research longer before purchasing. Keep the product price within a range that impulse buyers accept (Source C). [L0361.018]
- Products around $25 fall into an impulse-buy range, which makes them easier to sell cold to new audiences (Source C). [L1251.003]
- Dropship products for an Instagram viral approach are priced between $9.99 and $49.99 (Source C). [L1367.002]
- For shoes sold online, the best-selling price range is roughly $20 to $40. Above about $40, a shoe stops being an impulse purchase and buyers need more convincing (Source C). [L0661.009]
- Expensive niche products that do a narrow job, with limited capacity, rarely convert on price alone. If buyers need several units to get value, offer a quantity discount or rethink the price; otherwise most will buy just one (Source C). [L1186.012]
- Customers do not care about the retailer's margin. They choose by the outcome or benefit they expect from the product, so margin belongs in the decision of what to stock, not in the customer's decision to buy (2021-22, older). [L1456.018]
- Products with high perceived value, such as beauty, health, wellness and tech gadgets, make it easier to set a high price (Source C). [L0638.024]
- Lightweight products with high perceived value keep shipping cost low relative to price (Source C). [L0780.038]
- Phone cases and other cheap, very common products look easy to sell but compete with huge demand, so they usually earn little per order. [L1147.011]
- If a niche has much cheaper variants, do not advertise the cheap versions when they would pull buyers away from higher-priced items. List low-price items only when the margin is there, and never spend ad money on them because they erode profit (2020). [L1088.006]

### Price Tiers Within a Niche

- When choosing between price points in the same niche, higher-priced products are generally easier to make profitable, unless the product is a luxury good with different buying behavior (2018). [L1085.026]
- Keep a niche's products in the price range where the brand and product mix is strongest rather than mixing segments (2020). [L0967.006]
- Product tiers within a niche: choose the tier that fits your service capacity, as stated in the two-tier rule. [L0469.019]
- Within a niche, carve out a price tier above the cheap versions, for example studio lighting sets at $400 or more instead of $100 sets (2021). [L0801.010]
- Price variation inside a niche is normal and should be handled by choosing the tier with the strongest mix (2020). [L0967.006]
- Adding products above a range can still work if supplier quality and pricing are right (2018). [L1109.012]
- Products sold per square foot or per piece: to estimate the typical bundle size, look at competitor sites for bundle or multi-pack listings and use those sizes. No reliable estimation method was given beyond this. [L0359.020]
- Products priced well above the calculated range can still be sold, and higher-priced suppliers raise margin (Source A). [L1150.006]
- Products whose quality tier can absorb shipping are better than the same products at a lower tier. [L1180.015]

### Volume and Realism

- For a high-ticket niche product that sells around $1,000, a realistic monthly volume for a new store is about 10 to 50 units, with 20 as a plausible middle figure. A plan built on 1,000 units of such a product is unrealistic. [L1147.024]
- A smaller audience paying high prices can produce the same profit with far fewer orders and far less traffic than a large audience buying cheap products. Large, heavy or expensive products look harder to sell but can be profitable (no year). [L1147.012]
- Higher-priced products earn more revenue per order, so fewer orders are needed to reach the same profit (no year). [L0941.012]
- Plan the operation for fewer, more valuable orders when selling premium products (no year). [L1472.060]

### Decision Sequence for an Operator

Work through the tests in this order. Stop at the first failure.

1. **Price test.** Average of new, fixed-price products on the unfiltered first page of Google Shopping is at least $200, and at least half of results are at $200 or more. Average around $700 to $800 is the working target under Source B's framework (older). [L0667.070, L0451.009, L0451.013, L1281.021, L0458.017, L0994.003, L1329.013]
2. **Shipping test.** Check size and weight, then the COGS and shipping arithmetic. Standard parcels should sell at about $200 or more; large or heavy items should ideally sell above $1,000 and at $3,000 or more under the older working threshold. [L0015.001, L1179.010, L1179.011, L0994.006]
3. **Margin test.** Net margin target of about 30%, or 25% in some niches. Gross margin at least 3x purchase price with a minimum of $20 per product (Source C). [L0016.002, L0895.002]
4. **Supplier test.** Confirm wholesale-to-MAP spread after approval, or use the non-MAP procedure. Reject a 10 to 15% markup. [L0804.021, L0671.158]
5. **Service test.** Stay under $2,000 for phone-free operation, or plan service capacity for higher averages. [L0050.003, L0836.019]
6. **Buyer test.** Keep impulse-range prices for cold traffic, and be cautious above about $40 for shoes or about $79 for high-ticket items. [L0661.009, L1440.051]
7. **Volume test.** Plan around about 20 units per month for a new store at about $1,000 per product. [L1147.024]
8. **Ranking.** When several niches pass, choose the one with the highest average order value, ideally at least $1,000. [L1115.018]

#### Further details

- When screening niches before exact cost and shipping data exist, rough intuition about price points is an acceptable first filter. Those estimates should later be replaced with measured COGS and shipping figures. [L1179.012]

## Customer Demographics and Brand Loyalty

### Target segment and why it matters

- In Source A X, target the upper middle class exclusively. A demographic is a particular sector of the population, so the niche must appeal to a specific segment, not everyone. [L0018.001, L1517.016]
- Decide which income segment a niche serves before researching it. [L1517.016]
- A target market should be a small segment of a country's population. Even in the US, with about 330 million people, pick a specific subsection to sell to. [L1518.001]
- Demographics fall into three broad income classes: lower income, upper middle class and wealthy. These classes apply across most product types and online businesses, anywhere in the world. [L1518.003]
- Target only the upper middle class, not lower-income households and not wealthy buyers. [L1517.002]
- Niche ideas must appeal to upper middle class or affluent buyers and have low brand loyalty to be suitable for dropshipping research. [L0024.003]
- The best niche sits in a sweet spot where product price and target demographic match, typically the upper middle class at a mid-range price. [L1518.013, L1517.007]
- Niche quality depends on many combined criteria, not on any single factor. [L1518.013]
- Demographic rules have exceptions: some people outside their usual income bracket will still buy at any price point. [L1518.014]
- Some niches are highly saturated, so a sample product type should be treated as an illustration of the method, not a recommendation to enter that market. [L1518.014]
- Demographics are the first thing to get right: the right offer shown to the wrong group will fail. [L0523.039]

### Why the upper middle class is the sweet spot

- Upper middle class buyers have strong disposable income and need less pre-selling than other demographics, with fewer calls and emails before purchase. [L0018.002, L1518.006]
- They complain less, return less and need less customer service, so operations stay low-maintenance for a lifestyle business with limited time. [L0018.003, L1517.003, L1518.006]
- They are very comfortable buying high-ticket products online without hand-holding or consultation. [L0018.004, L1517.007]
- They already shop online regularly, have realistic expectations and buy without messaging the seller first. [L1517.007]
- Their purchases are routine rather than a major decision, which keeps interaction with the seller low. [L1518.006]
- Households in this group are accustomed to online shopping, have discretionary spending capacity and make substantial online purchases without significant price resistance. [L0019.002]
- Wealthy buyers also have disposable income, but the lower interaction costs of upper middle class buyers outweigh this advantage. [L1518.005]
- The upper middle class label describes the level of service a customer needs, not a price range. It does not apply to business buyers, who are used to spending money. (2018, older) [L1109.018]

### Why lower-income and wealthy buyers fail

**Lower income**

- Lower-income buyers spend a large share of their resources on purchases, which creates very high expectations despite low prices. [L0018.005]
- This leads to higher returns and customer support costs, with minimal profit margins and financial reward. [L0018.005]
- Expensive products sold to them lead to heavy pre-selling, frequent complaints, more service work and more returns, because a large purchase takes a big share of their savings. [L1518.007]
- If lower-income buyers are targeted at all, the product should be less expensive to limit these costs. [L1518.007]
- A product around $200 appeals to college students or budget-limited families and usually has lower quality. Buyers who spend most of their money or use credit on it have high expectations, more back-and-forth contact and a much higher return rate. [L1517.005]
- Avoid the lowest-priced tier of any niche, such as budget sleeper sofas rather than quality leather couches, where lower-income customers concentrate. This tier produces significantly more inquiries, complaints and returns that demand constant management. [L0019.004]

**Wealthy**

- Wealthy buyers expect high-priced custom or luxury products to be perfect and require significant pre-selling: emails, calls and hand-holding. [L0018.006]
- Returns are frequent if the product is not perfect, which makes this segment unsuitable for low-maintenance lifestyle businesses. [L0018.006]
- Very expensive products sold to wealthy buyers tend to have high return rates. These buyers ask many questions before purchase, expect a tailored experience and are used to getting exactly what they want. [L1518.008]
- Very expensive custom products attract wealthy buyers with high expectations who want calls and emails before buying. If the item does not match what they pictured, they return it. The model is then harder to run as a lifestyle business, even if it can make money. [L1517.006]
- Do not build the business around luxury products or the extremely high-priced sub-categories within niches, such as crystal chandeliers versus standard chandeliers. These require extensive pre-selling and individual nurturing, which does not fit a minimal-touch model. [L0019.003]

**Comparison**

| Segment | Typical price (source values) | Pre-sale work | Complaints and returns | Fit | Units |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Lower income | About $200 futon | High expectations, service issues | High returns, minimal margin | Poor; if targeted at all, use cheaper products | L0018.005, L0018.007, L1517.004, L1517.005, L1518.007, L1518.010 |
| Upper middle class | About $1,500 average sofa, or about $2,000 fabric sofa | Little | Few | Best fit | L0018.007, L1517.004, L1518.010 |
| Wealthy | About $7,500 custom designer sofa, or about $10,000 Italian leather | Heavy: emails, calls, hand-holding | Frequent if not perfect | Unsuitable for a low-maintenance model | L0018.006, L0018.007, L1517.004, L1517.006, L1518.008, L1518.010 |

### Income thresholds (sources differ)

| Figure | Use | When it applies | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Household income of $100,000 or higher | Target threshold for customers | General target definition | L0019.002 |
| Combined household income above $100,000 per year, one or two people, any combination (such as a married couple or two partners) | Definition of upper middle class | General definition | L1518.004 |
| Households earning $100,000 to $400,000 | Band for the demographics test | When running the demographic test | L0457.001 |
| About $150,000 combined per year (US) | Benchmark for purchasing power (2021 and 2022, older) | US benchmark; expect it to rise over time because of inflation | L1090.007, L1092.034 |
| $150,000 converted into local currency | Benchmark for other countries, such as Australia (2022, older) | When judging purchasing power outside the US | L1092.034 |

- Use $100,000 as the general definition and the $100,000 to $400,000 band for the test. Use the roughly $150,000 US benchmark only as a purchasing-power reference that rises with inflation. [L0019.002, L1518.004, L0457.001, L1090.007, L1092.034]

### Price points and demographic fit

- Sofa examples: a roughly $200 cheap metal futon is typically bought by lower-income buyers. A roughly $1,500 average sofa fits the upper middle class, and a roughly $7,500 custom designer sofa is typically bought by wealthy buyers. [L1518.010]
- Alternative sofa values: a $200 futon, a $2,000 three-seater fabric sofa (realistic price, proportional expectations, fewer issues, strong profitability) and a $10,000 custom Italian leather sofa (high profit, intensive pre-selling, high return rate). [L0018.007, L1517.004]
- The $1,500 product or the $2,000 fabric sofa is the best fit for an upper middle class target, depending on which example set you use. [L1518.010, L1517.004]
- A high-priced product with a high margin, such as a $7,500 item at a 30% margin, is not automatically the best choice. Price must match the target demographic, because a product that appeals to the wrong buyers creates more service and return costs. [L1518.011]
- Do not choose a niche because a very expensive version looks attractive. A high-priced niche aimed at wealthy buyers can produce sales, but it brings heavy pre-selling and high return rates. [L1517.010]
- Chandeliers with an average search-term price of about $400 pass the test. For households earning $100,000 to $400,000, that amount is not a big decision. [L0457.005]
- For real crystal chandeliers, the first organic row averaged about $1,000, while later rows showed prices from about $4,000 up to over $450,000. Many of the most expensive listings were presumed to be real crystal pieces. [L0457.007]
- When organic listings show a very wide price spread for one search term, do not treat the whole range as one price point. Wide spreads often come from premium versions of the same product, so judge the typical buyer by the more mainstream listings. [L0457.017]
