- A saturated offer aimed at an audience already heavily targeted by large players leaves little room for a new store. [L1382.013]
- If almost all brands on the supplier list average 20 or more stores on Google Shopping, the niche has too much competition for this method. [L1483.009]

### When Saturation Is Not a Blocker

- Competition is not a reason to drop a product if an ad for it was launched within the last 7 days and is getting good engagement, because the product is working for someone else. [L1382.009]
- A crowded product is not a reason to skip it when most competitors post inconsistently on organic TikTok and can be outperformed with steady posting and better videos. [L1384.061]
- A store can capture only a small fraction of a large high-ticket market and still be very profitable, so a crowded niche is not an automatic rejection. [L1483.002]
- A niche with many stores can still be workable if its individual products have little competition. [L1483.001]
- Existing competition is a sign of demand, so a market with established sellers is not automatically empty or unworkable. [L1441.033]
- An average of about 10 stores or fewer per brand is a green light to keep the brand in the niche. [L1483.009]

### Measures at a Glance

| Measure | Where it is taken | What it tells you | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Number of competitors running ads for the product | Meta Ad Library | Saturation; re-check right before testing a shared-list product | L1316.025, L1316.049 |
| Distinct stores per product, first page of free listings | Google Shopping | Product-level competition; 10 or fewer is a green light, 20 or more on almost all brands is too crowded | L1483.003, L1483.009 |
| Same top creative run by thousands of advertisers | Ad libraries | Avoid the product | L1479.007 |
| Sold in mainstream retail or easy to find on many online sellers | Observation | Usually saturated for dropshipping | L1444.066 |
| Ad launched within 7 days with good engagement, product not seen for about six months | Ad libraries | A positive signal; competition is not a reason to drop | L1382.009, L1436.013 |

#### Further details

- Analyze competition by counting reviews on competing products, not by counting total sellers. Products with 1,000+ reviews are practically untouchable due to accumulated momentum and ranking advantage. Target products with fewer than 300 reviews where you can realistically compete. [L0228.009]

## Fixing Failed Niches: Niching Up, Sideways and Down

### Failed Tests: First Decision

- A niche that fails the Demand Test can be either niched up (narrowed to a more specific subset) or removed from the candidate list. Note that this unit uses "niche up" to mean narrowing, while most other units in this section use it to mean broadening. [L0047.002]
- A niche that misses one criterion can often be adjusted sideways to meet all criteria, which is generally better than starting over from scratch. [L0247.016]
- A niche that almost passes all tests but fails one should be pivoted to a closely related niche, which keeps the good parts of the original idea instead of abandoning the research. [L0972.006]
- A niche that has real potential but fails the research criteria does not have to be dropped. You can pivot it into a different niche that passes the tests, or broaden it one level so the niche list gets more candidates. [L0807.051]
- A niche must pass every niche criterion. If demand is too low, widen it by moving up one category level, or sideways by adding related products that serve the same customer. [L0966.012]
- A niche is successful only if it passes all research criteria: minimum 20 suppliers, minimum 100 products, sufficient search volume, and realistic margins. If these are not met, niche up one level instead of adding unrelated product categories. (Older advice, 2023.) [L0274.001]
- If a rejected niche has few brands, the usual response is to tweak it rather than start over: keep the store and adjust the niche, for example by moving up a level. A rejected niche does not mean the whole store has to be deleted and rebuilt. (Older advice, 2019.) [L0960.020]
- Do not stop a niche after one weak store. Check the supplier pricing tiers and organic traffic first before moving to another niche. [L0805.045]
- In a niche with a busy season and few suppliers, stay with the core niche and keep following up with suppliers instead of expanding into related products. [L0857.039]
- Use the same analytics to compare lateral options as you used for the original niche. [L0920.017]

### Failed Test Procedures

**Narrow-niche recovery (older advice, 2023):**

1. If a narrow niche fails, niche up to the broader product type.
2. If the broader type still fails, niche sideways to a related product group, such as ergonomic desks.
3. Test each new niche against all criteria before committing. [L0855.084]

**Supplier-count recovery (older advice, 2019):**

1. Count the suppliers for the niche, including suppliers with only a handful of matching products.
2. If there are fewer than 20, broaden the niche one level, for example from gaming chairs to a complete game room setup with desks and chairs.
3. Repeat until you can find at least 20 suppliers. [L0960.018]

**Generic-to-specific retest (older advice, 2021):**

1. Research the niche against the criteria.
2. If it fails, broaden it one level, for example brown leather chairs, then leather chairs.
3. Repeat until the niche has at least 20 brands and 100 products. [L1279.002]

**Niche-up procedure for narrow niches (older advice, 2020):**

1. Research the narrow niche, for example electric fire pits, and count the possible products and brands that sell it.
2. If products or brands are below the thresholds (100 products, 20 brands), search the next broader category, for example fire pits.
3. Repeat the count for the broader category.
4. If it passes both thresholds, build a store in that category. If not, move up another level, for example fireplaces or patio furniture. [L1277.014]

**Rejected-idea rescue (older advice, 2022):**

1. Review the full list of dismissed niche ideas and look for similar products that could be combined.
2. Check the reason each one failed, such as too few suppliers or low demand.
3. Retest the combined version against the criteria instead of generating new ideas. [L0803.008]

### Niching Up (Broadening)

**Definition and purpose**

- Niching up means broadening to a related, larger category when a narrow product, such as standing desks, fails validation, for example moving to ergonomic office furniture. [L0853.118]
- Niching up means widening the product category to a broader group that includes your original product and related items. The combined search volume of the broader group can exceed the 10,000 minimum even when the single product does not. [L1072.007]
- Ergonomic furniture is a broader niche that includes stand-up desks, ball chairs and other products, so its combined volume can pass 10,000 in a smaller market where stand-up desks alone fail. In the UK, the search term "ergonomic chair" had a volume of 27,000, enough to stand as a niche on its own. [L1072.008]
- Broaden step by step as a normal part of research. Example: if only three brands make brown leather watches, broaden to leather watches. If that gives only six brands, broaden to all watches, which had 25 brands in the example. (Older advice, 2018.) [L0466.050]
- Example chain: brown leather chairs, then leather chairs, then leather furniture, until the 20-supplier minimum is met. (Older advice, 2021.) [L1090.002]

**When to niche up: supplier and product shortfalls**

- If a niche has fewer than 20 suppliers, niche up one level (add a closely related category) rather than restart. Example: fire pits plus fire tables instead of only fire pits. Stay within the same suppliers where possible to avoid re-approval. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0272.007]
- When niching up, choose the closest adjacent category already available from your suppliers. Example: if a supplier has 100 fire pit products and 20 are fire tables, upload those 20 fire tables the next day without re-applying for approval. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0272.062]
- If a niche has fewer than 20 suppliers or fewer than 100 products, move up one level (niche up) to a broader related category that has enough of both. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0671.024, L0671.163]
- If a niche has too few suppliers, for example only 13 found, go one level up to a broader niche with the same customer. Check how many brands and suppliers that broader category offers before deciding. (Older advice, 2025 source.) [L0941.010]
- If a narrow niche has too few suppliers to reach 20, broaden it one category level, for example from stand-up desks to ergonomic furniture. Then combine the suppliers from the product types that fall into the broader category until the total reaches at least 20. [L0935.003]
- Aim for at least 20 suppliers in a niche before building the store. If you only find about eight, broaden the niche by adding related categories until you reach about 20 to 25 suppliers. (Older advice, 2022.) [L1281.019]
- If a niche yields only about 10 viable brands while all other criteria pass, broaden it one level by combining related categories to reach 20 or more brands rather than starting over. The goal is enough suppliers to build a store with several winning products. [L0807.010]
- If a niche has too few brands and products to reach about 20 brands and 100 products, broaden it to a parent category. If it has thousands of brands and products, narrow it to one specific type. (Older advice, 2019.) [L0663.050]
- If a broader niche has few brands, count the brands in the next level up before deciding. If only 10 brands make file cabinets, move one level broader to office shelving and count the brands there. [L0962.083]
- If a treadmill niche yields only 10 brands and 50 treadmills, move one level up to treadmills and elliptical trainers. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0962.083]
- If demand, product count or supplier count is too low in a narrow niche, move one level up in the category, for example from brown leather recliners to leather recliners, then to living room furniture. Check again and stop at the most specific level that still meets all criteria. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0801.004]
- If a narrow niche (for example luxury family tents) fails the niche tests, step up one level to a broader niche (for example luxury tents) and test again. Typical failure points are fewer than 20 dropship-friendly brands or fewer than 100 products. (Older advice, 2023 source.) [L0964.003]
- If a niche has too little search volume or too few suppliers, broaden it one level, for example from a specific product to a wider category, without turning it into a general store that sells everything. (Older advice, 2020.) [L0967.004]
- If a niche has no or few suppliers in the country, niching up one level (for example from bathtubs to bathtubs plus vanities and mirrors) adds product variety, even though narrow niches normally convert better. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0969.023]
- Niching up is a fallback when persistent out-of-stock issues remain after contacting all suppliers. It is not the first response to slow supplier replies. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0969.024]
- If a niche yields few suppliers because suppliers want a longer track record, niche sideways or niche up and widen the product range to find suppliers that will approve. (Older advice, 2020.) [L1088.004]
- If a product type has low average search volume, for example under 10,000 search results, it is harder to grow into a store. Broaden to a niche level that combines it with a similar product type to get more search volume and traffic, and build the store for the bigger niche first. (Older advice, 2019.) [L0960.019]
- If one product keyword does not reach the volume target, combine related product types in the same category until the total does. Example: 1,000 plus 5,000 plus 8,000 monthly searches equals 14,000, which is called niching up a level. (Older advice, 2022.) [L1113.006]

**Limits on niching up**

- Do not niche up if the niche passes the verification criteria and at least 20 brands and 100 products are available. Keep the niche specific so the store speaks directly to its buyers. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0962.082]
- Niching up should add only closely related products at a higher price point. Avoid adding loosely related categories, because that turns the store into a general store. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0962.084]
- Expand into closely related niches to find more brands to contact when outreach to suppliers yields few brands. (Source year 2025.) [L0857.035]
- Niche up only when the real numbers stop matching the research results. A narrower niche usually converts better, provided the research criteria are still met without the extra products. [L1114.070]

### Niching Sideways

**Definition and purpose**

- Niching sideways means moving into a closely related sub-niche or adjacent product within the same niche when the original version fails the demographics test. It is used to find a price point and buyer group that match the upper middle class. [L0457.004]
- Niching sideways means switching to a different but related product, such as office chairs instead of recliners. [L0853.118]
- If you have exhausted your supplier research and cannot find enough suppliers for your chosen niche, broaden it slightly to find additional suppliers. This strategy, called niching sideways, expands your product category just enough to unlock a larger supplier pool willing to work with dropshipping retailers. (Source year 2025.) [L0255.070]
- Niche sideways when similar products from the original manufacturers sell better than the chosen niche. In the source, the speaker's similar products outsold the original niche, so a new store was built for them. (Source year not stated.) [L0832.026]
- If you cannot find enough suppliers, or if a niche lacks a path to 20 suppliers, work down your brainstorm list, niche sideways into a related category, or niche up one level. Pick the path that gets you to at least 20 suppliers. (Older advice, 2023 source.) [L0804.007]
- If your niche has no good options left, you may need to expand into a lateral niche by looking beyond your current niche into the wider market. (Source year not stated.) [L0920.017]

**Sideways examples**

- If a canoe niche lacks 20 suppliers or 100 products, add related products such as canoe motors, upgraded seats or fishing holders. Stay as close to the core product as possible while reaching the minimum numbers. (Older advice, 2020.) [L0852.019]
- Pivoting from futons to leather sofas keeps the same use case but raises the price point into a range the upper middle class buys. This lets the niche pass the demographics test. [L0457.011]

**Procedure for sub-100-product niches (older advice, 2019)**

1. Niche sideways by including all related product types, such as every type of office chair.
2. If that is still too small, niche up to a broader category, such as office furniture.
3. Judge the choice by the number of suppliers and products you can actually find. [L1110.016]

### Niching Down (Narrowing)

**Why narrow**

- Choose the most specific niche possible as long as it passes all validation criteria. If a specific niche fails, broaden it one level at a time, for example from a narrow product type to a broader category. (Source year 2024.) [L0471.054]
- Choose a niche as narrow as possible, provided it still meets the minimum supplier count and product count. (Older advice, 2020.) [L0468.021]
- Niche down as far as possible while the niche still passes all validation tests. If a narrower niche fails, niche up or niche sideways instead. The depth you can go is decided by the research results (number of suppliers and products). (Source year 2024.) [L0806.004]
- Be as specific as possible within a niche, but only as far as the niche still meets all niche criteria. [L0966.014]
- If all niche criteria hold, narrowing down to a more specific sub-niche usually increases conversion rate. The sub-niche keeps the search demand high enough to remain viable. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0963.096]
- A narrower niche usually converts better, provided the research criteria are still met without the extra products. [L1114.070]
- Narrow a niche as far as possible, but only while the sub-niche still passes every test: at least 20 suppliers, at least 100 products, evergreen demand and real search demand. Go to the narrowest level that still passes, such as closet organization instead of organization as a whole. (Older advice, 2021.) [L1090.001]
- Start niche research with the most specific product type you can name, such as ergonomic office chairs rather than a single color or model, and test it against your criteria. If it fails, broaden it one level, for example from ergonomic office chairs to ergonomic office furniture. (Source year 2025.) [L0807.008]
- Choose a niche at the product-type level, such as standing desks, not a narrow variant such as bamboo standing desks. (Older advice, 2023.) [L0855.083]
- A niche with a huge number of models or types can still work, but limit the store to one narrower product line, such as dirt bike suspension rather than all motorcycle suspension. (Older advice, 2023.) [L0855.093]
- A deeper niche has a better chance. Broad categories dominated by a few big brands are bad by default, but a narrower subcategory can still be an opportunity, such as wine refrigerators or kegerators compared with general refrigerators. [L0766.017]
- A broad category such as Fitness, Outdoors, Office or Kitchen contains many sub-products. Narrowing to one sub-niche, for example Squat Racks within Fitness or Pizza Ovens within Outdoors, makes the audience and ad targeting more specific. (Older advice, 2019 source.) [L0546.011]
- A multi-brand auto parts catalog works better as a sub-niche than as a general car parts store. For example, a store for Jeep Wrangler owners can sell wheels, tires, shock mounts, cages and lights for that vehicle. (Older advice, 2020.) [L0852.018]
- Furniture is too broad to be a niche. Break it down into specific furniture types and specific audiences who want them, then test each sub-niche against the validation criteria covering product count, supplier count and competition level. (Source year 2024.) [L1285.011]
- Do not sell furniture as a generic furniture store. Within furniture there are thousands of sub-niches that should be researched individually. (Older advice, 2022.) [L1281.023]
- A broad category can be narrowed into a higher-ticket subtype to target a higher price point, for example generic rugs to Persian rugs or generic sofas to leather sectionals. [L1179.013]
- If a broad niche such as dogs is too generic, brainstorm more specific and more expensive products within it, then run each one through the competition criteria. Only a specific product idea that passes the test should become the starting niche. (Older advice, 2023 source.) [L0804.012]
- A niche can be specialized by product type and still work. Among typical niche choices, the price tier is the way to narrow your space, while the brand selection is the way to avoid saturated brands. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0801.016]

**Beginner caution**

- Beginners should avoid common niches like pets and beauty, which are flooded with new drop shippers. A sub-niche of a large category with little online discussion is more likely to be underrated. (Source: Source C, year not stated.) [L0561.020]

**Narrowing mistakes**

- Choosing a niche so narrow that little search volume or brand opportunity exists is a mistake. Broaden the niche one level instead of forcing a narrow one. (Older advice, 2019.) [L1275.006]
- A niche built around a very narrow buyer group, such as one trade with one product type, often falls below the demand benchmark of about 10,000 average monthly searches for its core product term. If a narrow niche fails this test, widen it to a broader product category rather than forcing the narrow version through. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0803.094]

### Thresholds and Stop Points

| Check | Threshold stated in sources | Units |
|---|---|---|
| Suppliers | At least 20 (most units); aim for 20 to 25 | [L0272.007, L0274.001, L0960.018, L0935.003, L1281.019] |
| Brands | At least 20 brands | [L0663.050, L0962.082, L1279.002] |
| Brands as a trigger for combining | About 10 brands, then combine and retest | [L0803.006, L0807.010] |
| Products | At least 100 products | [L0274.001, L0962.082, L1090.001, L1277.014] |
| Products as a trigger for sideways moves | Fewer than 100 core products | [L1110.016] |
| Monthly search volume | About 10,000 average monthly searches | [L0803.094, L1072.007, L1072.009, L1085.020] |
| Search volume (lower-volume trigger) | Under 10,000 search results | [L0960.019] |

- Some units use "suppliers" and some use "brands" for the same supplier-count threshold. The sources treat them as interchangeable. [L0663.050, L0960.018, L0962.082]
- Demand threshold conflict: one example shows 8,000 monthly searches failing the demand target [L0803.007], while another shows a related line with about 8,000 monthly searches and 15 brands passing when combined with other criteria [L0804.114]. Demand alone does not decide; the combined niche must pass all criteria.
- Search volume may be measured as "search results" in one unit [L0960.019] and as "monthly searches" in others [L0803.094, L1072.007]. Use the same metric for all candidates when you compare them.

### Combining Sub-Niches

**When combining is allowed**

- Combine related sub-niches only if suppliers sell them together and customers would purchase them in sets, for example chairs, loveseats, sofas and ottomans in matching colors. Do not combine niches purely for SEO reasons. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0249.005]
- Combine niches into one store only when testing shows a niche has too few suppliers, too little demand or too much competition. Small niches that fail the research criteria are better candidates for combining than strong, large niches. [L0623.020]
- Combining two related product types is a fallback, not the default. Combine only when no single product or broader niche reaches 10,000 search volume in the target country, and combine only similar niches so that the combined volume reaches the minimum. (Source year not stated.) [L1072.009]
- If a niche only has about 10 brands, combine it with a closely related product type and count the suppliers and demand together. Combine them only if the combined niche passes the same criteria. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0803.006]
- Combine only categories that a customer would compare or buy together, such as stand-up paddle boards and surfboards. Do not combine unrelated categories, because the store then stops reading as one niche store. (Source year 2025.) [L0807.009]
- Combined demand and supplier count can turn a rejected niche into a viable one. Example: a product with 8,000 average monthly searches fell below the demand target, but combining it with a related product reached 10,000. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0803.007]
- Combining two related product lines into one store is valid when the combined niche meets all the criteria. Example: a sub-niche with about 5,000 average monthly searches and too few brands can fail the demand test, while a related product line with about 8,000 monthly searches and 15 brands can pass. (Source year 2023.) [L0804.114]
- Mixing related categories, such as several home goods types, can reach the target of 20+ brands and 100+ products where local-only suppliers are too few. (Older advice, 2019.) [L0663.051]

**Combining in smaller markets**

- Two small connected niches may be combined to reach the 10,000 monthly search minimum, which is common in smaller markets like the UK. The combined niche should still be a clear, specialized store theme rather than a general department store. (Older advice, 2018.) [L1085.020]
- For smaller markets or countries where drop shipping is less established, combine a few related sub-niches until the niche reaches at least 20 brands. A general store that sells a little of everything is the wrong model in those markets. (Older advice, 2021.) [L1279.003]

### One Niche per Store and Mixed Stores

- Mixing unrelated products in one store is a last resort, used only when no niche passes the approval criteria. Before accepting mixed products, try to build a loose theme around them, such as a room-style store. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0469.009]
- If sub-niche stores get little traffic while broader home stores get a lot, study the broader stores that sell your sub-niche plus a bit more to find where the traffic goes. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0469.015]
- Competitor stores that sell other categories alongside your niche do not require you to sell those categories too. Decide on the niche using its own research, and stay narrow as long as it passes the criteria. (Older advice, 2018.) [L0466.049]
- Adding categories should never turn the store into a general store that sells everything. [L0967.004, L0962.084]
- Niche expansion techniques are only for owners who have already completed the blueprint's niche and supplier validation and have a working store. They do not replace the blueprint's criteria, so always follow the blueprint first. (Source year not stated.) [L1125.009]

### Small Markets and Country Limits

- For markets with small populations (under 5 million), niche up one level broader than you normally would to reach enough potential customers. This typically lowers conversion rates but increases traffic opportunity. (Older advice, 2020.) [L0245.002]
- Market size for a small country can be too small for the product criteria. Two options are to niche up a level by adding more products to the range, or to sell in a larger market such as the UK. (Source year not stated.) [L0359.019]
- If you cannot find a supplier that sells to you because a niche is too small in your country, the answer is usually to niche up one level, not to abandon the market. Check whether the larger category gives enough volume, products and suppliers. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0801.017]
- If a niche cannot reach 20 dropship-friendly suppliers, especially in a smaller country such as Canada, Australia or the UK, move up one category level and test again. (Older advice, 2021.) [L1090.002]
- Smaller markets can be served by the broader ergonomic furniture level, where combined volume can pass 10,000 when a single product does not. [L1072.008]
- Note the tension: small markets call for broadening [L0245.002], while narrower niches usually convert better when the criteria still pass [L1114.070]. Broaden only as far as the criteria require.

### Price and Demographic Fit

- Do not mark a niche as wealthy or lower-income and drop it right away. First check whether a related sub-niche, such as general chandeliers instead of real crystal chandeliers, fits the upper middle class. (Source year not stated.) [L0457.009]
- Consider pivoting when price points reach the $5,000 to $10,000+ range, or when the product is mostly bought as a first or temporary purchase. Adjust the niche to move it back into upper middle class price territory. [L0457.012]
- A broad niche such as rugs covers an enormous price range, from about $30 to $40 for house rugs up to $500 or more for premium rugs. Broad niches make it hard to tell which demographic they serve, so split them into narrower sub-niches before researching. [L1517.009]
- Narrow niches differ in price: a niche with a $30 to $40 product and a $500 product serve different buyers. Pick the sub-niche that matches the target price tier before you test demand. [L1517.009, L0801.016]

### Fallback When All Ideas Fail

**Shortlist cycle (Source B, 2021-22, older advice)**

1. Take the next five ideas from the shortlist that have not been researched yet.
2. Research each of them in full.
3. Run the niche approval procedure on the five ideas.
4. Repeat the cycle until at least one niche is green. [L0490.031]

**Fallback order when all ideas fail**

- Work down your brainstorm list first. If the niche fails the competition test, niche sideways into a related category, or niche up one level, and pick the path that gets you to at least 20 suppliers. (Older advice, 2023 source.) [L0804.007]
- If a niche fails, pivot from the closest near-miss niche rather than brainstorming new ones. A niche that failed only one test is a good pivot starting point. (Older advice, 2023.) [L0855.085]
- Expand into a lateral niche when the current niche has no good options left. Use the same analytics to compare these options. [L0920.017]
- Keep a near-miss niche alive by pivoting it into a related niche that passes, or broaden it one level so the list gets more candidates. [L0807.051]
- Rescue dismissed ideas by combining similar products and retesting the combined version against the criteria. (Older advice, 2022.) [L0803.008]

#### Further details

- Niche up (broaden to a higher category) when you cannot find 20 dropship-friendly suppliers in your specific niche but can reach that number at a broader level, such as selling kayaks plus stand-up paddle boards plus surfboards as water sports. [L0249.004]

- When your niche has few suppliers, look at adjacent product categories, such as broader lines of similar products, to reach the minimum number of suppliers. [L0671.155]

- When your niche has few suppliers, look at adjacent product categories, such as broader lines of similar products, to reach the minimum number of suppliers. [L0671.286]

- If a niche like car seats only has about 10 suppliers, broaden to a related category such as child care products or products for new parents. Keep this step-up approach until the store reaches 20 suppliers and 100 products. [L0852.016]

- If a niche has too few suppliers in one product category, consider related product categories instead of broadening the whole store far beyond its focus. [L0905.025]

## Final Niche Decision, Verification and Store Scope

### Grading each niche against the criteria

**Source A validation tests (current)**

- A niche is ready to build on only if it passes every check on the Niche Research Worksheet, not just most of them. [L1080.001]
- A niche must pass all six validation criteria at once: pass every test on the Niche Research Worksheet; be dropship-friendly; have at least 20 viable suppliers; have at least one future competitor with a traffic rank under 100,000; have 20 or more suppliers with real contact information; and meet all thresholds for pricing, profit, target demographics, brand loyalty and seasonality. [L0058.001]
- Passing all four checks together is the threshold for treating a niche as likely profitable: drop-ship friendly, at least 20 suppliers, at least one competitor with a traffic rank under 100,000, and more than 20 reachable brands. Passing only some of them is not enough. [L1080.006]
- Judge a niche on measured data (supplier count, competitor traffic rank, reachable brand contacts), not on gut feeling. An expert's approval confirms data you have already gathered; it does not replace it. [L1080.012]
- Pick niches from the data, not from what sounds interesting. A niche that seems appealing may earn far less per sale than a data-backed alternative, as the woven rugs versus Persian rugs comparison shows. [L1081.014]
- Check every candidate niche against all criteria before building a store. A niche that fails the criteria should not be used as a store. [L0359.010]
- A niche qualifies as a winner only if it has enough search demand, has other stores already selling in it (drop-ship friendly), and can supply at least 20 distinct suppliers or brands. Those suppliers together must offer at least 100 products. Competitor stores in the target country should have a traffic rank below 1 million. [L1079.001]
- Traffic rank limits differ between sources. The stricter 100,000 limit appears in the six-criteria test and the four-check threshold; the 1 million limit appears in the winner definition. Apply the 100,000 limit when the test is the verification-stage check, and treat 1 million as the looser screen for qualifying a winner. [L0058.001, L1080.006, L1079.001]
- Approval checks the whole niche, not each individual product. Product-level questions are answered by the niche criteria and supplier approvals. [L1111.006] (older, 2020)
- Before committing, a niche must be checked by a manual procedure:
  1. Find competitor stores selling the niche or a broader category that includes it. [L0664.041] (older, 2020)
  2. Look in the target subcategory of those stores. [L0664.041] (older, 2020)
  3. Confirm at least 100 products and at least 20 brands you could source from. [L0664.041] (older, 2020)
  4. Test search demand with Google Keyword Planner or Ubersuggest and confirm enough search traffic. [L0664.041] (older, 2020)
  5. Disqualify the niche if the subcategory has only a handful of brands and products. [L0664.041] (older, 2020)
- Six-step check from the 2020 material:
  1. Check demand for the niche. [L0358.017] (older, 2020)
  2. Check the level of competition. [L0358.017] (older, 2020)
  3. Check saturation. [L0358.017] (older, 2020)
  4. Check seasonality. [L0358.017] (older, 2020)
  5. Check whether the niche is dropship-friendly. [L0358.017] (older, 2020)
  6. Check whether the dominant sellers are online-only or sell both offline and online. Heavy offline dominance is a reason to avoid a niche even when competition looks manageable. [L0358.017] (older, 2020)
- Five-step validation from the 2021 material:
  1. Search the niche keyword on Google Shopping and count the products on the results pages, aiming for at least 100 products available from suppliers before committing. [L0801.006] (older, 2021)
  2. List the brands behind those products and confirm at least 20 brands exist. [L0801.006] (older, 2021)
  3. Check which brands are sold by many retailers and avoid those. [L0801.006] (older, 2021)
  4. Check demand with keyword research and competitor traffic. [L0801.006] (older, 2021)
  5. Submit the top three candidate niches to the niche verification process and decide. [L0801.006] (older, 2021)
- Compare the number of brands, the number of products and the search demand before choosing. A niche must pass all three checks. Failing one means widening or narrowing the category. [L0801.177] (older, 2021)
- A niche should pass three checks: evergreen demand, a workable price point, and enough search demand. For a US-sized market the demand check used a target of about 10,000 in the demand data. The niche should offer at least 20 possible brands and about 100 products to stay specific. [L0962.146] (older, 2021)
- A niche should be evergreen, have demand, have at least 20 suppliers and 100 products in the target country, and face no excessive competition on the first page of Google Shopping. All criteria must hold before a niche is accepted. [L0963.095] (older, 2022)
- Niches are checked against a Google-based competition test and a drop-ship friendliness test. A niche is only pursued when all criteria pass. [L0969.026] (older, 2022)
- A niche idea should pass checks for seasonality, good price points, drop-ship friendliness, a healthy number of Google searches, and competitor websites that are popular enough. Failing one check can be enough to drop the idea. [L0972.005] (2025)
- Minimum niche viability: at least 20 different suppliers, at least 100 total products across those suppliers (not per supplier), non-seasonal demand, sufficient search volume, low-to-moderate competition, and appeal to upper-middle-class buyers. [L0272.006] (older, 2022)
- Approval requires at least 20 suppliers, at least 100 products from those suppliers, and enough buyers searching for the product every month. If a niche falls short, broaden it into a related set of products rather than abandoning the store concept. [L0469.007] (older, 2021)
- Before building a store around a niche:
  1. Confirm at least 20 suppliers. [L1068.083] (older, 2019)
  2. Confirm at least 100 products across those suppliers. [L1068.083] (older, 2019)
  3. Have the niche reviewed by an experienced person for a go or no-go decision. [L1068.083] (older, 2019)
  4. Build the store only after the niche passes the review. [L1068.083] (older, 2019)

**Source B approval procedure (2021-22, older)**

- Choose the target country first, because the competitor and supplier limits depend on it. Then run the following for each researched idea, in this order:
  1. Check average price: the average across the niche's products must be 800 USD or more. [L0490.001]
  2. Check shipping: the products must be suitable for shipping and not too large. [L0490.001]
  3. Check the enthusiast market: buyers should want the products for hobby or recreation rather than need them. [L0490.001]
  4. Count suppliers: more than 10 is needed for an Australian target, and the US target is 20. [L0490.001]
  5. Count direct competitors: at most 15 for the US and at most 10 for Australia. [L0490.001]
  6. Check recurring revenue: one customer should be able to buy several different products from the niche. [L0490.001]
  7. Check traffic volume: add up the monthly searches across all products in the niche. [L0490.001]
  8. Apply the strikeout rules: competition above the limit or average price below 800 USD means not approved, regardless of the other results. [L0490.001]
  9. Fill in the Approved? column: green if all boxes are ticked, red if there is a strikeout, orange or yellow if borderline. [L0490.001]

| Check | US target | Australian target | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Suppliers | 20 | More than 10 | [L0490.001] |
| Direct competitors | Up to 15 passes | Maximum 10 (13 fails) | [L0490.001, L0490.003, L0490.004] |
| Average price | 800 USD or more | 800 USD or more | [L0490.001] |

- Competition is a strikeout criterion. If the number of direct competitors is above the limit for the target country, the niche is not approved, whatever the other criteria show. This is the most important rule in the approval step. [L0490.002]
- For a US target, a niche with up to 15 direct competitors passes the competition check. [L0490.003]
- For an Australian target, the aim is a maximum of 10 direct competitors. A niche with 13 direct competitors fails there but could pass for the US. [L0490.004]
- Only competition and price are direct strikeouts. Weak recurring revenue, a low supplier count or lower traffic lower the grade toward maybe but do not reject a niche on their own. [L0490.014]
- A niche without recurring revenue can still be profitable, but it cannot grow to the same size. For this reason it is graded maybe instead of approved. [L0490.013]
- Seven-criterion market check, in order (local currency applies; the size rule has an exception):
  1. Average product price of at least 800 in your local currency. [L0994.028] (older, 2021-22)
  2. Products are not too big or heavy, unless they are valued at 3,000 or more. [L0994.028] (older, 2021-22)
  3. The market is an enthusiast market, not everyday household items. [L0994.028] (older, 2021-22)
  4. There is the right amount of competition: some, but not too much. [L0994.028] (older, 2021-22)
  5. Established, local suppliers exist, but the brands are not household names. [L0994.028] (older, 2021-22)
  6. There is enough online search traffic for the market. [L0994.028] (older, 2021-22)
  7. The market has recurring revenue potential. [L0994.028] (older, 2021-22)
  A market idea that meets all seven criteria is viable. [L0994.028] (older, 2021-22)
- Compare all brainstormed ideas against the six questions and choose the one with the most yes answers. An enthusiast market with a yes on every other question beats a market with weaker answers, even if the other market was researched first. [L0771.022] (older, 2021-22)

### Comparing graded niches side by side

- Compare candidate niches side by side in one worksheet, judging each on average price, average profit, customer demographic, brand loyalty, seasonality, demand, dropshipping friendliness and the estimated number of suppliers before choosing one. [L0543.002]
- Complete the research worksheets in this order:
  1. Fill out all remaining columns in the Niche Research Worksheet. [L0043.003]
  2. Complete the Future Competitors worksheet. [L0043.003]
  3. Complete the Master Suppliers worksheet. [L0043.003]
  4. Narrow your initial niche list down to your top candidates. [L0043.003]
  5. Submit your top niche ideas for verification. [L0043.003]
- Select exactly five niches for the top list. Each must meet all of these criteria: meets your pricing and profit requirements; appeals to upper-middle-class demographics; has low brand loyalty; sells year-round (passes the seasonality test showing all four seasons); and demonstrates strong average monthly demand. [L0045.004]
- Filter and rank the worksheet to find the top 5 niches:
  1. Right-click the demand column and choose sort sheet A to Z (smallest to largest). [L1081.015]
  2. Highlight every niche under 10,000 monthly searches and change its text color to red, marking them as losers. [L1081.015]
  3. Sort by the seasonality column A to Z and mark every niche that failed the seasonality test red. [L1081.015]
  4. Right-click the average profit column (column D) and sort Z to A (largest to smallest). [L1081.015]
  5. Cut the red rows and paste them at the bottom of the list, then delete the blank rows left behind. [L1081.015]
  6. Remove further weak niches that failed enough tests, such as off-grid solar kits in the example. [L1081.015]
  7. Keep only the top 5 niches at the top of the sheet. [L1081.015]
  8. Color the top 5 green, using a shade that is easy to read. [L1081.015]
- Winner list procedure:
  1. Open the main research workbook and list every niche that has already been tested in the research phase. [L1079.002]
  2. Check each niche's average price, average profit, demographic, brand loyalty, seasonality, demand and whether it is drop-ship friendly. [L1079.002]
  3. Keep only the niches that meet all of these criteria; these are the winners. [L1079.002]
  4. For each winner, open its Master Supplier list and count the suppliers found so far. [L1079.002]
  5. Enter that count in the column labelled Estimated Suppliers for the niche. [L1079.002]
  6. Compare the winners and choose the one to build the first store in. [L1079.002]
- Demand and results: demand is not the only predictor. A niche with lower demand can still outperform, and the actual outcome only shows after the store is built. [L1079.004]
- Grading scale: a niche can be a base hit (a modest, profitable store), a double, or a grand slam (a store that can reach very high annual sales). Early research can confirm a niche is profitable but not how big it will become, which only shows after months of running it. [L0806.014] (2024)
- Traffic against competition: when one niche has more search traffic but more competition, and another has less traffic and less competition, both can still be approved. Choosing between them is a judgment call, not a rule. [L0490.016]
- Several niches passing every criterion means there is no single best niche. Run the numbers for each one in the tracking sheet before choosing, and gut feeling should not replace the data. [L0941.011]

### Choosing the first niche

**Ranking and tiebreakers**

- Prioritize niches with a higher average selling price and a large number of possible suppliers. These two measures help narrow a long niche list. [L0968.087] (older, 2021)
- For a first store, choose the niche with higher average price points and more available suppliers when several niches pass the criteria. [L0855.086] (2023)
- If a niche has many suppliers and several niches pass the research test, pick any one that passes and keep the rest as a list for future stores. Higher-priced products are a reasonable tiebreaker. [L0665.004] (older, 2022)
- If several niches meet all criteria, choose the one with the most suppliers and a price point that feels right to you. Other qualified niches can be built later. [L0469.011] (older, 2021)
- A niche can contain a wide price range, so you can sell all tiers under one store. Example: a 3D printer niche could include a beginner kit under 300 dollars, a consumer model at 500 to 700 dollars, and a prosumer model at a few thousand dollars. [L1112.065] (older, 2021)
- Top niche rankings and example lists show what makes a niche strong; they are not a pick-one list. Choose a niche that meets the same criteria, not simply one of the listed names. [L1090.008] (older, 2021)
- Published lists of profitable niches are useful for widening the range of ideas, but a niche should be chosen only after it passes your own demand and supplier tests. A niche should not be picked simply because it appears on a list. [L1069.087] (older, 2019)

**Decision rules**

- Research niches until one passes every criteria test. One niche that passes everything is enough to move forward. [L0855.082] (2023)
- If several niches meet all criteria, there is no single best niche. [L0941.011]
- Once several niches pass all criteria, they all have a real chance to become strong stores, so no winner is clearly better on paper. [L1079.004]
- Choose based on the collected data and on your own confidence in the niche. Take a day or two to decide, and do not spend a week re-reviewing the same data. [L1079.005]
- If three niches pass all criteria, they are usually good candidates to choose from. Submitting two of them for verification is acceptable. [L0964.163] (2023)
- Brainstorming dozens of niche ideas usually produces several viable winners, so the goal is to validate the most promising few rather than find the single perfect one. Submitting two or three top ideas for validation gives extra confidence. [L1094.022] (2023)
- If a niche passes every validation test, choose it and start building rather than waiting for a perfect niche, because thousands of niches can work with this model. More stores can be built later to grow revenue and profit. [L0967.001] (older, 2020)
- Social media reach is not required when choosing the first niche. It becomes more relevant later when building more niche-specific stores or a brand around a niche with fewer suppliers. [L0967.009] (older, 2020)
- Once a niche passes the viability tests and meets the criteria, it is good enough to start with, so further research should not stall the launch. Some niches can be confirmed in as little as five minutes, so overthinking the choice is a common waste of time. [L1083.002]
- Limit the time spent choosing a niche: shortlist the three niches you feel most confident about, submit them for verification, and let the verification help you pick one. Do not rush the decision, but do not stay stuck on it indefinitely. [L0801.182] (older, 2021)
- A niche that passes all the criteria should not be dropped because of saturation rumors or a recession. Once you have doubts after passing the test, a downward spiral of changing niches tends to cost more than it saves. [L0804.015] (2023)

**Tiebreaker order for approved (green) niches**

- Procedure for choosing between several approved niches (older, 2021-22):
  1. Remove the red niches from the active shortlist and set aside the ideas that were never researched. [L0490.024]
  2. Compare the remaining greens on average price, supplier count, direct competitors and traffic. With approved niches these differences are usually small. [L0490.024]
  3. Use personal interest as the tiebreaker: which niche would you feel most excited to sell day to day through your website. [L0490.024]
  4. Pick exactly one niche and start the next phase with it. [L0490.024]
  5. Keep the full list with its scores for later use. [L0490.024]
- Sources differ on the role of interest. The Source B procedure uses it as the last tiebreaker after the measured comparison. The Source A material says gut feeling should not replace the data (see above). Use the data first and personal interest last. [L0490.024, L0941.011, L1081.014, L1079.005]

### Submitting for external verification

**Whether to submit**

- Before you submit a niche for an outside check, ensure that all worksheet data is complete, all future competitors are listed, and all suppliers are listed with their real contact information. [L0058.003]
- Submitting before the worksheet is fully filled out wastes the reviewer's time and weakens the review. Complete all research data first. [L1080.008]
- If all four checks pass and you are confident in the data, you may proceed without outside review. [L0058.002, L1080.007]
- If a niche passes all validation tests, proceed to store building without additional validation. Based on 20 years of dropshipping experience, completing these tests is sufficient to move forward with confidence. [L0058.002]
- Before committing to a first niche, submit the shortlisted top niche ideas for an outside check. The second opinion helps confirm which niche has the highest chance of success. [L0584.003]
- Submit the niche for verification before building the store. [L0857.037] (2025)
- Verification is optional and can be used as many times as needed. Adding a new product type within an already verified niche does not require a new verification. [L0666.054] (2024)
- Verification is typically done after completing module two, where the niche tests are finished. [L0964.006] (2023)
- Run the demand and competition check before spending money on products or ads. [L0675.009] (2025)
- If you are unsure whether a niche is viable, submit the niche idea through the niche verification system before contacting suppliers. Use it when you have a candidate you want confirmed, not as a substitute for the research steps. [L1088.091] (older, 2020)
- Before building a store, the niche must pass a review by an experienced person; the build starts only after the review. [L1068.083] (older, 2019)
- A shortlisted market that you are unsure about can go to an external reviewer before you move on. The reviewer checks whether the idea is viable and flags potential problems, and you receive an explanation of the findings. [L1058.006] (older, 2021-22)
- External market verification is optional. If a researched market clearly meets all selection criteria and you are confident in it, you can proceed without verification. [L1058.008] (older, 2021-22)
- Some high-ticket dropshipping programs offer a niche verification service. You send the proposed niche by email and receive an opinion on whether it is viable, which may confirm the choice or suggest changes. Using it is optional and not required for success. [L1059.008] (older, 2021-22)

**Procedure (full)**

- Niche selection procedure (2025 unit 0058.004 as written):
  1. Review your Niche Research Worksheet. [L0058.004]
  2. Confirm your chosen niche passes all required tests. [L0058.004]
  3. Decide whether to request optional niche verification from the instructor. [L0058.004]
  4. If requesting verification: click **Niche Selection Verification**, fill out the form with data from your research worksheet, and submit your completed research. [L0058.004]
  5. If not requesting verification: proceed knowing your niche is validated by the research process. [L0058.004]
  6. If verification was requested, wait for confirmation via email. [L0058.004]
  7. Mark this lesson as complete. [L0058.004]
  8. Move on to Module 3 to begin building your store. [L0058.004]
- Verification steps before the review step (2024):
  1. Submit niche ideas for verification. [L0276.065] (2024)
  2. Wait for response (check spam folder). [L0276.065] (2024)
  3. Requires minimum 20+ suppliers for approval. [L0276.065] (2024)
  4. Each application must include comprehensive supplier research showing names and contact information. [L0276.065] (2024)
- Verification procedure with a guided form (2024):
  1. Open the members area and find **Get your niche verified** in the sidebar. [L0360.086] (2024)
  2. Click it and submit your niche ideas, ideally the top two or three. [L0360.086] (2024)
  3. Expect feedback within about one day, and treat a green light as the signal to start the store build and supplier contact. [L0360.086] (2024)

**Form, entry point and cost**

- Niche verification is a free online form where you submit your completed niche research to an expert for review. The reviewer replies by email, either confirming the niche or recommending a pivot to a different one. [L1080.011] (undated)
- Niche verification is free. In the members area Blueprint sidebar, open **Get your niche verified** and submit your top one or two niches for feedback. If you are stuck between several, submit the two you are most torn between and let the reviewers pick. [L0941.101]
- Conflict on cost: the niche verification system is described as a paid review service in which the operator submits niche data and a team member checks it independently. It is meant for cases where two or three niches seem equally good and the operator lacks confidence. [L1079.007] The free status is stated in [L0941.101] and [L1080.011]. Confirm the current terms in the members area before submitting.
- Entry point differs by year and course. Use the path that matches your course version:

| Entry point as described | Year | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Members area, sidebar item **Get your niche verified** | 2020 | [L0967.104] |
| Training member area, the same sidebar link, step-by-step form | 2020 | [L0551.006] |
| Members area, **Start lesson** for the blueprint, then sidebar box **Get your niche verified** | 2022 | [L0803.009] |
| Members area, any lesson page, orange box **Get your niche verified** in the right-hand navigation | Undated | [L1083.014] |
| Course sidebar, item **get your niche verified**, after module two | 2023 | [L0964.006] |
| Blueprint sidebar, item **Get your niche verified** | Undated | [L0941.101] |
| Niche Selection Verification button | Undated | [L0058.004] |
| Discord ticket, channel #submit-product-research (Source D product research sheet) | 2026 | [L0491.026] |

- Niche verification form in the member sidebar lets you submit your top two or three niches for a second opinion before you commit to one. Use it to compare candidates rather than deciding alone. [L0807.012] (2025)
- Niche Verification is a listed resource in the December 2020 coaching call for checking a niche before committing to it. The lesson gives no further detail on how it works. [L0426.001] (older, 2020)
- A niche verification tool checks demand and competition for a niche before you commit to it. [L0675.009] (2025)
- Niche Verification is a tool for checking whether a chosen niche is viable before a store is built around it. [L0844.002] (2025)
- Niche Verification is a tool for checking whether a niche is suitable for drop shipping before committing to it. [L1096.002] (2025)
- Niche verification is a check run on a candidate niche before a store is built around it. It is used to confirm that the niche has real demand before committing money to it. [L1008.003] (2025)
- A niche verification tool guides you through checks on a niche idea and gives feedback after each run. The team then manually reviews the result at the end, which helps when you cannot choose between several ideas. [L1002.006] (older, 2019)
- Niche verification is available as a form in the members area, where shortlisted niches can be submitted for feedback from experienced researchers. It is useful when a list of 50 or more options cannot be narrowed down. [L1111.016] (older, 2020)
- A niche selection verification tool is available to members in 2020 and can be used to confirm a niche that has already passed the manual tests. [L0967.002] (older, 2020)
- The niche verification system is a paid review service in which the operator submits niche data and a team member checks it independently (see the cost conflict above). [L1079.007]

**How many to submit**

- Choose two or three niche ideas you feel good about, and go through the niche research material before submitting them. [L0551.006] (older, 2020)
- Submit your top three niche ideas. If the form does not open, email support with the subject line niche verification and list your niches there, ideally three at most. [L0960.021] (older, 2019)
- Start the niche verification with one niche, the one you are most excited about, rather than submitting several. The team responds with feedback whether the niche passes or fails, including how to adjust it or pivot. [L0804.016] (2023)
- Submit the top two or three niches through the niche selection form in the members area sidebar. Submitting too many niches produces more noise, so keep the list short. [L0963.094] (older, 2022)
- Narrow the niche down to the top two or three candidates before submitting them for verification. There is no limit on submissions, but too many make the review harder for everyone. [L1094.021] (2023)
- For new stores, submit two or three niche ideas for review; new stores are best limited to about two submissions, with preliminary research done beforehand. [L0969.016] (older, 2022)
- When you ask for an outside niche validation, send no more than two or three candidate niches at once and narrow the list yourself first. [L1113.084] (older, 2022)
- A niche can be validated by submitting two or three ideas to the niche verification process. The verification team then helps select one that passes the criteria. [L0962.085] (older, 2021)
- Limit submissions to the top two or three. If you are stuck between several, submit the two you are most torn between. [L0941.101]
- Conflict on count: the sources agree on two or three. Some say two is the working maximum for a new store [L0969.016], one may be sent when you have a single candidate [L0804.016], and no limit is stated but short lists are preferred [L1094.021]. Use two or three for a shortlist and one when only one candidate is in doubt.

**What the submission must contain**

- A niche idea can be submitted for external verification before you commit. The reviewer either confirms the niche or suggests a related niche that fits the selection criteria better. [L0970.160] (2023)
- Enter the top three competitors ranked by traffic that are closest to your niche. If there are no direct competitors, use multi-category stores that sell in your niche. [L0854.097] (older, 2022)
- A niche can be chosen when the demand data is strong, even if the competitors are general stores. Being the first focused store in the niche can be an advantage. [L0854.098] (older, 2022)
- Dropship friendliness is checked through the future competitors you list on the submission form. [L0837.061] (2025)
- Submit the niche information, including research on future competitor stores. The team reviews it within typically two business days and gives honest feedback on whether it meets the blueprint criteria. [L0836.020] (2024)
- Each application needs complete supplier research with names and contact information (see the procedure above). [L0276.065] (2024)
- Niche approval is decided by reviewers with long industry experience who have researched thousands of niches, combined with a fixed set of validation tests. It is not decided by a single checklist alone. [L0801.179] (older, 2021)
- Niche approval checks cover the whole niche, not each individual product. [L1111.006] (older, 2020)
- Niche ideas can be submitted for a verification review by a small internal team of two or three people who check them against the criteria. Submitted ideas are not exposed to others, so there is no real risk of a niche idea being stolen. [L0962.147] (older, 2021)

- Conflict on turnaround: the sources give 24 hours, one business day, one day, 24 to 48 hours, and two business days. Plan for up to two business days and check spam first.
- The verdict is direct: a niche submitted for verification comes back as looks good, looks bad, or should be pivoted, with the reason given. Use this feedback when you are stuck between several candidate niches that all look viable. [L1083.015]
- If no reply arrives, check the spam folder first, then send a follow-up to the support inbox. [L0801.178] (older, 2021)
- The reviewer's response is an email. After submitting, wait for confirmation through email. [L0058.004, L1080.011]
- The response either confirms the niche or suggests a pivot to a different niche. [L1080.007]
- Judge the response on the data you submitted. The reviewer's approval confirms the research and does not replace it. [L1080.012]
- Requests for outside verification are answered with honest feedback. The team reviews the submission and reports whether it meets the blueprint criteria. [L0836.020] (2024)
- Each review is an independent check. A reviewer may return a green light, a pivot suggestion or other recommendations. [L0551.006] (older, 2020)
- Verification is optional, and an outside check does not change the research requirements. [L0058.002, L1058.008] (older, 2021-22)
- The Source D course uses a different route for its product research sheet. Submit the completed sheet as a ticket in the community Discord, using the channel named #submit-product-research. Wait for the ticket result, which names the approved product, before starting any store work. [L0491.026] (2026)
- The same course describes the submission as going through the Discord ticket channel for product research. The submission is reviewed and the strongest product is selected before any store building starts. [L0491.013] (2026)
- Use the reviewer to compare candidates, not as a substitute for the research. [L0807.012] (2025)

### Niche-specific store rules

**One niche per store**

- Keep one niche per store. Add a second niche to the same store only when fewer than 20 suppliers or fewer than 100 products can be found for the first one. [L0469.008] (older, 2021)
- Each store should target one niche. A niche can hold many products and SKUs as long as they stay within that niche and meet the niche criteria. [L0967.005] (older, 2020)
- Build separate stores for each niche that passes all criteria, because separate stores convert better, allow more targeted ads and give a better return on ad spend. Combine niches only if neither had enough suppliers on its own or one of them failed the criteria. [L0359.011]
- A niche can stand as its own store when it passes all criteria and at least 100 products from at least 20 brands or suppliers can be found for it. If one niche does not reach that level, combine it with another niche. [L0359.012]
- Build one niche-specific store per niche only if you can find at least 20 brands and 100 products that meet all blueprint criteria. If not, move up one level, for example from motorized wheelchairs to all wheelchairs. [L1086.009] (older, 2019)
- Before moving a niche up a level, check whether a sub-category such as chandeliers already has at least 20 brands and 100 products. If it does, a dedicated sub-niche store can be built. [L1086.010] (older, 2019)
- Build a store around one niche that passes all validation criteria. Put several categories in one store only when they are closely related and naturally bought together. An example is a sofa sold with matching loveseats, ottomans and chairs. [L0853.119] (older, 2021)
- Only put products in the same store if they are logically related, such as a sofa with a matching loveseat and chair that buyers might purchase as a set. Otherwise, build separate stores, each with at least 20 suppliers and 100 products per niche. [L1112.063] (older, 2021)
- Build a store around a whole niche rather than one product, and include all legitimate brands in that niche that are based in the US and sell only through online-only stores. Multiple products in the same niche give more room for winners than a single item. [L0807.011] (2025)
- Only broaden the niche when a niche cannot pass the research criteria. More niche-specific stores generally convert visitors better than general stores that sell many unrelated items. [L0965.017] (2024)
- Keep a store as niche-specific as possible, as long as it still meets the minimum of 20 suppliers and 100 products. General multi-category stores are not recommended. [L0852.017] (older, 2020)
- Niche-specific stores convert better than broad multi-category stores, which is why the niche structure is kept whenever the supply criteria are met. Adding several categories is possible, but it is best kept close to the blueprint. [L1086.011] (older, 2019)
- Niche-specific stores often outperform a mixed-niche store with the same products. Build a second store once the first runs smoothly and the easy wins are captured. [L1112.064] (older, 2021)
- Single-niche stores consistently converted visitors into customers at a higher rate than multi-niche stores, according to the research author's reported decade of store building. The reasoning given is that a single-niche store can offer a more tailored experience for the product being sought. [L0891.008]
- Always build niche-specific first due to higher conversion rates. Multi-niche stores can be used only if a single niche fails to meet module two criteria and needs to be broadened to reach minimum demand or competition thresholds. [L0270.050] (older, 2021)
- A more specialized niche (for example office chairs instead of office furniture) lets you become the category authority and prevents customer distraction. Customers searching for a specific product type are more likely to buy from a specialist store than from a generalist. [L0251.002] (2023)
- A kayak-specific store has more SEO authority and customer trust in that category than a broader water sports store that sells kayaks, paddle boards and surfboards together. The more specific niche ranks better for category keywords and builds deeper expertise perception. Broaden only when supplier count requires it. [L0249.101] (older, 2022)
- A small, narrow product type can compete well when it is built into a standalone store with its own site and experience. Such niches should still pass the demand tests before launch. [L1069.034] (older, 2019)

**Store scope and combining**

- For a second store, avoid seasonal niches and apply all the full research criteria to it, as you would for the first store. [L0803.075] (older, 2022)
- Conflict on the second niche: the first-store rule requires year-round demand [L0045.004], and the second-store rule repeats the avoidance of seasonal niches [L0803.075]. Both apply.
- If the store domain is tied to one niche, related niches can be added to the same store when the current store is established and the new products sell well under the domain. A separate domain (around 12 USD for a new domain purchased through Shopify, per 2022 pricing) with a new logo is an option for brand-new projects. [L0429.008] (older, 2022)
- If several products in different types all meet the criteria, start the first store with one product type and add more stores later. [L0469.010] (older, 2021)
- A store can be pivoted to a different product type within the same niche without renaming it or building a new store. [L0671.030] (older, 2021)
- A store with one niche may use the category that already generates the best sales. Narrow the store to one product category rather than mixing unrelated products such as children's gadgets, men's accessories and dresses. Mixed categories reduce credibility when the brand is built around a person's expertise. [L0838.010]
- Specializing in one category works because visitors expect a personal brand to be an expert in one area. A mismatch between the person's stated expertise and the products sold creates a disconnect that undermines trust. [L0838.011]
- A jewelry brand can sell its bracelets through a fulfillment center instead of dropshipping and still keep a homepage focused on its top seller. Even when the store has a few minor categories, such as a small blanket section, the homepage should show mainly the best-selling product, here bracelets. [L0838.020]
- The first filter to add to a store should be by product type, matching the main niche category in the top navigation dropdown. This is the recommended single starting filter for a new store. [L0890.008]
- Adding decor or lighting to an established dining furniture store is not recommended. Cheaper, unrelated categories lower the average price point and average order value and can reduce the conversion rate. [L0623.017]
- A shopper buying a dining table usually does not buy lighting at the same time, so a lighting category attracts only a small share of customers. This is one reason not to merge closely related but different products into one store. [L0623.018]
- A single niche such as dining furniture can have well over 100 supplier brands, so there is usually enough depth within the main niche. Expanding into related categories is generally less valuable than working through the existing niche's brands. [L0623.019]
- A product in the same niche across several products (for example face, hair, shaving and personal care) keeps the store focused. Staying in one niche makes it easier to build a consistent brand and audience. [L0657.033]
- Subniche counts decide store structure:
  1. A subniche with many suppliers and products (for example around 40 suppliers and about 1,000 products) can get its own store. [L1110.017] (older, 2019)
  2. Subniches with fewer than 20 suppliers and few products should be combined. [L1110.017] (older, 2019)
  3. Where some subniches are strong and others weak, build the strong ones as their own stores, build the best one first, and skip or merge the weak ones. [L1110.017] (older, 2019)
- Choose a store name broad enough for future expansion, such as a name built on a larger theme like surfing or watches, instead of a narrow product name like leather watches. [L0466.051] (older, 2018)

**Brands**

- No sector is excluded by default, including beauty. Any niche that passes all the niche criteria can be used, and no extra restriction applies to a specific category. [L0359.112]
- Working with one to three well-known brands that people already search for brings traffic through brand searches. These brands also help sell the other products in the store and can be used for monthly promotions. [L0429.017] (older, 2022)
- Conflict on brands: the Source A material favours one to three well-known brands for store traffic [L0429.017], while the Source B market screen requires established local suppliers whose brands are not household names [L0994.028]. The first applies to the store build; the second applies to the market screen.
- Single-product stores or funnels are not recommended. Each product page should be treated as a sales funnel inside a full store, because one-product businesses depend entirely on that product. [L0801.018] (older, 2021)

### Catalogue size and product selection

- Upload only the products you want to sell, even if a supplier offers hundreds. A supplier with 100 products may have only 10 you need; uploading all dilutes niche focus. [L0274.002] (2023)
- Do not upload all products from a supplier's list. Upload only the products that fit your niche and are profitable. [L0671.182] (older, 2021)
- Minimum product count per store: at least 100 products; no defined maximum. [L0969.017] (older, 2022)
- Aim for as many sellable products in the niche as the market supports, not for a fixed number. About 300 products can be enough to launch, but more should be added whenever the niche has thousands of products available. [L0962.148] (older, 2021)
- Start a new store with about 10 products, then test them one by one rather than building a large list. Products that are not yet proven can be kept as a collection on the store. [L0661.010] (Source C)
- Conflict on launch size: about 10 products to start and test one by one [L0661.010]; about 300 to launch when the niche supports it [L0962.148]; at least 100 products per store as the minimum [L0969.017]. Use 10 to start and test if proof is still missing, and the larger counts when the niche is verified and the supply supports it.
- Prioritizing products when there are many supplier products:
  1. Go to the top future competitors' sites and open the category or subcategory. [L0666.033] (2024)
  2. Sort products by best sellers. [L0666.033] (2024)
  3. Upload the top 20 best sellers first, from brands you are approved to sell, then add the rest over time. [L0666.033] (2024)
- Adding products to a store increases the chance of finding new winners that may be more profitable than the current winning product. Do not rely on one or two winners; keep expanding the offer and adding products. [L0434.003] (Source C)
- Each new category can be tested as a separate product with its own ads. Any category that performs well can become an additional winner to scale on its own. [L0434.008] (Source C)
- A broader product range increases the chance of finding a new winning product that can outperform the current best seller. Stores should keep adding products instead of relying on one or two winners. [L0435.008] (Source C)
- Where a niche has a wide price range, sell the tiers under one store. [L1112.065] (older, 2021)
- Check whether product models differ in a meaningful way, such as size, power or technology, before building separate pages for them. Models that differ only in color rarely justify their own category page. [L0949.006] (Source B 2021-22, older)
- If suppliers and products are sold as a pair or set, upload them as sold, with the photos showing the pair or set. [L0671.031] (older, 2021)
- In niches where buyers want matching sets, such as furniture, offer complete sets rather than individual pieces, because buyers prefer to purchase the matching items together. [L0663.037] (older, 2019)
- Choose the collection list before creating products. Build the collection list from competitor stores before creating anything in Shopify:
  1. Open two to three future competitor stores. [L0371.010]
  2. Hover over the main categories to see their subcollections. [L0371.010]
  3. Note how they split the category, for example by type, by brand or by feature. [L0371.010]
  4. Open a document in Google Drive, Notes or similar. [L0371.010]
  5. Write each main collection first and indent its subcollections below it. [L0371.010]
  6. Keep the list short at the start and skip brand collections until suppliers are approved. [L0371.010]

### Demo products before supplier contact

- Demo store preparation: 5 to 10 demo products are sufficient before contacting suppliers. More than 50 products is excessive and delays supplier outreach. [L0249.003] (older, 2022)
- Demo products only need to look professional: 4 to 5 products with complete pages, no blank images and no dummy text. Full catalogs are not needed before contacting suppliers. [L1085.037] (older, 2018)
- Conflict on demo count: 5 to 10 products are sufficient [L0249.003], and 4 to 5 per collection is the working limit [L0452.007, L1085.037]. Both stop well short of a full catalogue. Use 4 to 5 when you need the fewest pages, and up to 10 if you want more coverage before supplier contact.
- Demo products are added in the Shopify admin under Products in the left sidebar. The Products page opens the product list; the **Find products** button is not useful for this task and can be ignored. To add one, click **Add product**, which opens the product editor. [L0452.001] (older, 2021-22)
- Find demo products from another store that sells the same product type but carries brands you do not plan to target, so suppliers on your list do not see their own products on your site. A supplier seeing its own products can create awkwardness. [L0452.003] (older, 2021-22)
- Demo product procedure:
  1. Open your initial supplier list from the earlier step. [L0452.004] (older, 2021-22)
  2. Turn on a VPN and set it to a country that is not your target market. [L0452.004] (older, 2021-22)
  3. Run a Google search for the product type you plan to sell. [L0452.004] (older, 2021-22)
  4. Pick a store from the results that carries brands not on your supplier list. [L0452.004] (older, 2021-22)
  5. Choose 4 to 5 products from that store's collection for your demo products. [L0452.004] (older, 2021-22)
- A VPN is used to search from another country so that Google returns e-commerce stores from that market. The video recommends NordVPN and notes that many other VPNs can be found through a Google search for good VPN. [L0452.005] (older, 2021-22)
- Choose the VPN country as a market where the brand is sold but not in your own country. For a store in Australia, set the VPN to the US and look for brands sold only there. For a US store, use Australia, the UK or a European country. This way there is no confusion with local suppliers about the products. [L0452.006] (older, 2021-22)
- Upload only products that fit one of the product-type collections you already created. Choose one collection and upload 4 to 5 demo products for it, not more than that. [L0452.007] (older, 2021-22)
- Before supplier contact, the demo store is a sample of the look and feel, not the catalogue. Use it to show suppliers the store style and the product type. [L1088.091] (older, 2020) [L0249.003]

### After approval

**Starting the build**

- Approval is the signal to start: a green light means you start the store build and supplier contact. [L0360.086] (2024)
- If a niche passes all checks and you have confirmed it, move on to store building. [L1080.007]
- Once you have confirmed the niche or completed the submission, move on to store building. [L1080.007]
- If a niche passes every validation test, proceed to store building without additional validation. [L0058.002]
- Once the niche is verified, the next step is Module 3, where the store is built. [L0058.004]
- After confirmation, the niche becomes the store niche. Store build and supplier contact follow the collection list in the procedure above. [L0360.086, L0371.010]
- Niche verification requests on the Source D course come back with the approved product. Wait for that ticket result, which names the approved product, before starting any store work. [L0491.026] (2026)
- Once a niche is confirmed, a new product type within that niche does not require a new verification. [L0666.054] (2024)

**Using the verdict**

- If the verdict is a pivot, use the suggested related niche. The reviewer either confirms the niche or suggests a related niche that fits the selection criteria better. [L0970.160] (2023)
- Use the verdict and reasons when stuck between several viable candidates. [L1083.015]
- A niche that passes all criteria should not be dropped because of saturation rumors or a recession. [L0804.015] (2023)
- A niche that passes the research can still be a base hit, a double or a grand slam. Early results show profitability; scale becomes clear only after months of running it. [L0806.014] (2024)
- Higher demand does not automatically mean higher results. The actual outcome only shows after the store is built. [L1079.004]

**Brand, reviews and affiliate content**

- Bulk-uploading manufacturer reviews is acceptable if a supplier agrees in writing that you can use their product reviews on your store. You can then bulk-upload reviews from the manufacturer's website in one day without risk of Google account suspension. Always confirm supplier permission first. [L0253.054] (2024)
- Affiliate links belong in the blog or content section of a store, not on product pages. Only link to directly related products that the store does not sell, such as a heating pad alongside a massage chair, or a drum lesson subscription alongside a keyboard. [L0472.060] (2025)
- Affiliate examples for related niches: a gun safe store can promote a firearms safety subscription; a keyboard store can promote online drum lessons. [L0472.061] (2025)
