- Problem-solving products are the preferred type. Wow-factor products are also viable if you add clear lifestyle or experience benefits. Both types should be checked for a real demand signal before testing. [L0335.030]
- Prefer problem-solving products over novelty products that only have a wow effect. Customers need problem-solving products rather than just wanting them, which supports longer-lasting sales. [L0363.007]
- Problem-solving products usually outlast pure wow-factor products because a group of buyers already looks for a solution. The same product can often be pitched through several marketing angles, which can revive an older product. [L0708.003]
- Problem-solving products usually keep selling longer than novelty products, which fade once the wow factor is gone. Novelty items such as a galaxy projector tend to die out faster. [L0693.010]
- Products that are only unique or novel, such as simple toys and gadgets, can produce a short burst of sales. They are hard to scale and keep going long-term because they solve little real need. [L0706.003]
- Consider leaving a product that has a strong wow factor but solves no real problem. Such products often get views without converting. A product with a clear use typically converts better. [L0501.024]
- A product works when the problem is specific and the ad shows the problem and the solution quickly. Choose products that solve a clear pain point for a defined market, and use a strong marketing angle to make a simple product stand out. [L0638.027]
- A winning product should feel new to the viewer, meaning they have not seen it on Amazon, in ads or on YouTube. On Facebook and TikTok the creative must stop the scroll, so the product needs an immediate attention-grabbing hook. [L0708.001]
- On Facebook a product can also work if the audience can easily relate to the problem or concept it represents. Pure wow-factor products are riskier than products that combine attention with a clear use. [L0708.002]
- Products that solve a clear problem and visually stop people while scrolling must make the stop themselves, because the product has to create it. [L0692.004]
- Choose products by the specific problem they solve for a defined customer, not by what the seller personally likes or would buy. A clearly stated problem makes ad copy and the offer easier to write. [L0549.051]
- Find products by identifying a problem people face in their country or season, rather than by chasing trending winning products. A clear problem is easier to communicate in ads, for example a product that keeps people warm in a cold winter. [L0562.019]
- Products that solve a clear problem with very low time delay, effort and sacrifice for the customer are easier to sell, for both the offer and the ads. [L0549.010]
- Products with fast, visible results are easier to sell than products that need long, effortful routines. A spray tan that takes about 10 minutes is an example, compared with hours of sun exposure to get the same look. [L0549.011]
- A product can sell without a wow factor if a strong community or culture surrounds it, such as pet owners or hobby groups. Community strength is a signal worth weighing when choosing a niche. [L0549.009]
- Products with a visible, demonstrable effect are easier to show in a short video. A water bottle that shows its temperature and keeps drinks hot or cold for about 12 hours was praised in TikTok reviews and later sold on Amazon. Confirm the product solves a real everyday need, because a wow factor alone may not sustain sales. [L0706.061]
- Problem-solving products that people need on an ongoing basis are a strong category. A specialised knee brace is an example: it was sold only in the US with credit card and PayPal and reached about EUR 3,000 revenue per day at an early stage. [L0660.009]
- Products with a clear problem solution and a fast, simple buying decision work best. Choose products that buyers can decide on quickly at first sight, since first-time buyers rarely accept a complex or high-priced product. Products that need more explanation or cost more are harder to validate with cold traffic. [L0661.011]
- Products that solve a problem, such as cold-weather leggings in winter, tend to sell well during their season. [L1185.012]
- Problem-solving products sell without a strong wow factor in health, wealth, happiness and relationship niches. During spy-tool research, check which problem a product solves and what wow factor it offers, because the problem size shows how large the market can be and which complementary products fit. [L0871.005]
- Entertainment is also a problem a product can solve, for example through a solid toy. The niche itself matters less than the product, so follow a structured product research process instead of chasing a specific niche. [L0694.010]
- For products that are attractive and have high perceived value, lifestyle pictures and UGC do most of the selling. Investing in these images is worthwhile. [L0693.014]
- Build products and ads around desires people already have, or around rising trends, instead of trying to create demand for an unwanted need. Riding a popular trend is far cheaper than creating a new habit. [L1261.036]
- When researching products, first identify the problem being solved and the benefits or use cases. Upgraded versions of older winning products and products with multiple use cases are strong candidates. [L0788.043]
- Choose products that solve a problem or have a visual element that makes a person stop scrolling, because the product itself has to create the stop. [L0692.004]

**Conflict: wow factor as a preference**

- Source C's full checklist lists a wow factor (new, innovative or upgraded) as a preference, while the same checklist, and most other sources, put problem-solving first. Use the wow factor as a tie-breaker when the problem is already clear, not as the reason to choose a product. [L1174.004, L0335.030, L0363.007]

### Upgraded versions and differentiation

- An upgraded version of an existing solution, such as a new design or an improved model for the same problem, can sell at a much higher price and scale. In health niches, new variations of older solutions repeatedly succeed because buyers keep looking for better results. [L0871.009]
- In a neck-pain niche, an upgraded version of a supplier product that cost about $50 to $60 on AliExpress or Alibaba was sold at about $244 by another seller. A better design for the same problem can support a much higher price than the basic version. [L0871.091]
- If a product has weak reviews but the same function exists in a better variation, source the better variation from the same supplier and sell that instead. The same function with better quality is a stronger product. [L0693.005]
- When a product in a niche is widely available, aim for quality above the average brand. When a common product has clear weaknesses, such as poor heat retention, bad handles or excessive size, each identified weakness is a possible point of differentiation. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1155.014]
- Creating a private-label version of a main product without differentiation makes the store just another seller of the same item, which competes on price alone. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1155.016]
- Customizing a product with your own creatives and messaging is recommended from the start, even though launch takes longer. Copying a product one-to-one launches faster but offers less differentiation. [L1187.010, L1187.011]
- A product that is customizable with your own creatives and messaging gives control over the ads, even if it takes longer to launch. Speed to launch is traded against control and uniqueness. [L1187.010]
- Product research should favour products that can be customised with your own creatives and messaging, even if launch takes about one to two weeks longer before the first product can go live. [L1187.011]

### Demand signals and proof of concept

- Products that already show proof of demand, such as steady sales on another marketplace or a store scaling them, are safer to test than completely unproven items. Taking a proven product into a new market or segment is a common strategy. [L0950.005]
- Prefer products with proof of concept: check whether competitors or other stores are scaling them, and use an ad spy tool to see what is trending before committing. [L0950.006]
- Trend research should look for products that already have an audience and are scaling, and should be combined with checking how saturated the product is before joining the trend. [L0950.009]
- If a product is already scaling on another marketplace or in another store, you can enter that market with an improved version, such as one with better features, provided the market is not overly saturated. [L0950.081]
- Start product research with products that are already selling, because a proven product gives more reliable evidence than an untested idea. The goal is to take a product that already works and improve its offer, store and ads. [L1172.001]
- Look for products that already sell on the platform and in the market where you plan to run ads, because that is the proof of concept. Avoid being the first to test an untapped product, especially as a beginner. You do not need to reinvent the wheel. [L1174.002]
- Pick products that already sell for competitors (market-proven) instead of testing untapped products with a wow factor, because the competitor has already paid for the market test. Untested products are risky because you do not know whether the market responds to them at all. [L1177.001]
- Evaluate a product on three data points together: how fast a competitor is scaling, how new the competitor is in the market, and how many sales the competitor makes right now. A product that passes all three is a strong candidate to test and scale. [L1177.002]
- Recently appearing products usually address a large market, often estimated at 50 to 100 million potential buyers, so a competitor with a few thousand likes has probably reached only a small share of it. [L1177.004]
- A product where a competitor has a fresh page, a scaling ad count and confirmed sales is low risk, because the market has already proven the sales. The seller should still improve the landing page, offer and ads to win against the competitor. [L1177.017]
- Products with no ad proof can still be tested by sourcing them from AliExpress or CJ, asking friends and family whether they would buy, and testing with image ads. This works best for items that need little explanation. [L1316.022]
- An original product idea with no visible sellers is worth examining, but the lack of competitors can also mean weak demand or hard sourcing. Before committing, confirm that buyers actually search for and pay for the product, and that suppliers will sell it to a dropshipper. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L0905.026]
- When a product is brand new with only one or two players in the market, it can sell with minimal marketing and a decent landing page, because novelty gives an advantage. This is luck-dependent and does not replace proper research. [L1158.008]
- New and unique products convert better on landing pages because fewer competitors are selling them and audiences have not yet been saturated with ads. Prioritise products that have been on the market for less than 1 to 2 months. [L0321.031]
- A product that is new to the market is a good candidate for a short test. Use the new-product window when the market is still uncrowded, and treat it as an early signal rather than proof. [L0321.031, L1158.008]
- Both types should be checked for a real demand signal before testing, so a new product still needs the same demand check as an established one. [L0335.030]
- Look for demand in a market already validated for a similar product: a competitor that sells the same product, or a product that succeeds in one country before it is tested in another. [L0388.025, L0950.081]
- Bottom-of-funnel ads work when a product category is universally understood (for example phone case, water bottle, posture belt) regardless of how many competitors exist. A niche with only two sellers can still support profitable bottom-of-funnel ads if the product needs no explanation. (Source D 2026.) [L0316.050]
- Amazon bestsellers and beginners: for beginners, products already proven on Facebook ads are safer than Amazon bestsellers, because a product that sells on search may not sell on a social platform. Once experienced, testing Amazon bestsellers on Facebook can be an advantage. [L0693.009]
- Concerning how many marketing angles a product needs, a product needs at least 5 distinct marketing angles drawn from detailed positive Amazon reviews to be kept, and more angles are better. [L0636.017]
- The first product-level check should be the product's problem, not its popularity: a product that is popular without a clear problem still needs a demand test. [L0280.003, L0335.030]

**Conflict: new products versus proven products**

- Some sources favour new or unique products because few competitors and fresh audiences help conversion. Others favour products that already sell for competitors because the market has paid for the test. Use proven products as the default for beginners and new products as an early test when the market is still uncrowded. [L0321.031, L1158.008, L1172.001, L1174.002, L1177.001]
- Being first to sell a product can be a long-term advantage, but only after you have gained experience and sales. [L1219.044]

### Market size and audience

- Estimate the total addressable market (TAM) for each product by asking how many people actually suffer from the problem it solves. In the lesson, a market of roughly 50 to 100 million potential people was cited as a large enough example. [L0363.008]
- A product must appeal to a large audience. A broad audience, such as several demographic groups plus seasonal gift buyers, makes a product easier to scale than a tiny niche. Broad appeal also creates more data for testing. (Source D 2026.) [L0347.008]
- Products with a niche angle are preferred over broad products such as general jewelry. Broad products depend more on luck, and whether they work can only be judged by their performance. [L1176.007]
- Products that are not sold in many stores but show strong ad counts and a clear niche can be tested, since many niche products are still under-tested. [L1176.008]
- Personal taste is a poor filter for product choice. Judge by market evidence, not by whether you would buy the product yourself. [L0577.032]
- A generic product, such as a plain sports jersey, has weak demand unless buyers have a clear reason to own it, such as supporting a specific team. Before testing, define who would buy the product and why. [L0577.075]
- Before testing a product, check who would use it repeatedly and whether cheap substitutes already solve the same job, such as jars or simple bag clips. A product that replaces a cheap everyday habit faces strong price resistance. [L1186.006]
- Phone accessories such as cases are a broad category because almost every buyer owns a phone, so a simple single-product store in that category can perform well. [L1186.005]
- Bottom-of-funnel and niche claims are not enough on their own; test the audience with a small budget before scaling. [L0316.050, L0678.045]
- Influencer marketing works best with small, affordable, high-margin products that can be given away free to creators. For products that are large or expensive, paid creators or other channels are more practical. (Source A.) [L0790.009]
- Find new products by looking for B2B-adjacent opportunities, such as office lighting for a home chandelier seller or a commercial-grade version of a home kitchen tool. A separate sister store is usually recommended for B2B sales, but combining B2B and B2C products in one store has also worked well. (Source A.) [L1357.017]

### Markup, margin and price rules

- A product must be sellable at a minimum of 3x markup over total cost (product plus shipping). [L1174.004]
- Electronics can sell at 4x to 5x or more because of their higher perceived value, but verify reviews before testing. [L1174.004]
- Real deal breakers are poor quality and insufficient profit margin. [L0361.036]
- The break-even ROAS for a product should be 1.4 to 1.5 or lower. [L0692.003]
- Prefer low COGS (product plus shipping), which improves cash flow and lowers break-even ROAS. [L1174.004]
- Products that are heavy or bulky are rejected, because shipping costs rise sharply and reduce margin. [L0692.007, L1171.006, L1172.010, L1174.004]

**Price guidance: two sources, two contexts**

| Source | Price guidance | When it applies | Ids |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source C | Around $50; avoid $40 or $60 starting points | Product selection criteria for a first product | [L0280.003] |
| Source A | $200 or more expected selling price | Brainstorm worksheet, where ideas are listed before testing (2020 and 2021 advice is older) | [L0474.011, L0474.013] |
| Source C | 3x minimum markup, 4x to 5x for electronics | Margin test after total cost is known | [L1174.004] |

- The Source A price threshold is a filter for brainstorming, not a rule for final product selection. Test each idea for demand before committing. [L0474.014]
- A neoprene wine bottle holder had a retail price of about $10 to $20 and a manufacturing cost of about $1 to $2, giving very high margins. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1152.009]

### Quality, reviews and ratings

- Require at least 4.2 stars on Amazon for a product, since this suggests acceptable quality and few refunds. [L0692.005, L0692.003]
- Avoid products whose Amazon reviews average under 4 stars. Poor reviews usually point to products that break after a short time, which damages customer trust and can increase the risk of bans. [L0693.004]
- The band between 4.0 and 4.2 stars is not defined in these sources. The 4.2 figure is the pre-test requirement, and under 4.0 is the avoid threshold. [L0692.003, L0693.004]
- If the identical product on Amazon has many ratings but a low average rating (for example 3.4 stars across 474 ratings), this suggests weak product quality. Rank such products lower on the list. [L1183.025]
- Avoid products with poor AliExpress ratings or recurring customer complaints. [L1174.004]
- Quality matters more than virality, because a viral video for a weak product brings little interest and few sales. Use going viral as a skill to be learned first, then choose only good products once you can reliably generate views. [L0372.014]
- Quality checks matter most for beauty and health products, because a poor-quality product can harm the buyer and damage a store's reputation. Quality problems should be treated as a red flag before any ad budget is spent. [L1382.011]
- When judging a product, check its size, weight and price first, then think about the customer experience. Choose products where customers are lenient about delays and mistakes, because satisfied buyers return and recommend the store. (Source A.) [L0766.011]
- Images and videos matter most in visual niches such as fashion and jewelry, but they matter in all niches. Beginners with small budgets can repurpose existing competitor or YouTube videos instead of paying for new shoots. AI tools such as Canva can also create product images. [L1174.005]
- Make sure high-quality images and 1 to 2 existing videos (Facebook video ads or YouTube videos) are available for repurposing. [L1174.004]
- Check Facebook ad comments for positive sentiment, realistic names from Western countries and no repeated or copy-paste comments, and click profiles to see their location. [L1174.004]
- Check Google Trends for the main keyword or niche to confirm it is trending or stable. [L1174.004]
- A simple product can sell thousands of orders without looking special. A sheet of paper with 100 ideas for a first date sold thousands of orders in a single season, which shows that a product does not need to look special and must be tested to know if it wins. [L0780.008]

**Case: a niche store reaches its first profit (Source C)**

- A dropshipper with about six months of experience had started with a done-for-you agency. He had about five years of marketing experience, mostly B2B work with Google, Facebook and LinkedIn ads, and had tested over 20 products without a clear selection method. [L0549.004]
- He pulled a list of 50 product candidates from TikTok, Facebook ads and spy tools, and filtered it with product criteria, which narrowed it to 2 products. He launched one of them, which became his most successful store so far. [L0549.004]
- He first tested Canada, then launched in Australia and New Zealand, where he got his lowest cost per lead and his first profitable sales. Before that he had been breaking even with one to two sales per day, and one Friday he got five sales. [L0549.004]

### Product types to avoid

**Avoid by material, size or shipping**

- Avoid glass products because of the high risk of breakage and returns. [L0692.006, L0692.003]
- Avoid heavy products, because shipping costs rise sharply and reduce the margin. [L0692.007]
- Avoid bulky products, because shipping costs eat the margin. Prefer small, light products that solve a clear problem. [L1171.006]
- Avoid very large or bulky products when selecting candidates, because the supplier can charge high shipping costs that reduce margin. Products of this size were excluded from the list. [L1172.010]
- Avoid liquids. [L1173.005]

**Avoid by category or sales channel**

- Avoid electronics, because they break quickly and generate complaints and returns. Home decor is a better choice when it is light enough to ship cheaply. [L1171.007]
- Electronics are an exception to the markup rule only if reviews confirm the product works. [L1174.004]
- Avoid products that can easily be bought at local stores. [L1173.005, L1174.004, L0280.003]
- Avoid products that look like established brands, since they are hard to differentiate. [L1173.005]
- Avoid products with visible Chinese writing or third-party brand logos, such as a Samsung logo, in the ad video or product. Do not test such products even if their ad counts look strong. [L1161.009]
- Avoid products linked to the Kardashians, or products from GoPure, MaryRuth, URO, Lemme, or any book from Global Brothers. [L1164.001]
- Avoid product categories such as shilajit, ashwagandha, perfumes, anything featured on Shark Tank, clothing and baby items when choosing products to test. [L1164.002]
- Avoid products tied to health risks, such as supplements or chemicals that touch the skin, unless certificates and proof exist. [L1174.004]
- Avoid products linked to a single event. Prefer products that can be sold for one to three years or more, can be branded and can reach new audiences. Products tied only to one event, such as Valentine's Day, Father's Day or Mother's Day, have a short sales window and cannot be scaled much after the event. [L0335.029]
- Pump-and-dump products are driven by a trend, season, aesthetic or impulse buying, are easy to copy and are not meant to become long-term brands. They usually have no brand moat, and many sellers can enter quickly. [L0347.003]
- Pump-and-dump products that win are usually simple, common and already sold, so the edge comes from marketing rather than invention. Beginners should not expect the product itself to be unique. [L0347.004]
- Pump-and-dump products fit the emotional vibe of a season through colour, sound and visual style. Warm, soft, cozy and neutral tones suit fall. Products that look like they belong to the season sell by feeling, not by specification. [L0347.007]

**Avoid by harm, use or sizing**

- Products sold for use on the skin, such as foundation, are not recommended for a dropshipping store. [L1161.012]
- Be careful with items applied to the face or ingested, such as cosmetics, because the buyer's trust and the product's safety are at stake. Only sell products you would use or consume yourself. [L1171.008]
- Reject products where wrong use can harm the buyer, such as non-prescription eyewear sold as corrective glasses. Harm leads to complaints, refunds and legal risk that outweigh the sales potential. [L1173.043]
- Customizable products are not recommended for beginners. [L1161.008]
- Swimwear is not recommended because of sizing issues and ad restrictions. [L1184.023]
- Avoid apparel that often causes sizing problems. [L1173.005]
- For fashion products, prefer items sold in one size where possible, because they avoid most sizing problems and the returns that come with them. [L1161.050]
- Pants and shoes caused fewer sizing problems than jackets and shirts. Products without sizing avoid sizing returns entirely. [L1128.017]
- A generic product, such as a plain sports jersey, has weak demand unless buyers have a clear reason to own it. [L0577.075]
- Products that are only unique or novel, such as simple toys and gadgets, are hard to scale and keep going long-term. [L0706.003]
- Avoid products whose Amazon reviews average under 4 stars. [L0693.004]
- Avoid products with recurring complaints about breakage or battery issues. [L1174.004]

**Avoid by buyer decision**

- Choose products that buyers can decide on quickly at first sight. First-time buyers rarely accept a complex or high-priced product, and such products are harder to validate with cold traffic. [L0661.011]

**Conflict: fashion as a niche**

- For a brand, fashion and jewelry are the easiest niches to build around, since almost any product can be branded. Start from knowing the target audience and build the brand around the product. [L0492.012]
- Fashion products were common among the trending items, and fashion was described as a good niche at the beginning of the year. Customizable fashion products are still not recommended for beginners. [L1161.008]
- One operator reported that roughly 80% of his sales came from women's fashion, so this category can be prioritised when shortlisting products. Treat this as a single-source signal and confirm it with your own test results before scaling. [L1173.045]
- Apparel is avoided where sizing causes returns, but one-size fashion items avoid most of that risk. [L1173.005, L1161.050]

### Product types to favour

- Jewelry and bags, such as shoulder or crossbody bags, are suggested for beginners, since they carry less sizing risk and can have strong margins when the perceived value is high. Jewelry sells well on Facebook. [L0693.012]
- Choose products based on data, quality and demand instead of limiting the options by category. A focused niche can be developed later, while a second store can use other niches. [L0693.013]
- Small, light products with a visible problem-solving use, a strong visual design, a fair price, and simple variants such as colour or plug type fit the favoured profile. Use these traits as a filter when shortlisting candidates. [L1172.057]
- Home decor is a better choice when it is light enough to ship cheaply. [L1171.007]
- Vacation-related products can work because demand for travel has grown after the lockdowns. [L1184.023]
- Products that replace a cheap everyday habit face strong price resistance, so favour products that solve a need the buyer does not already cover cheaply. [L1186.006]
- Choose products you can make content about two to three times a day, because a product that is hard to film or present will not be uploaded consistently. Convenience of content creation is a selection criterion. [L0706.004]
- An upgraded version of a winning product, or a product with several use cases, is a strong candidate. [L0788.043, L0871.009]
- Products in categories where the problem is ongoing and recurring, such as the knee brace, are favoured. [L0660.009]
- Look for products where a problem is recognised and the audience already looks for a solution. [L0708.003]

### Private label and white label

- Private label and white label products work well because they carry your own unique brand name and product identifier. Google will not associate your white-labelled products with competing brand names. (Source A 2024.) [L0276.035]
- Start by selling a generic product and watch which products get traffic and sell best and what buyers like or dislike. Then private label a product that is the best of the best in the niche. (Source A 2024.) [L0805.043]
- You do not have to sell every product a brand offers. You can choose which items to list from the catalogue, keeping only the products that fit your niche and margins. (Source A 2024.) [L0965.022]
- When choosing a product to develop as a private-label item, the lesson sorts candidates into four types: accessory, smaller item, lead magnet or large product. Each type can serve as a fit for a private-label launch, so match the product type to your own capacity and goals. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L0346.001]
- Accessories that you already sell, or that you should sell but skipped because the margin looked too thin, are good candidates for private labelling. Review both groups. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1152.004]
- Neoprene wine bottle holders protect bottles from knocking together during transport and help keep their temperature. Buyers of wine coolers, wine cellar equipment and other wine-industry products are a natural audience. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1152.023]
- Pellet grill accessories form a large range of white-label and private-label candidates: utensils, pellets, cedar planks, remote thermometers, smoking racks, grill covers, slicing knives, marinades and rubs, meat shredding claws, and cast iron cookware. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1152.014]

**Lead magnets and cross-sell**

- A lead magnet is a low-cost product that brings buyers into the store. Check whether its buyers already own or plan to buy a related main product, such as a wine cooler. Then remarket them with the main product or related items. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1152.010]
- Neoprene wine bottle holders fit a lead-magnet role for buyers of wine coolers, wine cellar equipment or other wine-industry products. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1152.009]
- Lead-magnet products can be sold on marketplaces such as Amazon or on Etsy, with custom sayings or designs, to reach customers in the same niche before they reach your own store. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1152.011]
- To find upsell and cross-sell products, check the "frequently bought together" section on Amazon for the main product. Alternatively, open the AliExpress store that sells the original listing, because each listing belongs to a store that usually carries related products. [L0363.013]
- Once a hero product is chosen, upsell and cross-sell products should be small and closely related to it. Complex unique products would need their own landing page, which adds friction. [L0363.014]

**Case: travelling pellet grill (Source B, older advice, 2021-22)**

- The store owner received white-label offers from a major pellet grill brand's manufacturer and wanted a version with clear differentiation. [L1155.013]
- Repeated customer feedback showed that portability was a real problem for pellet grill buyers. Only one grill on the market addressed it, and it sold strongly. [L1155.013]
- The owner bought two units to test them and found weaknesses: poor heat retention, clunky handles that doubled as legs, and a large size. [L1155.013]
- The proposed improvement was a smaller grill sized for a single brisket, with better heat insulation (for example, a fitted cover) and better handles. It was to be sourced from an American manufacturer and built out through manufacturer outreach, which was expected to be difficult but likely successful. [L1155.013]

### Air purifiers: a worked criteria set (Source B, older advice, 2021-22)

Competitor guides weigh tool-free filter changes, ozone emissions, upkeep costs over the unit's life, warranty length, weight and portability, and filter-change monitoring. Use these criteria to judge which brands are worth listing for buyers with allergies, asthma or chemical sensitivities. [L0937.018]

- A unit should exchange the room's air about 5 times per hour, with 2 air exchanges per hour as the minimum, depending on room size. A unit rated for a larger room than needed can run on lower speeds, which makes it quieter. [L0932.019, L0937.024]
- Room size is a major factor when choosing an air purifier, because the unit must exchange the room's air several times per hour. [L0937.024]
- A reliable warranty covers at least 5 years on the main fan and motor parts. The filters are the only part expected to need regular cleaning or replacement. [L0932.020, L0937.019]
- Any ozone emission from an air purifier is undesirable. It matters most for buyers with allergies, asthma or multiple chemical sensitivities, because ozone irritates the respiratory system. Filter out ozone-emitting models when selecting products for these buyers. [L0932.021, L0937.020]
- CADR (Clean Air Delivery Rate), certified by AHAM, shows how much purified air a unit delivers and is used to compare air purifiers. Higher CADR figures indicate higher output for the same type of unit. [L0937.021]
- Combining gas or odour filtration and HEPA filtration in a single cartridge is criticised, because the two filter types degrade at different rates. Separate filters are generally preferred. [L0937.022]
- Products with filters that are easy to change without tools are preferred. The best designs let the user open a door, pull out the filter and insert a new one by hand. Filters that need a screwdriver, the unit turned upside down or are hard to reach are often changed late, past the recommended date, which reduces performance. [L0932.022, L0937.031]
- Upkeep cost is often overlooked by buyers. Some of the most expensive air purifiers cost less to maintain over their lifetime, and units without filters, such as some air sterilisers, have no filter cost at all. [L0932.023]

### Product idea examples and brainstorm inputs

- Product ideas can come from items visible in everyday life. Each brainstorm candidate is a candidate to test for a price of $200 or more. [L0474.013]
- Product ideas on the first brainstorm list are hypotheses, not confirmed winners. [L0474.014]
- Selection should be based on criteria, not on the example products. Apply the selection criteria rather than copying the examples. [L1111.007]
- Passion is not a selection criterion. Product ideas should be selected on the expected selling price. [L0474.012]

**Conflict: passion, understanding and personal use**

- Passion for a product is not a valid selection criterion, and it is not required. [L0474.012, L1088.002]
- Only sell products you believe in and would use yourself, because selling something you understand makes the marketing and customer answers easier. Spend a couple of weeks researching which brands are actually best before choosing a product. (Source A.) [L0910.004]
- Do not try to sell products you do not understand, because you will struggle to connect authentically with the product, create convincing marketing or answer customer questions. [L0280.005]
- Choosing products only because you like them or would buy them is a mistake. Test for the average customer in your target market. A novelty window-mounted cat bed and phone cases sold little or nothing for one seller, because they had no wow factor and no culture around them. [L0549.008]
- Choosing a product because of personal passion is not a valid selection criterion. Product ideas should be selected based on the expected selling price. [L0474.012]
- Niche selection should be based on research criteria and market knowledge, not on familiarity alone. [L1111.020]
- Products that are not sold in many stores but show strong ad counts and a clear niche can be tested. [L1176.008]
- Only sell products you would use or consume yourself. [L1171.008]

Reconciling these: understanding the product and being able to use it is useful; passion and personal taste are not criteria. Judge a product by its problem, its price, its margin and the market's response. [L0280.003, L0549.051, L0577.032, L0910.004]

### Testing mindset and rules of thumb

- Pick a niche that meets the criteria and follow the process, because a perfect niche rarely exists. (Older advice, 2021.) [L1112.067]
- Product quality matters more than virality. [L0372.014]
- Product selection matters more than platform specialisation. [L0349.002]
- Do not run products with no ad proof without a small test. Use image ads and friend and family checks first. [L1316.022]
- Build the list of product ideas continuously; keep adding ideas from daily life. [L0474.016]
- Brand-new products with few sellers can sell with minimal marketing, but this depends on luck, so keep research as the main method. [L1158.008]
- Before testing a product, confirm it solves a problem and stands out. [L0950.076]
- Prefer products with only 2 to 3 variants. [L1174.004]

### Written Product Criteria and Pre-Research Steps

- Write the product criteria checklist before opening any research tool. Use about six to seven points for TikTok. The checklist defines what kind of product to look for. [L1436.001]

### Problem-First Product Selection

1. Identify a group of customers who already buy from you. In the lesson's example, these were women over 45. [L1432.014]
2. List the daily problems that group faces. [L1432.014]
3. Search for a product that solves one of those specific problems. [L1432.014]

- Example from the lesson: for a customer group that struggles with fitness, hair loss or weight, choose a product that addresses that specific problem. For women over 45 in Switzerland, emptiness and depression were noted as problems, and meditation-related products were considered as a response. [L1432.016]
- A proven audience can be used to test products across several niches. For example, a winter clothing brand and an astrology-themed product were both aimed at women over 45. [L1432.042]
- Choose test products by asking which daily problems the audience already has, not by copying random winning products. [L1432.042]

| Step | Question | Example from source | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| Audience | Who already buys from you? | Women over 45 | L1432.014 |
| Problems | What do they struggle with daily? | Emptiness, depression (Switzerland) | L1432.016 |
| Product | Which product solves one of those problems? | Meditation-related products | L1432.016 |
| Test | Which niches can this audience test? | Winter clothing, astrology | L1432.042 |

### Conversion Before Traffic

- Traffic alone does not produce sales. A high-converting product is essential. [L1429.020]
- Products that appeal to emotions tend to trigger impulse buys. [L1429.020]

### Problem-Solving Versus Wow-Factor Products

#### Two Requirements for a Product Worth Testing

- A product worth testing needs two things: room to scale, and support for many engaging short videos. [L1444.001]
- A product can fit a popular category and still fail if it is poorly built or poorly structured. [L1444.001]

#### Wow-Factor Products

- A wow-factor product that is hard to buy locally can go viral quickly, because viewers assume the seller has exclusive access. [L1444.003]
- Once viewers discover that the product does not work as shown, conversion drops sharply and the product is exposed. [L1444.003]
- A wow factor only carries a product if the product actually delivers what the video shows. [L1444.003]
- Before you publish a store for a wow-factor item, check that it works properly. [L1444.004]
- A simple, common item that buyers can easily get themselves is hard to sell at a high price. Example: an ice product listed at about 17 to 18 USD. [L1444.004]

#### Problem-Solving Products

- Products that solve a problem, especially medical-type or health-related solutions, were described as the best performers. [L1444.006]
- Slight improvements on proven products are also worth testing. [L1444.006]

#### Quick Money-Grab Products

- Quick money-grab products may not solve a real problem but can generate a few thousand USD. [L1444.005]
- Use them as a reasonable test to practise hooks, angles and video production before testing a product with higher potential. [L1444.005]

| Product type | What the sources say | When it applies | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| Problem-solving (health-related) | Best performers | Default choice for a main product | L1444.006 |
| Proven product, slight improvement | Worth testing | When a proven product already sells | L1444.006 |
| Wow-factor | Can go viral, but only if it delivers | Only after confirming it works as shown | L1444.003, L1444.004 |
| Quick money-grab | A few thousand USD, no real problem solved | Practising hooks, angles and production | L1444.005 |

### Quality, Safety and Red Flags

- Check product quality with extra care for beauty and health products. A poor product in these categories can harm the customer and creates a red flag. [L1436.012]
- Burns, poor quality, or a product that stops working after a few uses spread quickly through comments and buyer discussion. [L1444.069]
- Once buyers realise a product does not work, conversion can drop sharply within days. [L1444.069]

### Product Types to Favour

#### Economy-Driven Choices

- Choose products by the economy. In a cost-of-living crisis, people go out less and spend more at home. [L1440.050]
- In that period, home cooking, home entertainment and kids' board games sold well, and TikTok cooking content performed well. [L1440.050]

#### Household and Seasonal Items

- Household items were described as strong sellers in general. [L1444.008]
- A product priced too low may not carry a whole store, but it can work as an upsell. [L1444.008]
- Sunny locations near water were mentioned as a helpful factor for certain beach or summer products. [L1444.008]

#### Established Branded Products (older advice, 2021-2022)

- Start with established branded products that already sell in your target market, not with new untested products. [L1480.009]
- New products cost more, take more time, and carry a much higher risk of failure. [L1480.009]
- The wow-factor and quick money-grab guidance above (L1444.003, L1444.005) is more experimental. Use L1480.009 when choosing the core product for a store in a known market, and use the experimental tests on a small scale to practise and find new angles. [L1480.009, L1444.003, L1444.005]

### Cross-Sell and Bundle Candidates

#### Jewellery

- Choose cross-sell products that are highly relatable and easy to explain with one image. [L1410.035]
- Jewellery is one of the best niches for collection and bundle offers, if each product is simple to understand from a single photo. [L1410.035]
- Simple one-image pieces suit bundle and cross-sell offers. [L1412.041]
- Designs tied to meaning or feeling need more explanation and can lower conversion when cross-sold. [L1412.041]

| Design type | Cross-sell suitability | Units |
|---|---|---|
| Simple, understood from one photo | Suited to bundles and cross-sells | L1410.035, L1412.041 |
| Tied to meaning or feeling | Needs more explanation; can lower cross-sell conversion | L1412.041 |

#### Further details

- Do not test branded products; focus on unbranded or generic alternatives. [L0209.024]

- Local-brand products are already sold on the market, are tested, and are often trusted brands with histories of 20 years or more. Choosing such products lowers the risk compared with selling new, unknown items. [L0458.060]

## Finding Products with Ad Spy and Ad Library Tools

### Ad Spy Tools: Roles and Limits

- The Meta Ad Library is the most complete public ad archive for dropshipping research, because advertisers cannot hide their ads from it, while third-party spy tools can miss ads that advertisers pay to conceal. Use it as the primary source for finding products. [L0638.001]
- No spy tool shows every ad, and some products appear in only one tool. Each tool has its own library, so use several tools for a more complete list. [L0708.025, L0708.024]
- Some spy tools do not update their databases and keep showing the same products every day. Supplement them with manual searches in the Ad Library and on supplier marketplaces. [L1108.010]
- No tool gives exact competitor store data or sales for a product. Use the Ad Library and keyword searches to estimate competition. Spy tools with a product section show some stores that sell a product, but they miss many of them. [L0638.048]
- Product research with spy tools works best by studying the best sellers of competitor stores and the ads they run, rather than hunting for new products every day. Products with proven sales are a better starting point than constantly chasing new ones. [L0561.019]

| Tool | Role as stated in the source | Ids |
|---|---|---|
| AdLib | Product research tool showing real-time Facebook ads and trend volume; filter by Shopify stores to find products sold by working ecommerce operations. | L0209.014, L0209.015 |
| AfterLib (Afterlib) | Paid product research tool with ad analytics; product list sortable by active ads. Because it is pricey, a single-month trial is a reasonable way to evaluate it. | L0361.016, L1171.050, L0950.007 |
| Winning Hunter | Alternative product-finding tool; Meta ad library with ad cards showing estimated data (see the filter section below). | L0361.016, L0772.014 |
| Peak Star (PeakStar) | Winner list of products already performing well, usable as a starting list; store research and dashboard features. Free for beginners. Its newer version was not yet tested by the coach at the time of the lesson. The seller said its figures should be checked for accuracy before relying on them. | L0363.005, L0678.030, L0708.023 |
| Droppy Spy (DropiSpy) | Cheap alternative that also suits beginners. | L0708.023, L0335.019 |
| AdSpy | Large library but expensive, so not recommended for beginners. | L0708.024, L0661.003 |
| Peakster | Ad spy tool showing thousands of daily ads on TikTok and Facebook; filters products by set conditions over a period, such as the last month and a half. | L0561.018, L1108.011 |
| Peak (store and product tracking) | Monitors a competitor store's selling pace for a specific product, for example units per week. | L0950.008 |
| Shop Hunter | Checks the sales of a product, to confirm it is selling before testing it with ads. | L1108.009 |
| PPSpy | Used alongside Peak Star and DropiSpy to compare the engagement and comments of the same winning ad. | L0335.060 |
| Droppy Supply | Paid product-sourcing subscription in a different format from Peak Star; can surface products Peak Star does not show. Worth adding as a second product source after the first research tool has been used for a while. | L0639.041 |
| Find Shopify competitors with AI | Reverse image search over saved product images of almost every Shopify store; returns similar, not always identical, products, and the similarity is the signal to check. | L0892.003 |
| Magic AI | Accepts a text description or an uploaded image and returns ads and competitors sorted by similarity. | L0892.006 |
| PiPiAds (most likely) | TikTok ad search tool that can show large sellers running the same product on TikTok. | L1158.045 |

- Peak Star and Droppy Spy both offer a post type filter for Facebook ad research, but they can return different results for identical filters. Run the same search in both tools to avoid missing products. [L0708.053]
- If a competitor's Facebook page has no website link, check its ad activity in a TikTok spy tool before ruling it out, because some sellers run ads only on TikTok and do not appear clearly in the Facebook Ad Library. [L0895.035]
- Old Facebook winners from the past few years are a strong source of product ideas, because products that performed well as Facebook ads may not yet have been tested with organic TikTok content. [L0706.037]
- If a spy extension reports that a Facebook account has too few ads to analyze, create a separate Facebook account for product research and keep it apart from the business account. [L1108.015]

### Meta Ad Library: Setup and Basic Search

- The Meta Ad Library is a free public tool for checking which ads run for a brand or keyword, filtered by country and active status. It is used to validate products and to find winning ads for inspiration. [L0347.013]
- Log into a Facebook account before using the Ad Library, because without a login the results may not show everything. Start from the Ad Library page, choose the country, then open the All ads view. [L0638.002]
- Steps for checking a product in the Meta Ad Library: [L0347.014]
  1. Open the Meta Ad Library.
  2. Set the country filter to United States.
  3. Set the active status filter to Active ads and the ad type and media type filters to all.
  4. Search the product or brand keyword.
  5. Count the results and check the launch dates and Library IDs of the ads.
  6. Open the ads and check the impression label: ads marked with a low impression count (under 100 impressions) are weak performers.
  7. Look for the ads with more impressions and with multiple advertisers running similar creatives, since these are the likely winners.
- The Ad Library can show which products competitors advertise. Search the product idea and sort by newest to see which products have recently started running ads. Use this as a market check before testing. [L0577.077]
- The Ad Library shows which stores run ads for a product. If other stores run the same product creatives with their own landing pages and product titles, that helps validate demand. [L0361.014]
- Searching for an exact product name can return nothing, because some ads only run on general pages. When the exact product is not found, look at the ads of large niche stores in the same category to see what the market runs. [L0450.029]
- Searching by hand gives scattered and incomplete data. A paid ad spy tool with a large library and product filters produces more candidates and more reliable scaling data in less time. The aim is a list of at least 10 candidates, ideally 10 to 15. [L1174.036]
- Facebook Ads Library searches with niche keywords, such as kids toy or kids gift, show which ads are running in a niche and are used for manual niche and competitor checks. [L1108.008]
- Ad spy search by product keyword for a specific audience: AdSpy filters for female 40+ fashion research are Gender = female, Age = 40 to 65+, Country = United States, and Ad text = a product keyword such as shoe, sneakers, boot or slippers. To see a specific competitor store's ads, search by its URL. [L0661.003]

### Keyword and Offer Searches

- Keyword searches in the Ad Library are the first filter for dropshipping ads. Use typical offer phrases such as 30 percent off, 35 percent off, 50 percent off and free shipping. Broad phrases like percent off capture most discount ads, while 70 or 80 percent off are rarely used by dropshippers but can still be tested. [L0638.005]
- A single broad keyword is not enough on its own. The keyword percent off returned more than 50,000 results for the United States without other filters. Adding the Active ads filter and a narrow date window reduces the list to a workable number. [L0638.006]
- Combine several keywords in one search with OR logic, using the pipe character, to see ads containing any of the phrases, such as percent off together with get yours today. Use quotation marks for exact-phrase search when you need ads containing the exact phrase, such as free shipping. [L0638.007]
- Brand and dropship ads often appear side by side in the Ad Library. Large non-product advertisers such as brands, non-profits and political groups add a lot of noise. Use specific keywords, narrow date windows and product-related ads to filter them out. [L0638.015]
- Free research workflow with keywords: [L0895.005]
  1. Prepare a list of 5 to 10 keywords per product.
  2. Search each keyword in the Facebook Ad Library, the main free source for Facebook competitors.
  3. Review the last one to two months of data, including the previous month, to see who is running ads.
  4. Note each competitor, its ad count, creative reuse and launch dates in a sheet.
  5. Open the competitor's Facebook page and search its name in the Ad Library to check whether it is scaling.
  6. Check the competitor's landing page and copy.
- Search Google, Amazon, AliExpress, Alibaba and TikTok with the same keywords as the Facebook Ad Library, and compile the competitors found outside the ad tools, since ad spy tools do not cover every store. [L0693.006]
- Winning Hunter is not needed for a beginner's basic keyword check; the Ad Library workflow above is enough to start. [L0638.004]

### Date Windows and the Active-Ad Filter

- Set the Active ads filter in every research session, because it hides ads that have stopped running. Running ads show what other sellers are currently scaling or testing, which is the signal being looked for. [L0638.008]
- The Ad Library sometimes shows results that do not match the active filters, for example older ads when a recent date window is set. Re-check the filters and dates before trusting a result. [L0638.014]
- A short recent window with the Active ads filter shows which products other sellers are scaling right now, rather than just testing. Ads launched in the last few days give a current signal of demand. [L0638.010]
- Long-running active ads are a signal of profitability, because advertisers rarely keep ads running for months without return. An ad launched in March that is still active in May suggests the product is profitable for that seller, although a forgotten ad can also stay active. [L0638.011]
- Advertisers do not scale ads for products that fail to make money, so active advertising by others is a signal of profitability. Check which products have sustained ad activity before choosing what to test. [L1172.002]

**Date windows by purpose**

| Purpose | Window | Ids |
|---|---|---|
| Products others are scaling now (Impression date filter) | 2 to 3 days, for example 30 April to 2 May; avoid windows longer than about 3 days | L0638.004, L0638.009 |
| Proven older products (Impression date filter) | About 1 to 3 months, for example 1 March to 31 March, or 1 January to 31 March | L0638.004, L0638.012, L0638.013 |
| Ads launched recently (Ad Library date preset) | Last 90 days, to avoid older ads that may have stopped working | L0374.043 |
| Ad creation date in Winning Hunter | Last three days, then sort by longest running or days running | L0772.011 |
| Recently launched competitor ads (spy tools) | Last 1 month; extend to 1.5 to 2 months only if needed | L0708.027 |
| Fresh product launches | Ads launched in the last 1 to 2 weeks, with about one month as the widest window | L0335.005 |
| Widening a search that returns too few products | Date range about 45 days | L0335.018 |

- Ad Library date presets are Today, Yesterday, Last 7 days, Last 14 days, Last 30 days, Last 90 days, Last 180 days, Last 365 days and All Time. [L0374.043]
- Filter for ads launched in the last 1 to 2 weeks, using about one month as the widest window. The aim is to find products that competitors have only just started to scale. [L0335.005]
- Choosing a window that is too recent, such as April, mostly shows products still in testing or early scaling without product market fit. For a proven product, use an older window such as 1 to 31 March or 1 January to 31 March. [L0638.013]
- Filter for product ads created in the last 1 month, and extend to 1.5 to 2 months only if needed. Recently launched ads show which products are currently working for other dropshippers. [L0708.027]
- Winning Hunter has a Last seen date filter, separate from the Ad creation date filter. Use it to find ads still being shown recently, regardless of when they first launched. [L0772.040]
- Check when an advertiser's ads started before trusting their ad count. Ads that began only a day or two ago are not yet proof of profit, while ads that have run for about a week or more are a stronger signal. [L1161.047]
- Change the date range in the Facebook Ad Library to look at past ad counts for a product. A product that once had over 1,000 active ads in an earlier window has scaled before, even if the current count is lower. [L1161.048]

### Days Running and Video Filters

- Set Days running to a minimum of seven days. An ad that has run that long suggests the product is either working or at least breaking even. [L0772.009]
- Dashboard filter ranges include Days running from 0 to 365, Video length from 0s to 3600s, Product Price Range from 0 to 5000, and Products on Store from 0 to 100000. Combine them with Store Traffic (Monthly Visits) and Scaling to narrow results to stores that are already proven. [L0374.044]
- Set Media type to Videos, because the goal is to recreate video ads that already perform. [L0772.006]
- Set the Video length filter to a long range, with the default range 0 to 3600 seconds, to find VSLs. Long-video filtering works well for finding sales-video funnels. [L0772.005]
- Use the Ad copy length filter to surface native-style ads, which tend to carry long body copy. [L0772.004]
- Leave Page type blank, so advertorials, listicles, quizzes and blog-style funnels appear next to product pages. This lets you study the full funnel a brand uses. [L0772.007]
- Choose a niche relevant to your search (the example used Health) and leave the Apps and Theme filters blank. Winning Hunter warns that the niche filter may not show all ads, so use it only when it saves time. [L0772.008]

### Active-Ad Count Thresholds

The sources give different numbers for different purposes. Each row states the value and when it applies. Count only active ads that belong to the specific product. [L1172.005, L1174.031]

| Active-ad count | Meaning and use | Ids |
|---|---|---|
| Under about 50 | Skip the product in Facebook Ad Library screening; products with only inactive ads are dropped | L1161.001, L1161.004 |
| Under 100 | Below the shortlist minimum in AfterLib and Ad Library research; skip it, since fewer usually means weak demand | L1171.002, L1173.001 |
| Over 100 | Main filter for a winning product; a much stronger candidate than under 50 | L1161.001, L1173.002 |
| 200 or more | Stronger signal of a product that converts | L1173.002 |
| 300 to 600 | Strong performance, the rule of thumb for Meta ads | L1172.005 |
| Over 300 | Example: a pet product with over 300 active ads counted as strong validation worth testing | L1161.003 |
| Over 500 | Worth adding to a research list | L1172.005 |
| 600 or more (Facebook) | Strong scaling signal for a product on Facebook | L1174.038 |
| 1,000 or more | Strong trust signal that the product works and is worth testing | L1171.003, L1176.006 |
| Over 1,000 | Extremely strong signal of profitability; little further proof needed, though the store and margin are still checked | L1172.006 |

**Scaling thresholds for one product:** 20 or more active ads for scaling, 30 or more for solid proof of concept, and 50 or more for likely high revenue. [L1174.038]

- Products with 2 to 10 active ads: a seller with 10 to 15 active ads is usually still testing. [L0335.058]
- Products with a very high count that appeared only days earlier may be a short burst of testing; a product whose ads run weeks or months later is a stronger signal of sustained performance. [L1171.052]
- Ads that have run for a week or more strengthen the signal from a high active-ad count. [L1161.002]
- Skip products with very few active ads, such as 18, when comparable products in the same search have many more active ads. Come back to them later instead of testing them now. [L1171.005]
- A product with many active ads that drops to zero may simply have been stopped or replaced by the seller. It can still be tested in other markets, but its success probability is lower. [L1171.004]
- A falling number of active ads signals declining demand or quality. Treat such products as lower priority, even if they were strong in earlier research. [L1172.059]
- Track how many active ads a competing brand runs for a product over time, and check again after about two months. A clearly falling number signals the trend is fading and demand is being lost. [L0347.041]
- A product that had over 1,000 ads a few days ago and now shows fewer active ads may still be a proven winner. Check the Ads Library history and the active ad count together before rejecting a product. [L1173.004]
- A product that started running ads about a month earlier and already shows around 645 active ads is scaling very fast and is worth shortlisting. Compare its start date with its current active-ad count to judge growth speed. [L1173.044]

### Reading Ad Counts Correctly

- Read the active ad count as a signal of intent. Around 10 to 15 active ads usually means a seller is still testing, while a steady flow of several new ads per day suggests the seller has found audiences that convert and is putting budget behind them. [L0335.058]
- Multiple active ads running for a long time, combined with recent edits or new ads started within days, are stronger evidence than a single high count. A competitor who recently started or edited ads is actively testing and spending. [L1172.007]
- Check recent activity: when the latest ad was started or edited shows whether money is still being spent. [L1172.004]
- The Ad Library counts an ad that runs in several ad sets once per ad set, so an ad in five ad sets shows as five ads. A high count means the advertiser tests the product heavily, not that many separate creatives exist. [L1161.006]
- The unfiltered total on a competitor's page can be several times higher than the active count. For one product, 2,200 total against 640 active was shown. Apply the Active ads filter before counting. [L1174.035]
- Some tools show how one creative's ad count grows over time, for example from single digits to several hundred ads for the same creative. Rising counts mean the advertiser is scaling that creative and the product is probably profitable for them. Check the date range to confirm the growth happened recently. [L1174.037]
- A product with a high and growing ad count is a usable proxy for profitable demand, because advertisers do not keep paying for ads that do not perform. This makes ad volume a practical filter. [L1176.004]
- Sorting by active ads is the first filter for shortlisting candidate dropshipping products. [L1171.050]
- Sorting by percentage change in ad count shows which products are gaining ad volume fastest, not only which have the most ads. [L1176.002]

**Same-creative counts in the Ad Library**

Count ads using the same creative and copy. The table shows what the count indicates. [L0638.017]

| Same creative count | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 3 | Early test; not yet a scaling signal |
| 4 | Testing phase, or about to scale |
| 6 | Testing or initial scaling |
| 10 | Likely scaling; next scaling phase |
| 13 to 16 | Winning creative and clear winning product |

- A competitor running 5 or more ads with the same creative is probably scaling that creative, which usually means the product was profitable for them. [L0895.006]
- A competitor running 10 to 15 ads with the same creative is in an active scaling phase and is a strong competitor signal worth tracking. [L0895.007]
- For a product with ads at a scaling threshold, count the same creative across the advertiser's page to judge whether the product is being scaled or only tested. [L0638.016]
- Mark every competitor's scaling status (Y/N). Competitors who scale ads show the product is currently profitable for them. Count this with the competition and engagement numbers when deciding to test. [L1159.011]

### Likes, Shares and Comments as Filters

Engagement thresholds differ by tool and by product age. Use the row that matches your filter setup.

| Setting | Values | When it applies | Ids |
|---|---|---|---|
| Winning Hunter-style Facebook filter | Likes 500+, Comments 150+, Shares 100+ | Ad spy search with Post Creation Date last one month and a fixed country list | L0636.003 |
| Peak Star or Droppy Spy starting point | 300 to 500 likes, 50 to 100 shares | General Facebook spy research | L0708.028 |
| Flexible lower threshold | 200 to 250 likes | Some products with these numbers stayed profitable; lower the number based on search results | L0708.028 |
| DropiSpy starting thresholds | 250 to 300 likes, 300 shares, 300 comments | Starting point in DropiSpy | L0335.019 |
| First-month product | 100 to 200 likes | Good signal when the store is new and the ads are scaling | L0335.019 |
| Thin results | Lower from 1,000 likes to 500, or even 250 likes | Products with many likes are easy to miss; widen the date range to about 45 days | L0335.018 |

- Products with a large number of likes are easy to miss. If filters return too few products, lower the thresholds and widen the date range to about 45 days. [L0335.018]
- Likes and comments can be bought, so do not rely on engagement numbers alone. Check the comment section to see if buyers are real and whether they complain about quality. [L0708.029]
- Use the comment section to judge genuine demand. People tagging friends on an ad is a strong sign of real engagement. Repetitive comments or fake-looking profiles suggest bought engagement, and the ad should be discounted. [L1174.028]
- Engagement without sales is a weaker signal. A competitor ad shows market fit when its comments contain buying questions and people tag friends to buy. [L0363.078]
- Positive comments such as buyers asking about the product, sharing reviews and tagging friends signal real demand. Products with strong comments can be ranked higher. [L0708.030]
- A product with many positive comments about the concept, buyers asking for details, people tagging friends and reviews from real buyers is a good sign. Comments praising the concept or saying buyers want the product show real demand. [L0636.005]
- Many repeated short comments of 2 to 3 words posted by different accounts are a red flag, because bots may have added them. Ignore such comment sections as evidence of demand. [L0636.006]
- Comments that criticize product quality are a red flag and should lead you to drop the product. [L0636.007]
- Compare the engagement and comments of a competitor's winning ad across a second tool, such as PPSpy, Shop Hunter or DropiSpy. [L0335.060]

### Page Age and Advertiser Quality

- An older Facebook page is not automatically a warning sign. If a page created years earlier is adding many active ads quickly, for example rising from about 30 to about 57 active ads in one day, the product may still be worth testing. [L0335.057]
- Page age of a product's store is a soft guideline, often cited as four to six months. An older page is not an automatic deal breaker. A page older than a year that runs high-scale ads may have a well-trained pixel that is harder to compete with. [L0361.035]
- Competitor Facebook page age does not matter much for product selection, because pages and ad accounts get banned often and are replaced. Judge a product by its active ads and store, not by the advertiser's age. [L1173.006]
- A product that was popular a year or two earlier can return. Check its current ad activity instead of dismissing it because of its age. [L1176.005]
- A declining percentage in AdLib may indicate the advertiser's account was banned and recently restarted. [L0209.017]
- Avoid products when the competitor is a general store testing many products and the active ad count for the specific product is unclear. Without a clear count, you cannot tell whether the competitor is scaling it or profitable. [L1174.029]

### Store and Competitor Tracking

- Peakster has a store tracking feature showing a competitor store's revenue, last orders, and each last-sold product with its name and image, which reveals winning products. [L0561.018]
- To confirm a store found through Peak Star store research: [L0335.060]
  1. Check the store's active ads and scaling pattern in the Meta Ad Library.
  2. Open the About section of the store's page and read the page creation date.
  3. Find the same winning ad in a second tool, such as PPSpy, Shop Hunter or DropiSpy, and compare its engagement and comments.
- Use a competitor's store to find more candidates: [L1161.049]
  1. Open the advertiser's page in the Facebook Ad Library.
  2. Note the other products they currently run ads for.
  3. Screen each new product the same way: count active ads, check ad age, check the store, and infer the target country.
- When one competitor store sells several products, the product with the most active ads is usually the one they are scaling. Use that product's ads as the reference for your own test. [L1176.044]
- Each competitor's ad activity in the Ad Library: open the competitor's Facebook page, search its name in the Ad Library, and check whether it is scaling. [L0895.005]
- Recheck ad counts after a few days to confirm the ads are still running. [L1173.001]
- Check whether the store runs other products with many active ads, which shows what it is testing. [L1173.001]
- Peak Star-style tracking is used to monitor a competitor's selling pace on a specific product. [L0950.008]
- Shop Hunter confirms a product is actually selling before it is tested with ads. [L1108.009]

### Competitor Screening Workflows

**Product screening workflow (Ad Library)** [L1161.004]
1. Search the product in the Facebook Ad Library and count the active ads.
2. Skip the product if it has fewer than about 50 active ads or only inactive ads.
3. Check the advertiser's store: offer, price, and whether it is a product you would test.
4. Infer the targeted country from the store currency and language.
5. Find the supplier product via AliExpress using the camera (image) search.
6. Add the product to the test list with the Ad Library link and the store link.

**Product research procedure in the Facebook Ad Library** [L1172.004]
1. Open a product list sorted by performance or by number of active ads.
2. Open each product's store link and note the product, price, offers and bundles.
3. Open the Facebook Ad Library, find the product or store, and count the ads marked as active.
4. Check when the latest ad was started or edited; recent activity shows that money is still being spent.
5. Note the countries targeted in the ads.
6. Review the ad copy and videos, and save videos for reference.
7. Compare the store's problem and solution messaging, description and offers with what the ads promise.
8. Add the product to the research list with its store link and its Ad Library link.

**Product research in the Meta Ad Library, in order** [L1173.001]
1. Search for the product or brand.
2. Filter for ads that are currently active.
3. Sort results by number of active ads.
4. Keep only products with more than 100 active ads, since fewer usually means weak demand.
5. Open the competitor's store and check its offer, product description and landing page.
6. Check whether the store runs other products with many active ads, which shows what it is testing.
7. Recheck the ad counts after a few days to confirm the ads are still running.

**Product research with Afterlib** [L1171.001]
1. Sort the Afterlib product list by active ads.
2. Keep only products with more than 100 active ads in the Facebook Ad Library.
3. Open the product page and check whether the product clearly solves a problem and whether the store has room for a better page.
4. Search the product in the Facebook Ad Library and confirm its active ad count and the date the ads started.
5. Check which countries the ads run in and choose the test market from there.

**Product research process for Facebook and Meta** [L1174.020]
1. Choose an ad spy tool and set its filters.
2. List all potential products the filtered results show, aiming for at least 10 and ideally 10 to 15 candidates.
3. For each product, open the competitor page and find its Facebook Ad Library page.
4. Count the active ads for that specific product on the Ad Library page.
5. Record the data in the product research sheet: product name, competitor store link, Ad Library link, active ads, AliExpress link, COGS, competitor selling price and break-even ROAS.
6. Use the recorded COGS and selling price to calculate break-even ROAS and rank the candidates.

**Competitor count per product (scaling analysis)** [L1174.031, L1174.035]
- Only count active ads that belong to the specific product when doing the scaling analysis, excluding ads for other products on the same competitor page. Record the adjusted active ad count in the sheet for each candidate. [L1174.031]
- On a competitor's Facebook Ad Library page, apply the Active ads filter before counting. Count only the ads for the specific product and subtract ads for other products the advertiser tests on the same page. [L1174.035]

**Facebook Ad Library competitor research (full workflow)** [L0638.004]
1. Open the Ad Library and log into your Facebook account.
2. Select the country, for example United States.
3. Select All ads.
4. Enter a discount or offer keyword in the search field, for example percent off.
5. Open the filters and set Active ads so only currently running ads appear.
6. Set the Impression date range to a window of two to three days for recent scaling products, or to a window of about one to three months (for example 1 to 31 March) for proven older products.
7. Scroll the results and note the products that show a high number of ads using the same creative.
8. Open each candidate's ads, copy the ad link, and check the advertiser's full ad count in the Ad Library.
9. Record each candidate and rank products against your product criteria before testing them one by one.

**Find long-running products** [L0638.012]
1. Open the Ad Library and select the United States (or another chosen country) as the country.
2. Select All ads.
3. Enter keywords such as percent off, free shipping, or get yours today.
4. Set the Active ads filter.
5. Set the Impression date filter to a past window of one to three months, for example 1 March to 31 March, to find products whose ads have been running a long time.
6. Review the results and look for products whose ads are still active from that window.
7. Check whether the seller is still scaling, and note the product if the ad is still running.

**Verify a candidate's ads and store** [L0638.016]
1. Click View ads, Go to page, or the three-dot menu and Copy ad link on the candidate ad.
2. Open a new browser tab and paste the link to see the page that runs the ad.
3. Go back to the Ad Library, select United States, then All ads.
4. Search for the advertiser's page name to see the total number of ads that page runs.
5. Count how many ads use the same creative and copy to judge whether the product is being scaled or only tested.
6. Open the store and check the landing page and product proposition before deciding to test.

**Find products to test through the Ad Library as a buyer** [L1108.014, L0693.008]
- Click an ad on Facebook or Instagram, visit the advertiser's website, add a product to cart, start checkout and leave. Repeat, so the platform shows more ads from that niche. The same approach works on TikTok. [L1108.014]
- Click an ad that appears in the feed, land on the product page, add the product to cart and go to checkout. Expect Meta to show more ads for similar products afterwards, which signals a market. [L0693.008]

**Shortlisting volume** [L1171.005, L1171.009, L1171.003]
- Examples from the lesson: a magnetic absorption product with 686 active ads and a clothing item with 672 active ads were both kept for testing. A home decor item with 390 active ads and a product with 385 active ads were also shortlisted. [L1171.009]
- A product with 1,000 or more active ads is a strong trust signal that it works, so it is worth testing. [L1171.003]

**Trend research on Facebook and TikTok, as taught** [L0895.003]
1. Check spy tools (Peak Star, Droppy Spy) and the ad platforms for products that worked in the last month.
2. Check which products worked in the same period of the previous year, since seasonal products that worked last year often work again because they tie to events.
3. Check products from two years earlier in the same season for ideas that could be improved.
4. Build a list of 10 to 15 candidates with basic criteria and margin checks.
5. Run competitor analysis on each candidate.

**Products that worked before** [L1108.012]
1. Filter products with your conditions for roughly the last six weeks.
2. Go through all matches until none are left.
3. Go back to previous years and look for products that worked then and could work again now.

**Trend example** [L1176.003]
- A trend product rose from 618 ads on 27 November to 1,423 ads on 10 December, a sharp jump within about two weeks. A rapid rise in ad count like this signals that demand is growing. [L1176.003]

### Market and Country Checks

- Check competitors in the Meta Ad Library filtered by your target country before launching there. If many advertisers already run the same ad in that market, expect higher competition. [L0692.010]
- Searching by country, for example United States, reveals products that can be tested in another market. [L0678.030]
- Checking competitors in a new country with the Facebook Ad Library: [L1158.044]
  1. Open the Facebook Ad Library.
  2. Set the country filter to the target country.
  3. Search a broad keyword for the category around the product, such as women's care or healthcare.
  4. Search the exact product name.
  5. Note which brands run ads for the product, what they sell, how their ads are built, and on which platform they run them.
  6. If the product has no scaling competitors in that country, the market may be open; if strong brands already sell it, study their ads and offers before entering.
- When a product is over-run in one market, look at the same product sold in another physical form, such as a drink mix versus drops. That form usually has its own video ads from other sellers, which gives a fresh pool of creatives to study. [L0901.002]
- Markets to avoid for the US research filters: Exclude the European and UK countries GB, DK, NL, DE, NO, SE and FR from the country filter when researching the US, so non-US ads do not crowd the results. [L0772.002]
- Set Countries to the target markets in the spy tool, for example Australia and UK, with the Language filter left open. [L0708.026]
- Countries used in the spy-tool filter for broad research: USA, Canada, Australia, UK and Germany, with Language set to English. [L0636.003]
- Smaller markets such as Australia and New Zealand return a comparatively small library and can be used for a quicker overview; Germany and the UAE were also named as options. The United States produces a very large result set, so extra filters are needed. [L0638.003]
- Infer the targeted country from the store's currency and language. [L1161.004]
- Choose the test market from the countries the ads run in. [L1171.001]
- Home decor items are a good niche for picture-only ads, because they are visually self-explanatory and cheaper to advertise than video. [L0642.041]

### Winning Hunter Meta Ad Library Filters

**Country, language and technology** [L0772.001, L0772.003]
- In the Winning Hunter Meta ad library search, set Countries to the US, set Technology to Shopify, and set Languages to English while excluding the other listed languages. This keeps results on the target market's native-language ads. [L0772.001]
- Leave the EU adspend filter unused when targeting the US, because it mainly covers ads running in Europe. [L0772.003]

**Store traffic** [L0772.010]
- The Store Traffic (monthly visits) filter helps find stores that are booming. Beginners without e-commerce or dropshipping experience should skip it, because high-traffic products are often crowded and harder to enter.

**Saved presets** [L0772.038]
