- Avoid very large or expensive-to-ship products when choosing items to source. [L1184.021]

### Amazon Best Sellers: research procedures

**Procedure A: category scan**

1. Go to Amazon and search Google for "Amazon Best Seller." [L0227.004]
2. Click the Best Sellers link. [L0227.004]
3. Select a top-level category, such as Toys and Games or Kitchen and Dining. [L0227.004]
4. Scroll through the top 100 products and look for repeated items. Multiple knife listings, for example, indicate a hot category. [L0227.004]
5. For each product of interest, click to open its details. [L0227.004]
6. Check the Best Seller Rank in the top-level category, not the subcategory. [L0227.004]
7. Note the number of reviews. [L0227.004]
8. Record the price point. [L0227.004]
9. Assess whether the product could be private labeled (logo change, packaging change). [L0227.004]

**Procedure B: Best Sellers to ideas**

1. Open the Amazon Best Sellers page, which lists the top 100 products in each category. [L1153.015]
2. Drill into subcategories to see what sells within each one. [L1153.015]
3. Use these lists to generate product ideas. [L1153.015]
4. Brainstorm in parallel with store visits, recent purchases and questions to friends, using the same logic as dropshipping research at a lower price point. [L1153.015]

**Procedure C: keyword demand check**

1. Search Amazon for the product keyword, for example "resistance bands." [L1153.019]
2. Open the first 10 or more results. [L1153.019]
3. Scroll to the bottom of each product page and note the BSR in the main category. [L1153.019]
4. If most results have a low BSR (typically under 5,000 in most categories), demand is good, and it is worth looking at competitors and suppliers. [L1153.019]
5. If most results have a high BSR, the product is probably not worth pursuing. [L1153.019]

**Amazon sales signals**

- Movers and Shakers lists the biggest sales gainers of the past 24 hours and is updated frequently, so checking it daily reveals new products. [L1184.009]
- Best Sellers can be filtered by category on the left side. It shows the top sellers per niche with their review counts. Products that sell well on Amazon can also be sold in markets where Amazon is less dominant. [L1184.010]
- Amazon usually does not run strong promotions such as buy-two-get-one-free. A store can compete with bundles and special deals on products sold on Amazon. The product may be unknown to the target audience, so ads raise awareness. [L1184.012]

### Best Sellers Rank (BSR)

**What BSR is and where to find it**

- BSR is Amazon's ranking that estimates how many sales a product makes. The lower the number, the more it sells. It can be checked on any Amazon product page. [L1153.016]
- BSR appears at the bottom of every Amazon product listing page. It is the most reliable indicator of whether a product has real demand and is worth entering. [L0228.007]
- On the product page, BSR appears in the product details section just above the reviews, at the bottom of the page. Read the top-level category ranking (for example, Arts and Crafts), not the subcategory ranking. [L1153.018]

**Read the top-level category only**

- Check BSR in the top-level category only. A product ranked #1 in a subcategory may not sell well if its top-level BSR is 40,000. [L0227.005]
- Do not judge demand from a small subcategory ranking. A product ranked #2 in a subcategory may compete with only two or three products. Judge demand from the main top-level category. [L1153.020]

**BSR targets and their conflicts**

The sources give different thresholds. Each applies under different conditions:

- **General target, 1 to 5,000 (top-level category):** This range indicates sufficient sales velocity. [L0227.006]
- **General starting point, under 5,000:** The usual target is under 5,000, but the threshold depends on the category. Use it as a starting point and adjust it for the category. [L1153.017]
- **Low-demand categories, stricter cut-off:** In categories such as Musical Instruments, 5,000 is far too loose. Use a stricter cut-off, for example under 1,000. [L1153.022]
- **Sports & Fitness:** A BSR of 5,000 or lower means roughly 10 to 15 units sold per day. [L0228.008]
- **Sales equivalents, which differ by source:** A BSR of 2,000 in a top-level category equals about 45 sales per day. [L0227.006] The category table below gives different figures for a BSR of 5,000. The sources do not say which category the 45-per-day figure refers to, so use the figure for the category you are researching. [L1153.021, L0227.006, L0228.008]

| Demand level | Amazon category | Approximate sales at a BSR of 5,000 |
|---|---|---|
| High | Home and Kitchen | 23 |
| High | Sports and Outdoors | 18 |
| High | Health and Personal Care | 26 (one of the most competitive markets) |
| High | Beauty | 18 |
| Medium | Toys and Games | not stated |
| Medium | Pet Supplies | not stated |
| Medium | Home Improvement | not stated |
| Medium | Office Products | not stated |
| Low | Industrial and Scientific | 4 |
| Low | Automotive | 7 |
| Low | Musical Instruments | 2 |

[L1153.021]

- Categories differ in demand, so read a BSR cut-off against the category's sales level. One BSR number across all categories can lead to a bad product choice. [L1153.023]
- Prioritize BSR over review count. A product ranked 10th with a low BSR (selling 10 to 20 units daily) is more valuable than a product ranked 1st with many reviews but a high BSR (selling only 1 to 2 units daily). High sales volume creates room for growth even in competitive conditions. [L0228.010]

### Competition: reviews and listings

- Avoid products with 1,000 or more competitor reviews, which indicate heavy competition. The ideal competitor review count is 200 to 300, which indicates an established market without excessive saturation. [L0227.008]
- On Amazon, a product needs at least one listing with a 4+ rating and at least 20 reviews. Drop it if any listing has 5,000+ reviews with a 4+ rating. The two thresholds are both kept as stated; the source does not say how they combine. [L0636.013]
- Example: a listing with about 1,400 reviews and a rating near 4 stars was estimated at roughly 10,000 orders. Heavy Amazon sales signal demand, but they also make organic TikTok sales harder. [L0372.044]

### Amazon category trees and idea lists

- Find ideas by checking your own purchase history (credit card and bank statements for online purchases), walking through department stores and Walmart, photographing potential products, and browsing Amazon's Top 100 bestsellers by category and subcategory to find under-tapped products. [L0228.006]
- Marketplace category trees, such as Amazon's, cover almost every category sold online. Browse them for individual products or small niches within large categories. *(Older advice, 2021 to 2022.)* [L0996.020]
- Browsing path: Departments > Industrial & Scientific > Robotics, then drill into the subcategories to see individual products. *(Older advice, 2021 to 2022.)* [L0996.027]
- On an Amazon results page, use the Sort by dropdown and choose Price: High to Low to see the most expensive products in a category first. *(Older advice, 2021 to 2022.)* [L0996.028]
- Case: a robotics subcategory showed 146 results. Sorting by price (high to low) revealed only a few expensive products, so the subcategory did not look rich in high-ticket items. Subcategories with few high-priced listings are weaker candidates. *(Older advice, 2021 to 2022.)* [L0996.029]
- Amazon's Industrial & Scientific department is split into many subcategories, including Cutting Tools, Fasteners, Food Service Equipment & Supplies, Lab & Scientific Products, Material Handling Products and Professional Medical Supplies. Drill into each one for individual products or small niches. *(Older advice, 2021 to 2022.)* [L0996.037]
- Example: in the Robotics subcategory sorted by price (high to low), the top items were a robot arm kit (uArm Swift Pro), an indoor GPS starter set (Marvelmind), a 1350W DC power supply (Venom Pro Power) and a robot arm (Tinkerkit Braccio). Only a few items at that price appeared among 146 results, so the subcategory looked thin for high-ticket products. *(Older advice, 2021 to 2022.)* [L0996.038]
- Free category pages on large marketplaces such as eBay and Amazon are good sources for product ideas. Search their category lists for product types you could sell. *(Older advice, 2020.)* [L0961.045]

### Libraries and physical retail

- Local libraries show real demand without ad spend. Look up the books with the highest borrow rate, or ask staff which titles are borrowed most. This works in many countries, including Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, the Philippines, the US, Canada, Germany and Europe. [L1195.012]
- Libraries are a free source for market ideas. Their special-interest magazine collections often include back issues, and their non-fiction books are sorted by topic, which makes interest areas easy to find. *(Older advice, 2021 to 2022.)* [L0996.019]
- Seeing a product stocked in physical retail, such as a seasonal costume store, is a validation signal that demand exists beyond social media. Check whether a trending gadget is also sold in shops before judging it a fad. [L1186.037]
- Products sold mainly through physical retail stores are often not yet dropshipped online. A product with that profile, a good idea and proven demand can be tested by calling suppliers. *(Older advice, 2021 to 2022.)* [L0905.012]
- Many products seen in large retail stores are sourced from AliExpress. Spotting them offline and checking their supplier is a valid method. [L0690.008]
- A product featured on a TV investment show may be worth checking as a sourcing idea if it is not yet on AliExpress. When it appears there later with only a few sellers, the number of competing listings stays low, which makes it easier to test. [L1194.056]
- As Seen On TV (free to use) is a source of product ideas. The speaker says almost anything listed there performs well, but this is an opinion, not a tested rule. [L0690.010]

### Store marketplaces: Flippa and sold stores

- Flippa lists Shopify stores for sale together with their revenue and profit figures, so it can be used to find products and niches that already sell. Browse its listings at least weekly to spot stores with working products. [L0549.001, L1184.019]
- Shopify once ran its own marketplace where every store figure was verified by Shopify. Flippa offers verified listings that work the same way. Apply the verified-listing filter in the left-hand panel and ignore unverified profit claims. [L0549.002]
- Procedure:
  1. Open flippa.com and browse Shopify store listings. [L0549.003]
  2. Apply the verified-listing filters in the left-hand panel. [L0549.003]
  3. Read the verified monthly profit or revenue of each listing. [L0549.003]
  4. For promising listings, copy the store domain and open the store. [L0549.003]
  5. Study the store's products, niche and price points. [L0549.003]
  6. If no domain is available, photograph the product image and use AliExpress image search to find the same product. [L0549.003]
  7. Search the brand in the Facebook Ad Library and check how long its ads have been running. [L0549.003]
  8. Check the age of the store and repeat this review at least weekly. [L0549.003]
- Case: a Shopify home decor store was listed on Flippa for $1,000,000. The seller claimed Shopify had verified the data and showed about $100,000 profit per month. This was not independently checked. The analyst used AliExpress camera (image) search on the store photos to find the matching supplier products. Then a Shopify best-selling collection URL was appended to the store domain to show the top sellers. The first four best-selling products were tested in Switzerland and Germany. The store sent visitors to a collection page instead of a single product page, and the ads were carousel ads showing several products with the offer "buy two, get the third free." The campaign performed well. A relaunch was planned about one month ahead of spring, because home decor demand rises in spring, while the cold, snowy months had produced little interest. [L0388.031]
- While browsing listings, also look at other niches, including print on demand, which can be tested as an additional business model. [L0549.007]

### Print-on-demand stores on Flipper

Procedure:

1. Create a free account on flipper.com and log in. [L1214.024]
2. Go to Browse, then Websites. [L1214.024]
3. Search for "print on demand," or a keyword such as "fashion," and click Search. [L1214.024]
4. Sort by highest price, highest revenue or most profitable. [L1214.024]
5. Open a store to read its monthly profit, profit margin, years in business and annual revenue. Some listings hide their figures. [L1214.024]
6. Open the About Us page, which shows the niche and sometimes admits to using print on demand. Stores without an About Us page are harder to assess. [L1214.024]
7. Read the product descriptions and check what the store sells, since descriptions can reveal the fulfillment method. [L1214.024]

### AliExpress

- AliExpress orders come mostly from Russia, other Asian countries and parts of Europe. Sales there say little about buyers in the US, UK, Canada or Australia. Use AliExpress for sourcing and quality checks, not as proof of demand in your target market. [L0335.061]
- The AliExpress app camera works as a reverse image search. Photographing a product, such as a shoe, shows matching AliExpress listings. This takes you from an ad found in AdSpy to a supplier listing within minutes. [L0661.004]
- Multiple listings of the same product with a rating of 4.6 or higher and at least 50 reviews indicate that quality is probably acceptable. More reviews make this stronger. Ordering a sample is the most certain check, but it takes time. [L1382.008]
- AliExpress and Temu hold many products, but search with a clear idea of what you want, such as personalized jewelry or fashion items. Browsing without a plan is slow. [L1108.013]

### Temu

- Product and content research sources include competitor ads, Amazon, AliExpress, Alibaba, TikTok, YouTube and Temu. Temu is cited as offering good product pictures, which are better than AliExpress pictures. [L0349.014]
- Temu best sellers can be used to find trending dropshipping products. Cross-check each product on TikTok before testing it. [L1219.039]
- Cross-check procedure:
  1. Take a product from the best sellers list. [L1219.040]
  2. Search TikTok for active organic accounts that show it. [L1219.040]
  3. Confirm proof of content by tracking the store or placing an order and checking the order number. [L1219.040]
  4. If it is proven, look for a different angle for organic posts, ads or both. [L1219.040]
- Check whether a new marketplace such as Temu offers dropshipping integrations and fulfillment before treating it as a supplier option. Confirm it works for your business model first. [L1216.032]

### Shein

Procedure for a trending dropshipping product:

1. Search Google for "bestsellers Shein," which leads to Shein's bestseller pages. [L1439.010]
2. Browse the bestsellers, starting with categories that performed well in earlier products. [L1439.010]
3. Take a phone photo of a promising product. [L1439.010]
4. Open AliExpress on the phone and use its camera search to find the same product. [L1439.010]
5. Check the supplier that appears and source the product from it, for example through CJ Dropshipping. [L1439.010]

- Trending products on Shein are often picked up by TikTok users under 25, so the same products can be advertised on Facebook in markets outside the United States. Products that already trend on one platform can be a useful source of ad products on another. [L1439.011]

### CJ Dropshipping and Alibaba

- Look for products on CJ Dropshipping and AliExpress that look eye-catching and fit your product criteria. Use CJ to find products, then compare suppliers on AliExpress, since AliExpress often offers a wider variety. [L1444.011]
- The date when a CJ product price was last updated is not a reliable sign that a product is inactive. Judge the product by its ad results and test it. [L0661.008]
- Alibaba is listed among product and content research sources. [L0349.014]

### Trend tools and free sources

- **Google Trends:** Choose a country, type in a broad niche such as "fitness," and look at the related keywords and rising searches. Check which sub-topics are rising. [L1184.017, L1184.018]
- Procedure:
  1. Choose a country in Google Trends (for example, the United States). [L1184.018]
  2. Type in a broad niche such as "fitness." [L1184.018]
  3. Scroll down to the related keywords and check which sub-topics are rising. [L1184.018]
  4. Search those keywords or products on AliExpress or Amazon. [L1184.018]
  5. Check whether the product sells well there before testing it. [L1184.018]
- **Exploding Topics** (explodingtopics.com) lists currently rising trends and lets you filter by category. Use it to check whether a product or niche is growing. [L0895.025]
- **Instagram hashtag search** can be an extra source of product ideas alongside spy tools such as Peak Star and Droppy Spy. Add promising candidates to the same ranked research list. [L0708.051]
- **Jungle Scout** shows niches and products that Amazon FBA sellers research, which can be used to find products to source on AliExpress. [L1184.021]
- **Seller Pulse** shows how many sales a product gets from a specific country. Use it to check market opportunity for a design or product before investing in branding. [L1217.030]
- **Dsmoz** is a database of niches and suppliers, with close to 400 niches and about 10,000 suppliers at the time of the call, and it was being rebuilt. Niche and supplier lists go stale quickly, so still find current suppliers by researching the future competitors of a niche. [L1287.013]
- **Callow** is a source to check for items that already sell well, including seasonal kids' toys ahead of the Q4 Christmas period. Looking there lets a beginner spot proven demand without guessing. [L1454.021]
- **Wayfair:** Best-selling products on competitor stores can be spotted before launch by checking collection pages sorted by "recommended" or best-selling on large retail sites such as Wayfair. [L0971.023]
- **Google Shopping:** Shopping ads show a product picture, title, price and retailer. Retailers upload product data to Google to advertise. The dedicated Shopping tab is useful for fast price research and is also a future marketing channel. *(Older advice, 2021 to 2022.)* [L1329.010]
- **Google Shopping, broad search:** Search the broad niche term without filters and study the first page. Google's first results reflect the products most often bought for that search term. *(Older advice, 2022.)* [L1113.009]
- Use trend tools to filter candidates, not to decide on a product. Combine them with TikTok and Temu research. [L1219.043]
- Stay open-minded and look beyond supplements. Products already selling well in other channels or marketplaces reduce guesswork. [L1454.014]

### Validate before testing

Procedure, from trend to supplier:

1. Find a trending product on Amazon Movers and Shakers or Amazon Best Sellers. [L1184.011]
2. Open the AliExpress app and tap the camera function. [L1184.011]
3. Upload a photo of the product. [L1184.011]
4. Review the similar products AliExpress returns and choose a supplier listing. [L1184.011]
5. Test the product with ads. [L1184.011]

Procedure, cost and competition check:

1. Narrow down to products you understand or care about. [L0280.002]
2. Use the Koala Inspector extension (a free Shopify spy app with freemium searches) to find competitor stores selling similar products. [L0280.002]
3. Right-click the product image and select Google Lens (built into all browsers) to reverse image search. [L0280.002]
4. Examine the results for cheap suppliers and specifically search AliExpress. [L0280.002]
5. Use the AliExpress image search browser extension to find suppliers only on that platform. [L0280.002]
6. Add the product to the supplier's cart and complete a fake checkout with a fake address to reveal the full cost, including hidden shipping fees. [L0280.002]
7. Add the supplier's product price plus shipping cost. [L0280.002]
8. Compare the total against competitor selling prices to verify profitability. [L0280.002]
9. Check the product against your selection criteria before adding it to your list. [L0280.002]

- Example: a product featured on a TV investment show, if it is not yet on AliExpress, can be checked again later; few sellers on AliExpress means fewer competing listings. [L1194.056]

## Specialty Product Types: Books, Digital Products, Print-on-Demand and Gadgets

### Kalodata book research: filter setup

The base filter set for US book research is shown below. [L0354.002]

| Filter | Value |
|---|---|
| Dates | Last 30 Days |
| Category | Books, Magazines & Audio |
| Revenue(S) | 0-10000 |
| Revenue Source (Content) | Video |
| Revenue Growth Rate | >30% |
| Avg. Unit Price($) | 30-100 |
| Region | United States |

Set the filters in this order: [L1175.007]

1. Open the product search in Kalodata and set Country to United States.
2. Set Category to Books, Magazines & Audio (the top-level category, not the subcategories).
3. Set Dates to Last 30 Days.
4. Set the Revenue ($) filter to 0 to 10K; a 0 to 100K range gives too many products and is not used as the working range. [L1175.007]
5. Set Revenue Source (Content) to Video.
6. Set Revenue Growth Rate to 30% or more.
7. Set Avg. Unit Price ($) to 30 to 100.
8. Leave all other filters (launch date, commission rate, creator number and similar) untouched.
9. Click Submit to apply the filters, then use Save selected filters to keep the setup for reuse.
10. Scan the results, discard products in the excluded categories, bundles and multi-book listings, then check the revenue trend and highest revenue videos and validate the candidates with Reddit, Amazon and emotion valence research. [L1175.007]

### Revenue range: which value applies when

The sources give different revenue ranges. Each applies to a different step.

| Range | Where it applies | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 0 to 10K (0-10000) | Filter setting in the base set and in the step-by-step procedure | L0354.002, L1175.007 |
| 0 to 100K | Not used as the working range; returns too many products | L1175.007 |
| About 0 to 8K to 10K | Practical working range; winners in this filter are typically low-revenue products, often below about $1,000 over the period | L1175.008 |
| 0 to 8K | Sweet spot for manual selection | L1175.009 |
| Up to 5K or 8K | Only if the manual scan is still manageable; above these values the list grows too quickly to check every product | L1175.009 |

### Revenue growth rate

- A growth rate above 30% narrows results to products whose sales are rising fast. The presenter argued that a higher threshold also means higher margins because costs are lower, but this is not proven, so check unit economics before acting on it. [L0354.003]
- Growth rate alone does not decide a product. A book with a negative growth rate can still be a winner, and a trend that looked strong in the past may no longer hold. Check the current revenue trend and treat it as a signal, not a guarantee. [L1175.010]

### Ranking screenshot workflow

Use this procedure to feed Kalodata ranking pages to Claude. [L0354.004]

1. In Kalodata, set the filters for the category, revenue range, growth rate and unit price.
2. On Windows, press Windows + Shift + S and drag a box around the ranking table.
3. Switch to the Claude chat and paste the screenshot.
4. Switch back to Kalodata, go to the next ranking page (page 2, 3, and so on) and repeat steps 2 to 3 for each page.
5. Once you have sent about six pages, give Claude the research prompt.

- Ranking screenshots can run past six pages, and capturing more pages gives the AI a fuller picture than a shortened sample. Six pages is a time-saving shortcut, not a rule. [L0354.028]
- Zoom the browser out before capturing so the full ranking table, including product titles and revenue columns, fits into one screenshot. [L0354.029]

### Research prompt for ranking screenshots

Use this prompt, unchanged, after the screenshots are sent. [L0354.019]

```
Hey Claude, find me a winning product that is in Kalodata. I am sending you screenshots of the Kalodata ranking with these filters: last 30 days, category Books, Magazines & Audio, revenue 0 to 10000, revenue source video, revenue growth rate above 30%, average unit price 30 to 100, region United States. Read up the demand metrics (revenue, revenue per day, revenue growth rate, items sold, launch date, creator count, creator conversion ratio, video revenue) and find which kids (genre) book has a unique mechanism and solves a specific pain point for parents and children. You may look into TikTok; I want it to be specifically organic content without paid ads. Check whether the book's author has large YouTube subscribers, or whether the book is an old book that has been in the industry for quite some time, and tell me which of these justifies its authority. Also look into the Meta Ad Library: find out whether any competitor is running the same niche title or the same book or author, and tell me how many paid Meta ads each competitor is running. Mark clearly which numbers come from my screenshots and which you could not verify, because you cannot query the Meta Ad Library directly. Then cook it for me and make me money: give me the product concept, the niche reasoning, and the next test steps.
```

[L0354.019]

- Before judging a niche in a ranking, remove unrelated genres such as romance, Bible and survival titles that add noise. Only then look at the remaining titles for real organic traction. [L0354.006]

### Book winner profile

A winning book candidate should meet several criteria at once. [L0354.007]

- A unique mechanism.
- A specific and emotionally charged parent pain point.
- Authority from a big author with large YouTube subscribers, or from an old book established in the market for many years.
- Organic traction on TikTok without paid ads.

Authority can come from two sources:

- An old book, meaning one published many years ago (for example in the 1980s), whose long market presence creates trust and authority for buyers. [L0354.008]
- A well-known author with a large YouTube audience. [L0354.008]

The winner profile for books is an older title by an aged author with a long market history and proven validation. Strong signals are high YouTube subscriber counts in the niche and active Reddit discussion in the genre niche. [L1019.033, L1195.016]

For book niches, the strongest profile is an older title by an author born in the 1950s or 1960s (boomers) or the 1970s or 1980s (late millennials), with a long market history and proven validation. Their long-running sales are a demand signal, and high YouTube subscriber counts in the niche add to it. [L1195.059]

### Pain point and mechanism

- A strong parent pain point combines the visible problem with a deeper fear behind it. For learn-to-read products, the visible problem is a child who guesses words, and the deeper fear is that the parent will fail at teaching reading themselves. [L0354.009]
- Decodable text is a useful mechanism because the child only sees letter-sounds already taught, so the child reads rather than guesses. The method also makes the parent's job scripted, which removes the need for teaching expertise and gives the product a clear hook. [L0354.010]
- Before testing a book, understand what the author or the ad is trying to say and which problem the buyer wants solved. The meaning and the audience matter more than the translation or the format of the product. [L1175.018]
- Judge each book on whether it solves a durable problem for a clear buyer. Some books tied to specific US requirements stay in demand for years, while others are short-lived fads. [L1175.020]
- A book with a map or content tied to a region far from the target market is hard to sell. Example: a map centered on the Middle East is difficult to sell to a US audience unless the buyers want to travel there. [L1175.019]

### Niche tailwinds and sub-niches

- A wider trend can strengthen demand for a niche. In the learn-to-read example, US parents rejecting whole-language reading methods and looking for phonics is a tailwind for decodable products. [L0354.011]
- Children's books cover many sub-niches: parenting and family, learn-to-read, early activity cards, financial literacy workbooks, Bible stories, handwriting and writing, and emotional or puberty guidance. Each sub-niche can be tested separately. [L0354.012]
- The same niche logic can be applied to other book genres such as gardening, construction or handyman DIY. [L0354.012]
- In the US, handyman and DIY books can have demand because hiring a contractor is expensive, so people try to do repairs themselves when they can. This is the presenter's reasoning and is specific to the US market. [L0354.013]
- Books in the kids, parenting, nursing, survival, independence and practical skills categories tend to sell well and appear among the stronger candidates. Confirm each product with the revenue trend and sales data rather than assuming the category always works. [L1175.017]
- Books are a beginner-friendly niche because they are less saturated than supplements, beauty and pet niches. Lower competition and cheaper CPC/CPM make test budgets less painful. [L1175.003]
- Spanish-language books are an untapped category, because few sellers test them. This is an opportunity for sellers who have the translation and creative skills. [L1175.038]

### Book niches to avoid

- Avoid legal, regulation and tax books, financial and investment books, and trading or chart books. These niches do not convert well, and trading content is too subjective. Financial books were specifically excluded by the source. [L1175.012]
- Avoid food and beverage (F&B) books for beginners. They show high competition and did not perform in the tested cases. [L1175.013]
- Avoid EQ, emotional intelligence, psychology and inner-child books. These niches did not perform in the tested cases. [L1175.014]
- Case: an EQ and psychology book was tested with about $1,000 in ad spend and produced little or no profit, so the test was a net loss. Avoid this niche when the budget is small. [L1175.015]
- Example: a farming book and a plumbing book were tested and did not work, although some books in the category do convert. Testing a book in an unfamiliar subject can waste budget without a clear reason to expect demand. [L1175.016]
- Skip books sold as bundles or as multi-book listings with different content. They are hard to run as a single product, even when the listing has high revenue. [L1175.011]

### Sourcing book candidates

Pull three product candidates in the same week, one from each source. [L1019.035]

1. Kalodata, filtered to Spanish (Kalodata workflow: filter by language, select Spanish, then find book ads that are already converting). [L1019.030]
2. Library or Taobao data.
3. Amazon or eBay bestsellers.

- Besides Kalodata, product sourcing can come from local libraries (books with the highest borrow rates), Taobao (items with the highest purchase counts), and the bestseller lists on Amazon and eBay. [L1019.032]
- Building an original product that follows a public method or blueprint, rather than copying an existing book, avoids rights-holder risk. The product can then stand on its own. [L0354.014]

#### Spanish-language book workflow

1. In Kalodata, filter products by language, for example Spanish.
2. Find reading-book ads that already convert in that language.
3. Convert the narration to English with an ElevenLabs voiceover swap.
4. Replace the book cover with an English version using GPT image editing.
5. Convert the ad itself to English. [L1195.009]

#### Taobao book workflow

1. Open Taobao and search for books.
2. Sort the results by the highest number of purchases.
3. Rip the video and test it.
4. If you can produce custom ads, do that for a better result. [L1195.013]

#### Amazon and eBay book workflow

1. On Amazon and eBay, sort books by the highest sales count.
2. If no VSL rips are available to pull from, build a custom VSL yourself. [L1195.015]

#### Ripping ads: conflicting guidance

The sources disagree on copying competitor ads. Both apply, depending on the step:

- The Taobao and Amazon/eBay workflows above describe ripping a video and testing it. [L1195.013, L1195.015]
- The presenter also warns not to rip ads just for the sake of ripping, and to understand the ICP and USP before testing. [L1019.034]
- Kalodata is used to find the competitor ads that sellers of a product run, and copying those ads creates DMCA and competitor-report exposure. Custom covers and custom UGC avoid matching them. [L1030.029]

In practice, the source's own guidance favours understanding the ICP and USP first and building custom ads when possible.

### Books: running an uncustomized book

- The default for running books is to customize every book before selling it, rather than listing the generic version as it is. Customization can cover the title, cover, interior content and overall look. [L1255.001]
- Customizing books is a strongly recommended best practice rather than a hard rule, so the seller ultimately decides. The recommended default is to customize each book you run. [L1255.010]
- Running a book straight off the shelf with no changes means you sell the same product as every other seller, which weakens differentiation. The speed gained by skipping customization is lost if competitors undercut the identical listing. [L1255.007]

Test-first approach for an uncustomized book: [L1255.006]

1. List the book unchanged to test demand quickly.
2. If it sells, decide to customize it.
3. Create a new, completely separate book listing with the changed title, cover or content, since the customized version cannot simply replace the original.

The trade-off is speed now versus extra work later.

### Supplements

- Avoid the supplement category unless you have significant cash reserves. Competitors in supplements generate $1M+ monthly revenue and can engage in predatory tactics. These include mass-buying your entire inventory on day one, opening all units (making them unsellable), posting 2,000 negative reviews, then returning everything for a refund, erasing your investment. This risk is too high for new sellers with limited capital. [L0228.040]
- In niches where most advertisers have poor quality scores and low CTRs, such as supplements, the platform can penalize new advertisers from the start. Expect a weaker starting position and factor it into the budget. [L0510.009]
- Beginners should first test broad, mass-appeal products such as gadgets. Supplements and other complex niches should be tested only after the beginner has the cash flow and marketing experience to handle them. [L1454.013]
- Ingredient-led supplement products such as ashwagandha were skipped during screening in the lesson, so such products need extra scrutiny before testing. [L1187.008]

#### Supplement winner screening (after filters are set)

1. Skip the first five result pages and start the review at page 6.
2. Skip products whose video ads are TikTok Shop-only and depend on the TikTok Shop platform.
3. Skip products whose ads are mostly in Spanish if you are a beginner. If you do run them, customize the landing pages and translate everything into Spanish.
4. Check the Last 30 Days revenue graph and prefer a curve that rises and falls with recovering peaks over a flat or steadily rising line.
5. Open the Video & Ad list and check the mix of top-funnel, middle-funnel and bottom-funnel ads.
6. Skip the product if nearly all ads are bottom-funnel with no variety.
7. Check that the ads use a wide range of avatars across genders, ages and ethnicities.
8. Judge the editing and creatives of the strongest ads and note which videos have the highest conversion rates.
9. Compare 30-day revenue, units sold, price, shipping fee and commission rate against the test budget.
10. Check the Last 90 Days graph. If the product peaked and is now slowing, rethink the plan or skip it.
11. Decide to build custom ads rather than copy a competitor, and plan for roughly one to two weeks before the first launch.
12. For supplements, consider timing the test toward the Q4 peak around Black Friday and Christmas.

[L1187.027]

### Electronics and gadgets

The sources disagree on electronics. Each statement applies in its own context:

| Statement | Context | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Avoid electronics as FBA products | Amazon FBA; electronics become outdated quickly and have higher defect rates than non-electronic products, limiting their appeal and longevity | L0227.041 |
| Electronic gadgets are strong niches for Facebook ads | Starting hypothesis only; validate each product with competitor research and look for a clear gap a competitor is missing | L0637.067 |
| Gadgets sell at higher prices | High perceived value; a strong supplier connection is essential because of defect risk | L0788.052 |
| Gadgets are the beginner's first test | Broad, mass-appeal products are easier to sell without deep marketing skill | L1454.013 |

- Example: a gadget seen selling on X was reported to be doing around $5K in daily sales. A visible, broad-appeal product like this is a signal worth testing when a beginner is researching what to launch. [L1454.022]
- Gadget niches such as locks often get attention without converting. Treat them as low-priority tests unless you have seen them convert. [L1186.007]

#### AliExpress electronics criteria

For electronics on AliExpress, choose products with: [L1218.027]

- An average rating of at least 4.7.
- At least one listing with more than 1,000 orders.
- About 50 to 100 plus ratings.

Check the same product on Amazon for a rating of 4 or higher.

### Digital products: principles and niche selection

- Digital products such as ebooks have no fulfillment cost and instant delivery, which makes them a low-cost way to test offers. [L1212.017]
- Digital products often have low competition, so a narrow niche topic that solves a specific problem can be tested with ads and may stand out with little rivalry. [L1212.018]
- Choose a niche that can make money, where buyers are willing to spend, and where you have real knowledge or the willingness to learn it quickly. Without knowledge you cannot provide the value that makes a buyer pay, so avoid a product about a subject you know nothing about. [L0513.007]
- Example niche categories with proven demand include health (weight loss, fitness, healthy living), financial investment, making money online, dating and relationship advice, hobbies (for example chess, where buyers may pay 20 to 30 dollars for a good ebook), language learning, and personal development. [L0513.008]
- Ebook niches suggested for testing include dating advice for young men and dating advice for women above a certain age. [L1212.019]
- Hobby niches are the easiest place to add information product offers after a physical sale, because buyers already spend money on learning and community around that hobby. Before choosing a niche, check whether paid courses, ebooks or memberships already exist for it, since that shows buyers will pay for extra value. [L0923.054]
- Digital products such as Lightroom presets, Apple themes, iPhone wallpapers and ebooks sell well when they match a passion or niche of the seller. They can be made on Fiverr if you do not create them yourself. [L0577.070]
- Platforms for digital products: Pinterest, Etsy and Facebook were named the best platforms for digital product sales. Etsy ads can be run via Google. [L0577.071]
- Sales counts shown on Etsy listings can serve as a demand signal. For example, one design selling 200 times versus another selling 7,000 times. Compare counts across similar listings before choosing which digital product to test. [L1184.066]
- Etsy hosts digital products such as iPhone icon packs and digital planners, which have no fulfillment cost because the buyer receives a download link to a file. [L1184.013]

### Digital products: ebook sourcing and reselling

- PLR Hustle is a site where private label rights ebooks can be bought, downloaded, branded and resold. ChatGPT can also be used to write an ebook from a chosen outline. [L1212.020]
- Free ebook libraries can supply ebooks that are resold or used as free upsells after a light rebranding with a new cover and after checking the content first. [L1184.015]
- Use only free-to-use stock images and legally usable templates. Do not download or resell other brands' ebooks or copyrighted content. [L0513.012]
- Digital products like printable planners or icon packs need no shipping or fulfillment, but resellers must check copyright. Ask the original seller for permission, or hire a designer on Fiverr to create a very similar product. [L1184.014]
- Etsy can be used to download and study existing ebooks in a niche to see how they are structured and what value they include. Use this only to learn the structure and gaps, never to copy the content. [L0513.041]

The sources disagree on reselling ebooks from free libraries. Use material whose license allows resale, such as PLR or free-to-use content, and never resell others' copyrighted ebooks. [L1184.015, L0513.012, L1212.020]

#### Turning a free PLR ebook into a sellable product

1. Download the ebook and check that the content is strong.
2. Replace the cover and reformat the layout in Canva.
3. Export the final PDF for delivery.

Done properly this takes roughly one hour. Sending the unchanged file is not recommended. [L0513.046]

#### Setting up a PLR or private-label digital product

1. Find digital products by checking free PLR download sites and ebook libraries as a base, then validate demand with Google Trends.
2. Create the product with a copywriter or ebook specialist on Fiverr, and make it specific to the niche and the trend, such as seasonal editions. [L0789.047]

- Use seasonal or multiple editions of a digital product, such as winter, summer and fall editions, so that a later edition can serve as an upsell. Bundle editions by category, such as relationships, growth mindset or abundance mindset. [L0789.049]
- Free ebooks work well as upsells. Offering a bonus ebook worth about $20 with a purchase increases conversion. Automating delivery through an app that sends a PDF immediately after each order is preferred over manual sending. [L1184.016]

### Digital products: validation and competitor research

#### Ebook product research (Source C)

1. Look at what big brands sell and which problems they target.
2. Choose problems that buyers actively face, such as gut health, skin, dental health or joints in pets.
3. Build one ebook per problem.
4. Check that the solution helps before creating the full product. [L1131.036]

- A recipe ebook for one problem should contain 15 to 20 recipes. With 20 recipes, a buyer using one recipe every second day has enough content for more than a month. [L1131.037]

#### Niche and competitor validation for a digital product

1. Choose a broad niche with proven money potential that you understand.
2. Narrow it to a sub-niche with a specific problem people want solved, for example weight loss for men above 40, memory loss, anti-aging or gut health.
3. Find the top five competitors selling digital products in that sub-niche.
4. Analyse each competitor's offer, copy structure, headlines, price and guarantee.
5. Build a better offer with more value and a stronger angle.
6. Create the ebook cover first and sell before the ebook is written.
7. Once orders come in, create or source the ebook and fulfil it. [L0513.009]

Find competitors by searching these places: [L0513.010]

- ClickBank (rank top offers by gravity).
- Digistore24.
- Warrior Plus.
- The Facebook Ads Library (search the problem term to see who runs ads).
- TikTok (who promotes a product on the problem).
- Google (first two result pages).
- Twitter/X.

ClickBank is the largest affiliate marketing marketplace and shows the top offers by gravity. Open the offers to study how they name the problem and persuade the buyer. Use it to learn new offers and copy structure, never to copy content. [L0513.011]

#### Pre-sale validation before writing the ebook

1. Create a book cover and a table of contents.
2. Run ads to an offer priced at 19 USD per ebook.
3. Only after people actually pay, write the full ebook, for example with ChatGPT.
4. As an alternative, buy a private label rights ebook from PLR Hustle, download it, add your own branding, and resell it.

[L1212.051]

A low-cost ebook test at about 19 USD per book was run to see whether people spend money on the offer before the full product is created. [L1212.021]

#### Pricing digital products for ads

- Before selling a product for ads, check the competitor price and the cost of acquiring one customer via Facebook ads, then price the product so the margin stays large enough. Example from the lesson: if one customer costs 13 dollars to acquire, do not price the ebook at 15. [L0513.013]
- Example: a competitor selling an ebook on quitting gaming addiction charged 27 dollars and used a personal story on the sales page. The response was judged a good but improvable offer. [L0513.014]

### Digital products: stock video and organic reach

- Digital products can be promoted by downloading free stock videos from Pexels, adding a quote on top, and posting them as short-form videos for organic reach. This aims at zero ad spend and zero fulfillment costs, but takes more time than paid ads. [L1439.013]

Stock video steps: [L1439.014]

1. Download a free video from Pexels that fits the product topic.
2. Add a short quote on top of the video that explains what the product helps with in which situation.
3. Upload the video as Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts.
4. Post consistently to generate organic traffic.

### Digital product variants: monthly plans and white-label

- Custom phone icon packs can work as a digital product for an influencer's niche, with the designs commissioned from Fiverr. Offering a monthly plan that adds new icon sets every month or season turns a one-time sale into recurring revenue. [L0789.056]
- For a physical product in a specific niche, such as photography gear, a white-label item like a tripod can be branded with the influencer's name. This gives the influencer a product that fits their audience. [L0789.057]

### Print-on-demand designs

- Print-on-demand designs sell when they tie into a trend or a strong emotional interest, such as a football team. Use names, quotes, players or memes that suggest a team instead of official logos, to avoid trademark problems. [L1214.027]

Pattern for trend-based slogans: [L1214.064]

- Formula: take a well-known phrase or catchphrase from a popular show or trend, and change it to describe an everyday activity that many people share at the same time.
- Why it works: buyers recognize the reference and enjoy wearing a joke that matches their current situation, so the product sells during that moment.
- Examples in the same pattern: "Remote and rested" for people working from home, and "Snooze and bake" for people stuck indoors during a lockdown.

### Customized and personalized products

#### Customized jewelry and products

- Customizable products with multiple options (parent and child variants, personalization features) sell better because buyers perceive higher value. [L0209.022]
- Customizable products such as engraved jewelry, bracelets, necklaces and frames can perform well, especially on TikTok. Customization creates an emotional attachment for the buyer. [L0363.010]
- Jewelry products require only still photography for ad creatives. Video content is optional. [L0209.025]
- Customizable jewelry performs well because it combines jewelry's photo-only requirement with personalization appeal. [L0209.026]
- Customized products sell better in a narrow niche than as generic items, for example jewelry tailored to a specific region or country, a specific religion, or a specific language. Pet products are another customization option. [L1017.034]
- Customized jewelry tends to sell better when it targets a narrow group, such as a necklace featuring a specific country's map, a religious symbol, or text in one language. Choose the audience first, then design the piece around it. [L1017.045]
- Customized or personalized products, such as gifts for a sister, mother or father, can work better than broad jewelry because they target a narrower buyer with less competition. Broad jewelry has many competitors and is harder to sell. [L1185.011]

#### Finding a customization niche

1. Search small, broad keywords such as "engraved", "custom", "bracelet" or "necklace" on the marketplace or research tool.
2. Repeat with other short keywords to surface more listings. [L0363.012]

#### Production, delivery and beginner fit

- Customized products justify longer delivery times, so the product page can state 7-12 days or up to 7-15 business days. [L0363.011]
- For made-to-order products like custom furniture, state the production lead time on the product page, for example four to six weeks. Customization options can be added with the Bold product options app, which has a 14-day free trial. [L0804.027]
- Custom-sized or custom-configured products sold via dropshipping work this way: the customer chooses options, the supplier builds the item to order, and then ships it to the customer. [L0805.044]
- Personalized products often sell well, but they are not recommended for complete beginners because they need more production effort and logistics to arrive undamaged. In the lesson's experience, personalized products work best in the US market. [L1172.009]

The sources give both signals: customized gifts can outperform broad jewelry [L1185.011], but personalized production is not recommended for complete beginners [L1172.009]. Start with a narrow customized niche only once production and logistics are under control.

### Category-specific warnings

- Before selling a smart home device such as a light-bulb security camera, confirm whether it needs a subscription, how footage is stored (for example an SD card slot for local playback), and what the companion app requires. Check these points in the product listing or the manufacturer's information so you can answer customer questions. [L0372.046]
- For electronics that the buyer uses on the body, order a sample and test it yourself before listing, or check the product description and manual for safety and performance. This prevents selling a poor-quality product that causes chargebacks and disputes. [L1218.038]
- Gadget niches such as locks often get attention without converting. Treat them as low-priority tests unless you have seen them convert. [L1186.007]
- Ingredient-led supplements such as ashwagandha need extra scrutiny before testing. [L1187.008]

#### Further details

- Books, supplements, and gadgets are the runnable niches discussed for this approach. The customization principle is framed around books. [L1255.002]

## Seasonality, Timing and Market Selection by Country

### Season and timing principles

- A product must match the season that is active in the target market. A cold-weather product should not run in hot summer months, and seasonal timing matters more than most beginners expect [L0347.005].
- The same offer can fail in one month and succeed in another. A winter product that did not sell in April started selling in November when the weather turned cold [L0502.034].
- A product that did poorly in August or September can be retried in November (Q4) and may perform better [L0501.034].
- Seasonal products sell most when launched well before the event, because early sellers capture most of the demand. For Christmas products, the recommended timing is a launch in late October, on Halloween or on the day after [L0352.031].
- Seasonal products can be copied quickly, and supplier shipping times can delay launches. Prepare the next seasonal product as early as possible to avoid competing with copycats [L0352.032].
- Seasonal ideas need early timing. A trend from last year, such as a holiday costume trend, is usually too late once the season has started, so list seasonal products well before the peak [L0372.018].
- Seasonal products can be planned months ahead. Check whether competitors already post content for the season, and search older seasonal terms to see whether demand existed in past years [L1186.008].
- Use Google Trends to confirm a spike before testing, and check the trend for the product itself, not only its category [L0638.025].
- Test seasonal ideas before the season begins. For a summer product, prepare the offer several weeks before the season starts [L0577.034].
- Time the test of cooling or ice-based products ahead of the warm season, so the test runs while buying interest is rising. A product tested out of season may show weak sales that do not reflect its real potential [L0657.048].
- Time the launch to the start of the season in the target market. The speaker launched a summer-type product in Australia around September, when the weather there turned warm [L0661.012].
- Seasonal products must launch in their peak window. An ice cream product tested late in summer converted poorly, and early summer (about May to June) is the better launch window [L0764.027].
- Timing can matter more than the video. A pen product generated about 30,000 USD in one month (August) with about 6 million views because it matched back-to-school demand [L0764.028].
- Start research by identifying problems or needs people have in a specific period, then look for trending products that solve them. Do not hunt for winning products at random [L1108.005].
- Before a Q4 push, choose a product unique enough to stand out in a crowded marketplace, such as one that solves a problem differently from common alternatives [L0950.068].
- Products that are not yet saturated in January and February often have low CPC, because there is less competition for ad space. If you find a working product before that period, buy stock early, since factories may close during the Chinese New Year period [L1347.026].
- Seasonal products such as kids' toys can be tested before Q4 and Christmas. Start searching early enough to have stock and ads ready before demand peaks [L1454.015].

### Seasonal calendar windows

| Product or market | Window | Note | Units |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kids toys | September to December, before Christmas and year-end holidays | High-opportunity period | [L0209.020, L1454.015] |
| Christmas products | Launch late October, on Halloween or the day after | Recommended launch timing | [L0352.031] |
| Ice cream | Early summer, about May to June | Late-summer test converted poorly | [L0764.027] |
| Back-to-school pens | August | Matched school demand | [L0764.028] |
| Cooling products | Test ahead of the warm season | Out-of-season tests understate potential | [L0657.048] |
| Gardening and fishing | March to August or September | Confirm spike with Google Trends first | [L0638.025] |
| Winter products in Switzerland | Start in October | Launched after February arrive too late before spring around March | [L0562.021] |
| Health supplements | Q4, around Black Friday and Christmas | Time the test to the peak | [L1187.009] |
| Gym and home-workout products | Q1, New Year's resolutions | Fitness products worth testing in Q1 | [L1220.021] |
| Kitchen items and home decor | End of Q4 and start of the new year | Seasonal demand | [L1172.011] |
| Home fitness and outdoor fitness | Expected to rise in January | New Year resolutions | [L1172.011] |
| Summer product (Apple Watch straps) | Summer | Prepare the offer several weeks before the season | [L0577.033, L0577.034] |
| Valentine's Day | Campaigns from late November or mid-December | Pre-test content 2 months before the event | [L0309.017] |

### Q4 and gift products

- Products that peak in Q4 (October through December) include gadgets, jewelry, kids' items, dog and pet products, fashion items, customizable gifts, toys and baby products. Gift products sell especially well because customers buy for others, not only for themselves [L0309.003].
- Gift niches that performed strongest in Q4 were kids toys, personalized jewelry and winter clothing. Christmas gifting drives this demand [L1108.006].
- Winners in Q4 included children's gifts, winter clothing, winter shoes that keep feet warm, and personalized jewelry such as name or message pieces. These categories are not to be copied exactly but used as a basis for product research [L1220.019].
- Personalized gifts and gifts for parents, kids or grandchildren sell well around Christmas and in Q4. Kids toys were also a Q4 product for the lesson's seller [L0774.045].
- Gift products such as personalized necklaces, and gifts for parents or kids, suit Christmas [L0773.047].
- Non-electronic gifts are preferred over electronics because they carry less customs and quality risk. Children's toys work well in Q4 [L1220.012].
- Giftable products tend to perform strongly in winter, but shipping times must be reliable, because late delivery is a serious risk around gift periods [L0387.036].
- Seasonal winners in Q4 2024 included:
  - hoodies that began in five simple colors and later grew into many designs;
  - family matching clothing for kids, babies and adults in the winter, when energy prices were high;
  - games, toys and puzzles, which also performed well in Q4 when people stayed at home during lockdowns [L0780.007].
- Health supplements show strong Q4 demand around Black Friday and Christmas [L1187.009].

### Climate and weather-linked products

- Fashion and seasonal apparel align with climate shifts. Push sweaters and cold-weather items in fall and winter, when customers actually need them [L0209.023].
- Look for products that solve a seasonal or environmental problem in the target market. In Switzerland, summer runs roughly from May to the end of September, so cold-weather products have demand during the rest of the year [L0492.007].
- Energy shortage concerns in Europe from 2022 onward made warmth a stronger need, which supported a cold-weather product. Watch current events that affect how people heat or warm their homes. (Dated: this reflects the 2022 situation.) [L0492.008]
- Climate-related products sell better where the cold is extreme. Sweden at minus 20 degrees compares with Switzerland at minus 4 degrees. Check where the use case is strongest before choosing the test market [L1316.028].
- Warm-weather products such as summer outfits or swimwear should be tested in warm markets such as the US or Australia rather than Europe at the start of the year. Cold-weather products, such as winter items, can be tested in every market [L1161.007].
- A season-tied product, such as golf scratch repair in winter, may have low demand at certain times. Cold and rainy weather in Europe can make a warming or comfort product relevant [L1176.009].
- In cold months in Europe and the US, products that fit the weather and winter gifting can be tested, such as heated tea cups or tea warmers. Choose products by what fits the current season in the target country, not only by what a spy tool shows [L1108.042].
- Tool-type products that solve a practical home problem may work best in Australia, the US and Canada. Weather-related products, such as summer dresses, should be tested in countries where the season is only starting, using a seasonal angle such as a pre-summer sale [L1171.010].
- Relaunch a seasonal niche ahead of its demand peak. For home decor in Switzerland, the spring cleaning season starts about one month before the relaunch, and cold, snowy months showed little interest [L0388.030].
- Weather-linked and seasonal products can be good niches, such as cooling products for summer and warm or pet protection products for winter [L0774.044].
- Niches such as camping and adventure perform well when targeting Australia, New Zealand, Canada and the US. Sub-niches with passionate audiences also work well because they make audience targeting clearer [L0788.042].
- Seasonal product example: Apple Watch straps are a summer product because people walk and do outdoor activities more and the watch is used more. Heat-friendly fabric and bright colors help. In the lesson's test, TikTok ads were cheaper per acquisition than Facebook ads for these straps. A free wallpaper or theme download was used as an add-on offer [L0577.033].

### Hemisphere shifts and extending a season

- A seasonal product can be extended by switching to a market in the opposite hemisphere. For example, a winter product can be sold to US buyers in winter while the Australian audience is in summer. This keeps sales going after the home-market season ends [L0347.006].
- Seasonal products sell well only in their season, so a seasonal brand needs extra tactics and new markets in the off-season. Testing winter products in Australia while it is summer in Europe can keep sales going [L0502.033].
- Seasons are reversed in the Southern Hemisphere. A product that sold well in the Northern winter can be tested in Southern winter markets such as Australia. Summer products that worked in the Northern hemisphere can be tested there during the Southern summer [L0562.022].
- Winter products depend on hemisphere. It is summer in the southern hemisphere while it is winter in the north, so check the target market before choosing seasonal items [L0387.036].
- Seasonal niches can be tested by checking what sells in one hemisphere's season for the other market. For example, winter products in the US can be tested in Australia during its winter. Searching for a product in the US and selling it in another market is a valid test method [L0678.031].
- Products that did well in summer can be tested in Australia, where summer starts when the Northern Hemisphere is in winter. Products that sold well in Australian summer can be tested in Europe or the US during winter [L0773.047, L1108.007].
- Products that worked in the northern summer can be tested in Australia, which enters summer in Q4 [L0774.044].

### Holiday and event launch deadlines

- A holiday is only worth targeting if there is time to prepare and run ads before it. If the holiday is only two to three weeks away, it is generally too late, so choose the next upcoming event instead [L0577.035].
- Avoid testing a product with a very close deadline, such as Halloween when it is only a day away. Products for a holiday need to be tested well ahead of time [L1220.020].
- Launch windows and deadlines differ by step, not by contradiction: the Christmas launch window is late October through Halloween or the day after [L0352.031], while a product with a deadline one day away should not be tested [L1220.020].
- Seasonal products such as Valentine's Day and Mother's Day can be sold, but orders must be delivered before the date to avoid chargebacks. The presenter avoids fixed-date products because of delivery risk and Chinese New Year timing [L1184.024].
- Q4 gift products should be tested early enough to arrive before Christmas. Establish the last date an order can be shipped and still arrive on time [L1220.013].
- For a Valentine's Day campaign, pre-test content 2 months before the event. For gift products that overlap with Christmas, such as love bracelets and charm jewelry, use the same products and content with adjusted messaging 2 weeks before each occasion [L0309.017].
- For a Valentine's Day campaign, the store is built about one month before the holiday, and the winning product should be found at least about 15 days before the holiday [L1469.023].

### Choosing the target market

- The same niche can be approved in one country and rejected in another, because competitor and supplier targets differ per market. Set the target country before grading any niche (older: Source B course, 2021 to 2022) [L0490.006].
- When researching high-ticket dropshipping products, choose the market to sell into first, then select the specific products within that market. This keeps product ideas tied to a market that can support them (older: 2021 to 2022) [L0913.001].
- Infer the target country from the competitor store. A store in US dollars and English is assumed to target the US. Traffic-estimation tools were unreliable in the mentor's own checks, so trust their country data only when it points overwhelmingly to one country [L1161.005].
- Competitors running ads for the same product usually target the same top four or five countries. Use that cluster as the starting market list for a new test, and expand to other markets only after the first data comes in [L1176.043].
- Most dropshippers in the lesson examples target the top markets of the US, UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand. Products that target the US, Australia and Canada were treated as the main markets to evaluate [L1172.008].
- Starting countries for first testing: the US, Canada, Australia and the UK are the strongest. They are English-speaking, accept credit cards and PayPal, and have good online buying habits [L0645.036]. (Conflict note: this is the default for English-speaking tests; when CPM in these markets is too high, the European choice applies instead, see the competition section.)
- The Big Five markets (USA, UK, Canada, Australia, New Zealand) are the usual default. Smaller markets such as Greece are weaker because of lower buying power and higher shipping cost, which makes dropshipping harder, even though simple pages may convert more easily there [L0691.026].
- Targeting options for initial tests: the US, the UK or Australia, or a native-language market such as Germany or France if the operator speaks that language [L1173.009].
- Test first in a market whose language you speak and whose buying habits you understand, such as your home country. There is usually less competition from dropshippers there. Once you have results you can expand, and you do not have to stay in that country [L1219.016].
- Germany, Switzerland and Austria can offer lower competition for many products and strong buying power. Test them when capacity allows [L1185.025].
- When a shortlist is built for one home market, only test products that suit that country's buyers. A list of 5 to 10 products may yield only two or three candidates for a single market such as Switzerland [L1185.039].
- For a trend-based approach, find products trending in the US or Canada over the last two months, then test them in smaller markets such as Australia, New Zealand, Germany and Switzerland [L1184.008].
- Pick products that could sell in German-speaking and English-speaking markets, such as Germany, Switzerland, Austria and Australia. Build a separate store branding and language for each market [L1431.006].
- The ideal product idea is one that is already selling well in another market and can be brought to a new one. Find the problem first, then the solution [L1432.015].
- Sending a product to multiple countries may reveal different results. A product that failed in one market can work in another. Consider countries with e-commerce potential beyond the usual German-speaking markets, and test them [L1316.027].
- Start in the country where you speak the language well. For an English speaker, that is the US. Starting in a country with a language barrier adds work at the beginning (older: 2021) [L0962.090].
- France was one of the first markets where shoppers encountered dropshipping, so French buyers easily recognize generic dropshipping stores. A French launch needs custom content and full native translation, and it still requires research into local brands and trust [L1158.052].
- In the EU, fashion is presented as a strong niche for general stores, especially in France, where fashion and orthopedic sneakers sell well. Beauty products also perform well in France [L0660.008].
- Test products through pricing and messaging in a single market first, then expand to other countries once the audience is clear [L0995.046].

### Competition, CPM and market-size checks

- Check market competition in each country before choosing it. Alternative markets such as Germany, Switzerland, Austria, the Scandinavian countries, France and Belgium were recommended over the US and Canada, where ad costs are high [L0492.013].
- Canada, Australia and the US were described as expensive for testing in recent periods, which pushed the choice toward European markets. Check current CPM in each country before choosing a test market [L1219.015].
- A store focused only on Canada usually faces less competition than a store primarily targeting the US market. The same logic applies to other English-speaking markets such as Australia or the UK (older: 2021 to 2022) [L0905.019].
- Products trending in the US can be sold in other markets, where competition is lower. A US trend tested on TikTok produced weaker results than expected [L0492.014].
- Choose products that are trending in the United States and sell them in other markets such as Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Australia, New Zealand or Canada. Competition there is lower, and the combined German-speaking market (Germany, Switzerland, Austria) is about 100 million people [L0519.019].
- Saturation in the US does not rule out a product. Being an early adopter in a new market and offering a better offer can still produce strong results, even if many advertisers run the same product in the US [L0519.020].
- Avoid launching a product in the United States when it is already heavily sold there, since saturation makes it hard to win. Test instead in markets where the same product is not yet common, such as Australia, New Zealand, Germany, Switzerland or Austria [L0661.005].
- Products already advertised heavily in one market are proof of demand, so they are a good starting point for research. Take such a product and test it in a different market where competition is lower [L0661.001].
- An ad running in only one country tells you that the product may already sell there, not that it will fail elsewhere. A product with strong engagement in one market can be tested in another [L0661.006].
- A product that is saturated in the US, which has high CPMs, can still be a valid candidate when moved to a cheaper market, where competition is often lower and ads cost less. Test the transferred product in the new market before judging it [L1161.011].
- Target countries where the product is in season and CPMs are lower. For seasonal holidays such as Halloween, consider other countries with lower CPM if the US CPM is too high [L0773.048].
- Halloween is celebrated in many countries, not only the US. For seasonal demand such as Halloween, sell in countries where CPM is lower if the US CPM is too high [L0774.046].
- Niche criteria must be adjusted to the market size. The US demand numbers are not comparable with Canada because of population differences [L0805.042] (2024).
- Countries with small populations, such as Canada, do not work with the same niche criteria as the US. Use revised criteria for smaller markets instead of applying US thresholds [L1285.013] (2024).
- For a demand test in a smaller country, a population share can justify a lower target. If the UK has about 20 percent of the US population, either find a bigger niche or move one level broader rather than lowering the target blindly [L0962.089] (older: 2021).
- The US niche validation uses a demand threshold of 10,000. Smaller markets such as Australia have fewer sub-niches, so sellers there may need to niche up a level to reach that threshold (older: 2020) [L1088.003].
- Niches selling to a small population should be widened to a broader category so enough visitors arrive. Large-population markets can use very specific niche stores, which convert better (older: 2020) [L1111.010].
- Pandemic conditions in 2020 did not change the product selection criteria. Recession or fear-driven concerns should not be used to drop a niche that passes the tests, because online buying remained strong (older: 2020) [L0967.011].

### Research steps for a new country

1. Set a VPN to the target country, then search the supplier name or product on Google Shopping to see the local results (older: 2022) [L0665.008].
2. Use the Source A research tool with the target country selected to see whether people search for the product there (older: 2022) [L0665.008].
3. Search results depend on location. When researching a market for a country you do not live in, use a VPN and set the location to the country you plan to sell in, or results may come from your home country or other countries (older: 2021 to 2022) [L1329.012].
4. Use a VPN set to the target country so Google returns local results. Without it, search results in another country distort competitor and niche findings (older: 2021) [L1279.014].
5. Market size check for the Facebook Ad Library:
   1. Search for the outlook for growth or market valuation of the industry (for example the pet industry).
   2. Check the ad library for each target country (for example Germany) to see how many sellers run ads there.
   3. Countries with lower saturation are better test markets [L0895.023].
6. Facebook Ad Library country check:
   1. Search a product keyword in the Facebook Ad Library and use the country filter to limit results to one market, such as the United States.
   2. Compare it with a test market such as Germany. Low scaling in the test market suggests room for a new seller [L0895.036].
7. Check whether a product is popular in each target country before testing. A product that sells well in one country may not sell in another. For example, air fryers are less common in Switzerland than in the US [L1176.010].
8. Compare the new country's shipping infrastructure and supplier responsiveness with a market you already know. Check how quickly suppliers reply and how reliably parcels arrive before committing money to ads or inventory [L1441.045].

### Language, translation and language arbitrage

- Test products with English-speaking markets before translating the store into other languages, even if competitors are not marketing there. Translation requires both professional translation services and a customer service virtual assistant fluent in that language, which adds significant cost and complexity [L0280.006].
- Start product research with English-language ads. The US English market has a larger total addressable market (TAM) than smaller language markets. Study which creatives and messages already run there before looking at underserved markets [L1195.055].
- Language arbitrage: take an ad that already converts in one language and run it in a language market that has not seen it yet. The Spanish-speaking market in the US has about 60 million people, a smaller total addressable market than the English market, but far less competition [L1195.008].
- The Spanish-language market in the US is largely untapped. Its total addressable market is smaller than the white and Black American markets, but auctions are less saturated, so demand is proven while competition is not [L1019.029].
- Products whose ads are mostly in Spanish can be run, but only if the landing pages are customized and everything is translated into Spanish. This is harder for a beginner, so beginners should skip Spanish-language ad products at the start [L1187.007].
- Taobao videos mostly feature Asian presenters and may underperform in the US market. Recast them with white or Black American talent when producing custom ads for the US [L1195.014].
- When the market is English-speaking, a product that worked for a long time there can be tested in other languages such as German or French. Native-language markets often have less competition [L1173.008].
- Validate a product that sells well in one country by running the same product with ads in the language of another target market. If the new market also shows a strong hook rate and CTR, the product is worth more store work [L1108.041].
- When testing an ebook or digital product in a new country, translate the mockup and ad copy into that country's language before running ads. The lesson's example built a German mockup for a German market test, which makes it possible to judge whether the offer itself is attractive to local buyers [L1131.063].
- Entering an untapped market needs only minimal effort beyond the product. Native translations and local payment methods are required, and Stripe lets you enable the most used payment methods for each country. Custom branding or UGC is not needed from the start [L1158.013].
- Study what works in other markets to find message patterns, but do not copy a competitor's exact wording. Adapt the underlying structure to your own market [L0378.014].
- Pricing differs by market. Australian dollars look cheap to US buyers, so pricing and currency must be checked per country [L0995.046].
- When pricing in countries where the local currency is significantly smaller than USD (such as Malaysia at 4 MYR to 1 USD), do not automatically adjust price points by converting wholesale cost. Validate your intended prices against what other online stores in that country are selling for, and use market-based pricing (older: 2022) [L0249.103].
- For an Italian-market test in Q4, classic, mid-priced jewelry was suggested because Italian buyers were said to prefer classic styles over expensive fashion. Treat this as a hypothesis and validate it with a small test budget before scaling [L1219.058].

### Testing a proven product in a new market

- Do not reinvent the wheel. Take a product that sells well in one market and test it in a market where nobody is selling it in volume. Check the product in the new market before scaling [L0388.026].
- Start by testing products that already show scaling ads in the USA or Australia, because a product that works there may also work in other countries. Adapt the store to the new market, including language and payment methods [L0361.017].
- Differentiating by market: take a product proven in the US and launch it in English-speaking countries such as Australia, New Zealand, the UK and Canada, or in European markets such as Germany, France, the Netherlands and Switzerland. Check in the Facebook Ad Library whether the product is scaling in the new market. Low competition there is the differentiator [L1158.012].
- Comfy case: a sleeved blanket, first sold in the US market, was adapted with minor product and design changes and launched in Australia and New Zealand, reaching over 300 million dollars in sales. The same concept was later launched in Switzerland under a different brand name by another seller, who knew the market well and sold well there [L1158.014].
- Question for research into a new product market: if a product is not selling in a new country, check whether competitors exist there, whether their store and ads are good, and whether the market accepts this product type. A lack of sales usually comes from missing trust, missing native-language content, or the market not yet knowing the product, which requires educating customers [L1158.042].
- Competitor products proven in one market can be tested in another by copying the product and store and changing the store currency (for example to euros or Australian dollars) and the language. Stores in weak condition with good ad counts still prove the product sells, so the offer and store can be improved [L1161.010].
- Example Swiss test: an early dropshipping test in Switzerland with about 200 to 300 USD in ads produced roughly 3,000 CHF in sales. That low-spend result was the signal to test the product further [L0492.010].
