- A/B testing should be iterative and ongoing: after a win is achieved and deployed, continue testing different recommendation ranking logic, design variations, and customer segments to identify further improvements beyond the initial test. [L0197.024]

- Do not turn off ad campaigns after 1 or 2 days unless performance is extremely poor; analyze performance around day 3, not before, because early data is incomplete. [L0280.015]

- Testing optimization priority: (1) Find creative with high CTR (1%+ on Facebook, high engagement rate on TikTok), this proves ad is getting attention. (2) Once creative is locked, test offer variations (discount level, bundle structure, bundle price) to find highest converter. Don't optimize both simultaneously, isolate variables. [L0307.028]

- If testing different offers, maintain consistency first. Don't increase price mid-campaign because sales slowed-lower the price back to consistency baseline. Test one variable at a time. Kill offers that don't work; keep and duplicate what works. [L0308.030]

- 1. Pick one element to test, such as a bonus offer or the button text. 2. Run version A for one week with enough traffic. 3. Run version B the following week and compare the results. Use this only when enough visitors come in, because time-based testing is less reliable. [L0356.042]

- Page-builder based split testing changes the content on the same URL and shows each variation to about 50 percent of visitors, instead of splitting URLs. Typical test items are offers, bonus items, and button text. [L0356.043]

- In Google Optimize, the weights of the variants determine the share of traffic each receives. With three variants use 33 percent each; with two variants use 50 percent each; any uneven split can be set to favor one variant. [L0387.011]

Set up a split test in Google Optimize:
1. Create the page variants, one per angle or version you want to test.
2. Open Google Optimize and set up a split test (A/B test).
3. Add the variants and set the traffic weights (e.g., 33/33/33 for three variants, 50/50 for two).
4. Copy the generated link and use it in ads, bio, or organic posts.
5. Read the performance data per variant to see which one converts best.
[L0387.012]

- Testing completely different marketing angles in one split test (for example gaming, home decor, and a therapeutic angle for the same product) shows which audience converts best, without needing separate ads for each angle. [L0387.013]

- When the target audience and angle are already known, test one element of the landing page at a time (for example the headline first for about five days, then the product pictures, then the brag bar), because changing several elements at once makes results hard to attribute. Only test multiple different angles together when the audiences and angles are truly different. [L0387.014]

- ABC testing adds a third or further variant of the same element, for example three possible positions for the add-to-cart button, with traffic split across all variants. Multivariate testing combines several elements, such as 3 button sizes and 3 copy options, which means 9 combinations and a much larger sample size. [L0390.009]

- Test conversion changes one at a time and expect a result over a fixed period, such as two weeks. Run changes long enough to measure a clear result before adding the next change, so the cause of any sales movement is identifiable. [L0410.011]

- Change tests every one to two weeks is a typical rhythm for active store owners, so a changelog becomes necessary early on. Log each change with its date and platform so that the many simultaneous tweaks can be separated later. [L0410.012]

- A candidate test worth logging as an idea is replacing an exit-intent offer of a percent-off discount code with a short product-finder quiz that routes visitors to the product type that suits them. Writing the idea into the changelog before testing it means it can be found again later, so it is not forgotten or retested blindly. [L0410.013]

- A/B testing compares two versions of one element to check one specific hypothesis. For example, you could test whether moving the add-to-cart button higher on the product page increases conversions. [L0423.007]

- Split testing compares two distinct solutions against each other to see which performs better. For example, two different brand or product options can be shown to visitors to find the stronger one. [L0423.008]

- A/B/C testing checks one hypothesis against three potential solutions. For example, it can show which of three positions for a call-to-action button converts best. [L0423.009]

- Multivariate testing examines a complex hypothesis that combines several variables, which makes it the most complicated method. The number of combinations equals options multiplied by variants: 3 options for 2 variants gives 9 combinations, and 3 size options with 3 copy options gives 9 combinations for one call-to-action. [L0423.010]

- Each version in a test needs a sufficient sample, with the benchmark being about 10 samples per version. Results from smaller samples are unreliable. [L0423.012]

- Running split tests is technically demanding, so setup errors can easily invalidate results. Verify that each variant is delivered correctly before reading the data. [L0423.013]

- Test several ebook cover designs for the same product to see which one converts best, instead of committing to the first cover. Change only the cover between tests so the result shows which design performs. [L0513.042]

- For an A/B test, aim for at least 1,000 samples per variant before treating the result as meaningful. In a 50/50 split this means 2,000 total recipients or visitors in the funnel, not 500 per variant. [L0570.001]

- A result at 1,000 samples per variant can reverse once more data arrives, because small samples produce unstable winners. The confidence score rises as the sample grows, so decisions should wait for more data where possible. [L0570.002]

- The three elements with the largest effect on conversion to test are images, headlines and colors. Focus tests on these before smaller changes. [L0570.008]

- Declaring a winner after only 1,000 samples per variant risks choosing a version that loses once more data is collected. Wait for a larger sample before acting on a result. [L0570.012]

- Split testing compares two versions of one element, such as an opt-in pop-up offering 15% off the first order versus one offering a free set of examples. The winning version is the one that earns more money, which can differ from the one with more sign-ups. [L0572.011]

- Judge the landing page by its add-to-cart rate and judge creatives by CTR and CPC, so each asset is optimized on the metric that matches it. Use a sample of about 200 landing page visitors before judging a change. [L0871.028]

Test the five first-view elements:
1. Create a version of the page with three features or elements in the first view.
2. Create a second version with five features or elements in the first view.
3. Run both versions in an A/B test and measure the conversion rate of each version.
4. Keep the version with the higher conversion rate.
[L0916.023]

- 1. Split incoming shoppers 50/50 and show the pre-purchase return option to only one group. 2. Keep the other group on a normal cart and checkout with no return option. 3. Run the test for about two weeks, recording checkout conversion, cart abandonment and AOV for both groups. 4. If the option group does not lose conversion and AOV rises, test two fee levels such as $2.99 and $3.99 and compare uptake. 5. Roll out the fee that gives the best uptake without a drop in conversion. [L0955.054]

- Price testing in Shopify by changing the price of the live store is less reliable than split testing, because it compares two periods rather than two groups at the same time. Use split testing for prices. [L0999.067]

## Prioritizing and running the optimization plan

### Entry conditions: when conversion work starts

- Start optimizing as soon as the store makes its first sale, because that proves the checkout works and customers want the product. Before any sale, begin conversion work once the store reaches about 40 unique visitors per day. [L1293.001]
- At 40 unique visitors per day, the store should make at least one sale every other day. If it does not, fix the conversion problem before spending more on traffic. [L1293.002]
- Run these basic checks first: 1) confirm Google Product Listing Ads are running, 2) confirm Amazon Product Listing Ads are running, 3) confirm the store has at least 50 products. [L1293.003]
- Action plan from the lesson, in order: [L1293.034]
  1. Check traffic and confirm at least 40 unique visitors per day. [L1293.034]
  2. If traffic is low, confirm Google Product Listing Ads and Amazon Product Listing Ads are running. [L1293.034]
  3. Set up free bonus gifts for the top three products. [L1293.034]
  4. Brainstorm on paper or log into the shop and make the changes. [L1293.034]

### Order of operations

Work in this sequence. Each step points to the section that holds its full detail.

1. **Confirm entry conditions.** Traffic, basic ad checks and the 50-product minimum from the entry section come first. [L1293.001, L1293.002, L1293.003, L1293.034]
2. **Audit the store as a paid visitor sees it.** Run the cold-visitor review, then the full-funnel audit at about one and a half months in. [L1346.035, L1017.005]
3. **Choose where to focus.** Rank products by traffic and work on the products that already get visitors. [L1446.013, L1446.014, L0208.007, L0941.049]
4. **Build the first product page, then duplicate it.** Build the page structure on one product page first. Once its add-to-cart ratio meets the platform minimum, duplicate that page for the other products. [L1194.032]
5. **Run the conversion setup in order.** Follow the setup sequence. [L0393.009]
6. **Roll out the marketing message in stages.** Start with best-sellers, test, then extend. [L0396.034]
7. **Build the test backlog and run tests continuously.** [L1364.004, L0399.001, L0399.019]
8. **Hold the weekly routine.** [L1293.005, L1088.060, L0390.051]
9. **Change scale or strategy only on evidence.** Use the scaling, cut and maintenance rules. [L0686.012, L0744.053, L1228.008, L0639.046]

### Store audit procedures

#### Cold-visitor review

*Older (2021-22)? No. Source: Source A, undated.*

Review a store the way a cold visitor from a paid ad sees it:

1. Note the product and offer promised by the ad that brought the visitor. [L1346.035]
2. Open the homepage and check within a few seconds whether it shows the same product type, and whether a stranger can tell what the store sells. [L1346.035]
3. Open a product page and check whether the featured image shows the product clearly, whether the description sells it with benefits, features and dimensions, and whether reviews, stock count, delivery estimate and live chat link are visible. [L1346.035]
4. Check the product page tabs or sections for the description, the shipping policy and any price match policy. [L1346.035]
5. Scroll to the footer and check that get-in-touch details, support hours, support email, live chat link, social media links and policy links are present and point to relevant pages. [L1346.035]
6. Check that the social media accounts exist and show recent activity. [L1346.035]
7. Write down every point where you would hesitate to buy, and fix those points first. [L1346.035]

#### Full-funnel audit at about six weeks

1. Once the store is built and ads are running, around one and a half months in, audit the whole store. [L1017.005]
2. Go through every page and every step of the funnel from the ad click to the completed order, including minor details that tutorials may not cover. [L1017.005]
3. Look for small problems that cause drop-off, such as a missing element or unclear step, instead of waiting for the student to report low conversion or many abandoned carts. [L1017.005]

#### Standing assumption

- Assume your store has issues that need constant fixing, since even large companies have teams fixing bugs and reports every day. Regularly review your store with fresh eyes and check trends in your data. [L0390.051]

### Setup and rollout sequences

#### Conversion setup, in order

1. Install an urgency app and a review app on Shopify. [L0393.009]
2. Modify the content page templates. [L0393.009]
3. Create Facebook and Instagram business pages. [L0393.009]
4. Install Klaviyo on Shopify. [L0393.009]
5. Set up automated emails and actions for bounced visits and abandoned carts. [L0393.009]
6. Apply for a financing app. [L0393.009]
7. Complete all remaining conversion action tasks. [L0393.009]

#### Marketing message rollout

*Older (2021-22): Source B.*

1. Start with the best-selling products, not the whole catalogue. [L0396.034]
2. Test the new descriptions against the old ones. [L0396.034]
3. Optionally run conversion rate tests and compare the results. [L0396.034]
4. If the new approach works, implement it across the rest of the products. [L0396.034]

#### Seven store optimizations for a winning product with no sales

Run these in this order when a winning product gets traffic but no sales:

1. Split-test landing page design or theme. [L0773.009]
2. Test prices. [L0773.009]
3. Test lead magnets (free gifts). [L0773.009]
4. Add automatic discounts. [L0773.009]
5. Improve copywriting. [L0773.009]
6. Improve product description and trust signals (images, GIFs, reviews). [L0773.009]
7. Break down ad data by placement, gender, age and country before relaunching. [L0773.009]

#### Store optimization sequence (alternative order)

*Source: Source C. No trigger stated. See the conflicts section.*

1. Test different themes. [L1108.024]
2. Test different bundles. [L1108.024]
3. Test different prices. [L1108.024]
4. Add a clear sense of urgency. [L1108.024]
5. Improve the copywriting on the store. [L1108.024]
6. Once the conversion rate is good, keep scaling the product. [L1108.024]

*Mistake to avoid:* Do not leave the store unchanged from day one while only adjusting ads. Working on the store is part of testing every product. [L1108.025]

### Choosing where to focus

#### Product pages first

- Improving product pages where you already receive traffic increases conversion rate without requiring additional ad spend, directly improving ROAS. This is the highest-leverage starting point for optimization. [L0208.007]
- Improve product page optimization for products that already convert before scaling their traffic. Better pages turn the same clicks into more sales. [L0941.049]
- Optimize the top 20 percent of product pages first, since they usually produce about 80 percent of sales, and then work through the remaining products. [L0966.072]
- Optimized product pages support free Google traffic, Google Ads clicks and conversions, so optimizing the products already getting traffic gives the fastest return. [L0966.073]
- Start conversion work on pages that already get the most traffic, since these produce the fastest gains. Check Google Analytics for your most visited pages before deciding what to change. [L0972.035]

#### Ranking products by traffic

Two cut-offs appear in the sources. Both are kept here, and the sources do not say which applies to which store size.

1. Look at the product analytics and rank all products by the traffic they receive. [L1446.013]
2. Identify the top 100 products that actually get visitors. [L1446.013]
3. Focus optimization on those product pages rather than trying to perfect every page. [L1446.013]
- Focus optimization effort on the top 20% of products that receive traffic, since these are likely to be the initial money makers. Other products can wait until traffic data shows they matter. [L1446.014]

#### 80/20 across pages and channels

- Use the 80-20 principle for SEO optimization: start with the top 20% of pages by traffic. Optimize these first to boost conversions, then slowly expand to other pages. Do not try to optimize the entire catalog on day one. *Older (2022).* [L0249.033]
- Use an 80/20 approach when deciding where to focus: for an established store of about three to four years, paid search and organic search are almost always the largest traffic sources and therefore where conversion work has the most impact. Compare sources in Google Analytics to see which converts and which does not. *Older (2021-22).* [L1456.004]
- Focus on the top 20% of products by traffic and conversion first. (Derived from the two rules above.) [L1446.014, L0966.072]

#### Representative analysis

- Changing website elements at random based on personal opinion wastes effort. Improvements should follow from evidence of what customers need to see to move toward purchase, judged with empathy and in comparison with competitor pages. *Older (2021-22).* [L1456.035]
- When a competitor comparison reveals a problem on one product, the same problem usually exists on other products in the store. Analyse a few representative products in the comparison matrix instead of checking every product separately. *Older (2021-22).* [L1456.039]

#### Traffic versus conversion

- If traffic is high but conversions are low, improve the product page and retarget visitors. If traffic is low, first focus on getting relevant traffic. Conversion levers include social proof and compelling offers, and retargeting drove most of the owner's sales. [L1077.040]
- When traffic already arrives but sales lag, improve the conversion rate before buying more traffic. A store's conversion rate is never finished and should be improved continuously. *Older (2019).* [L0663.034]
- On-site conversion changes produce small, incremental gains and do little if the traffic is poorly matched to the offer or the offer itself is weak. Fix the audience match and the offer before spending time on these details. *Older (2021-22).* [L1522.001]

### Checklists

#### CRO action checklist (full sequence)

*Older (2021-22): Source B. Google Optimize and Neat are named as in the source; check that each tool is still available before use.*

1. Set up a CRO tracking system, such as a Trello board, spreadsheet, Google Sheet, Asana or another project management tool, to log every conversion test. [L0399.001]
2. Connect a CRO testing tool to the e-commerce site (Google Optimize or the Neat A/B testing tool on Shopify), and test with one or both. [L0399.001]
3. Fill the first column of the tracking system with a list of future CRO tests, based on what you think needs testing after reviewing the material. [L0399.001]
4. Review your competition analysis, covering competitors' offers and USPs. [L0399.001]
5. Compare your current offer with competitors and judge where you stand in your market. [L0399.001]
6. Improve the offer toward a strong C.U.R.V. offer where you are behind, and record it in the curve offer builder. [L0399.001]
7. Show the curve offer on the home page, product page and About Us page at minimum. [L0399.001]
8. Review product descriptions against the marketing message parts. [L0399.001]
9. Write a marketing message for one or more current bestsellers, or for high-traffic products with low conversion rates, and share the mechanism with any external copywriter. [L0399.001]
10. Implement the review multiplier call system, share the script with customer service, and schedule post-purchase calls. [L0399.001]
11. Add video review requests to every review request, with image reviews as a second option. [L0399.001]
12. Set up the off-site customer survey and the emails that invite visitors, opt-ins, pre-purchase prospects and existing customers to take it, choosing questions from the template list. [L0399.001]
13. Choose and implement one on-site survey mechanism, such as an online chat widget or Hotjar. [L0399.001]
14. Identify other on-site CRO tests, plan them and start testing. [L0399.001]
15. Review the list of smaller on-site factors and add the promising ones to the test plan. [L0399.001]
16. Keep the surveys and testing running continuously. [L0399.001]

#### On-site factors procedure

*Older (2021-22).*

1. Check whether your store already does each factor. [L1522.002]
2. For each factor you do not yet have or are unhappy with, add it to a conversion test backlog (a Kanban-style board such as Trello works). [L1522.002]
3. Decide when and how each test will run, then implement and measure it. Not every factor has to be implemented. [L1522.002]

#### Checklist of easy wins

- If visitors come to the store but do not buy, work through a list of 18 easy-win conversion tips before making deeper changes. *Older (2018).* [L1274.007]

### Test backlog and test design

- Keep at least one conversion test running at all times and treat testing as a permanent item on the to-do list. Even small tests add up to long-term change, and new test ideas should always be collected. *Older (2021-22).* [L1364.004]
- Conversion rate optimization is an incremental process built from many small, repeatable improvements. Waiting for one rare change that doubles conversion rate is not a plan for growth. *Older (2021-22).* [L1364.002]
- Make many small changes to the store, such as offer placement and wording, and test them one after another rather than waiting for one large redesign. Each small published change can noticeably move results, so check the effect of every change. [L0549.053]
- Store design tests make sense only after the store already makes sales. Before that, use design changes only when the offer and the traffic are both confirmed to be working. [L0388.005]
- Rewrite the marketing message first for products that already sell well. Then prioritize products with high traffic but low conversion rates, since they offer the biggest conversion upside. *Older (2021-22).* [L0399.011]
- Add the smaller on-site factors that may improve conversion to the test plan, and test them after the larger tests are planned. Use the tracking system for this list too. *Older (2021-22).* [L0399.019]
- Many popular conversion tips and hacks change very little on their own. The larger gains usually come from fundamental changes to the store, offer and purchase path, so these should be prioritized over minor tweaks. *Older (2021-22).* [L0598.002]
- Conversion improvements fall into two kinds: quick actions that can be taken immediately, and ongoing processes that take weeks or months to build and pay off. Both should be planned, and the ongoing ones should be treated as continuous work inside the business. *Older (2021-22).* [L0598.003]
- Conversion optimization is a foundational system. These 11 tasks form a foundational conversion system that requires continuous revisiting and refinement beyond initial implementation. [L0040.010]

### Quick wins versus tests

- Split the roadmap into quick wins (fixes to do now, such as making a guarantee, free shipping or free gifts visible) and testing ideas (hero positioning, risk reversal, comparison modules), and tag each with the metric it should move. [L0886.020]
- In an example 30-day roadmap, the first block (days 1 to 3) was labelled a quick win with high impact. The days 1 to 5 block included rewriting the homepage hero to explain the premium tool, its technology and its benefits (less damage, less frizz, less styling time); adding a comparison section against standard hot tools near the homepage and product page; and making the guarantee, free shipping and free gifts visible, which was rated low effort. The metrics to improve were homepage conversion rate, product page engagement, add-to-cart and checkout start. [L0886.035]

### 30-day CRO roadmap

#### Prompt

Use this prompt to turn a store review into a plan:

```
Turn this review into a 30-day CRO plan. Rank each step by expected impact, amount of work, and how confident we are it will succeed. Separate immediate improvements from experiments, and name the metric each change is meant to move.
```

[L0886.004]

#### Roadmap layout

The roadmap has these columns: Timing, Priority, Impact, Confidence, Metric to Improve, with rows of actions. The example timings are below. Cells marked "not stated" are not given in the source.

| Timing | Priority | Impact | Confidence | Metric to Improve |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Days 1-3 | Quick win | High | not stated | not stated |
| Days 1-5 | not stated | not stated | not stated | Homepage CVR, product page engagement, ATC, checkout start |
| Days 4-7 | not stated | not stated | not stated | not stated |
| Week 2 | not stated | not stated | not stated | not stated |
| Week 3 | not stated | not stated | not stated | not stated |
| Week 4 | not stated | not stated | not stated | not stated |

[L0886.019]

Metrics named in the roadmap include CVR (homepage and product page), PDP engagement, ATC (add to cart) and checkout start. [L0886.019]

Example content for the days 1 to 5 block is in the quick wins section. [L0886.035]

### Weekly routine and ongoing maintenance

#### Weekly cycle

- Repeat the full optimization process every week, for example every Monday, instead of doing it once, because a store either grows or slips backwards. [L1293.005]
- Conversion optimization is an ongoing process. After the initial setup, keep checking how ads and pages perform over time and review each optimization area again. *Older (2020).* [L1088.060]
- Monitor ad spend every two weeks (self-auditing), identify ads and products not generating profitable sales, and verify ROAS is stable or improving. *Older (2020).* [L0245.043]

#### Reading trends

- A small, short-term dip in traffic or sales is not always a problem. Check whether it continues into the next weeks before concluding something is broken. *Older (2020).* [L1088.061]
- Slow sales periods are a good time to work on conversion rate optimization, adding products and suppliers, improving content, and expanding sales channels. The aim is to be ready when orders return at a higher rate. *Older (2021).* [L0801.117]

#### Measuring compounded gains

- Improving each funnel step by 10% compounds: 1.1 x 1.1 x 1.1 = 1.331, so three separate 10% gains give about 33% total, not 30%. Funnel steps to optimize include the visit to next-page rate, the add-to-cart rate, the checkout click rate, abandoned-cart recovery, and pre-purchase emails. [L0572.013]

### Dashboard organization

- Organize the dashboard with decision metrics on the left, top-of-funnel metrics in the middle, and bottom-of-funnel metrics on the right. This structure allows you to see everything that drives daily decisions without scrolling, then use the funnel metrics (reach, impressions, link clicks, add to carts, checkouts, purchases) to quickly identify where drop-offs occur in the customer journey. Everything you need to make decisions should fit on one screen. [L0290.009]

### CRO team and agency compensation

- CRO agency success is harder to measure than paid media because conversion improvement is influenced by many factors. Structure compensation as base plus incentive tied to incremental revenue or conversion rate improvement, but beware revenue share percentages that favor the agency. [L0217.036]

### Ad-level and product-level cuts

#### First 24 hours (ad level)

- Within the first 24 hours, evaluate individual ads within the ad set (not the ad set level). Turn off any single ad that has spent $10 or more, shows a cost per unique link click (CPC) of $3.50 or higher, and has generated no add-to-cart events or purchases, because such CPC is not sustainable long-term. [L0229.003]

#### Product break-even (product level)

- A product with no sales in its first two days can still become profitable after the landing page or offer is fixed and the ads have collected more data. Cut a product at the pre-set break-even limit rather than at the first disappointing day, and change one weak funnel stage at a time. [L0639.046]
- Changing the ad budget at product level: monitor, cut, redirect and verify. (See the reallocation procedure below.) [L0245.043]

#### Reallocating budget from losers

*Older (2020): monitoring every two weeks.*

1. Monitor ad spend every two weeks (self-auditing). [L0245.043]
2. Identify ads and products not generating profitable sales. [L0245.043]
3. Cut spend from underperforming products entirely. [L0245.043]
4. Redirect that budget to products that are converting or have historically converted. [L0245.043]
5. Verify return on ad spend (ROAS) is stable or improving. [L0245.043]

#### Recovering a store that almost breaks even

*Older (2022).* To improve a store that is almost breaking even after several months of ads:

1. Review all ad and analytics data to see which ads and products lead to the best results. [L0803.056]
2. Identify losing products because of low margin, supplier issues or high ad cost. [L0803.056]
3. Stop advertising losers, renegotiate with the supplier, or focus only on organic traffic for them. [L0803.056]
4. Reinvest the cut budget into the top 20 percent of products and optimize those product pages for higher conversion. [L0803.056]

#### Launch budgets

- Pouring large budgets into untested campaigns is a mistake. Start with small budgets to see if a campaign is profitable before scaling, and if results are poor, delete and restart the campaign rather than modifying it extensively. *Older (2020).* [L0210.027]

### Scaling and changing strategy

#### Scaling checks

- Cost structure example: £15 cost per £45 sale equals 33% of revenue spent on ads. Use this ratio when calculating whether to double budget during 4-hour scaling checks. [L0308.011]

#### Raising bids

- To justify a higher bid while keeping your target profit per sale, you must first raise the conversion rate. Confirm that the new bid is profitable at your current conversion rate before increasing it. *Older (2021-22).* [L0686.012]

#### Google Shopping ceiling

- Once the profitable Google Shopping limit is reached, raising conversion rate is the only remaining lever inside that channel, and it also has a ceiling. After that, keep the account profitable in maintenance mode and focus on other channels. *Older (2021-22).* [L0744.053]

#### Low conversion on paid traffic

*Older (2021-22).*

1. Check that the traffic targets the right audience. [L1228.008]
2. If the ads look good but conversions are low, reduce ad spend. [L1228.008]
3. Focus effort on the website and raise the conversion rate. [L1228.008]
4. Increase ad spend again only once the website can support the cost of the traffic. [L1228.008]

#### Scaling a product

- Build the page structure on one product page first, and duplicate it only after its add-to-cart ratio meets the platform minimum. [L1194.032]
- Improve product page optimization for products that already convert before scaling their traffic. [L0941.049]

### Where sources disagree

1. **Design changes before or after sales.** Source C says store design tests make sense only after the store makes sales, and before that only when the offer and traffic are confirmed to work. [L0388.005] Source A says to start conversion work at the first sale, or before any sale at about 40 unique visitors per day. [L1293.001] Source C also says not to leave the store unchanged from day one. [L1108.025] Apply the design rule to design tests. Use the pre-sale rule for general conversion work, once traffic reaches about 40 unique visitors per day.

2. **Order of first store tests.** One Source C sequence starts with the landing page or theme, then prices, lead magnets, discounts, copy, product description and trust signals, and ad breakdown. [L0773.009] Another starts with themes, bundles, prices, urgency and copy, then scaling. [L1108.024] The first sequence has a stated trigger (a winning product gets traffic but no sales). [L0773.009] The second has no stated trigger. [L1108.024] Use the first when that trigger applies.

3. **Many small changes versus fundamental changes.** Source B says small tips change little and fundamental changes to the store, offer and purchase path come first. [L0598.002] Source C and Source B both recommend many small tested changes, and an ongoing process. [L0549.053, L1364.002] Use fundamental changes when the offer or purchase path is weak. Once those are planned, run small changes continuously. [L0399.019, L1364.004]

4. **Cut-offs for product focus.** The top 100 trafficked products is one cut-off. [L1446.013] The top 20% of trafficked products is another. [L1446.014] Both are kept above. Use the top 100 as the working list and the 20% rule to rank within it, if the sources' stated numbers are applied to the same store. (Derived; the sources do not say which applies to which store size.)

5. **Ad cut level.** Ad-level cuts happen within the first 24 hours at $10 spend and $3.50 CPC. [L0229.003] Product-level cuts happen at the pre-set break-even limit, not on the first disappointing day. [L0639.046] These apply at different levels and do not conflict.

#### Further details

- Product recommendation and discovery tests require strong product categorization and merchandising to achieve their full potential lift. Before running tests on product recommendations, out-of-stock alternatives, or quick navigation links, audit and optimize your product catalog structure and categories. [L0197.026]

## Platform-specific conversion tactics

### Amazon conversion benchmarks

- Conversion rate is a number to track weekly, not once. Even small changes to images, copy or product features can move it. Once conversion is optimized, stop changing things to avoid regression. [L0227.023]
- The sources set the "exceptional" line differently. L0227.023 puts exceptional at 18% and above and says to stop further changes once a listing reaches it. L0227.024 uses a fuller scale: 5% is poor, 10-18% is good, 20% and above is excellent, 30% and above is exceptional. Use the L0227.024 scale for grading and the 18% point from L0227.023 as the freeze point. [L0227.023, L0227.024]
- A supplement product averaged 38% conversion on Amazon, with some days above 50%. Other platforms typically reach 2-3%. [L0227.024]
- Amazon shoppers are in a buying mindset. Baseline conversion is 15-20%, rising to 33% on some days and above 50% in supplement categories. Dropshipping stores typically convert around 2%. Amazon ads are therefore the best traffic source for FBA products, despite high cost-per-click. [L0228.025]
- Amazon conversion is much higher than on a website, but the sources set different working bars:
  - L1153.032 treats 3% as good on a store, and on Amazon treats a rate under 15% as a bad sign. It cites an 8% rate as a poor week.
  - L0227.024 counts 10-18% as good on Amazon.
  - Use L0227.024 as the general benchmark and L1153.032 as the stricter alarm level. [L1153.032, L0227.024]
- Amazon shoppers already want to buy, which is why conversion is high compared with traffic from Google, Bing or Facebook. Items under $50 need little thought from the buyer and support fast purchases. [L1153.033]

| Context | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Good conversion on a store | 3% | L1153.032 |
| Typical dropshipping store | About 2% | L0228.025 |
| Typical rate on other platforms (vs. Amazon) | 2-3% | L0227.024 |
| Amazon, poor week | 8% | L1153.032 |
| Amazon, bad sign | Under 15% | L1153.032 |
| Amazon, good | 10-18% | L0227.024 |
| Amazon, baseline | 15-20% | L0228.025 |
| TikTok scaling target | Above 1.5% to 2% | L1375.005 |

### Amazon listing optimization

- The product page elements that influence Amazon conversion are the title, images, bullet points and description. Optimize each one to match the problems and benefits buyers find in competitor reviews. [L1153.035]
- Research competitor reviews in this order:
  1. Open the product pages of competitors and read the positive and negative reviews. [L1153.034]
  2. Note the recurring problems buyers mention. [L1153.034]
  3. Use these problems in your title, bullet points and description to show how your product solves them. [L1153.034]
  4. Use the same insights to make small product improvements instead of building a new product. [L1153.034]

### Amazon advertising sequence

Run the sequence in order. Do not run automatic and manual campaigns at the same time.

1. Set up an automatic Amazon ad campaign for one week. Amazon selects keywords and displays the product. [L0228.026]
2. Review which keywords produced conversions and which wasted spend. [L0228.026]
3. Build a manual campaign that targets only the converting keywords. This gives you control over cost-per-click and bid amounts. [L0228.026]
4. Do not run automatic and manual campaigns simultaneously. You will outbid yourself and waste budget competing against your own ads. [L0228.026]

- In the short term, losing money or breaking even on Amazon ads is acceptable while you accumulate sales and conversions to improve organic ranking. Long-term profitability needs a margin high enough that each sale can reinvest in ads and still be profitable. Higher price points make this strategy possible. [L0228.027]
- If Amazon ads are already profitable (for example, spending $10 to make $20), increase the budget. Keep scaling until conversion rates plateau. More sales improve organic ranking, which generates additional unpaid traffic. [L0228.028]

### Dynamic product ads

- Running dynamic product ads and optimizing them for CTR is the target for a 26% lift in conversion rate. [L1031.032]

### Service-business websites

- Use shorter text on a service website. Visitors rarely read long blocks, so services must be communicated quickly and clearly. [L0440.025]
- On mobile layouts, page builders such as Gem Pages or PageFly can create side-scrolling carousels and drop-down (accordion) menus. Use them to compress feature lists and benefit copy while keeping detail accessible. [L0918.013]

### High-ticket and bulky items

- Older (2021-22): For high-ticket products, a phone call call to action can convert better than a buy button. End the copy with an instruction to call today on a visible phone number and offer to discuss purchase options. [L0461.013]
- Older (2018): White glove delivery, meaning professional delivery and setup, can increase conversion rate for large or bulky items. [L1109.044]
- Older (2019): Mobile hesitance is common for high-ticket products. Expect many mobile visitors to convert later on desktop, and measure performance with that in mind. [L1275.070]
- Older (2018): There is no fixed rule that conversion falls as price rises. Traffic quality and how targeted it is matter more than the price point. [L1109.045]
- Conversion rates for high-priced products can be higher, lower or similar to standard products. Measure conversion for each high-priced product after launch rather than assuming a figure. [L0970.099]
- The social pages support high-ticket orders, with buyers placing orders of roughly $500, $1,000, $2,000 or $5,000. Credibility matters more than viral reach for purchases at this level. [L0654.021]
- Older (2021-22): A search bar in the header is important for high-ticket dropshipping stores, because the catalogue grows over time and visitors need a fast way to find the product they want. Present it as a conversion measure that helps more people find the right product. [L1371.008]

#### Products that require assembly

- Older (2022): For products that require assembly, request photos from the supplier showing what the product looks like when delivered in boxes or pallets. Display these alongside assembly time and instruction videos on the product page, so customers understand the unboxing and assembly reality. [L0249.098]
- Older (2022): Example. Outdoor swing sets for backyards are sold for $5,000 with photos of children playing and climbing. Delivery arrives as three pallets of 1,000 pounds of lumber, while customers expect an assembled product. The fix is to show assembly time in videos, include delivery photos, and list assembly requirements prominently. [L0249.100]

### Dropshipping-specific rules

- Do not copy a competitor's landing page, video or ad creative exactly. If the original advertiser is banned, your account and store can be banned too. Change images, text, layout and creatives. [L1213.073]
- Older (2021-22): Hide stock levels on a high-ticket dropshipping store, because showing stock levels gives no advantage in that model. [L1371.019]
- Where stock is genuinely low on a standard store, the low-stock message can help conversion. See the inventory settings below. [L0976.033]
- Hide the expiring coupon block until the store receives real traffic, because demo products do not need urgency messages. Re-enable it at any time with the same settings. [L0976.021]
- Enable the out-of-stock alert for items that are backordered for a long time, so you can build a waiting list instead of taking orders. [L0976.010]
- Test landing page themes before anything else. The procedure is in the page builder section below. [L0774.010]

### Shopify setup order

Work through conversion tasks in this order:

1. Install an urgency app and a review app on Shopify. [L0532.011]
2. Modify the content page templates. [L0532.011]
3. Create Facebook and Instagram business pages. [L0532.011]
4. Install Klaviyo on Shopify. [L0532.011]
5. Set up automated actions and emails for bounced visits and abandoned carts. [L0532.011]
6. Apply for a financing app. [L0532.011]
7. Complete all action tasks of the conversion step. [L0532.011]

### Theme-native conversion features

- Theme-native features aim to raise conversion rate and average order value. For most of these needs, the theme covers the function without a paid third-party app. [L0973.002]
- Exit pop-up: enable it in Theme settings, optionally turn on an image, and offer a discount code. It appears to visitors who are leaving the site, displays text only, and captures no email. [L0973.007]
- Social proof pop-up: enable it in Theme settings to show recent store orders in the bottom corner of the website. The format is "[Customer name] recently purchased [product name]", and a frequency setting controls how often it appears. [L0973.011]
- Social proof pop-ups are optional. The built-in version avoids a monthly fee for a separate app. [L0973.012]
- Sticky content on desktop: turn it on in Theme settings and save. The image stays in place while the text column scrolls. This helps on monitors where the page does not fill the screen, and the option is recommended on. [L0976.004]
- Price colors: under Theme settings you can change the color of the list-price savings text (red by default) and the color scheme of the sales badge. Both can be set to any colors. [L0976.012]
- Sticky add to cart: the button stays visible at the bottom while the visitor scrolls. It is optional and can be tested. Icon, colors and font size are set under customize add to cart button. [L0976.027]
- Share button: keep it on. Visitors can copy the product link or share it on social media or by email. The link updates to the product page URL automatically, and the button text can be changed. [L0976.030]
- Image block: add it at any position on the product page, and add several if needed. It suits a promotion banner, such as a sale graphic showing a discount and the checkout code. Prepare the image in advance in a design tool such as Canva. [L0976.045]
- Countdown timer: it needs a tag on the individual product in the Shopify admin, not in the theme settings. The tag begins with the word sale and carries the offer's end date, which must lie in the future, because the timer counts down to that date. [L0976.047]

#### Inventory display

- The low inventory threshold defaults to 10 units. When stock falls below that number, a low stock message appears. It can be dragged to sit directly below the buy button. [L0976.032]
- With show inventory count turned on, the page displays the exact number left next to the low stock message, for example "low stock with 8 left". This can help conversion when real stock is actually low. [L0976.033]

#### Trust badges

- The trust badges block sits across the bottom of the page by default, unlike the side placement of the shipping text block. Its title can be changed and aligned center, left or right. Each badge can have an image, a link and optional text under the icon. [L0976.037]
- The block allows a maximum of seven badges. Enable display trust badge text to add a caption under each icon. The caption text comes from the badge boxes. [L0976.038]
- The trust badges block lets the store show reasons to buy below or beside the product. It is an advanced option and can be turned off for a basic demo store. [L1189.023]
- Switch a feature such as trust badges on temporarily in the theme editor to see how it looks on the product page before deciding to keep it. If it is not needed yet, switch it off again instead of building it out at the demo stage. [L1189.029]

#### Estimated delivery block

- The block shows text such as "estimated arrival between", followed by the earliest and latest delivery days, counted from the day the order is placed, plus the shipping country. That country should be the country you ship to. Its text and color can be changed. The block is recommended once the store goes live. [L0976.023]
- In the theme used in L1192, the block sits in the Product information section of the theme editor. Click its eye icon to make it visible. It then appears under the discount code with the label "estimated arrival" and a date range. [L1192.021]
- The date range is built from the earliest and longest delivery days entered in the estimated delivery settings. Example: 4 days as the earliest and 7 days as the longest, shown as two calendar dates. [L1192.022]
- The dates update automatically every night at midnight based on the day count, so the range stays current without manual edits. [L1192.023]

#### Setup procedure for coupon and delivery on the product template

1. Create the discount code in the Shopify Discounts section first. [L1192.030]
2. Turn on and configure the expiring coupon on the product template, matching the code name exactly. [L1192.030]
3. Turn on and configure the estimated delivery section and set the delivery day range. [L1192.030]
4. Save the template and check the product page in preview. [L1192.030]

#### Review widget and hero slide

- Older (2021-22): Hero slide text in the Shopify theme editor:
  1. Open the slideshow section and click the first slide. [L1310.019]
  2. Select the image, upload it, and check how it looks. [L1310.019]
  3. If the image is too dark, remove the overlay so it looks brighter. [L1310.019]
  4. Enter the Heading and Subheading, and set Text alignment to Left. [L1310.019]
  5. Remove the button by clearing its Label field if no button is needed. [L1310.019]
  6. Click Save. [L1310.019]
- To place the review widget, go to Online store > Themes in Shopify, click Edit theme, and switch from the homepage to a product page template. The review widget appears in the apps section of the sidebar and can be dragged to a different position. By default it sits directly under the product description. Save with the theme save button. [L1245.005]

### Visually A/B tests (Shopify)

#### Running and reviewing experiments

- The Pages setting "All Pages" covers the homepage, product pages, collection pages and the rest of the store. To test only one template, choose a specific page type such as Product Pages or Cart page, so the change does not affect unrelated pages. [L0389.027]
- A running experience appears in a live list showing its start date, last edit date, pages, audience, device and allocation (for example 50%). From there you can Edit, Pause or Preview the experience without creating a new one. [L0389.028]

#### No-code A/B test setup

1. Hover over the element on the live page and click Edit Visual. Change the text, font, size, spacing or color, then click Save. [L0389.001]
2. Enter an Experience Name. [L0389.001]
3. Set the Audience (for example All Visitors), Pages (for example All Pages or Product Pages), Devices (for example Mobile) and Trigger (PAGE LOAD). [L0389.001]
4. Click Next and set the experience as an A/B test with a 50-50 allocation. [L0389.001]
5. Select the goals: Conversion Rate as the primary goal, and Per Session Value and Profit as secondary goals. [L0389.001]
6. Tick the box that sends the events to Google Analytics. [L0389.001]
7. Publish. [L0389.001]

#### Social proof widget below Add to Cart

1. Add the Social Proof element through Content Blocks, placed directly under Add to Cart. [L0389.003]
2. Choose Bought instead of Viewed. [L0389.003]
3. Set the General Customization to BOUGHT IN THE PAST X TIME, with Timeframe WEEK and Rounding (50's) for rounded numbers. [L0389.003]
4. Set the threshold to a minimum of 150 purchases. [L0389.003]
5. Style the text block: font Commons Sans-serif, 16px, bold, black to match the brand, with reduced padding. [L0389.003]
6. Save. Then set Audience All Visitors, Pages Product Pages, Device Mobile, and name the experience (for example "mobile BDP social proof"). [L0389.003]
7. Set the A/B test to 50-50 with the primary goal, send the events to Google Analytics, and publish. [L0389.003]

- Choose Bought over Viewed, because bought counts show stronger proof. Timeframe options are day, week, month and year. Rounding (50's) shows a rounded count instead of the exact number. The Set threshold field hides the widget until the purchase count exceeds the chosen number. [L0389.005]

#### Trust elements (USPs) in the cart

1. Copy the USP block from the product page (shipping, returns policy, lifetime warranty, active promotion). [L0389.008]
2. Paste it into the cart page directly below the upsells and above the shipping line. [L0389.008]
3. Set Audience All Visitors, Pages Cart page only, Device Mobile, and name the test (for example "mobile cart USPs"). [L0389.008]
4. Set the A/B test to 50-50. [L0389.008]
5. Add returns rate and profit as goals, because a visible return policy can raise the return rate. [L0389.008]
6. Tick the Google Analytics box and publish. [L0389.008]

#### Opening a feature dropdown on page load (Fake Click)

1. Add a Fake Click element from the element list. [L0389.015]
2. Hover over the dropdown (for example Features) and click it, so the interaction is recorded. [L0389.015]
3. Preview the page to confirm the dropdown opens on load. [L0389.015]
4. Set Audience All Visitors, Pages Product Pages, Device Mobile. [L0389.015]
5. Name the test, set it as an A/B test, set the goals, send the events to Google Analytics and publish. [L0389.015]

### Cart, announcement and progress elements (Shopify)

#### Announcement bar

- Header > Add > Announcement Bar: use it to promote sitewide sales or discount codes inside the cart. With several messages, they slide across the top of the bar. A single message stays static, without the sliding animation. [L1230.005]
- An announcement bar can hold several announcements that scroll as a marquee, with a default display timing of roughly five seconds. The character limit was not stated, so keep messages short and watch for unwanted line breaks. [L1231.023]

#### Tiered progress bar (free shipping goal)

- Goal Box > Add > Tiered Progress Bar shows customers their progress toward offers such as free shipping, free products, an order-wide discount, or a decorative tier with no reward. Up to four tiers can be configured. [L1230.007]
- Tiered Progress Bar > Configure Tiers > Free Shipping: enter the unlock price as a dollar amount (the lesson uses $50). The free shipping options are Free Shipping on All Products with no minimum, Free Shipping on Subscription Product, and Enable Presentment Currencies. [L1230.008]
- Example: with a $50 unlock price, a cart holding $29 in products shows that the customer is $21 away from free shipping. The bar updates as items are added or removed. [L1230.009]

#### Cart footer components

- Footer > Cart Subtotal controls how the subtotal text appears in the cart. [L1230.019]
- Footer > Checkout Area > Express Checkout Buttons: Shop Pay, Apple Pay and Google Pay can be shown in the cart through Accelerated Checkout. Pre-checkout options (Terms and Conditions, Pre-Purchase Pop-Up), standard buttons (Checkout Button, View Cart Button, Continue Shopping Button) and Installments are configured in the same area. [L1230.020]
- Footer > Add > Discount Code Input lets customers enter a discount code inside the cart, so the saving is visible before the checkout page. The field can be dragged to any position in the footer. [L1230.021]

### Section settings (Shopify themes)

- The Instagram stories section displays images and testimonials as a stories-style feed. Add user post blocks inside the section. The section fills with stories automatically once content is added. [L1330.018]
- Instagram stories section settings in the theme editor:
  - Display section ID: the ID can merge two sections in the Sections group, and can be placed in any button link so the button scrolls to this section.
  - Display on: All devices.
  - Heading.
  - Heading words highlight 1: words in bold get the highlight style (for example with Text color #6D388B).
  - Heading words highlight 2: words in italic get the highlight style. Choose None to keep the default italic style.
  - Heading size, Margin and Remove section. [L1330.019]
- Older (2021-22): Highlights banner settings: Section background color, Desktop section spacing (set to 60px in the tested build), Mobile section spacing, and Banner text alignment set to Center. Colors: Banner headings, Banner text, Icon, Dividers and Background. [L1310.023]
- Product information section in the Shrine theme: Display section ID, Enable sticky content on desktop, Color scheme (Background 1), Media settings, Display first variant image as featured image, Disable prepend of the new active media, Hide other variants' media after selecting a variant, and Active variant images filtering. Use the sticky option to keep the purchase block visible while the visitor scrolls. [L1331.021]
- Product template block order in the Shrine theme: Title, Rating stars, Price, Variant picker, Quantity selector, Buy buttons (with Add to cart), Shipping checkpoints, Sticky Add To Cart, Description, Reviews, then Image with text sections and an Icon Bar. Remove blocks you do not need so the page does not get busy. [L1331.022]

### Demo-store configuration

- Hide the expiring coupon block until the store has real traffic. [L0976.021]
- Turn off the trust badges block for a basic demo store. [L1189.023]
- Keep the demo store simple: test features temporarily and remove them if they are not needed yet. [L1189.029]

### Landing page builders and theme testing

#### Theme split test

Split-test landing page themes before anything else:

1. If you do not use PageFly yet, build the landing page with PageFly and test it. [L0774.010]
2. If you already use PageFly, switch to the Source F theme for the test. [L0774.010]
3. Run ads for two days on one theme, then two days on the other, and compare results. [L0774.010]

- Some products convert better on PageFly and others on Source F, so do not commit to one design. Both PageFly and Source F are free to use. [L0774.010]
- Older (2024 source, no date mark needed): A store with a low conversion rate (for example 0.03%) on an older theme should be rebuilt on the current theme (Manhattan). A fresh build on a newer theme should show a much higher conversion rate. [L0856.038]

#### Page builders

- Gem Pages is the page builder named in the lesson, and it has carousel and drop-down features. PageFly is a similar builder with duplicate-and-edit functionality for creating variant landing pages per audience. [L0918.021]
- Instant is a page builder used for pre-landers, listicles and advertorials. GemPages has better templates, but Instant is easier to work with. PageDeck is another builder option. The choice of builder matters less than the flow: clean copy, then pre-lander, then funnel. [L1299.008]

#### Button styling in PageFly

- To build a button, add a button element, enter the button text, set the background color and text color (for example white text on a dark background), and set the text to bold. Add inside padding so the button has space around its label. [L1462.029]
- Set a button's border radius to 50 px to round its corners into a pill shape. Increase the value until the corners look fully round for the size of the button. [L1462.030]
- A fixed-position button with bottom 30 px and left 30 px floats over the page while the visitor scrolls. This works as a sticky add-to-cart button on mobile product pages. [L1462.032]

### Pinterest conversion setup

- Pinterest conversion campaigns need a checkout event fired on a purchase-style trigger. Use this snippet, which has a sample value of 80 and a placeholder product. Replace the product name, ID, price and value with the real trigger product's details before use. [L1133.006]

```
pintrk('track', 'checkout', {
  value: 80,
  order_quantity: 1,
  currency: 'USD',
  line_items: [
    {
      product_name: 'Trigger Product',
      product_id: '6789',
      product_price: 80,
      product_quantity: 1
    }
  ]
});
```

[L1133.006]

#### Activating conversion events

1. Open a product page on your store. [L1135.027]
2. Open the browser developer tools: right-click the page and choose Inspect, or go to More tools > Developer tools if inspect is blocked. [L1135.027]
3. Open the Console tab. [L1135.027]
4. Paste the Pinterest conversion event code into the console and run it 10 to 20 times. [L1135.027]
5. Wait five to 10 minutes. [L1135.027]
6. Return to Pinterest. The conversion campaign option should now be active. [L1135.027]

#### Pinterest audience growth

- Add a pop-up on the store that invites visitors to follow the store on Pinterest or check out new boards. This increases the number of people who follow the store and share its content automatically. [L1136.033]
- Place a Pinterest follow button in the website header. Add links to boards and the profile in the sidebar or footer, so visitors who want to interact on Pinterest can find the profile easily. [L1136.034]

### TikTok conversion setup

- Set the TikTok pixel's Data Sharing to Maximum during the Shopify connection, so the pixel receives the most event data for optimization. [L1373.003]
- Do not scale a TikTok campaign until the store conversion rate is above 1.5% to 2%. [L1375.005]
- Set the call to action to standard Shop now, or to Dynamic to let TikTok choose the most suitable button. Both are valid. Test which converts better. [L1383.053]
- If a video goes viral but produces no sales, the audience is probably wrong, even if the product is good. Switch the coins or Spark Ads objective to conversions to reach buyers. [L1429.012]
- Views versus conversions in one example: $10 with a conversion objective produced 1 to 2 conversions and about 500 views. The same $10 on a views objective could double the views but produce no conversions. [L1429.015]
- Conversion objectives cost more per result and give fewer total views, so choose between sales and reach based on your goal. If conversion targeting produces no sales, go back to views, because TikTok may still find the audience either way. [L1429.016]

#### Mixed coins strategy by stage

1. Spend about $10 on coins for views in the first stage. [L1429.049]
2. Once the account reaches about 1,000 followers, switch the remaining about $20 to a conversion objective. [L1429.049]
3. If growth slows, use views and conversions again to re-balance. [L1429.049]

### Common mistakes

- Do not copy a competitor's landing page, video or ad creative exactly. Change images, text, layout and creatives to protect the account and store. [L1213.073]

## Other details

### Foundations for conversion

- Market knowledge, content development and customer understanding feed directly into conversion rate optimization. Outdated basics therefore weaken every later marketing and sales effort. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L0761.005]
- A small store with good suppliers and steady traffic can make money before organic traffic builds. Organic traffic grows over time as Google recognizes the site as high quality. (Older advice, 2020.) [L1111.085]

### Sales channels and store setup

- The Shop sales channel can be added to Shopify sales channels. It rarely generates significant volume but does not hurt to include. [L0278.013]

### Product images in Search product ads

- Image extensions in Search product ads have an approval rate of approximately 50%, with no clear rejection reason. [L0210.037]
- Upload product images anyway, because approved images generate more clicks. [L0210.037]

### SEO titles and SKUs

- Adding the SKU number to the SEO title is fine and helps SEO. [L0805.048]
- The product title follows what the top competitors put in their titles. [L0805.048]
- Products without variants show the SKU in the SEO title. Variant products do not include the SKU. [L0805.048]

### Ad funnel (older advice, 2021)

1. Run targeted Google Shopping ads to product pages optimized for trust. [L0270.051]
2. Use dynamic Facebook remarketing ads and email marketing to bring back visitors who left without buying. [L0270.051]
3. Optimize lead value by earning more from every sale once a customer purchases. [L0270.051]
4. Repeat to maximize revenue per customer. [L0270.051]

### Affiliate banners in Refersion (older advice, 2021-22)

- When uploading a banner creative to Refersion, set the landing page URL to match the banner type. [L0288.017]
  - General business-wide banner: link to the homepage. [L0288.017]
  - Product-specific banner: link to the specific product page. [L0288.017]
- This ensures visitors land on the appropriate destination, where they find details about the offer. [L0288.017]

### Trade buyer capture (2024)

1. Create a page with a name such as "interior designer discounts" or "to the trade", and link it from the homepage and the footer menu. [L0360.024]
2. Add an exit-intent overlay that asks whether the visitor is an interior designer and collects their email for trade discounts. [L0360.024]
3. Send the captured emails a personal reply that offers custom quotes. [L0360.024]
4. Create a separate trade contact page with its own contact form. The form collects name, email, phone, products of interest and quantity. [L0360.024]

### Returns benchmark (older advice, 2020)

- Aim for a return rate under 1 percent. [L1277.080]

### Case: high Facebook CTR, no sales

- **Starting point:** A store with a high Facebook CTR but no sales. [L0773.061]
- **Changes:** Changes were made to the store, including the store adjustments covered in this section. [L0773.061]
- **Result:** Within a couple of hours, the store received two sales. [L0773.061]


# 7. Offers, pricing and bundles

## What an offer is and how buyers judge value

### Definition of an offer

- An offer is the full set of what a visitor is shown to convince them to buy. A discount may be part of it, but the offer also includes everything else presented to persuade the purchase. [L0408.007]
- Anything that makes the buyer more likely to say yes, such as a bonus, a bundle or a guarantee, counts as part of the offer. An offer is more than a product on sale at a discount. [L0757.014]
- (Older advice, Source B 2021-22) In marketing, an offer is the full package a buyer sees when deciding whether to buy from you: the product, the business behind it, and everything that persuades them. A discount or bundle is only one possible part of that package. [L0411.002]
- (Older advice, Source B 2021-22) A complete offer has nine elements: marketing messages for the product, the product itself, product price, shipping or delivery, a USP package, risk reversal, customer service, trust factors, and bonuses with value delivery or perceived value. [L0411.021]
- (Older advice, Source B 2021-22) Resellers compete mainly on the business. Own-product brands compete more on the product. [L0411.021]
- (Older advice, Source B 2021-22) A total offer includes the product and its benefits, the marketing message, the price, the unique selling proposition, risk reversal (protection if something goes wrong), shipping or delivery arrangements, customer service, trust factors such as reviews, and any special offer such as a discount, sale price or free gift. A discount alone is only one small part of the offer. [L0414.017]
- (Older advice, Source B 2021-22) The USP package is how the unique selling proposition is presented on the page. It can overlap with other offer elements, such as risk reversal, but it can also be entirely separate. [L0411.025]
- The offer is more than the price. Branding, the unique selling point, bundle or BOGO structure, and the perceived value of the whole deal all shape it. Add-to-cart rates depend on these elements. A weak offer is often the first reason a landing page does not convert. [L1260.016, L1345.012]
- Customers buy an offer, not just a product. The same item can look far more valuable with a free bonus, free shipping and quantity discounts, without any change to the item or its base price. [L0860.001]
- The offer must be relevant to the buyer's problem. High perceived value does not require adding more items. Speaking directly to the prospect's situation raises perceived value more than a generic "buy this" message. [L0643.008]

### The value equation

- Customer perceived value follows a ratio. Dream outcome and perceived likelihood sit in the numerator; time delay and effort and sacrifice sit in the denominator. This ratio determines purchasing decisions, and all four components influence whether a customer buys.
  - Sum form: `(Dream outcome + Likelihood of achieving it) / (Time required + Effort and sacrifice)` [L0233.001]
  - Product form: `Value = (Dream outcome × Perceived likelihood of achievement) / (Time delay × Effort and sacrifice)`. Raise the first two factors and shrink the last two to make an offer more valuable. For a product, show customers how little time and effort they need. [L0502.002, L0549.025]
  - The worked example in [L0233.004] uses the sum form.
- The four factors, judged from the buyer's point of view:
  - **Dream outcome:** what the buyer wants to become. [L0502.003]
  - **Perceived likelihood:** how possible the buyer believes it is to reach that outcome. [L0502.003]
  - **Time delay:** how long it takes. [L0502.003]
  - **Effort and sacrifice:** what the buyer must invest. [L0502.003]
- Dream outcome examples: a necklace promises looking stylish and expressing identity; fitness promises a great body. Identify your product's dream outcome and communicate it throughout the offer structure, naming and product description. [L0233.002]
- Build perceived likelihood through high-quality customer reviews, before-and-after photos, testimonials and comparative evidence showing results. [L0233.003]
- Worked example: a gym membership scores `(100) / (50) = 2`. Supplements for the same goal score `(100) / (10) = 10`. The outcome promise is identical, but supplements have 5x the perceived value because they require less time and effort. [L0233.004]
- Gyms and supplements sell the same dream outcome, but supplements win larger demand because they promise faster results with almost no effort. A six-pack through training can take two to three years or more, which makes the time delay and effort very high. [L0502.004]
- Numeric check: a numerator of 10 divided by a denominator of 2 gives 5. Lowering the denominator while keeping the numerator high raises the result. [L0502.043]
- As time and effort approach zero, perceived value approaches infinity. Sources differ on how this compares with the other levers:
  - Cutting time and effort matters as much as strengthening the promise. [L0502.002]
  - This asymptotic multiplier drives purchasing decisions more powerfully than improving the dream outcome or the likelihood of success. Products that need minimal time and effort will substantially outperform identical-outcome products with more friction. [L0233.022]
- Shorten the time delay by promising short delivery, such as one to two weeks instead of months. Fast competitors such as Amazon can offer same-day shipping, so the gap matters. [L0502.006]
- Sales copy should shrink the time, effort and sacrifice in the buyer's eyes, for example by showing a simple three-step process. This makes a high price feel justified. [L0919.037]
- Buyers pay for the value they expect to get. If the offer delivers little perceived value, selling and convincing people to spend money on the store becomes very difficult. [L0502.001]
- Buyer types differ:
  - Impulse buyers purchase quickly from a clear offer.
  - Comparison buyers check other stores.
  - Facebook and TikTok ads draw attention. Google Ads and comparison-shopping buyers look for the best deal.
  - The store offer has to convince both types. [L0502.031]
- Before launching a landing page or offer, ask whether you would buy it yourself at that price with that offer, and why someone else should. Add as much value as possible until the answer is yes. [L0502.013]
- Perceived value created through brand, presentation and marketing angles lets a product sell at a much higher price than its cost suggests. Prefer products with high perceived value potential. [L0708.007]

### Making the offer valuable (CURVE and bonuses)

- A CURVE offer stands for Clear, Unique, Risk-free and Valuable. Each letter is a test the offer must pass, and the offer should be reviewed against all four. [L0411.007] (older advice, Source B 2021-22)
- **Valuable:** the customer perceives more value or benefit than from competitors. Improving one element while keeping the others equal can make the whole offer more valuable. [L0411.020] (older advice, Source B 2021-22)
- **Unique:** position the total offer so it is perceived as unique within the market. A different offer from competitors raises conversion more than changing a button colour. An average presentation can sell a great offer, but a poor offer cannot be saved by a great presentation. [L0414.018] (older advice, Source B 2021-22)
- **Clear:** simple offers convert best because shoppers spend mental effort understanding complicated deals. A complex offer such as "50% off your third item" loses buyers. A simple, obvious deal makes customers act quickly. [L1404.017]
- An offer works best when the buyer would feel unreasonable refusing it, usually through a clear saving or added value tied to their problem. [L1131.059]
  - A bonus that duplicates the main product adds little, because a buyer who needs one item does not want a second one.
  - A complementary product that solves a related problem feels more valuable. Example: an organiser for a wallet buyer. [L1131.059]
- Bundles and products with extra value, such as a case or accessories that help the buyer complete the job the product solves, increase the perceived value of the offer. [L1218.030]
- Perceived value makes a product look more valuable than a competitor's without a large product change. Ways to add it:
  - bonus ebooks
  - a coupon code
  - a lifetime guarantee
  - bundling the product with a smaller item from the supplier [L1153.029]
- Irresistible offers maximise perceived value so the customer feels they are getting a bargain. Tools include discounts, free gifts, free resources, money-back guarantees and bundles that stack value. [L0919.020]
- Discounts raise conversion rates because a visitor perceives a discount as a valuable offer. This is the underlying reason behind most promotion types used to increase sales. [L1400.010]
- Explain the cost to develop the offer, such as expert teams, lab testing and the number of repetitions a product went through. This turns a feature list into a story of value. Identical features and benefits written with development detail sound more valuable than the same product described briefly. [L1370.071]

### Offer types

- Offer types available to an e-commerce store, with their variants:

| Offer type | Variants or notes |
|---|---|
| Percentage off | Sitewide, specific SKUs, tiered (e.g. spend $100, get 20% off after that) |
| Dollar off | Sitewide or specific SKUs |
| Buy one get one (BOGO) | Free, or discounted (e.g. 30% off the second item) |
| Mystery box | Bundle of unknown contents sold as a 'trust us' pack |
| Free express shipping | Upgraded shipping at no cost, used before cut-off dates |
| Bundle deals | Multiple products sold together, often combined with % or $ off |
| Subscribe and save | Recurring orders with a discount |
| Gift with purchase | Free product from another range added to a paid order |
| Post-purchase upsell or cross-sell | Offer made after checkout |
| Lifetime warranty | Extended guarantee as the offer |
| 100-day free trial | Long trial period as the offer |
| Just pay shipping | Product free at checkout, customer pays shipping only |
| Exclusive memberships | Paid or sign-up access to exclusive deals |
| Loyalty program | Points or perks for repeat customers |
| Purchase to go in draw | Purchase entitles the buyer to a prize draw | [L1404.034]

- Monetary offer types with example forms:

| No. | Offer type | Example form |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Percent off each purchase | 10% off each purchase |
| 2 | Spend X, save X | Save $X when the order is over $Y |
| 3 | Buy one, get one free | Second item at no charge |
| 4 | Free expedited shipping | Faster shipping at no charge |
| 5 | Free white glove delivery | Premium delivery service at no charge |
| 6 | Free extended warranty | Longer warranty at no charge |
| 7 | Entered to win a prize | Entry into a prize draw |
| 8 | Make an offer | Shopper names a price | [L0757.018]

- The offer must fit the product, the audience and its price point. For low-ticket items a free second item can be affordable because the extra cost is small. Weak offers such as BOGO at 20 percent off are seen as boring and ineffective. [L1469.005]
- Offers improve ad conversion. A brand running a promotion can afford to spend more on Meta ads than a competitor selling the same product without one, and still win the customer. [L1404.003]
- Offers reduce customer acquisition cost and lift revenue, clear slow inventory, create urgency and generate buzz and word of mouth. The main goal is revenue growth, driven by scarcity, urgency and the confidence buyers feel while a promotion runs. [L1404.002]
- Offers can roughly double revenue and make forecasting harder, because a well-matched offer can cause a sharp jump in sales. Plan for offers as a regular growth lever rather than an occasional event. [L1404.001]
- (Source D 2026) Strong offers are the primary lever for scaling. A well-designed offer combined with existing ad quality and conversion rates can increase ROAS from 2x to 4x overnight and CVR from 1.5% to 2.5%. [L0232.001]

### The no-brainer gap

- A no-brainer offer creates a large gap between perceived value and price. This is achieved by adding a lot of value, lowering the price, or a combination of both. Focus on increasing value, since a strong offer can make even average copy convert. [L1365.034]
- Value stack: total value = sum of the stated value of each item in the offer, shown as value rather than price. The final price is a fraction of that total, so the gap between total value and final price makes the offer feel irresistible. Example: items with a stated total value of $12,000 offered for $990 show a gap of about twelve times the price. [L1365.038]
- Bundle build-up: list every component of a bundle with its standalone price, add up the total hard value, then show a much lower total price. Name, value and state each bonus as free. Example: a training package whose parts were valued at over $5,200 but priced at $3,895 for a 24-month contract, with bonuses listed as free. [L1370.072]
- Anchoring: build perceived value by anchoring a higher price against a comparable product that offers a similar result, such as a hedge fund strategy costing six figures, so your price looks like a good deal. [L1365.036]
- Scarcity, by limiting the number of units available, raises perceived value and adds urgency. [L1365.036]

### Why price alone is a weak lever

- Price is part of the offer, but competing only on price is a weak strategy. If the rest of the offer matches competitors, a slightly lower price can make the total offer stronger. [L0411.023] (older advice, Source B 2021-22)
- Cutting the price to attract buyers makes the product look cheap, since shoppers assume the best products in a category are not the cheapest. A lower price lowers perceived value and can reduce sales, which is why many businesses price themselves out of the market. [L1365.035]
- Never build a store around the lowest price. Raise the price by increasing the value you provide, since higher prices often signal higher quality and build trust. [L0788.051]
- Price should match what the buyer believes the product is worth. Compare against what competitors charge for similar products, and aim to make the buyer feel they get more for a higher price. Products with high perceived value include electronics, advanced products and items made from premium materials. [L1215.003]
- Sources differ on when to price competitively:
  - Very simple products, such as a basic knife, cannot gain much perceived value, so price them competitively. [L1217.063]
  - Products with several features or benefits can justify higher prices. [L1217.063]
- Price shock: a price noticeably higher than competitors' or unfamiliar pricing can lead to abandonment. Check product pricing against the market and make the offer attractive before lowering the price. [L0640.043]

#### Further details

- The 40-40-20 principle (credited to Ed Meyer, adapted for e-commerce) splits the chance of conversion this way: 40% from reaching the right audience at the right time (traffic), 40% from the offer, and 20% from how the offer is presented (website design). Most people focus only on the 20% presentation part. [L0414.016]

## Choosing a price range and ticket size

### Why price point changes the work

- Building and marketing a store takes the same time and effort whatever the average price. Niche selection, supplier research, website creation and ad investment stay constant, whether products average $10 or $1,000. [L0011.001]
- At 10 sales per day, an average price of $10 gives $100 daily revenue and about $30 daily profit. The same 10 sales at $1,000 average give $10,000 daily revenue and about $3,000 daily profit. With constant work, price point is the primary variable determining profitability. [L0011.003]
- At 30% net margin, a $10 cell phone case yields $3 per sale and a $1,000 stand-up paddleboard yields $300 per sale, a 100x difference per transaction. [L0012.003]
- Higher-priced products need more visitors to convert into buyers, so their cost per acquisition is higher. Product price therefore determines what acquisition cost is acceptable. [L0440.041]
- A $50 product with $20 profit needs many more sales than a $3,000 product with $900 profit to reach the same total. A high-ticket product with a clear price and a niche-matched audience makes every sale meaningful. (Older, Source B 2021-22.) [L0458.041]
- The higher the price point, the longer the customer journey and the more touch points a prospect needs before buying. Around $30 to $40, the whole journey can happen within minutes on a single site visit. (Older, Source B 2021-22.) [L0481.011]
- A very low price can signal low quality and lower perceived value. For products where value perception matters, a higher price can increase sales, and the right price depends on the product. [L0388.006]
