  5. Action: introduce the product and place a clear call to action that leads to the product page.
  6. Add photos throughout the text to keep the reader engaged.
  [L0578.030]
- Native-style long-form ad pattern: a large primary text that reads like an article. Structure: a bold headline, a first-person story of a small symptom that grew slowly, an ordinary check-up that found nothing alarming, a turning point where the person tried the product, then the product as the answer, and a disclaimer at the end. It works because the story earns attention at the top of the funnel, and the disclaimer keeps it compliant. Two new examples: "I Kept Losing Track of My Running Times for Two Years. A Coach Found the Cause in One Session." and "My Desk Routine Had Stopped Working by Spring. A Physiotherapist Showed Me What I Was Missing." [L1164.061]

### Direct mail and envelope techniques

- Mail-order ads must make the full sale on a single run, so they pack the greatest number of intensification devices into one long ad. They are often frozen and repeated after three to six months. National advertising keeps the product in front of the public constantly, so it runs far more often, and its product lifespans are much longer. [L0330.083]
- Catalog-style direct mail: open the first paragraph of each product ad with several very short sentences of two to four words, which pulls the eye down the page and keeps readers moving toward the offer. Use the same opening rhythm across product ads to keep the reader moving through the page. [L0340.075]
- Operator note on the rhythm rule: the repeated opening rhythm applies across separate product ads. Inside one ad, every consecutive line must still escalate and must not echo the line before it. [L0340.075, L0039.012]
- Envelope technique: no knowledge units were supplied for this topic.

### Core principle: one reader, one action

- Direct response copy is a writing style built to make a reader take one specific action right away. Its formula is: name the reader's problem, show the product as the answer, and end with one clear instruction. It works because every sentence pushes toward that one action rather than informing for its own sake. Example in the same pattern: *Tired of cracked phone screens after one drop? This case absorbs the impact and ships in 48 hours. Tap to see the protection.* [L1460.002] (older advice, 2021-22)
- Each piece of copy must aim at exactly one action, chosen by its place in the funnel. On a product page the action is adding to cart and buying. In an ad it is clicking through to the website. In an email it is visiting the website. [L1460.003, L1460.014] (older advice, 2021-22)
- Adding a second competing action to the same piece weakens the first. [L1460.014] (older advice, 2021-22)
- Ads that try to make the viewer buy directly fail when the ad does not allow purchase on the spot, because the viewer must first visit the site. The ad should only earn the click, and the sale happens later on the site. [L1460.004] (older advice, 2021-22)
- Ads do not sell the product; they sell the click. A few lines of text cannot sell a product effectively, so the ad only needs to arouse enough curiosity that the person wants to visit the page. [L1507.002] (older advice, 2021-22)
- Words in emails, search text ads and social ads all count as copy and must be written with one defined action in mind. This includes Google search text ads and Facebook ads. [L1460.011] (older advice, 2021-22)
- The purpose of ecommerce copy is to move the reader to the action the business wants, which in most cases is buying the product. Every headline and text block should be judged by whether it pushes toward that purchase. [L1493.004] (older advice, 2021-22)
- Today's online copywriting methods largely come from direct-response text marketing developed from the early 1900s through the 1950s and 1960s. Before TV and the internet, mail and newspaper advertising sold almost everything through text alone, which forced writers to become very skilled. [L1523.002]

### Voice and reader focus

- The word "you" matters more than any other word in a sales letter, so the copy should focus on what the reader wants rather than on the seller. People are interested in their own goals, so the letter should speak to them directly. [L1365.012]
- Copy written as one person speaking directly to one reader, using I, you and me, feels personal and converts better than copy written as if addressing a crowd. A byline with a real person's name strengthens this feel. [L1366.014]
- Personal first-person invitation (pattern): rewrite a crowd-directed corporate line as a note from one person who would like to meet the reader again and show the new product.
  - Impersonal form: *We invite all customers to visit our booth.*
  - Personal form: *You may remember me from the last show. I would love to see you at the next one and show you the new machine.*
  - The personal version creates warmth and a direct invitation. [L1366.080, L1366.015]
- Honesty shows through the copy. Hidden flaws or evasive claims are noticed by readers, while a candid tone about the product builds trust and makes the buying environment feel real. [L1366.064]
- Creative and personal writing shows through the copy. Readers sense the personality of the writer, so write in the voice that represents the company rather than mimicking someone else. [L1366.065]
- Logic does not have to be strictly correct to work, as long as the phrase conveys the intended feeling clearly. A reassuring phrase about returns can sound odd when read literally and still be effective, because it signals a prompt and caring company. [L1366.017]
- The goal of all copy is to get the reader to exchange their hard-earned money for the product or service, so every choice in the copy serves that exchange. [L1366.059]

### Buying environment and layout

- The first paragraphs of an ad set a buying environment, and layout and copy tone must match the price and nature of the product. A premium product needs a refined, confident look and tone, while a bargain needs a busy, deal-focused look and tone. [L1366.012]
- In print, the copywriter controls the buying environment completely through layout and word choice, unlike a store where setting it up costs thousands. Use this control on purpose instead of leaving the mood to chance. [L1366.013]

### Word choice and emotion

- Single words carry emotional associations, so word choice can change the reader's feeling even when the facts stay the same. Choose the more evocative word when it is accurate, for example *cottage* instead of *motel office* for a small building, and do not change the facts to suit a mood. [L1366.019]
- Word-level emotion choice (pattern): when the facts allow it, choose the more evocative word, such as *cottage* instead of *motel office* for a small building, without changing the facts. Test single-word swaps on high-traffic claims, because one swapped word can change response measurably. [L1366.081]
- Test case: in a mail order offer, replacing *repair* with *fix* raised response by about 20 percent in the original test. Test single-word swaps on high-traffic claims, because small wording changes can move response measurably. [L1366.020, L1366.082]
- Readers respond more to vivid, emotional description than to a dry specification list. People enjoy emotion at any time but must be pushed to study facts, so put life and occasionally a light touch into the copy to stir the reader out of indifference. [L1369.057]
- Replace long lists of points with a few vivid images the reader can see. Long sequences of *firstly, secondly and thirdly* put readers to sleep and lose the attention you have built. [L1369.058]
- Sensory description (pattern): describe the product through a few concrete sights, sounds or textures the reader already knows, rather than through a list of specifications. The reader pictures the product in his own life, which makes the benefit feel real and memorable. [L1369.119]
  - Example one: *The lamp throws a warm, even pool of light across the desk, and the dial turns without a flicker.*
  - Example two: *The jacket feels heavy and soft in the hand, and it closes with a sound that tells you the zip will hold through a wet walk home.* [L1369.119]
- Build a word picture in the reader's mind: [L1369.059]
  1. Pick a familiar object or scene the reader already pictures. [L1369.059]
  2. Add one point of interest at a time, in logical order, starting with the framework and then the parts that matter. [L1369.059]
  3. Stop when the reader can build the complete picture himself. [L1369.059]
- Use sensory language and big-impact phrases that let the reader see and feel the benefit, such as describing a cold, dark office late at night when selling a fast computer. Build a card file of vivid phrases from advertising, novels and television, and use reference works of descriptive words when stuck. [L1370.049]
- Sell an emotional story first and back it up with logic. Buyers decide on emotion and then justify with logic. Cold, purely factual letters rarely work, so the letter needs an enthusiastic voice to compensate for being ink on paper. [L1370.052]
- Boredom is the most serious sin in marketing copy, so find something to be excited about even for dull products. Excitement can come from the feeling of owning the product, the enjoyment of the money or time it saves, or from exaggerated and passionate language that the reader will still find moderate. [L1370.053]
- Passion exercise: write a letter that tries to persuade someone to do something risky but exciting, using vivid sensory detail, bold promises and the removal of each objection as you go. Then carry that energy into the real offer. Example for a hardware retailer: *Picture the first morning your shop opens with the new displays up. Your customers walk in and see exactly what you promised them. Here is how to get that morning ready in ten days.* [L1370.055]

### Readability and simplicity

- Write sales copy in very simple language, keeping sentences and words basic and introducing one new idea at a time. Simple wording makes it easier for a reader on a phone to follow the argument and reach the offer. [L1365.055]
- Make copy readable with short, punchy sentences, sentence fragments, short paragraphs of three or four sentences, everyday language and no jargon. Writing that sounds like speech moves the reader along, and grammar rules matter less than momentum. [L1370.048]
- Write at a simple reading level. The target audience is often less literate or less patient than the writer assumes, a trap called the sophistication trap. Assuming sophisticated readers costs money, and the simpler approach is safer because even TV commercials are pitched at about a sixth-grade reading level. [L1370.059]
- Reduce the perceived effort of your offer by stating the time it takes in plain terms, such as 15 minutes a day. A small, specific time commitment makes the reader more willing to start. [L1369.066]

### Opening and first page

- Answer the first two questions, what is new and what is in it for the reader, on the first page. Readers often browse on phones and look for a reason to leave. If the prospect does not see their benefit quickly, they will leave and return to what they were doing. [L1365.011]
- Structure the first paragraph as an extended headline that sells the reader on reading the letter, and only then sell the offer. Cut any preamble, such as apologies for not writing a personal letter or long explanations of why the mail matters. [L1370.044]
- Write the headline so that it makes the reader feel the letter is welcome. [L1370.040]

### Core belief and planning

- To find the core of a promotion, ask: what is the single most important thing the reader must believe? Write the answer as one sentence before drafting anything, because it works as the mission that every later section must support. [L1365.046]
- Planning sequence for a promotion idea: [L1365.044]
  1. Write the one belief for the promotion idea. [L1365.044]
  2. Answer the first seven questions with a couple of lines each. [L1365.044]
  3. Map out the whole promotion, which takes about 5 to 10 minutes. [L1365.044]
  4. Do the research the promotion needs. [L1365.044]
  5. Write each section in order, starting with the sections the map has already defined. [L1365.044]
- Full sales letter sequence, in order: [L1370.040]
  1. Research the buyer thoroughly with the ten questions and connect with their priorities. [L1370.040]
  2. Use the offer yourself or talk to its users, and list every feature with its benefit, sorted by importance. [L1370.040]
  3. List every objection and identify the flaws in the offer, then decide how to admit them. [L1370.040]
  4. Plan delivery: postage class, envelope design, and whether it is a letter, postcard or self-mailer. [L1370.040]
  5. Write the headline that makes the reader feel the letter is welcome. [L1370.040]
  6. Build the reading path with subheads, bold text and short paragraphs so skimmers get the gist. [L1370.040]
  7. Minimise price impact with comparisons, value stacking and payment framing. [L1370.040]
  8. Use the proven persuasion techniques: scarcity or intimidation, ROI, ego, a strong guarantee and a story. [L1370.040]
  9. Write a first draft without editing or worrying about length. [L1370.040]
  10. Rewrite for strategy, adding repetition, a yes sequence and page-ending teasers. [L1370.040]
  11. Rewrite for style with short sentences, big-impact words and personality. [L1370.040]
  12. Answer every question and objection. [L1370.040]
  13. Create urgency with a deadline, premium or limited availability. [L1370.040]
  14. Add a P.S. that restates the offer. [L1370.040]
  15. Run the checklist. [L1370.040]
  16. Add graphic devices and build the layout with the copywriter involved. [L1370.040]
  17. Rewrite for passion and edit aggressively for clarity. [L1370.040]
  18. Compare the draft with strong examples. [L1370.040]
  19. Pretest it aloud and with real customers at no cost. [L1370.040]
  20. Prepare the final version, mock it up, cool off for a day, get second opinions, do a final review, then print and mail. [L1370.040]

### Flow and the slippery slide

- The first seven questions should be answered within the first third of the letter. By then the reader should be emotionally sold. Only after the emotional sale is complete should the copy turn to logic. [L1365.030]
- Once the reader understands how the mechanism delivers the result, they are pre-sold and ready for the offer. Present the offer only then, because the reader has already accepted that the new opportunity is the key to what they want. [L1365.033]
- Story formula (pattern): [Background fact] and [supporting context], BUT [conflict or problem], THEREFORE [result or conclusion]. Use *and* to set up background and momentum, *but* to create tension, and *therefore* to deliver the conclusion.
  - Why it works: stories are how people process information, and the *but* creates the tension that keeps the reader reading. Proof and quotes should therefore be wrapped in this structure instead of being listed. [L1365.016]
  - Example 1: *Reorders had been climbing for two years, and the team celebrated, BUT the newest customers had stopped coming back after month two, THEREFORE we rebuilt the onboarding sequence around month-two results.* [L1365.016]
  - Example 2: *Our waitlist grew every week and the signups looked healthy, BUT more than half of those people never bought, THEREFORE the first purchase offer now appears on the confirmation page.* [L1365.016]
- Each sentence should only have to earn the next sentence, so the reader moves through the copy like a train gathering speed. Once the reader is moving, the next lines become easier to read, which is why short opening sentences work. [L1366.004]
- Slippery slide rule: every element and sentence must pull the reader forward so strongly that they keep reading to the end. Once a reader gets past about 25 percent of an ad, they are likely to read the whole ad, so the goal is to get them past that point. [L1366.006]
- Seed of curiosity (pattern): end a paragraph with a very short line that promises the next paragraph holds something worth reading, so readers keep going through slower sections. Use it sparingly, because overuse makes copy feel manipulative. [L1366.008, L1366.074]
  - Examples: *The catch is hidden in paragraph four. Most buyers miss the one detail that changes everything, so keep reading.* [L1366.008]
  - *Most buyers miss the detail that changes everything. Keep reading.* [L1366.074]
  - *The cheapest fix takes less than a minute. Here is why it works.* [L1366.074]
- Hidden payoff (pattern): state a real benefit near the top of the ad and say it will be revealed later, so the reader has to read the full copy to get it. The payoff should be real and should arrive at the end. [L1366.009, L1366.073]
  - Examples: *Your refund question gets answered in the final section, after the warranty details.* [L1366.009]
  - *The cheapest way to run this setup is explained at the bottom of the page.* [L1366.009]
  - *The fastest way to cut your phone bill is in the last paragraph, and most readers skip it.* [L1366.073]
  - *The one setting that doubles battery life is explained after the list of features.* [L1366.073]
- Never end a page with a complete sentence, since that gives the reader permission to stop. End each page mid-sentence or at an exciting phrase, and add teaser copy at the bottom of the page that works like a headline for the next page. [L1370.046]
- Copy flows like a one-way chain: each block must anticipate the question raised by the one before it. A reader who stops at any question will not reach the order request, so check each transition. [L1366.050, L1366.124]
- Create a double readership path. Impulsive readers skim headlines, subheads, photos with captions and boxed short paragraphs, while analytical readers read every word and want facts, figures, charts and statistics. Write the skim path so it carries the full offer, then use it as signposts along the full text for analytical readers. [L1370.045]
- Repetition in one letter (pattern): restate the core promise in six different forms: as a plain statement, as an example, as a short true story, as a testimonial, as a quote from an expert or customer, and as a numbered summary. Repetition is one of the two ways people accept new ideas, the other being shock, so vary the wording on each pass. [L1370.041]

### Length

- Copy length rule: copy should be long enough to create the buying environment, build interest, relate to the buyer's needs and make the full case, and no longer. Judge length by whether the reader takes the requested action, not by word count. [L1366.054, L1366.089]
- Higher-priced products need more copy to justify the price and create the need. A low price that looks like a clear value needs less copy, while a low price that seems too cheap to be credible needs more copy to build trust. [L1366.090]
- Short copy works only when the photos, the price and the medium already do the environment-building work, as in a catalog with strong photography and low prices. Otherwise write more copy. [L1366.091, L1366.057]
- Readers read long copy when they care intensely about the subject. Interest drops once the reader has mastered the topic, so long copy pays off mainly for a target reader who is still learning and deeply involved. [L1366.092, L1366.058]
- The more unusual a product, the more copy it needs to relate it to the user, build the buying environment and explain its new features. Mail order suits unusual products that need that much copy, because most retail settings do not allow it. [L1366.056]
- Long copy works when it targets qualified buyers, because most readers will glance and discard, and that is acceptable. Write for the buyer, not for the non-buyer, and add pages until the buyer has every fact needed to act. Some letters grew from one or two pages to many and got better results with each addition. [L1370.042]
- Research cited by the author found that readership of industrial ads with extensive text drops sharply for copy under about 50 words, and drops much less between 50 and 500 words. Do not shorten copy just to fit a format or page limit; write to tell the whole story. [L1370.043]

### Drafting process

- Practice produces the largest gains in copywriting. Write every day in small forms such as letters, postcards, articles for local papers and ads, because volume builds skill faster than study alone. [L1366.045]
- A first draft is expected to be weak. Do not judge the draft by how it reads, because the first draft is an emotional release of everything you want to say and the real quality comes from editing. [L1366.046]
- When drafting, get the copy out first and ignore spelling and grammar, then switch to logic when editing. Write with the intuitive, emotional side of the mind and edit with the analytical side. [L1366.047]
- Write the first version as a print direct response ad, even when the final product will be sold on the internet, in a catalog or on TV. The print version reveals the core selling points that can then be used in every other medium. [L1366.060, L1366.093]
- Use a checklist as a mid-course correction in the writing process, scanning the draft against every formula, technique and strategy in the playbook, because drafts drift from good practice as they are revised. [L1370.061]

### Editing

- In editing, refine copy so that it expresses exactly what you intend with the fewest words. You can rearrange sentences, cut words that add little, substitute stronger words, or add words for clarity, but keep the same emotional feel. [L1366.048]
- Edit aggressively to clarify, not only to shorten. Remove any word or phrase that does not advance, strengthen or reinforce the core sales story. Edit the draft in several passes, setting it aside for hours between passes, because the shorter version usually follows naturally from clearer wording. [L1370.056]
- Compare your draft with several strong examples, not just one. Check whether your text flows as smoothly, speaks to the audience as well, is structurally sound, is as easy to understand, and moves the reader to act as effectively. [L1370.057]

### Objections, admissions and proof

- List every objection, fear, doubt and excuse a prospect could have for not responding, writing each one on its own card. Then answer each objection in the copy, because a letter that leaves an objection unanswered lets the reader stop at that doubt. [L1370.007]
- Damaging admission (pattern): openly state the real drawbacks of the offer and who it is not for, then show why the trade-off is still worth it for the right buyer. This raises credibility because readers trust a seller who admits weak points.
  - Example: *This is not the cheapest option, and it takes two weeks to ship. If you need it tomorrow, a local store is the better choice, but if you want a tested product that lasts five years, this one is built for you.*
  - Second example: *We do not offer same-day installation or phone support after 6 pm. If you can plan a week ahead and want a repair done right the first time, you will be glad you waited.* [L1370.008]

### Closing

- Use a P.S. after every sales letter, because many readers look at the end first. A P.S. that restates the offer or promise acts as a second headline. Do not consider the letter finished until a P.S. is written. [L1370.060]

### Envelopes: attention and first impression

- Assume recipients sort their mail over a wastebasket and decide in seconds. In business settings an assistant may screen the envelopes first. The envelope must therefore earn the open before the letter is read. [L1370.014]
- Never be half-way in envelope design. If the envelope reveals that the mail is business or sales material, use the whole face as a billboard with teaser copy and a strong image. Choose the disguised look or the billboard look deliberately, not a mix of both. [L1370.016]
- Whatever the envelope promises must be delivered inside, such as a *Personal* label followed by something personal in the mailing. Unfulfilled envelope promises destroy the credibility of everything enclosed, while fulfilled promises increase it. [L1370.015]
- Sneak-up envelope (pattern): a plain white envelope with no business name, only an address, a person's name as return address, no teaser text, individual or ink-jet addressing and a live stamp, so it looks like personal correspondence. The author estimated about a 98 percent chance of delivery and opening with first-class postage. Use it when prospects are cold and you want the envelope read before it is judged. [L1370.012]
- Avoid gummed white address labels, which look like junk mail. Individually addressed or ink-jet addressed envelopes produce better response. The author paid home workers to hand-address envelopes because testing showed the lift justified the cost. [L1370.011]
- A mailing to doctors that used the individual doctor's name and address as return address, with no company name, pulled up to 300 percent better than the same letter in envelopes showing the company. The author reports this from his own tests with a professional audience. [L1370.017]
- Hybrid envelope (tool): combine personalisation with teaser copy. For example, use a window envelope showing a personalised letter headline with the recipient's name and city, plus printed teaser text on the front and testimonials on the back. Personalised headlines, body copy and enclosures are now easy to produce with printing technology. [L1370.018]
- Use an attention-getter on the envelope only with a clear purpose. On third-class mail a catch-phrase pulls readers into the envelope, but on first-class mail a plain corner card usually pulls better because it looks like a personal letter. Test both versions against each other. [L1369.070]
- If you use a catch-phrase or attention-getter on the outside of an envelope, send the mailing third class to save about half the postage. Otherwise the postage cost of a first-class letter is wasted on an envelope that already looks like an advertisement. [L1369.071]
- Envelope picture (pattern): place a picture linked to the recipient's work or organization on the envelope, with the recipient's name line replaced by a care-of line for his company. A picture of a person he recognizes from his trade flatters him and draws favorable attention before he reads the letter.
  - Example one: a photo of a shop owner from a trade magazine, addressed as care of the owner's store and street address.
  - Example two: a photo of a plant manager from an industry newsletter, addressed care of the plant's name and city. [L1369.072]
- When a mailing carries a named person's name as the return address, enclose a small notepad-sized note signed by that person. The note says the information helped them and asks the reader to go through everything enclosed. This note is the promise the envelope makes, delivered inside, so the reader trusts the rest of the mailing. [L1370.121]

### Postage and delivery

- Third-class bulk mail can have a non-delivery rate of 10 to 30 percent according to older postal audits, and the author believed it was worse. Bulk mail is only justified when the economics cannot support first-class postage, since non-delivery can wreck a campaign without the sender ever knowing. [L1370.009] (older advice)
- Use first-class postage with a real stamp instead of a meter imprint to improve delivery odds, because postal workers are least likely to discard mail they believe the recipient expects. Automated stamp-affixing machines are available for mailers who cannot hand-stamp. [L1370.010]
- Stamps and small postage details (historical tests, US mail of the 1930s):
  - Two red 2-cent stamps pulled more replies than one 4-cent stamp, and one red 2-cent stamp pulled better than two green 1-cent stamps. Test stamp color and denomination before a large mailing. [L1369.082]
  - A brown 1.5-cent stamp looked like a 4-cent stamp and pulled better than a green 1-cent stamp, but no better than two half-cent stamps. Postage stamps also pulled better than metered postage or postal indicia in the same tests. [L1369.083]
  - Printing the 1-cent metered postage in black ribbon may outpull a 2-cent stamp or meter in some post offices. Small details such as ink color and postage type are worth testing, but only after the core letter already works. [L1369.084]
- Fold, indents, postage and stamp color are minor details that matter only after the opening, description, argument and close are working. Adding them to a weak letter will not produce results. [L1369.085]

### Gatekeepers

- When a gatekeeper such as an assistant screens mail for an executive, send the sales package this way: [L1370.125]
  1. Place the sealed sales package inside a plain kraft envelope. [L1370.125]
  2. Address the kraft envelope personally to the decision-maker, with no company name on the front. [L1370.125]
  3. Put the sender's personal name in the return-address corner. [L1370.125]
  4. Send it by overnight courier, placed inside the courier company's outer envelope. This makes the piece look like a personal, urgent item rather than advertising. [L1370.125]

### Letter presentation and folds

- Fold the letter so that only the salutation and first line show when the reader picks it up, using a military-style fold. This fold raised orders by as much as 10 percent in tests. [L1369.080]
- Indent the paragraph that carries your most important point. In tests, indentation drew more attention than underlining or all-capital text. [L1369.081]

### Executive mailings and grabbers

- For executive and business-owner mailings, use superior paper and an envelope with texture or watermark, keep enclosures to a minimum, and place brochures and order forms in a second sealed package inside the main envelope. Prestige words such as *exclusive, select, superior, charter member, prominent, worthwhile, yield* and *individual membership* raise perceived status. [L1370.029]
- A grabber is a physical object attached to or sent with the letter to create curiosity, such as a coin, tea bag, miniature object or a trade-show invitation in a bottle. Pairing the grabber with a message that explains why the object was sent gives a reason to read the letter. [L1370.030]
- Cases: a seminar operator mailed a miniature trash can with peanuts and a letter framed as a squirrel calling the prospect *nuts* for not responding, with the point that not responding equals throwing a large sum of money away. Separately, a trade-show mailing sent a bottled treasure-map invitation with a compass, magnifier and highlighter, and produced a 75 percent increase in targeted traffic compared with prior years. [L1370.031]
- Consumer mail needs bold, colourful and attention-grabbing pieces that give the reader something to do in every section, such as tear-off stamps, scratch-off cards, tokens or stickers. Colour is practically essential in consumer mailings, and colour photographs help. [L1370.032]

### Folders and multi-panel mailings

- A folder works like a magazine advertisement and needs the same parts: an illustration and headline to win attention, an opening that arouses interest, a clear description, a logical argument, a clincher, and a coupon or card that makes ordering easy. [L1369.073]
- A circular enclosed with a letter adds about 25 to 33 percent to the pulling power of almost any letter. The enclosure should carry the illustrated detail and the letter should carry the argument. [L1369.074]
- Layout of a multi-panel mailing folder: [L1369.120]
  1. Front panel: place a headline and illustration that win attention on their own. [L1369.120]
  2. Opening pages: use a story or question that arouses interest in the offer. [L1369.120]
  3. Center pages: describe the offer and present the logical argument with its key features. [L1369.120]
  4. Last page: place proof, such as a letter from a third party who verifies the claims. [L1369.120]
  5. Include a card or coupon that makes ordering a single action. [L1369.120]

#### Further details

Build opening-line ideas from published books:
1. Go to a physical bookstore and pick up novels from authors who write in your reader's genre.
2. Write down the first line of each book and note the hook it uses, such as danger, a question, or a loss.
3. Group the lines by hook type and see which types appear most often.
4. Write several opening lines for your own product using the most common hook types, then test the strongest ones against your current opener.
[L0378.116]

- Sales copy is a core online marketing skill, because it sells through words in print and in search results. Developing this skill can improve results more than most other changes. [L0382.049]

## Social ad copy by platform

### Facebook and Instagram primary text: principles

- Primary text is the most critical element of a Facebook ad because users see it prominently and it must look organic. Most advertisers fail by writing it in marketing language, which makes the ad read as corporate promotion. Getting it right matters more than perfecting headlines or descriptions. [L0205.012]
- Write it as a first-person narrative in three parts: the problem you experienced, trying the product, and the positive result. Conversational phrases such as "I've been noticing," "switched to," "honestly," and "seriously loving" make it sound like a real person sharing an experience. [L0205.011]
- It must appear organic and natural, like a personal recommendation or story, not marketing copy. [L0205.004]
- Include the closing phrase word for word: "click below to get yours here." [L0205.004]
- The first one to two lines carry most of the attention, so open with a bold claim, a benefit-led headline, or a question to the viewer that names their pain point. [L0647.024]
- On mobile News Feed, only the first three lines show before the "see more" link (older advice, 2021-22). Put the key message and the reason to click in the opening lines. [L1342.033]
- Keep paid social copy short, direct and bullet-pointed, with a clear call to action and an offer. Very long text reduces readability on feeds such as Facebook. [L0515.023]
- Short, simple copy still performs well for proven products, so competitor ads with minimal text are a valid model. Judge performance by ad activity rather than copy length. [L1172.041]
- Long and short copy should both be tested, because on many niches and products longer copy often outperforms very short copy (older advice, 2021-22). [L1238.010]
- The opening line of a long Facebook ad must be interesting enough to make people click to read more, because text beyond the visible start is truncated. [L1238.010]
- Ad copy for a proven video should use a formula: open with a surprised first-person line that names the buyer's hope, introduce the product by name as the answer, promise one result without fuss, then remove the main objection about feel or texture. The surprise stops the reader, the named product makes the offer specific, and the objection removal answers doubt before it forms. [L0707.032]
  - Example one: "Thought I would never find a moisturizer that sinks in fast. Meet [PRODUCT], my go-to for softer skin without the greasy feel." [L0707.032]
  - Example two: "Tired of serums that pill under makeup? Meet [PRODUCT], my secret to a smooth base without the heavy layer." [L0707.032]
- Pattern for a home decor ad: an emotional benefit statement plus a call to the customer to build a space. It sells the feeling of the product rather than only its features, which fits the ad's job of attracting clicks. [L0642.029]
  - Example one: "Turn any room into a place you love with pieces that feel personal." [L0642.029]
  - Example two: "Add warmth to your space with decor picked for everyday comfort." [L0642.029]

### Facebook copy prompts (ChatGPT)

Use the three prompts below as written and fill in the placeholders. The procedure that uses them follows in the next group.

```
Write two separate Facebook posts promoting [INSERT PRODUCT HERE] that read like authentic personal updates rather than ads. Both should acknowledge the core problem customers face, describe the positive result after using the product, feel conversational with emoji accents, and finish with exactly this closing: "click below to get yours here"
```
[L0205.001]

```
Draft a Facebook headline for [INSERT PRODUCT HERE] with a natural, peer-to-peer tone that avoids advertising language. Include both the customer's pain point and the benefit they'll experience. Keep it notably shorter than a full post.
```
[L0205.002]

```
Create a brief Facebook supporting text for [INSERT PRODUCT HERE] that sounds like user feedback while naming the problem solved and the improvement gained. Make it substantially shorter than the headline version.
```
[L0205.003]

### Facebook copy generation procedure

1. Identify your product name and the main customer problem it solves (for example: acne problem, focus problem, skin dryness). [L0205.010]
2. Open ChatGPT and use the Primary Text prompt, filling in [INSERT PRODUCT HERE] and [NAME MAIN PROBLEM CUSTOMERS HAVE]. [L0205.010]
3. Generate 2 primary texts from ChatGPT. [L0205.010]
4. Copy one or both primary texts and paste into your Facebook ad's primary text field. [L0205.010]
5. Add your website URL to the primary text field in the ad. [L0205.010]
6. Create two headlines: use the first headline for your offer (for example: "Buy 1 Get 1 Free Ends Midnight"), and generate the second headline using the Headline prompt in ChatGPT. [L0205.010, L0205.005]
7. Use the Description prompt in ChatGPT with your product name and customer problem. [L0205.010]
8. Copy one description from ChatGPT into the Facebook description field, ensuring it is shorter than the headline. [L0205.010, L0205.006]
9. Review all three elements before launching the ad. [L0205.010]

### Facebook copy generation example

- Example for an organic hyaluronic acid serum powder addressing skin dryness:
  - Primary post: "I've been noticing my skin getting drier and duller lately, especially with the seasons changing. Switched to this organic hyaluronic acid serum powder, and my skin's honestly never felt more hydrated and smooth. Seriously loving the natural glow it's giving me! Click below to get yours here." [L0205.009]
  - Headline: "Finally found something organic that actually keeps my skin hydrated all day. No more dry patches or dullness! Click below to get yours here." [L0205.009]
  - Support text: "My skin used to feel so dry and tight, especially in colder weather. Ever since I started using this organic hyaluronic acid serum powder, it's been noticeably softer, hydrated, and glowing naturally. Seriously, mixing it fresh each morning has been a game-changer." [L0205.009]

### Facebook headlines

- Keep headlines short enough to read fully on a phone. Place an emoji only at the end, and only when it matches the event and brand tone, because an unrelated emoji adds noise instead of attention. [L0547.012]
- Create two Facebook headlines with different purposes: one contains your specific offer (such as "Buy 1 Get 1 Free Ends Midnight"), and the other is generated with the headline prompt in ChatGPT. [L0205.005]
- Check each ChatGPT-generated headline for the phrase "click below to get yours here." If it appears, remove it. This closing belongs only in the primary text; headlines must stand independently as compelling statements or offers. [L0205.013]
- The headline is the most visible text, so include either a trust factor (a number of happy customers, or a star rating such as 4.8 out of 5 from reviews) or an offer such as free shipping or buy one get one free. [L0647.029]
- Headline formula: [trust element or offer] + [short supporting detail]. Shoppers look for proof that the brand is trustworthy or for a concrete deal, so one of these must be visible immediately. [L0647.030]
  - Own examples: "Over 2,500 five-star reviews" and "Free returns on every order." [L0647.030]
- Headlines in a Facebook ad are shown only on Facebook; the headline does not show on Instagram. [L0865.045]
- Social proof for the description field, in the format "[Rating] out of 5 by [number] happy customers":
  - "4 out of 5 by 15,000 happy customers" [L0204.021]
  - "[Decimal rating] out of 5 by [number] happy customers," for example "4.8 out of 5 by 15,000+" [L0204.021]
  - "[Number] happy customers worldwide," with no star rating [L0204.021]

### Facebook descriptions

- The description is shorter than the headline because the platform display requires brevity. [L0205.006]
- The description sits under the headline in small type and should carry an offer or a scarcity signal, such as "Limited time only" or "Get yours today." [L0647.031]
- Description formula: [urgency or scarcity phrase] + [action to take now]. A short urgency line gives the viewer a reason to click immediately, so keep it to a few words. [L0647.032]
  - Own examples: "Only 48 hours left at this price" and "Order before this batch sells out." [L0647.032]
- Keep the description very short, with one benefit, feature or trust line such as free shipping or 24/7 support, because longer text is cut off. [L0648.025]
- Conflict on whether the description is shown: Source E states the description is never shown on Facebook or Instagram and does not need to be filled in. [L0865.045] The Source C source treats it as a visible line that carries the offer or social proof. [L0647.031, L0204.021] Check the Advanced preview for each placement before deciding whether to fill it. [L0865.050]

### Facebook ad copy structure

Use this structure in order.

1. Bold headline: a pain point, a controversial statement, a question to the customer, or a big claim such as a rating or ranking. The product name can also work as headline. [L0648.025]
2. Product introduction line. [L0648.025]
3. Benefits: two benefits and one feature. [L0648.025]
4. Trust factor: a customer count or the accepted payment methods. [L0648.025]
5. Star rating: four star icons followed by a rating such as 4.8 out of 5 from 1000+ customers. [L0648.025]
6. Offer plus scarcity: a discount with a limit, such as 50% off for the next 50 orders. [L0648.025]
7. Call to action: Shop now, with the link. [L0648.025]

### Facebook primary text templates

Benefit-led version (use one version during testing):

```
[Bold claim, benefit headline, or question to the reader that names their pain point]
[Product name] is your answer to that problem: [one line on how it solves it].
- [Benefit 1]
- [Benefit 2]
- [Benefit 3]
- [Benefit 4]
[Exclusive offer, e.g. X% off, matching the offer on your site]. Limited time only.
Shop now: [product page URL]
```
[L0647.025]

Pain-point version (use one version during testing):

```
Struggling with [customer pain point]?
Say hello to [product name], your answer to the problem.
- [Benefit 1]
- [Benefit 2]
- [Benefit 3]
[Exclusive offer, e.g. X% off, matching the offer on your site]. Limited time only.
Shop now: [product page URL]
```
[L0647.026]

Short-form version (a shorter alternative to the templates above):

```
[One benefit-led top line about the product]
- [Benefit 1]
- [Benefit 2]
Shop now: [product page URL]
```
[L0647.027]

### Trust labels and call to action

- Trust labels: in the ad, open Edit info and click Create new label to add lines such as free shipping, free returns, PayPal accepted, Klarna, Google Pay or Apple Pay. These labels appear under the ad before the customer clicks. [L0648.026]
- Call to action button: Shop now. [L0647.033]
- Destination: the product page URL, not the home page, because the product page holds the product information the viewer needs after clicking. [L0647.033]
- Use Shop Now as the call-to-action button for standard sales ads. [L0865.046]
- Shop for product retargeting is the CTA for product retargeting, though it does not appear in every placement; use it where it shows. [L1342.035, older advice 2021-22]
- Add a strong offer such as 40% off near the start of a video to grab attention. [L1077.018]
- Ad copy for a proven video's link card: a bestseller label in the headline, a Shop now button, and a time-limited discount line such as "50 percent off today." These three elements together push the click at the end of the ad. Use a real sales rank or real offer. [L0707.031]

### Ad setup in Meta Ads Manager

- Creative setup: under Set up creative, add the headline in the Headline field (the Add headline option is available for more variations), and add the Primary text in its own field. The ad preview shows how the ad will look in Feeds, Stories and Reels. [L0614.014]
- Media picker: under Ad creative, the source tabs are Media from you and Media from AI, and the account's Business, Instagram and Page media appear under the Account and Page tabs. Only one image or video can be selected per ad, and a search field filters the media library. [L0614.023]
- Text section: Primary text (a line explaining what the ad is about), Headline, Description (extra detail, optional) and a Call to action button. [L0614.024]
- Several headline options let Meta show the version it predicts will perform best. [L0614.024]
- Creative testing can compare up to 5 creative versions, which is not needed for a warm-up. [L0614.024]
- Text & Links fields: Primary text (main copy), Headline (short, optional), and Description (additional details, optional). The Destination is Website, and the Website URL must be the landing page. The display link is the URL shown on the ad and must match the website URL. [L1342.034, older advice 2021-22]
- Settings > Ad > Languages: an ad can be created in several languages, and Facebook shows each viewer the version that suits them best. Add a language version when the store serves more than one language. [L1342.037, older advice 2021-22]
- Multiple text options: the primary text and headline fields can hold several text options, and Meta shows the option it predicts will perform best. [L0865.067]
- If full control over the copy is wanted, add only one primary text and skip Meta's generated variations. [L0865.067]
- Facebook's AI-suggested copy variations are optional and worth using only once they look good on their own. [L0647.028]
- Ad preview: the preview on the right shows the ad as it will look on Facebook, including the catalog below it when enabled. Advanced preview shows every placement the ad may run on and should be checked before publishing. [L0865.050]

### Placements, crop, video length and previews

- Crop: in Ad > Creative > Crop, choose 1:1 or 9:16 for the placements that need it. If Original is kept, the image may be cropped automatically, but this is unreliable. To control the crop, upload a separate 9:16 version with Replace in the vertical slot. Horizontal formats are rarely shown and can be ignored. [L0865.044]
- Primary text position: on Facebook the primary text appears above the ad and on Instagram it appears below the ad. [L0865.045]
- Carousel: in a Meta carousel ad, the primary text appears above the product cards on Facebook and below them on Instagram. One primary text entry therefore serves both placements, and the preview shows how it appears on each. [L1029.033]
- Carousel closing card: the destination URL entered in the final ad setup step is also used for an extra closing card at the end of the carousel. A click on that card takes the viewer to the store. [L1029.034]
- Ad copy length on Meta: keep ad copy to three lines because Meta shows only three. Use emojis, a clear offer and a direct link. [L0649.033]
- Video length cap: some placements, such as Instagram, cap video length at 15 seconds. A 30-second video still publishes but simply will not show in that placement, so make shorter cuts and both vertical and landscape versions. [L0649.037]
- Story aspect ratio warning: if Facebook or TikTok Ads Manager shows a story aspect ratio warning under automatic placements, it can be ignored when the video follows the format from the tutorial. [L0363.050]
- Copy space by platform: Google Search ads have limited character space and need short, concise copy. Facebook ads provide substantially more space, allowing longer paragraphs, detailed benefit explanations, and customer review quotes. Tailor copy length, depth of explanation, and proof elements to each platform's constraints. [L0241.013, older advice 2021-22]

### Facebook ad testing structure

- Inside one ad set, create several ads with different images and text so the creatives can be split tested against each other. Each ad holds its own image, headline and link text, while the ad set keeps the audience and budget. [L0641.022]
- During testing, use one ad copy version per ad. [L0647.028]
- Product test structure (Source D): read the 5 headlines and 5 primary texts generated by the prompt, and do not use all five. Pick the two headlines and two primary texts that feel strongest. [L1193.021]
- Product test entry (Source D): enter the two headlines and two primary texts into the ad, add one description, paste the landing page URL as the website URL, and select Shop Now as the CTA. [L1193.021]
- Only one description is needed per ad in a product test. Add it alongside the two headlines and two primary texts. [L1193.023]
- Conflict on copy per ad: the Source C rule of one copy version per ad [L0647.028] applies when each copy version must be read on its own. The Source D product test [L1193.021, L1193.023] puts two headlines and two primary texts into one ad. Choose the structure that matches the test's goal. Note that a single primary text gives full control and skips Meta's selection. [L0865.067]
- Image ads and carousel ads can perform as well as video ads on Facebook, so test them as a separate format next to the winning video creatives. Image ads with a short text overlay and an emoji were reported to work well for a brand. [L0774.056]
- When a proven video ad is the source, keep the proven video and add a call to action, urgency text and other conversion elements; change only what is needed for conversion. [L1429.050]

### Facebook audience-matched copy

- Facebook reads the text and the context of the video or image, including detected objects in the visual, to decide who sees the ad. Creatives should be relevant to the target audience, and a narrow interest may need messages that clearly match it. [L0995.029]
- Creatives should speak to the target audience intimately by naming who they are or the specific problem they face. Facebook uses the creative's visual context and text to match the ad to the right audience. [L0999.035]
- Pattern for niche creative and copy: name the specific audience and its specific problem or situation in the ad, and show that situation in the video or image. A broad message with a broad audience performs worse than one relevant to a narrow group. [L0995.028]
  - Example for a self-defense product: "Heading out on a late-night walk? Keep a personal alarm in your pocket." [L0995.028]
  - Example for a pet hair brush: "Shedding dog on your bed every morning? This brush pulls out the thick German Shepherd undercoat." [L0995.028]
- Interest targeting and broad targeting: when budgets are small, test a specific interest (e.g. camping, snowboarding, pets, home and garden), reduce the audience size, pick an interest, and make sure the ad clearly matches it. In the case described, broad targeting was not working and interest-specific targeting performed better. [L0995.030]

### Retargeting copy

- Retargeting Facebook copy works when the primary text reminds the visitor of the exact product they viewed, adds one concrete reason to return now, and the headline names the next action. [L1342.036, older advice 2021-22]
  - Example 1, primary text: "Still thinking about the [product name] you looked at? It is in stock and ships in [X] days." Headline: "Get Yours Before It Sells Out." [L1342.036]
  - Example 2, primary text: "Your [product name] is still waiting. Order today and get [offer] on your first purchase." Headline: "Complete Your Order." [L1342.036]
- Retargeting copy prompt for Meta and Google Display (use the email text as the foundation):

```
Great, thanks. I'm also launching retargeting ads on Meta and the Google Display Network. Use the email text above as the foundation for this ad copy. Meta needs main body text, a headline, and a call-to-action button labeled Shop Now. For Google Display, write one headline and one description per ad, with each ad matched to the email it follows, covering the opening two days, the middle days, and the final days of the promotion.
```
[L1287.050]

- Google remarketing ads allow only short copy, so the text must be brief there. [L1238.010, older advice 2021-22]

### TikTok ad copy

- Creatives must show what is being sold. On TikTok, users need a clear hook and an explanation of the offer. [L0577.059]
- Good TikTok creatives explain product features through sound and visual effects, with no on-screen text, no talking presenter, and no sales argument. This satisfying, fun style makes viewers feel entertained rather than sold to. [L1374.004]
- Native pattern: a newspaper-style analogy shows that traditional bold ad formatting gets skipped, while an advertorial that looks like useful content holds attention until the viewer realizes it is an ad. Make the ad match the native look and feel of the feed and provide value first. [L1374.003]
  - Example for a kitchen gadget: a 10-second clip of a slicing-hack sequence with sound and no text, showing the product working. [L1374.003]
  - Example for a pet accessory: a quick "what your dog does when you leave" scene that reveals the product as the answer at the end. [L1374.003]
- Ad copy pattern: a four-to-five-word phrase taken from how a customer would describe the main benefit, phrased in the customer's own words. It matches the native, conversational tone and names the concrete result the buyer wants. [L1376.020]
  - Examples: "My back finally stopped aching" for a posture corrector; "Sleep feels different now" for a sleep mask. [L1376.020]
- Offer-led text: a clear discount plus an urgency phrase, such as a percent-off message and a limited-time notice. [L1377.036]
  - Example patterns: "Save 40% today only" or "Free shipping ends tonight." [L1377.036]
- Short video ad text: name the product, add a short offer with its price, and keep the call to action simple. The price sits in the text so viewers understand the offer in one line. [L1378.021]
  - Examples: "Portable blender for only 39.99" and "Foot massager for only 49.99." [L1378.021]
- Ad copy formula: an offer line that states the discount and a call to action, such as a percent-off figure followed by "get yours today" or "ending soon." The discount and urgency are the first things a TikTok viewer reads, and the line fits the ad text limit. [L1382.027]
  - Examples: "40 percent off, shop today before the sale ends" and "50 percent off this week, get yours now." [L1382.027]
- Tone: use a fun, relatable tone in ad text and reactions, such as a funny quote or a customer reaction after receiving the product, instead of only a discount message. Offer messages still work well and are common. [L1377.038]
- Thumbnail: a human face smiling in the ad image or thumbnail has worked better than a product image or store graphic in tests. The face need not be tied to the product, and the brand name and a logo should stay visible. [L1377.037]
- Reuse across platforms: a TikTok ad creative that works on TikTok can usually be reused on Facebook and Instagram placements, but a Facebook ad generally does not perform on TikTok. Use TikTok-native creatives as the source when expanding to other platforms. [L1374.005]

### TikTok duplicate content and freshness

- TikTok reduces the reach of duplicate content, and ads are treated as ordinary videos on the platform. Creatives that were already widely posted or running for a long time lose reach, so new or freshly uploaded videos are preferred. [L1382.021]

### TikTok Spark Ads

- Spark ads on an organic video can lower that video's organic reach, so use videos that are roughly 20 to 30 days old or older. Recent viral organic posts are better left out of paid tests. [L1377.026]
- Spark Ads performed better than regular TikTok ads in the tests, so test both formats on the same product. Spark Ads are the preferred option when running ads from an organic account. [L1381.030]
- Spark Ads kept the comment filters set on the account, while comments on traditional TikTok ads are harder to monitor. Filter negative comments on the account before running ads. [L1381.029]
- After a Spark Ad was rejected by TikTok, organic views on the linked account dropped below 600 and stayed low. Rejected ads may coincide with a drop in organic reach, so review the rejection before testing more ads from the same account. [L1381.014]

### Instagram Reels and Trial Reels

- For Instagram Reels repurposed from TikTok, add a call to action such as Shop Now, and make the text more ad-like near the end of the video. The owner reported no account penalty on Instagram, while TikTok was more sensitive to reports. [L1077.018]
- Trial Reels works as a low-risk testing ground for content styles and can be removed from the profile grid afterwards, so a polished brand page keeps its look. Creators also use it to test many hooks before pushing an ad on Facebook. [L1397.006]
- When Instagram is a main source of income, the ad can link to the Instagram page instead of the store, since the goal is for customers to check out the brand page first. This is an exception to the usual approach of linking directly to the store. [L1439.024]

### Pinterest audience and targeting

- Pinterest audience size: 400+ million users. [L0296.016]
- 80% of Pinterest users have previously purchased items on the platform. [L0296.017]
- Pinterest's primary audience is women age 30 and older; this demographic is the majority and the best fit for products targeting this group. [L0296.018]
- Pinterest requires 7-15 days to optimize; expect very high CPMs and poor results in the first 2-3 days as the platform tests. [L0296.019]
- Not all products work on Pinterest; the platform works best for niches related to DIY, crafts, and inspiration content. [L0296.020]
- Audience size: use stacked interests, selecting seven to ten (or five to twenty) specific sub-interests related to the product and target audience, not only broad parent categories. Keep audience size between 5 and 10 million as the sweet spot; up to 30 million is acceptable, and above 30 million is too big. [L1134.021]
- Select individual sub-interests rather than only the parent interest, because Pinterest reports which interest drove sales only for individually selected interests; the breakdown view then shows which interest is performing. [L1134.023]
- Demographics: if only women fit the product, select female only; an age range of 21+ is good, and 25+ was also reported to work well. Location can be all US or a specific country; language and device restrictions are not needed. [L1134.022]
- Optimization and delivery: select Checkout as the conversion event and automatic bidding. [L1134.022]
- Keep keywords and interests in separate campaigns. Start with interest-based targeting, and test keyword targeting only after the product has been confirmed as a winner. [L1134.024]
- Keywords: Pinterest changed its search results so that keywords appear as separate, segmented items, which makes the platform more advertiser-friendly. Promoted pin targeting is built on these keyword segments, so choose keywords that match the exact terms users search for. [L1136.039]

### Pinterest creative

- Pinterest creatives should be TikTok-style vertical video in 9:16 format, 15 to 20 seconds long (20 seconds is seen as best), with quick transitions within one to two seconds. Show the product in use within the first three to five seconds; in the speaker's tests such clips reached over 3 percent CTR. [L1134.026]
- Video outperforms static images on Pinterest in the speaker's tests across beauty, health, home decor and home improvement; fashion may be an exception where images can work. [L1134.027]
- Creative can be reused for six or seven months because there is little saturation on Pinterest. [L1134.027]
- TikTok-style videos produced the best CTR in the lesson's tests, and simple image pins and standard pins performed worse. [L1135.041]
- Pinterest users recognize product images immediately, so the product must be visible. [L0577.059]

### Pinterest ad setup and copy

- Creating a Pinterest ad: click Select pins or Create pin (upload a video from the computer). Use the same headline as on TikTok ads as the title, and add a short description of three to four lines that names the pain point and the benefit and ends with a call to action, such as "flawless skin is just a click away." The description can be generated with ChatGPT. [L1134.028]
- Creating a video pin at the ad level:
  1. Click Select pins. [L1135.043]
  2. If you have no existing pins, click Create pin. [L1135.043]
  3. Upload the video from your computer. [L1135.043]
  4. Enter the ad headline in the title field (the same one used for TikTok ads). [L1135.043]
  5. Enter the ad text in the description field. [L1135.043]
- Pattern for Pinterest ad description copy: write three to four lines that name a pain point, state the product benefit, end with a call to action, and optionally finish with a short benefit-driven line. [L1135.044]
  - Example one: "Tired of frizzy hair after every wash? This comb smooths in one pass, so tap now for salon-smooth results at home." [L1135.044]
  - Example two: "Sore feet at the end of the day? These insoles add cushioning under every step, so shop today and walk easier tomorrow." [L1135.044]

### YouTube ads

- YouTube ads need studio-quality creatives with a hook that grabs attention within the first six seconds. Videos that work on TikTok or Facebook often do not perform the same way on YouTube. [L0788.037]
- Production polish is not a prerequisite. YouTube video ads can be produced cheaply, even with a phone and a plain setup where the presenter stands in front of the product and talks. [L1510.001]
- Authenticity can outperform high production values. A phone-shot video of a person talking in front of a product, with a near-zero production budget, can become one of the most-watched YouTube ads of its kind. [L1510.002]
- Simple YouTube ad formula: a product video with product promotion aimed at a retargeting list that has not purchased, plus a top-of-funnel video aimed at competitor fans. [L1510.009]

### Demand Gen ads

- Informational images should be paired with a headline that matches the image, since Demand Gen combines headlines with images. The image's job is to create curiosity, not to give the answer. [L0882.024]

### Native ad networks

- Native ad networks such as Taboola place advertorial-style ads on large news sites. This is a separate channel from Meta ads. [L0691.003]

## Search, shopping and display ad copy

### Principles for search ad copy

- **Write for one action.** Before writing a search text ad, define exactly which action the searcher should take. [L1351.001]
- **The ad sells the click, not the product.** Its only job is to make the searcher curious enough to visit the landing page, where the offer and the full sales argument belong. (older, 2021-22) [L1351.002]
- **The landing page must match the search term.** The visitor should find what the ad promised. Because the ad only creates curiosity and sets expectations, its copy can stay short within the limited character space. (older, 2021-22) [L1351.003]
- **Earn the click to lower effective cost.** The main job of a Google search text ad is to earn the click. A higher click-through rate usually lowers the effective cost per click compared with competitors bidding on the same queries. [L1401.001]
- **Lead with the buyer's benefit, not the product name.** Either move the buyer away from a pain (for example, weight gain) or toward a gain (for example, muscle growth). Benefit lines can be framed around the seller ("we have helped a million customers") or around the buyer ("seven ways to build muscle"). [L1401.002]
- **Trigger an emotion tied to the outcome.** Write for how the buyer will feel after the result, not only for what the product does. "Feel beautiful" instead of "look beautiful" connects emotionally when the product improves how people live. [L1401.009]
- **Avoid copying competitor offers.** If every competitor in the auction uses the same offer, such as "40% off", the ads blend together and clicks drop. Check competitor ads before writing yours and find a distinct angle. [L1401.006]
- **Reflect the searched keyword in three places.** Include the targeted search keyword in the display URL, the headline and the description text. Google bolds the matching keyword in these three places, which makes the ad stand out and signals relevance. (older, 2021-22) [L1351.004]
- **Address the reader directly.** Write as if speaking to one individual, using direct words such as "you" and "you can" instead of dry factual statements. (older, 2021-22) [L1351.005]
- **State the next action explicitly.** Always include a clear call to action and state the action directly. Do not assume the searcher knows what to do next. (older, 2021-22) [L1351.007]
- **Make the call to action match the landing page.** Use a call to action that tells the searcher what happens after the click, such as a shop page, a quiz or a product comparison, so the click matches their expectation. [L1401.012]
- **Use symbols where they fit the offer.** Registered trademark (®), percent (%) and dollar ($) symbols can make a Google text ad stand out and are worth using where they fit the offer. [L1401.011]
- **Use ad extensions.** Include ad extensions in Google search text ads and choose which ones to use based on the specific ad type during setup. (older, 2021-22) [L1351.006]
- **Keep the copy simple.** Ad copy does not need overthinking. Keep it simple, personal and clear about the next action; the detailed setup of campaigns and ads follows in the campaign setup stage. (older, 2021-22) [L1351.009]
- **Show the promotion when one exists.** Shoppers search for the exact product and compare sellers. Name the product and its use clearly, and show the promotion in the ad when one exists, since a promo tag raises clicks. (older, 2021) [L0801.131]
- **Match the ad to its page.** Google Shopping ads always link to product pages, so ad creative and page content should match. (older, 2021) [L0801.132]

### Search text ad formulas and structures

**Standard formulas**

- **Result-plus-keyword formula.** State the result the buyer wants in a time-bound, concrete way, then add a keyword the searcher typed. This works because the searcher sees the exact outcome they came for, which raises relevance and clicks. Examples: "Stop back pain in 30 days" with keyword "back pain relief" in the display URL; "Dry skin fixed by Friday" with keyword "dry skin cream" in the display URL. [L1401.003]
- **Simple Google text ad structure.**
  1. Headline: include the keyword or the buyer's goal.
  2. Description line: state one benefit or feature.
  3. Second description line: add social proof (for example, a customer count) or an emotional hook.
  4. Call to action that sets the expectation for the landing page.
  5. Put the keyword or search query into the display URL path.

  [L1401.014]
- **Three-line text ad pattern.** The headline names the result the buyer wants and includes the searched keyword. The first description line turns that result into a feeling or confidence benefit. The second description line adds social proof with a customer count. The call to action states the next step. The keyword is repeated in the display URL path. Each line answers one question the searcher has at that moment (is this what I want, why this one, what happens next), and the URL confirms the match. Examples:
  - Example 1 (US sleep supplement): headline "Fall asleep faster in 7 nights" with keyword "sleep aid" in the URL; line "Wake up rested, not groggy"; line "Trusted by 250,000 sleepers, see the results"; URL path sleep-aid.
  - Example 2 (running shoes for flat feet): headline "Run pain-free this month" with keyword "running shoes flat feet" in the URL; line "Every stride feels supported"; line "Chosen by 80,000 runners, shop today"; URL path running-shoes-flat-feet.

  [L1401.019]
- **Keyword-and-benefit formula with personal address.** Put the targeted keyword in the display URL, headline and description; address the reader as "you"; end with an explicit instruction such as "Get yours now". The keyword reflection signals relevance, bolding draws the eye, the direct address feels personal, and the explicit instruction removes doubt about the next step. (older, 2021-22) [L1351.008]
  - Example 1 (running shoe keyword): Headline "Trail Running Shoes - Free Returns", description "You'll find trail running shoes built for rocky paths. Shop the range today."
  - Example 2 (dog leash keyword): Headline "Reflective Dog Leashes For Night Walks", description "You can walk your dog safely after dark. Order your reflective leash now."
- **Offer-and-shipping headline formula for online stores.** The headline is the product category plus a clear price offer, such as a percentage off or an up-to discount, and then a short benefit such as free shipping. The description line adds a reason to act now, such as a limited-time sale, a free-shipping threshold, a fast pickup option, or a generous return window. Shoppers scan these quickly, so the offer and the shipping or return promise do most of the persuading. (older, 2021-22) [L0751.014]
  - Example 1: "Ceiling Fans - Up to 35% Off | Free Delivery Over $75", description "Weekend Clearance Ends Sunday. Order Today for Next-Day Dispatch and 45-Day Returns."
  - Example 2: "Kitchen Organisers - 25% Off Storage Sets | Fast Local Pickup", description "Limited Stock at This Price. Free Shipping on Orders Over $60 and Easy 30-Day Returns."

**Branded product search ads**

- **Exact name headline.** The headline is the exact brand name plus product name. The description repeats that name, then adds stock status, shipping speed, price and a short call to action such as "order now". It works because the ad mirrors the search query, so the searcher sees immediately that the exact product is available. [L0837.048]
  - Example 1: Headline "Northline Trail Backpack 30L". Description "Northline Trail Backpack 30L in stock, ships fast, $89. Order now."
  - Example 2: Headline "Brightwave Air Purifier H13". Description "Brightwave Air Purifier H13 in stock, ships fast, $179. Shop now."

**Informational and transactional headlines**

- **Informational headlines (guide titles).** Use a "how to choose" or "what to look for" phrase, followed by the product type, followed by the use case or the reader's situation. The searcher is looking for help, so a headline that reads like a helpful article matches their intent and avoids a sales tone. Examples: "How to Choose Ski Boots for Wide Feet" and "What to Look for in Hiking Boots for Rocky Terrain". [L1350.015]
- **Transactional headlines.** Use "Shop" plus the product type, plus the use case, plus one purchase trigger such as free shipping or free returns. This works for bottom-of-funnel queries where the searcher is ready to compare or buy. The same wording fails on informational queries because it signals that a sale is the only goal. Examples: "Shop Waterproof Hiking Boots for Wet Trails, Free Returns" and "Shop Kids Rain Jackets for Muddy Play, Free Shipping". [L1350.016]

**Restricted categories**

- **Savings offer instead of a direct call.** For remarketing copy in restricted categories, replace a direct call to a person with a plain savings offer that names the store and a percentage. Formula: offer percentage + product or store + store domain, without addressing the viewer as someone who needs the product. Examples: "Save 5% on your next order at [store domain] this week." and "Get 10% off [product category] at [store domain] before the offer ends." [L0807.032]

### Dropshipping keyword signals in search ads

- **Phrases that surface dropshipping products.** Search ad copy keywords such as "percent off" combined with a discount figure and phrases like "get yours today", "get yours now" or "get yours" are used by about 90 to 95 percent of dropshippers in their ad text, so these keywords surface dropshipping products. [L1436.005]

### Google Responsive Search Ads

**Headline and description mix (current, 2025-26)**

- **Use AI for volume, with a clear brief.** AI-generated ad copy solves the volume problem of manual copywriting, producing on-theme, intent-matched variants that Google rewards through Quality Score. The key is understanding what effective copy does (matching search intent and enabling combination testing) before feeding material into AI. [L0220.003]
- **Split headlines into two intent categories.** Allocate Responsive Search Ad headlines roughly two-thirds to keyword-relevance headlines that mirror the search theme, and roughly one-third to promotional headlines containing offers, guarantees or trust signals (free shipping, lifetime warranty, verified reviews). [L0220.005]
- **Do not write every headline yourself.** Do not write all 15 Responsive Search Ad headlines yourself. Populate the required headlines with keyword content and reserve slots for promotional headlines controlled at the ad group level, allowing Google to test which combinations perform best. [L0220.006]
- **Split descriptions the same way.** Structure Responsive Search Ad descriptions with the same two-part split: approximately two descriptions containing keyword-relevant content, plus one or two descriptions featuring calls-to-action, social proof or differentiators. [L0220.007]
- **Punctuation limits.** Responsive Search Ad headlines cannot contain exclamation marks. Each description may contain a maximum of one exclamation mark. [L0220.008]
- **Vary lengths.** Vary headline lengths within Responsive Search Ads instead of making them uniform. Different device widths and ad slots require both short and long text options for optimal display. [L0220.009]

**Conflict: number of headlines and descriptions**

Sources disagree on how many slots an ad has. Apply each value to its ad format:

| Ad format | Headlines | Descriptions | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Responsive Search Ad (current, 2025-26) | 15 headlines, with keyword and promotional slots as above | Approximately 3-4: two keyword-relevant plus one or two call-to-action, social proof or differentiator lines | [L0220.005, L0220.006, L0220.007] |
| Older text ad format (2021-22) | 3 headlines, each maximum 30 characters | 2 descriptions, each maximum 90 characters including spaces | [L0262.006, L0262.007] |

**Older text ad guidance (2021-22)**

- **Headline 1 carries the keywords.** Write 3 headlines, each maximum 30 characters. Only the first headline always displays completely; others may be truncated. Always put target keywords and the product identifier in Headline 1. (older, 2021-22) [L0262.006]
- **Headline 1 matches the search term.** In search ad headlines, include the target search terms (the keywords being bid on) in Headline 1 to create relevance between what the customer searched for and what is shown. (older, 2021-22) [L0262.010]
- **Headline 2 names one differentiator.** For product-specific search ads, focus Headline 2 on one best feature or unique selling point that differentiates from competitors, not a generic description. (older, 2021-22) [L0262.011]
- **Use the description space.** Write 2 descriptions, each maximum 90 characters including spaces. Use most of the available space to maximize information displayed. (older, 2021-22) [L0262.007]
- **Create curiosity in descriptions.** In ad descriptions, create curiosity by hinting at benefits without fully explaining them. Guide readers to click through to the landing page to learn the full story, and use the landing page to answer their curiosity and provide conversion opportunities. (older, 2021-22) [L0262.013]
- **Address the reader with "you" and monetary bonuses.** Personalize description copy using "you" to address the reader directly. Include special offers or bonuses with their monetary value (for example, "$700 in bonus accessories") to spark curiosity and desire. (older, 2021-22) [L0262.014]
- **Use two curiosity hooks.** Build multiple curiosity hooks across your descriptions to pull readers through to the landing page. Create a primary curiosity element in the first description by teasing a key benefit without fully explaining it. Introduce a secondary curiosity element in the second description with an additional benefit, bonus value or special offer. Answer both curiosity elements on the landing page to drive conversions. (older, 2021-22) [L0262.030]

**Example: product-specific search campaign (older, 2021-22)**

- **Campaign and ad group structure.** Name the campaign with product identifiers combined with geographic targeting (for example, "Product IDs - Search Text - US"). Create ad groups organized by specific product models, such as the Sunray Cayenne Sauna HL400D. [L0262.025]
- **Bid and keywords.** Set the default cost-per-click bid (this example uses $0.50). Target keywords with broad match modifier syntax (the + symbol before core terms, such as +cayenne +hl400d) to capture variations while maintaining relevance. [L0262.025]
- **Headlines.** Write three headlines with varying character limits (30, 30 and 21 characters). Lead with product identification and purchase intent, then highlight key benefits such as space efficiency for compact areas, and emphasize shipping advantages. [L0262.025]
- **Display path.** Use a display path that reflects the product URL structure, for instance bathvault.com/sunray/cayenne-hl400d. [L0262.025]
- **Descriptions.** Compose two description lines with character limits (71 and 83 characters). Explain the functional advantage, such as fitting into small outdoor spaces, and communicate a concrete incentive, such as $700 in bundled accessories. [L0262.025]
- **Extensions.** Enhance the ad with call extensions containing business contact information and callout extensions that communicate competitive strengths: price-match policies, service quality and complimentary shipping options. [L0262.025]

**Callouts and sitelinks**

- **Use callouts, not sitelinks, on conversion ads.** Use callout extensions (not sitelink extensions) on product-specific conversion-focused ads. Sitelinks distract from the conversion goal by providing links to shipping pages or other products. Callout extensions can highlight offers like free shipping, guarantees or special bonuses. (older, 2021-22) [L0262.012]

**Pinning and display paths**

- **Pin headlines that must appear.** Responsive search ads do not always show every headline and description, and the ad editor warns about this. To guarantee that a specific headline or description appears, pin it to a fixed position in the ad, then check the desktop and mobile previews before saving. (older, 2021-22) [L1391.019]
- **Display path fields.** Each text ad has two display path fields after the domain, in the form www.yourdomain.com/Path 1/Path 2, and each path field is limited to 15 characters. Use them for short, relevant labels that reflect the brand or the product category. (older, 2021-22) [L1391.020]
