- Choose the sizes with the most inventory and highest performance. Google itself names these as top-performing. [L1238.003]
- Google static ads are an image with text and call to action baked in, so one design can be resized through each size with small alterations. [L1238.003]
- Pinterest: use vertical images that are taller than they are wide. Vertical pins take up more space in the home feed and produce clearly higher click-through rates, repins and traffic than wide pins. The preset Pinterest Pin size is 735 x 1102 px. [L1136.020, L1169.028]

### Banners and display ads

- On Facebook, text covering the image may not exceed 20% of the image area. Text on Facebook images is optional, but can help text stand out when used. (Older, 2021-22.) [L1238.003, L1238.004]
- To check the 20% limit, lay a grid overlay over the image in any image tool. [L1238.004]
- A retargeting image has one job: stop the scroll on social media. It can do this by showing something the viewer has seen before, such as branding or a known product picture, or by standing out visually, for example with contrasting colors or something interesting. (Older, 2021-22.) [L1238.007]

### Store graphics and hero images

- A desktop hero image should be about 1600 px wide and 400 to 600 px tall. A taller hero image pushes the rest of the homepage below the fold, and the customer may never see it. (Older, 2021-22.) [L1310.006]
- A checkout banner at 1500 x 300 px can carry the logo, privacy/secure icons and payment processor logos. [L1260.026]
- Landing page graphics: export as PNG and compress before upload, then check the fonts in PageFly under the procedure above. [L1363.027]

### Logo, profile and cover images

- The profile photo is a square 1:1 portrait, direct to camera, warm and friendly. It must not look like a corporate headshot, stock-photo perfection or heavy polish. [L1475.015]
- Never use a logo or a product shot as the profile picture. [L1475.015]
- The cover photo uses a 3:1 aspect ratio and shows a warm, aspirational, editorial lifestyle scene from the character's world, such as a desk setup, gym or outdoor space. It may show the character or the scene alone. [L1475.016]
- Profile and cover photos must contain no product shots, logos or text overlays. [L1475.016, L1476.056]
- Putting a product shot or a discount graphic on the cover or profile photo immediately signals a brand and undermines the character. Keep those images strictly lifestyle and personal. [L1475.017]
- Whitelist character page images use two formats: a square 1:1 direct-to-camera profile portrait, and a wide 3:1 lifestyle scene for the cover. [L1476.056]

### Letterheads and printed samples

- A picture on the letterhead must add essential background to the offer, such as the setting of a product's use, because decorative pictures alone may not help. Test a plain letterhead against a pictorial one before you commit. [L1369.075]
- A colored nature scene printed across the top and one side of a letterhead doubled the orders for a book series offer compared with a plain letterhead. [L1369.076]
- A small full-color reproduction of the product in the upper left corner of the letterhead added nearly 50 percent to the pulling power of one letter. [L1369.077]
- When a business was built around one person, a photograph of that person on the letterhead added 10 to 20 percent to the pulling power of the letters. [L1369.078]
- Tip a small sample of the product onto the letterhead, such as a fabric swatch for a coat or a leather swatch for luggage, so the reader can judge quality. A tactile sample is an effective attention-getter when the product has a visible quality. [L1369.079]

### Video thumbnails

- Thumbnails must be attractive and clearly show what the video will deliver, because YouTube rewards a higher click-through rate, as it does on other Google properties. (Older, 2021-22.) [L1511.012]
- Preset YouTube sizes: Thumbnail 1280 x 720 px, End Screen 1920 x 1080 px, Channel Art 2560 x 1440 px. [L1169.028]

### Text legibility on mobile

- Put overlay text near the bottom of the frame and shrink it if it is too large, so the main action and the product stay visible. [L1427.073]
- Check the layout on a phone-sized preview before exporting. [L1427.073]
- Keep body type normal and readable, not oversized. Larger type adds cost without adding response. [L1261.064]

## Product photography and image editing

### Sourcing and licensing product images

- Search order for finding images: Pexels, Pixabay, Google Images, Alibaba, AliExpress. If none works, search for a very similar product or research hashtags on Instagram and use raw UGC-style images. [L1260.024]
- Stock photo sites suit homepage images. Product pages need the actual product photo, so use filtered Google image results or supplier images there. [L0359.075]
- Stock sites cost about $1 to $2 per image. [L0804.054]
- Canva's free stock photos work well for popular niches. For niches with few stock photos, such as mechanical or basic furniture products, download photos from a stock photo website and upload them to Canva. [L1045.022]
- Google Images, licensed use (2023 method): [L0804.054, L0934.046]
  1. Search the product on Google Images.
  2. Click Tools.
  3. Click Usage rights and pick a Creative Commons option.
- Google Images, licensed use (2019, older method): [L0960.045]
  1. Search for the product on Google Images.
  2. Click Tools below the search bar.
  3. Open the usage rights menu.
  4. Filter for images labelled for reuse, and use only those.
- Google Images results are often small and their licensing is unclear. Check the dimensions of every result before deciding to use it. (Source B 2021-22, older.) [L1310.005]
- Do not use Alibaba pictures on product pages. Most listings do not match the product you sell, and the images are not licensed for resale. Replace watermarked supplier photos too. [L0804.055]
- AliExpress and CJ Dropshipping photos are often good enough for home decor ads, so a photographer is not needed to start testing these products. [L0642.054]
- For early fashion tests, use supplier photos from AliExpress as ad creatives instead of paying for a photo shoot. Keep production cost low until the product has validated sales. [L0661.037]
- Once you scale, avoid showing raw AliExpress images on a product page. Use a sizing guide built in your brand colours instead of a generic supplier image. [L0387.028]
- Generic supplier photos from marketplace-style listings look unbranded and reduce trust. Replacing them with Canva-edited images that match the store's branding improves credibility. [L0692.052]
- Use royalty-free images, or photos supplied by the brand that you have permission to use. Do not use competitors' product images on the store or in ads. (2020, older.) [L0468.127]
- Competitor photos can be modified for uniqueness. AI tools can transform original photos into unique variations. [L0276.064]
- Images can be sourced from competitor websites if they are not protected. If a site blocks saving images, take a screenshot on a Mac or use an image enhancement tool. [L0577.057]
- Image enhancement tool: a website that upscales low-resolution product images to higher quality. It can be used for free after creating an account. [L0577.058]
- Stock Images (Free) was named as a free stock photo source in the December 2020 coaching call. The lesson names the resource without naming the provider or describing its licence. (2020, older.) [L0426.012]
- Until a supplier is approved and its images can be used, use placeholders such as AI-generated demo product photos or licensed stock photos. This avoids using supplier images without permission. [L0970.122]
- Stock product photos with a single angle are fine for demo products. Use real photos once products are approved and sold. [L0855.148]
- Supplier product photos that look like 3D renders are a weak choice. If you must use them, disclose that they are renders and ask customers for real photos. (2021, older.) [L0968.095]
- Keep watermarks very subtle and hard to see. Do not set a watermarked image as the primary image for a product variant, because Google Merchant Center rejects listings whose primary image has a watermark. Keep them on the product page. [L1357.035]

| Source | Use it for | Limit | Ids |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stock photo site | Homepage, demo products, niches with few stock photos | Product pages need the real product photo | [L0359.075, L1045.022, L0855.148] |
| Google Images (licensed filter) | Images with reuse rights | Check dimensions and licence; 2019 method is older | [L0804.054, L0934.046, L0960.045, L1310.005] |
| Supplier or AliExpress photos | Home decor tests, early fashion ad creatives | Not for product pages; avoid raw images at scale | [L0642.054, L0661.037, L0387.028] |
| Alibaba pictures | Not for product pages | Not licensed for resale | [L0804.055] |
| Competitor photos | Modified for uniqueness (2024) | Not used as-is (2020, older) | [L0276.064, L0468.127, L0577.057] |
| AI placeholders | Until a supplier is approved | Disclose renders | [L0970.122, L0968.095] |

- Adding an external stock photo to Canva: [L0342.022]
  1. Download the free image from a stock photo site to the computer.
  2. Drag the file into Canva; it uploads to the Uploads section and may take a moment for large files.
  3. Open Uploads, drag the image onto the page, right-click it and choose Replace background (or Set image as background).
  4. The image is cropped to the template size automatically.

### Own photos versus supplier and stock images

- Taking your own product photos is usually not worth the cost, because matching supplier-quality images requires a professional photo shoot. Use supplier-approved images when available. (Source A 2023.) [L0934.045]
- Keep production cost low until a product has validated sales. [L0661.037]
- Invest in photo shoots and edited videos once a product shows success. Generic supplier footage on Google performs poorly. [L0577.056]
- Shooting your own photos of received samples is a practical starting point when no professional production shoot is available. [L1438.027]
- Images and video must look professional. [L0577.056]
- Reconciliation: stock and supplier images apply while a product is untested. Shoot your own photos once sales validate the product. A low-budget home setup is covered below. [L0934.045, L0642.054, L0661.037, L0577.056, L1438.027]

### Low-budget and home photo setup

- Budget smartphone setup (USD): a used coil light bought second-hand for about $20 works as the key light. Cheap LED ring lights from Amazon at $10 to $15 serve as additional or fill light. White card plus a few sheets of paper from a stationery shop cost about $7 in total. Add a sturdy stand with a spirit level, an adjustable tripod, and a cheap smartphone clamp adapter. [L1199.001]
- Home photo procedure (Photoshop costs about £10 per month): [L0561.054]
  1. Photograph the product on an ordinary surface such as a bed or a table.
  2. Cut the product out of the background in Photoshop.
  3. Place the cutout on cleaner or different backgrounds for the ad.

### Starting from a clean source photo

- Before generating a Shopping image with AI, start with a clean source photo: front-facing, high resolution, with the product clearly the focus. Input quality determines output quality, so replace a weak source photo first. [L0882.007]
- Delete photos that are too soft or pixelated, even if they look usable at a glance. They will look worse once enlarged. [L1178.019]
- Discard shots that are too low in resolution for the intended use. Camera resolution matters. [L1132.013]
- If product images are pixelated, edit them with an AI image tool, or hire a Fiverr freelancer for about $5 to $10 to retouch the background and make the product stand out. [L1260.025]
- Never enlarge a small image to fit a larger banner space. It becomes pixelated and unprofessional. The image should be at least the size of the area where it is displayed. (Source B 2021-22, older.) [L1310.007]
- Resize an image before cropping it. Reduce width or height to the target first, and crop only the side you do not need if one dimension is still too large. (Source B 2021-22, older.) [L1310.008]
- Before cutting out a product, check the original shot. A straight-on, centred angle and a clean, well-lit photo give a better result. Odd angles or low-quality sources are harder to cut out. [L1257.007]
- Product photos should be shot straight on at a suitable angle. An odd angle can look awkward even after a clean cutout. [L1258.007]
- A perfectly head-on, dead-centre shot can look flat on a product page. Choose a better angle during the shoot, because background removal cannot fix composition. [L1257.010]
- Products that already sit on a clean, separated background need little or no cutout work. [L1257.009]
- A white product on a white backdrop is hard to cut out because the edges blend in. Shoot light-coloured products on a plain grey or contrasting backdrop. [L1199.028]
- Good lighting and correct setup matter more than heavy editing. Good light lets the phone capture the most detail. Blurred or dark images can be partly rescued, but not fully corrected. [L1199.024]

### Photo shoot setup: backdrop and surface

- Use a matte white or neutral backdrop that is monochromatic, with no blue or green tones, because colours bleed into the product. Matte surfaces avoid harsh reflections. Darker backdrops such as black or grey also work if they are monochromatic. [L1199.002]
- Set up the surface: [L1199.003]
  1. Lay white paper over a flat surface such as a chest of drawers so it curves upward into the wall in a cove shape with no visible horizon line.
  2. Tape it to the wall and floor.
  3. Make it large enough to frame the product from several angles.

### Photo shoot setup: light

- Diffuse hard light before it reaches the product. A direct source creates harsh glare and shine. An umbrella-style diffuser in front of the light, or a white pillowcase hung in front of a ring light, softens it into cloud-like light. [L1199.004]
- Natural light works best, ideally from large windows on an overcast day, because clouds filter sunlight into soft light. When natural light is unavailable, use artificial lights with a diffuser. [L1199.005]
- Adjust the key light's distance before adding diffusion, since moving it changes how strong and harsh the light is. The diffuser then works on the right level. [L1199.029]
- Reduce shadows with a fill light: [L1199.006]
  1. Place a second light or a white reflector card on the opposite side of the key light.
  2. Move the fill light farther away so it only softens the shadow edges.
  3. Check the result by watching how the shadow lightens when the card is introduced.
- Watch for shadows the photographer casts on the product. Keep the camera's position on the side opposite the key light so it does not block the light. [L1199.011]
- For apparel shoots, check that light falls evenly on the product. Lighting that falls on elbow pads or blocks the face makes the subject hard to cut out cleanly. Re-shoot with more even light rather than trying to fix it in Photoshop. [L1132.028, L1178.025]

### Photo shoot setup: camera and phone

- Use a camera with at least 1080p resolution, which most phones support. Use the basic camera app and avoid manual settings such as ISO or aperture. Turn on the 3x3 grid overlay to keep the product centred and level, and tap the subject to set focus. [L1199.007]
- Smartphones show a level guide when tilted. Use it together with the 3x3 grid to align a straight product shot so both sides are symmetrical. [L1199.032]
- Do not use the telephoto or zoom lens on a smartphone for product shots, because image quality is poor. Use the standard main camera and move the phone closer for close-ups. Shoot wider than the final crop so the image can be cut to a square later. [L1199.008]
- Keep the phone away from shutter buttons on the stand. An accidental tap can fill the camera roll with duplicates. Position the stand where no physical buttons sit under the lens or near your hands. [L1199.026]

### Photo shoot setup: angles and details

- Shoot a product from several angles: [L1199.009]
  1. Take a dead-level straight-on shot at product height.
  2. Take additional angles from the sides, front and back.
  3. Take a high-angle shot from above.
  4. Take a flat shot from below; for drink cans, this makes them look powerful.
  5. Take a top-down angled shot.
  6. Keep the camera fixed and rotate the product to capture other sides if it has several good angles.
- Shoot a wide variety of angles, since not every shot will be usable. Choose the best few for cutout and keep the others for social use without editing. [L1178.024]
- For apparel, capture several angles such as front, side, bent-arm and full-body frames. Accessories or equipment should not cover the model's face. Only the best frame of each angle needs a full cutout. [L1132.028]
- Photograph product features: take close-ups of buttons, controls, bases, lids and other distinctive details. Show functional features, such as a product floating in water. [L1199.010]
- Shoot close-ups at minimum focus distance. Move the phone back slightly until the focus is sharp. [L1199.010]
- A product image must show the entire product in its natural state and highlight its unique features. Pick sharp, well-lit shots and include a close-up of the most distinctive feature for each product. [L1199.012]
- Capture close-ups of fabric, weight and detail so buyers understand quality before purchase. [L1438.027]

### Lightroom corrections

- Division of work: Lightroom handles quick crops and simple exposure adjustments. Photoshop handles masking, cutouts and retouching. [L1132.013]
- Basic light correction order: [L1199.013]
  1. Exposure: brighten dark photos.
  2. Contrast: sharpen or soften the difference between light and dark areas.
  3. Highlights down: reduce overly bright white areas.
  4. Shadows down: add depth.
  5. Check Whites and Blacks for the tonal range.
  6. Use the crop tool and choose the 1:1 square ratio for product images.
- Colour Mixer (HSL panel): select a colour channel such as yellow and increase its saturation to make it pop, or desaturate a channel such as purple to remove an unwanted colour cast. [L1199.014]
- Keep the product's true colours. Adjust colour only to correct a colour cast or to match the real item, because heavy shifts make the product look different from what the customer receives. [L1199.030]
- Judge exposure and contrast by eye on the screen, not by fixed values. Move each slider until the image looks right, then check the result side by side with the original. [L1199.031]
- Use a simple Lightroom crop for photos that only need framing. [L1178.020]
- Once a cutout is saved from Photoshop, the file returns to Lightroom. [L1178.001]

### Square canvas and image size

- Standard product image size is square at 1080 × 1080 pixels. Crop to a square with the 1:1 ratio and save at this size for consistency across listings. [L1199.023]
- Non-square product images create uneven gaps in the image layout. Crop all product images to the same square ratio before uploading. [L1331.020]
- Set up a square canvas in Photoshop: [L1132.002]
  1. Hold the Selection tool icon in the toolbar to reveal the Artboard tool.
  2. Draw a square artboard and resize it to the size you need.
  3. Fit the product photo inside it so the subject sits roughly centred.
- Draw the square artboard with the Artboard tool, hidden under the selection tool group, then scale it with Ctrl+T while holding Shift to keep the ratio. [L1178.001]

### Background removal in Photoshop: full workflows

- Cutout workflow, Photoshop (eight steps): [L1178.001]
  1. Draw a square artboard with the Artboard tool (hidden under the selection tool group), then scale it with Ctrl+T while holding Shift to keep the ratio.
  2. Click Select Subject in the top bar and check the result.
  3. Add missing areas with the brush (plus) or remove extra areas with the brush held in minus mode.
  4. Deselect with Ctrl+D and refine openings and edges by brush or lasso.
  5. Add a layer mask with Select and Mask, using the left toolbar to clean up the cutout first.
  6. Smooth, feather and Shift Edge in the right-side panel last.
  7. Click OK with Output To set to Layer Mask, so the original photo is kept.
  8. Retouch spots with Spot Healing Brush and Clone Stamp, and save with Ctrl+S so the file returns to Lightroom.
- Cutout procedure, Photoshop (six steps): [L1132.004]
  1. Click Select Subject in the top menu bar.
  2. Check the result, and add or subtract missing areas with the Quick Selection tool (plus sign to add, hold Shift for minus, or Alt for minus in the lasso).
  3. Open Select and Mask.
  4. Refine edges with the Refine Edge brush for hair and the brush for gaps.
  5. Use Smooth, Feather, Contrast and Shift Edge in the right-hand panel.
  6. Under Output To choose Layer Mask (not Selection, which would delete the background) and click OK.
- Cutout checklist, Photoshop (eight steps): [L1132.014]
  1. Cut out the subject (Select Subject, then refine).
  2. Refine edges with the brush, lasso, and Refine Edge for hair.
  3. Smooth the edge subtly.
  4. Feather only if the background contrast is low.
  5. Apply Shift Edge (about 30 to 40) to remove dark fringes.
  6. Output as Layer Mask.
  7. Remove spots with Spot Healing Brush, and blemishes or stitching with Clone Stamp.
  8. Add an E3E3E3 fill layer behind the subject, and resize the subject as needed.
- Select Subject, then Layer Mask: [L1199.016]
  - Check the edges after Select Subject.
  - Add missing areas with a Layer Mask brush set to hard brush hardness (100%).
  - Use the Polygonal Lasso tool for straight edges.
  - Use Select and Mask to smooth edges and shift the edge inward slightly, then click Layer Mask.
- If a selection is active when you click Add Layer Mask, the mask is built from that selection and the background is hidden automatically. Use this right after Select Subject for a non-destructive cutout in one step. [L1178.028]
- Use a layer mask rather than deleting pixels. The mask is non-destructive: the original is preserved, the mask can be deleted to restore it, and it can be edited later by clicking it. [L1132.008, L1178.013]
- A layer-mask cutout can be reversed or reworked. Drag the mask onto the trash icon and confirm to restore the original photo. Or click the mask thumbnail in the Layers panel to reopen Select and Mask. In Select and Mask, use the brush in minus mode to remove leftover background, and check the result before clicking OK. [L1178.029]
- Always edit through layers rather than painting directly on the photo. Adjustment layers and layer masks keep the original intact. [L1178.013]

### Select and Mask settings

| Setting | Typical value | When it applies | Ids |
|---|---|---|---|
| Shift Edge | About 30 to 40 (pixels) for product cutouts | Product cutouts on a light background; move left to pull in dark or coloured halos, right to expand; check each step at zoom | [L1132.006, L1178.015, L1199.016] |
| Smooth | Small value | Keep subtle; too much pulls corners inward | [L1132.006, L1178.014] |
| Feather | Hardly used | White-background shoots, where dark and white contrast is already crisp; use feather only when background contrast is low | [L1132.006, L1178.014, L1132.014] |
| Contrast | Rarely changed | Only needed for low-contrast backgrounds | [L1132.006, L1178.016] |

- Shift Edge removes dark or coloured halo pixels left around a cutout. Shifting inward removes the fringe; shifting outward expands the selection. Do rough selection work first with the left toolbar, then smooth and feather in the right-hand panel. [L1132.007]
- Brush controls: hold Alt, right-click and hold, then move left or right to change brush size and up or down to change feather. Ctrl+D deselects. Alt with the mouse wheel zooms in and out. [L1132.005]
- Lasso or polygon selections create pixelated, jagged edges. Smooth them only after all cutout edits are finished, and keep edge refinement subtle so the outline does not look like a polygon at normal size. [L1132.009]
- If a cutout is a bit off, refine it with the brush or lasso, but keep it close to the natural outline. Parts of clothing that look odd when cut out, such as jeans at the leg, can stay if they look correct in the final image. [L1178.018]

### Halos, edge fixes and colour differences

- A thin dark or blue halo after cutout comes from the original background colour. Fix it with Shift Edge inward. Then remove remaining colour tint with a Hue/Saturation adjustment layer that reduces saturation on the affected area. [L1178.017]
- For minor colour differences between garments and the background, use a Hue/Saturation adjustment layer clipped over only the affected area to reduce colour cast. For small differences it is often not worth the extra layering. [L1132.012]
- Resize a cutout subject inside its frame: [L1132.003, L1178.027]
  1. Select the subject's layer in the Layers panel.
  2. Press Ctrl+T to open free transform.
  3. Hold Shift to keep the aspect ratio, and hold Alt to scale outward from the centre.
  4. Drag to the target size, then press Enter to confirm.

### Retouching in Photoshop

- Spot Healing Brush removes small spots, hair and blemishes. Use short sharp clicks rather than dragging, keep the brush small, and use some feather so the repair blends in. Dragging across high-contrast areas can smear the repair. [L1132.010]
- Clone Stamp: hold Alt and click to sample a clean source area, release Alt, then paint over the defect. Clone from an area with matching light direction, because lighting changes make the copy look too light or too dark. Use it for stitching or larger blemishes the Spot Healing Brush cannot fix. [L1132.011]
- Remove overlaid text or a white background from a lifestyle shot: [L1132.027]
  1. Cut out only the subject (for example an arm) with Select Subject and refine it in Select and Mask.
  2. Add a layer mask so the subject is isolated without deleting pixels.
  3. Add a grey fill layer (Edit > Fill, Colour E3E3E3) behind the subject so the overlaid text and white areas disappear.
- When a photo has text or other objects on it, cut out only the usable part of the subject and place it on the plain grey background, so the text disappears. [L1178.020]

### Background fill and backdrop colour

- Standard product backdrop: a neutral light-grey, hex E3E3E3 (RGB 227, 227, 227). In Photoshop, add a new layer, choose Edit > Fill, set Contents to Color, enter the value, and place the filled layer below the product photo. Place it below the photo, not above. [L1132.001, L1178.002]
- Use one consistent light-grey background (E3E3E3 in the lesson) across all product images so the set looks uniform. Apply the same fill to every cutout and check it visually after placing the subject. [L1178.003]
- Off-white looks more attractive than pure white for product photography. Add a new layer under the product, use Edit > Fill, and set the colour to off-white. [L1199.017]
- An off-white or slightly grey backdrop hides cut-out edges better than pure white. Choose the final background colour before cutting out the product, so the edges are planned for it. [L1199.027]
- Pure white is still the standard for product listing ads. Keep standard white-background photos for them. [L1094.105]
- A light-grey background matching the website's colour scheme is a practical default, so cutouts fit the store's look. [L1258.004]
- Product photos for a store with a light-grey colour scheme can use a plain light-grey background that matches the theme. Other colours are possible in Canva, but light grey suits that palette. [L1257.006]

| Background | Use when | Ids |
|---|---|---|
| E3E3E3 light grey | Standard product backdrop, consistent across the set | [L1132.001, L1178.002, L1178.003] |
| Light grey matching the site | Store colour scheme is light grey | [L1257.006, L1258.004] |
| Off-white | Clean, neutral product background, hides edges | [L1199.017, L1199.027] |
| Pure white | Product listing ads | [L1094.105] |
| Matte monochrome white, black or grey | Studio shoots | [L1199.002] |
| AI-generated background | Social posts, email, occasionally product pages | [L1094.105] |

### Shadows

- Add a simple shadow in Photoshop: [L1199.018]
  1. Draw an ellipse with the Ellipse tool, set fill to black and stroke to none.
  2. Convert the layer to a smart object.
  3. Apply Filter > Blur > Gaussian Blur.
  4. Position it under the product.
  - A thick, tight blur gives a shadow close to the floor. Blur more and move the shape further back for a shadow that looks farther away.
  - Side shadows: copy the layer, use Alt or Option to clip it to the image layer, and transform it with Command+T.
- Refine a shadow with a layer mask: add a mask to the shadow layer, then paint away parts with a black brush, or use the Gradient tool to fade the shadow along the left edge. Tune it until it looks convincing. [L1199.019]
- Canva background removal also removes the shadow. Add shadows back using Elements > Shadows. [L1199.020]
- PhotoRoom's AI Instant Backgrounds places the product on a pre-made background with shadows. [L1199.022]

### Generative Fill and AI-based background work

- Remove a background with Generative Fill in Photoshop: [L1199.015]
  1. Use the Lasso tool to draw around the product. Keep the shadow inside the selection if you want to keep it.
  2. Press Ctrl+Shift (Command+Shift on Mac) to invert the selection to the background.
  3. Right-click and choose Generative Fill, then click Generate to create a clean background.
  4. Pick one of the generated options.
- Canva's Magic Media tool handles most product image creation and editing needs. [L0276.034]
- Canva's AI erase tool is a basic option. [L1199.025]
- Use AI-generated background images for social media posts and email campaigns, and occasionally for product pages. Keep standard white-background photos for product listing ads. [L1094.105]
- Before a Shopping image is generated with AI, check the source photo. Replace a weak source first. [L0882.007]

### Canva background removal and edits

- Canva background removal: open the uploaded image, choose Edit photo, then select Background remover. Canva's Magic Grab lifts the object off the page. [L1199.020, L1093.006]
- Canva one-click removal, with refinement: [L1257.001]
  1. Open the image and click Edit photo.
  2. Click Remove background and let Canva process it.
  3. Check the result; for a clean look, choose a plain light-grey background, which matches a website colour scheme.
  4. If parts were cut out wrongly, refine after the fact: click Adjust, then Configure, then use Remove and Restore.
  5. Use the brush-size control and zoom in to erase leftover lumps with Erase, or restore cut-out areas with Restore.
  5. Check edges for thin black lines and remove them manually.
- Refinement tools are found under Adjust > Configure, which offers Remove and Restore. Brush size can be changed and the area zoomed in for finer work. [L1257.002]
- Canva's background removal may leave thin dark lines around the edges of a cutout. Erase them manually with the Erase tool at high zoom, or the image looks unpolished on the product page. [L1257.005]
- Canva's auto cutout does not always get edges right. Check every edge and remove leftover fragments before exporting. Hair, small gaps and white fringes are common problem areas. [L0754.033]
- Canva's one-click removal is fast and works well when speed matters more than precision. It gives less control than Photoshop: blemishes are hard to remove, shadows are harder to handle, and edges may not be clean enough for a premium product page. [L1257.003]
- Canva's refinement is rougher ("a ball park") than Photoshop's precise edge tools. [L1257.004]
- For a precise cutout, such as clothing with blemishes or detailed edges, use Photoshop: the selection tool, brushes, and edge refinement such as Shift Edge. [L1257.004, L1257.008]
- Canva colour adjustment: open Edit photo > Adjust > Color, pick individual colours Canva detects, and change saturation or vibrance. Canva's contrast control is less precise than Lightroom's. [L1199.021]
- Canva can make a simple change to a supplier image: cut the product out and change the background colour. This is enough to make a generic image look distinct when no major edit is needed. [L1218.035]
- Edit supplier product photos so their backgrounds match the colour scheme of the landing page, using Canva or Photoshop, to create a branded look. [L0387.022]
- Canva's Magic Grab, Background remover and AI erase tools form the cheaper beginner option, with basic colour correction. [L1199.025]

### PhotoRoom and paid tools

- PhotoRoom's AI Instant Backgrounds costs $9.99 per month. It removes the background automatically and places the product on a pre-made background with shadows. It is a faster paid alternative to manual editing. [L1199.022]
- Tools overview: [L1199.025]
  - Lightroom: basic colour correction and cropping.
  - Photoshop: cutting out products and adding shadows.
  - Canva: cheaper beginner option with basic colour correction, background removal and an AI erase tool.
  - PhotoRoom: AI cutout service.
- Photoshop costs about £10 per month for the home photo procedure. [L0561.054]
- A freelancer can remove backgrounds and produce clean white-background images when a supplier's photos show busy showroom backgrounds that Instagram rejects. (2021, older.) [L1279.048]

### Making supplier images look unique

- Procedure: [L0921.031]
  1. Take the supplier product image.
  2. Remove the background in Canva.
  3. Place the product on a new background.
  4. Adjust the colouring slightly so it looks like a different image.
  5. Add your brand name to the image before publishing.
- Modify competitor photos for uniqueness; AI tools can transform original photos into unique variations. [L0276.064]
- Replace generic supplier photos with Canva-edited images that match the brand. [L0692.052]
- Edit backgrounds to match the landing page colour scheme for a branded look. [L0387.022]
- Use a sizing guide built in your brand colours instead of a generic supplier image. [L0387.028]

### Product page image set

- Every product page needs more than one photo. A single photo makes a purchase unlikely. If the supplier has only one, ask for more, search the internet, or create variations: the product alone, the brand logo, and the available colour options. [L1293.009]
- Upload the clean white contoured studio images first, plus at least two styled images in the product media section. Use both studio and lifestyle images with people wearing the product. [L1331.019]
- Order product images for a listing: [L0470.090]
  1. Place the main straight-on product shot first, as customers expect.
  2. Add images of the product from different angles.
  3. Add close-up images showing material or mechanism.
  4. Add lifestyle images showing the product in use, optionally embedded in the description instead of the gallery.
  - Upload all images that are relevant to the purchase decision.
- Image set order, Source D 2026: [L0887.025]
  1. Product hero image: the product on a pure white background, generated with the hero image prompt.
  2. Value proposition headline image: an image with a large caption based on the value proposition headline.
  3. Homepage photos.
  4. Product photos for the product page.
  - Every image headline, bullet and visual suggestion must reflect real customer language and the emotional desire of the target buyer.
- A homepage hero image is valuable space and can be a tight crop of one of the product photos. Use a strong product photo for it. [L0884.013]
- Show the product's dimensions and benefit callouts on the images. [L1346.031]
- Apparel product set example: [L0884.012]
  - An indoor morning-light living room scene.
  - An early-morning urban coffee room scene.
  - A mirror selfie.
  - A zoomed hero image.
  - A close-up of the fleece layer.
  - Each scene should show the product in a different everyday setting.
- Use high-quality product imagery and close-ups showing fabric, weight and detail. [L1438.027]
- For a product that solves a problem, show it in use in the main product images and in a short how-to-use video, such as a person using it while sitting or lying down. Where the product suits presents, also offer it as a gift option. [L0549.052]

### Lifestyle images and the emotional brief

- Product photos should create emotion and desire by showing the life the buyer wants, not only the item. Plan each image around what the target consumer aspires to. [L0884.001]
- Lifestyle photos can sell an aspirational version of a product's use, even when most buyers do not actually do that activity. Choose scenes that match the dream of the target consumer. [L0884.002]
- Show the product in use, such as a parent using a baby product on a picnic or a traveller using a bag, to demonstrate outdoor, travel and everyday uses. [L1346.031]
- Models showing the product in use, including opening the package and comfort, give buyers a clear picture. Use real people, not only the product on its own. [L0492.046]
- Product photos can include recognisable local scenery, such as mountains behind the model, and local products on the table. These cues signal that the brand is local rather than shipped from abroad, which helps build trust. [L0492.069]
- Use original photos and models instead of supplier stock or AliExpress images. Original content can be reused in Facebook ads and makes the product look more trustworthy. [L0492.043]
- Benefit-led product images: one image per benefit, each showing the product solving a specific problem, with a short callout. [L1346.033]
  - Example: a camera bag photographed with a laptop inside, labelled "fits 15-inch laptops".
  - Example: a kitchen knife set photographed on a cutting board, labelled "razor-sharp blades for daily use".
- Product images and GIFs that show exactly how the product is used are strong selling assets. They can convert buyers even when the store is simple. [L1172.043]
- The product image should show the product in its intended setting and look like it does when set up. A plain product shot grabs less attention than a product in use, so use the strongest image available. (Source B 2021-22, older.) [L1169.014]
- Photo styles can be set by describing the camera look: a film photo, an iPhone-style snapshot, or a studio shot by a professional photographer. Asking a chat assistant which style the target consumer prefers is a valid way to choose. [L0884.006]
- A candid hard flash style fits a trendy, authentic look that resonates with consumers from short video platforms such as TikTok. It pushes existing iPhone-style photos towards a stronger, more distinctive look. [L0884.007]
- Model clothing can be changed to brand colours, such as dark purple or a pink sweater, so the photos reinforce the brand palette. Adjust clothing in the prompt instead of accepting the default colours. [L0884.014]
- Apparel case: [L0884.015]
  - Starting point: an apparel brand's website used eight product images: five on the product page, one homepage hero, one fleece interior detail, and one everyday-wear shot. The existing photos were already candid phone-style shots, and the goal was to replace all eight with a stronger brand look.
  - Actions: a chat assistant generated eight scene prompts. The first image run showed the same woman in every photo, so the prompts were edited to describe a different woman each time. The hard flash style prompt was added, product photos were attached as reference, a night scene was changed to daylight, and clothing was set to brand colours such as dark purple and pink. All eight images were then generated and placed on the site.
  - Result: the before and after comparison was judged a large improvement, the photos looked good on mobile, and no conversion figures were reported.
- Discount sticker on product photos: [L0387.009]
  1. Take the product photos from the supplier or AliExpress listing.
  2. Open Canva and search for a Black Friday sticker template.
  3. Upload the sticker, remove its extra layers if needed, and place it on the product photo.
  4. Resize the sticker and fit the text, for example "60% off" or "50% off".
  5. Put the sticker on all product images, for example in the top-right corner, to improve click-through rate.
- For home decor and furniture ads on Pinterest, the visual quality of the product images is the main driver of performance. Invest in strong product imagery before testing campaigns. [L0788.059]

### Social and Pinterest imagery

- Pin images should show the product in use and the result or feeling it creates, not only a product shot on a white background. Lifestyle scenes such as a summer picnic engage the Pinterest audience more than plain product photos. [L1136.021]
- Dropshippers with only supplier photos should create their own images showing people using the product and getting the desired benefit. Story-based images are the main way to make dropshipped products stand out on Pinterest. [L1136.022]
- Raw user-style images found through Instagram hashtag research produced a conversion rate of about 8% to 9% in one test with a weighted hula hoop. Real-looking UGC-style photos can outperform polished shots. [L1345.030]
- The same Instagram hashtag research produced a conversion rate of 8-9% for one product. [L1260.024]

## AI-assisted copy and creative

### Tools and project setup

- Claude Projects (Claude or ChatGPT) keeps a persistent knowledge base across chats. Upload your reference files once, and every new chat in the project reads them automatically. [L0039.021]
- When you run Step 9 and Step 10 of the Source D ad workflow, open a new chat inside the project for each angle you test. A new chat keeps the logic of each angle separate, and the project still reads all five reference files. [L0039.022]
- Ad Manage.ai can save ad copy templates containing primary text, headlines, description, call-to-action button and URL parameters with UTM tracking. Create a template from an existing ad, write custom copy, import from another ad set or paste a URL. Load a saved template into new campaigns to keep messaging consistent across launches. [L0207.004]
- The Inspiration Library shows competitor ads across platforms and can be searched by brand name or keyword. You can clone an ad and have Claude regenerate it as a custom version by specifying brand colours, fonts, product name, logo and creative brief. The system adapts design and messaging to your brand identity. [L0207.007]
- Canva's AI Magic Media generates product images that do not exist and carry no supplier logos or brand names. Describe the product in a text prompt. Use it for demo products or when stock images are unavailable. [L0253.029]
- Shopify Email's built-in Generate Text feature creates subject line alternatives and email body copy with selectable tones (playful, formal, professional). Use it to improve abandoned checkout messages while keeping brand consistency. [L0266.014]
- Voice Control for ChatGPT is a Chrome extension. Hold the spacebar and speak to dictate prompts. It saves a lot of typing when you write long, detailed prompts. [L0353.006]

### Briefing the AI before prompting

- Before you ask an AI tool for ad copy, know the product's desire, its features and the benefits those features give the customer, the target persona and the problem it solves. The AI only amplifies the inputs it gets. Weak inputs produce weak copy. [L0353.001]
- Copy generated without product inputs comes out generic. Always give the AI the unique selling points, the target audience and the framework before asking for headlines or scripts. [L0524.060]
- Generic AI copy written without knowing the target audience stays generic. Give the model the audience, the problem, the market position and the unique features first. Check every output for accuracy before you publish it. [L0552.033]
- A general chatbot such as ChatGPT, used to write ad copy without best-practice training or explicit instructions, usually gives weak results. Teams that skip this training often decide AI does not work and go back to human copywriters. Write detailed instructions and best-practice rules first, then judge the output. [L0464.024]
- Keep one brief in a spreadsheet: the desire, features and benefits, persona, awareness and sophistication stages, and principles. All of these feed the headline and body copy. With the brief kept up to date, you can generate Facebook ad copy, landing page copy and video scripts from the same inputs. [L0516.052]
- Start with one long, complete brief covering the product, desire, features and benefits, audience and chosen principles, ideally dictated by voice. Then refine with a few short corrections. In a worked example, strong copy took about five rounds. The number of prompts is not the goal. [L0353.054]
- Use short prompts with minimal wording and refine in several rounds. In one comparison, a single long voice prompt followed by a few corrections was faster than many separate prompts. Read this together with the long first brief in L0353.054: the brief comes first, then short corrections. [L0353.039]

### Ad copy workflows

**Basic AI-assisted ad copy workflow (Source C)**

1. Dictate the product, the problem, the desire, the features and their benefits, and the target audience into the chatbot in one long prompt. [L0353.004]
2. Ask for three headlines and three body copy texts for the Facebook and Instagram ad. [L0353.004]
3. Check whether the headline names the problem and hints at the solution. If the market is crowded, ask for the unique feature to appear in the headline. [L0353.004]
4. Paste the list of psychological principles and ask for the copy to be rewritten with the best ones. [L0353.004]
5. Ask for bullet points and emojis to format the ad. [L0353.004]
6. Refine in several short follow-up prompts instead of starting over. [L0353.004]

**Paid-plan ChatGPT workflow (Source C)**

1. Describe the product in plain words, its main target audience, the situation the audience struggles with, and its unique features. [L0515.021]
2. Send the psychological principles, desire, benefits and persona you wrote. [L0515.021]
3. Ask for three headline examples and body copy. [L0515.021]
4. Review the output. Remove generic phrases (for example "experience the magic of") and tighten the benefit and the unique mechanism. [L0515.021]
5. Give the market awareness and sophistication stage with the competitors' claims, and ask for a rewrite that features the unique mechanism in the headline. [L0515.021]
6. For paid social ads, ask for a shorter version with bullet points, a clear call to action, a limited-time offer and fear of missing out, plus emojis if wanted. [L0515.021]
7. Ask for variations of a headline using a named principle, for example how to intensify a headline. [L0515.021]

**Drafting prompt (ideation)**

```
I want you to write headline and body copy for a [PRODUCT: product name and what it does]. Main target audience: [PERSONA: demographics, behavior, pains and fears]. Desire the customer wants to reach or escape: [DESIRE]. Unique features and benefits: [FEATURE 1 => BENEFIT 1; FEATURE 2 => BENEFIT 2]. Market awareness stage: [AWARENESS STAGE: unaware, problem aware, solution aware, product aware or most aware]. Market sophistication stage: [SOPHISTICATION STAGE 1 to 5] with these existing competitor claims: [COMPETITOR CLAIMS]. Give me three headlines that name the unique mechanism and feature a new mechanism or feature in the headline. Apply these psychological principles where they fit: problem-agitate-solution, curiosity, social proof, authority and presupposition. Then write body copy that moves from the problem, through the features and their benefits, to a call to action with a limited-time offer and fear of missing out. Keep the language plain, specific to the persona, and free of vague phrases.
```
[L0515.022]

**Two-step breakthrough prompt**

**Primary text process (one chat per product)**

```
Generate Facebook ad copy for a product using the following process. Input: the product page URL, the ad creative description (the hook, the visual and the angle), and the brand name. Output: 3 headlines and 3 primary texts. Headline 1 (Problem-Aware): a headline about the offer. Headline 2 (Solution-Aware): a curiosity gap that makes the reader want the mechanism. Headline 3 (Transformation): an identity shift that makes the reader see themselves already using the product. Primary text V1 (Problem-Aware): open with the reader's pain point, show you understand their struggle, hint at what is possible, create curiosity about the solution, plant a seed of urgency, end with a soft call to action; tone empathetic, understanding, hopeful. Primary text V2 (Solution-Aware): acknowledge they have been looking, address why most solutions fail, show what is different about this product, introduce the mechanism, stack proof and credibility, create urgency, end with a confident call to action; tone knowledgeable, trustworthy, confident. Primary text V3 (Transformation and offer): paint a picture of life after using the product, show the exact transformation, state the core benefits, show what is included in the offer, make the offer undeniable, create urgency to act now. Use the current price, original price and discount percentage from the product page, and keep each text short, scannable and free of unsupported claims.
```

**Meta primary text and headline prompt (alternative format)**

This prompt sets a stricter layout (12 words per paragraph, four emoji lines). Use it when you want a fixed structure. The process prompt above (L0348.008) produces three headlines and three primary texts with V1 to V3 labels. Use the process prompt for product pages with full offer details, and this prompt for quick high-intent variations.

```
Act as a direct-response copywriter who focuses on high-converting Meta ads. Your job: review the product or creative you're given, pinpoint its central marketing angle, and then produce three alternative high-intent primary texts plus three headlines.

Input fields: Brand or product name: [Insert brand or product name here]. Audience notes: [Insert any notes about your audience here, or leave blank so the AI infers them]. Creative attached: [Yes or No; refer to the file name if relevant].

Stage 1 - Creative and avatar review. Write a brief analysis in three sections:
1. Marketing angle: the hook (the instant visual, emotional, or vanity payoff) and how it naturally moves the reader toward the functional, long-term, or technical advantage of the product.
2. Avatar: the buyer's core pains and desires, and the precise reason this creative and angle will halt their scrolling.
3. Awareness level: the single main awareness stage this ad aims at (Unaware, Problem Aware, Solution Aware, Product Aware, or Most Aware).

Stage 2 - Primary text. Produce 3 Meta-compliant primary text variations for the brand or product, each following this exact layout:
- Paragraph 1: an arresting hook centered on the main benefit or pain point (12 words at most).
- Paragraph 2: a transition linking the hook to the product's distinctive mechanism, quality, or solution (12 words at most).
- Benefit stack: exactly 4 standalone lines. Every line opens with one fitting emoji, followed by a short, punchy benefit written as [Benefit name].
- Paragraph 3: a clear call to action or a closing value proposition that is hard to dispute (12 words at most).
Hard rules: no paragraph may go over 12 words, so count each paragraph's words before you output it. Keep emojis out of the paragraphs; they belong only at the start of the 4 benefit-stack lines. Do not make any claim the product page fails to back up.

Stage 3 - Headlines. Write 3 headlines: an offer headline aimed at problem-aware readers, a curiosity-gap headline for solution-aware readers, and an identity-shift headline for readers focused on transformation. Where it fits, use the current price, original price, and discount as displayed on the product page.

Deliver the Stage 1 analysis first, then the three primary text variations, then the three headlines.
```

**Short-form and caption requests**

Ask for three headlines and three body texts for a Facebook and Instagram ad. - UGC scripts: name the product and use a problem-agitate-solution framework. Refine the output before you send it to creators or agencies. [L0353.044]

- Before you name a persuasion framework in a prompt, ask the AI whether it knows that framework by name. If it confirms, it can apply the framework directly. If not, describe the framework briefly inside the prompt. [L0353.053]
- Refine iteratively. Treat the AI as an assistant for back-and-forth refinement, not as a one-shot writer. The first output is often broad or misses the unique feature. Steer it with specific corrections such as "this word is too much" or "surface the feature in the headline". [L0353.007]
- Ask for a specific tone of voice or persona, for example a friendly everyday person, a mum, or a target group. Then have someone from that target group read the copy to check whether it sounds authentic. [L0353.008]

**Worked example: pet hair removal brush (Source C)**

- Starting point: a pet hair removal brush with a static microfiber head and a storage lid, aimed at owners of German shepherds who let their dogs on the bed. [L0353.055]
- Step 1: the first AI brief produced broad headlines and body copy that named the problem but not a unique feature. [L0353.055]
- Step 2: because the market was solution-aware, the headline was rewritten to name the microfiber head as the differentiator. [L0353.055]
- Step 3: a list of persuasion principles was added and the copy was rewritten. This introduced future pacing, scarcity and curiosity angles. [L0353.055]
- Step 4: bullet points and emojis were requested for the Facebook ad format. [L0353.055]
- Outcome: copy much more competitive than the first draft, but it still needed a human check for tone and claims. [L0353.055]

**Principles for AI-assisted creative**

- AI has changed ad creative more than any shift since social media took hold. It lets a team produce ideas, variations and finished assets much faster, with more variety and far less manual effort. [L0498.001]
- Using AI to generate ads without knowing how to direct it usually produces low-quality ads that perform worse. The tool alone does not create good creative. The operator's strategy decides the result. [L0498.002]
- Brands that keep winning with AI-assisted creative follow a small set of underlying principles, not a single tool or prompt trick. Understanding those principles lets an advertiser adapt when platforms change their rules. [L0498.004]
- Input quality decides the result of ChatGPT concept work, and a human must check the output. Overreliance makes the work weaker, so write the core copy yourself and check it against customer pain points. [L0646.042]
- Adjust copy and creative direction to match your brand voice and the customer psychology insights from your research. [L0221.012]

### Research-first ad creative (Claude Project)

Run this procedure in one Claude project named after your product.

1. Create a Claude project and name it after your product. [L0221.001]
2. Set up three prompts as project instructions: Market Research, Emotional Valence Framework, and Target Evidence. [L0221.001]
3. For the Market Research prompt, provide your website and product information, then add information about customer surveys, personas and behaviour data. More detail produces better output. [L0221.001]
4. Run the Market Research prompt, review the full research document to understand your market, and add the insights to the project. [L0221.001]
5. Copy and paste the Emotional Valence Framework prompt into the same project. Review the analysis thoroughly to understand your customers' psychological drivers. [L0221.001]
6. Copy and paste the Target Evidence prompt and provide your Facebook ad account data from 2 to 3 days of running the product. Include gender and age breakdowns, spend patterns, top creative themes and geographic concentration. [L0221.001]
7. Ask Claude to generate bottom-of-funnel ads using all the research insights you have gathered. [L0221.001]
8. Customise and refine the generated ads with specific tweaks and details suited to your business. [L0221.001]

### Ebooks and free-gift content

**Ebook generation prompt**

```
Act as a seasoned ebook writer and content strategist. Produce a finished, high-grade ebook of 15 to 25 pages to serve as a free giveaway for [TARGET AVATAR: who they are and the problem they have], linked to [PRODUCT NAME], which assists with [PRODUCT PROBLEM]. Pick a widely applicable, timeless theme suited to this readership, for example productivity, mindset, health routines, personal finance basics, or something similar. Execution counts for more than the subject: the piece should demonstrate what a well-crafted free-gift ebook looks like in practice.

Deliver the complete ebook from start to finish, containing:
- An attention-grabbing title and subtitle
- A short welcome note or author introduction
- 4 to 6 chapters of substantial, truly practical material, with no placeholder text
- Practical takeaways or exercises wherever they fit
- A closing section offering one clear, gentle next step

Quality benchmarks:
- A warm, direct, engaging voice, never stiff or generic
- Brief paragraphs, subheadings, and bullet points where they improve readability
- Each chapter provides genuine value rather than padding
- The tone should read like a thoughtful present, not a sales pitch
- The ebook serves as a reference model for others, so its structure, voice, pacing, and the way the content leads into the closing next step should all be polished.

Closing: refer to [PRODUCT NAME] a single time, softly, as support that complements the habits in the ebook, not as a cure or hard sell. Include a call-to-action link only when one is supplied: [OPTIONAL CALL TO ACTION LINK]. Finish with a brief note stating the content is for educational purposes and does not replace advice from a qualified professional.
```

**Performance image parameters**

When you generate image prompts for AI-created ads, specify exact visual parameters:

- Colours: hex codes sampled from brand assets, for example #FDE734, #0F1034, #FEC941, #2B2A4C, #101041, #DDE9FE. [L0221.016]
- Composition: for example, upper 62% photograph, lower 38% solid text panel. [L0221.016]
- Lighting angle in degrees, for example 35 degrees. [L0221.016]
- Colour temperature in Kelvin, for example 5200k daylight. [L0221.016]
- Aperture, for example f/2.2, and lens type. [L0221.016]
- Photography style: documentary-reportage rather than styled advertising. [L0221.016]
- Product: render it as a fully native scene element, never lifted or composited from reference images. [L0221.016]
- Details: describe wood grain direction, shadow edges, worn surfaces, household objects and soft-focus background elements. [L0221.016]

### Shopping and Demand Gen images

**Google Shopping image prompt**

Note from the source: the lesson displayed only the first question in full. The lesson states that the prompt also contains the further requirements: aspect ratio, no text, logo or badge overlays, and no borders or colour-wash backgrounds.

```
Act as an AI image generator that makes product pictures for Google Shopping ads. Whenever a user uploads a product photo, your first reply must be a question, before any image is made, asking which style they want: a plain white or neutral backdrop (the most typical choice for Shopping), a lifestyle or in-context setting, a flat lay, or something else they describe themselves. Once they choose, create the image in that style using the uploaded photo as the reference for the product, with an aspect ratio suited to a Shopping listing. Put no text, logos or badges on the image, and no borders or colour-wash backgrounds. Show the product straight on, sharp, and as the clear focal point, leaving visible empty margin around it so Google's automatic cropping and centring does not clip it.
```
[L0882.009]

- ChatGPT's image generation can create Shopping images directly from a product photo. A custom GPT with a fixed instruction set can enforce the question-first workflow. Other image models such as Gemini or Nano Banana can be used the same way. [L0882.010]
- A prompt is not strictly required for Shopping images, because current image models can work from the product photo and a described style. A prompt is still useful to enforce the required dimensions, the no-text rule and the no-border rule. [L0882.011]
- Do not expect a usable Shopping image on the first generation. Results usually need several rounds of refinement. Plan time for iterations, because each round takes a while to generate. [L0882.012]
- Refine each generation by naming the specific change, such as zooming in on the use case or enlarging the product on one side of the frame. When ideas run out, ask the model for concept ideas for the next round. [L0882.013]

INFORMATIONAL: spark curiosity without resolving the problem. COMPARISON: suggest that someone has done the research. Possible directions: editorial flat lay, lifestyle evaluation scene, or side-by-side hierarchy. 3. OFFER-FOCUSED: the product is the hero, and text on the image is permitted. Direction: a high-contrast product hero shot with negative space reserved for headline or urgency text. Rules for ALL angles: photorealistic, no heavy filters, no clutter. Format (choose one): Landscape (1.91:1), 1200 x 628 px (best for YouTube in-feed); Square (1:1), 1200 x 1200 px (works across both); Portrait (4:5), 960 x 1200 px (best for Discover). [User specifies angle and format]

### Brand Remap and book scene images

**Output sizes and aspect options**

- A4 portrait is 210 x 297 mm, a ratio of 1:1.414, which the tool uses for page proportions. For 300 DPI print, the page is 2480 x 3508 px. The tool does not produce that size directly, so upscale the PNG output afterwards. [L0794.016]
- Brand Remap aspect options:

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| Match competitor | Default. Keeps the competitor image's ratio. |
| 4:5 portrait | |
| 1:1 square | |
| 9:16 vertical | |
| 16:9 wide | |

[L0794.018]

**Content filters**

- Relax content filters is checked by default. It sends permissive safety settings so legitimate brand creative is not falsely blocked. Some server-side filters still apply regardless, so a blocked output must be rerun with an adjusted prompt. [L0794.019]

**Brand Remap: competitor layout re-skin**

```
Rebuild the arrangement, composition, element positions, framing, and general visual look of the attached competitor layout so the structure clearly matches it, but fully re-skin it in my brand's colours, logo, fonts, and identity taken from my brand reference. If the competitor layout includes a book or book cover, swap it for my own book cover so the book carries my branding. Never reuse the competitor's logo, brand name, trademarks, or text branding; replace every branded element with mine. Photorealistic, high resolution, clean composition, no watermark, no nonsensical text. All text must stay legible and spelled correctly.
```
[L0794.020]

- The Brand Remap tool places the brand images first, then the book cover if one is uploaded, and the competitor layout last so the model knows which image to recreate. The tool also adds a line stating the chosen aspect ratio. Check the instruction and image order before every run. [L0794.021]

**Book in user-generated-content style**

```
Create a photorealistic product photo in the style of user-generated content. The attached image IS the book: copy its front cover precisely, matching the title, author, subtitle, layout, artwork, colours, typography, and proportions. It must read as the same physical book in every frame. Do not redesign, restyle, recolour, translate, relabel, crop, or change the cover in any way; only the setting changes. Keep the front cover clearly visible and facing the camera. Natural, realistic hands with the correct number of fingers and realistic proportions, no nonsensical text, no watermark. Adjust this section if the book needs special notes, such as 'hardcover, glossy finish'. Setting: [one line from the scene list]
```
[L0794.036]

**Scene lines for Book Scene Studio**

Write one scene per line. Each line describes who holds the book, how they hold it, where they are, the camera angle and the light. Examples:

```
a woman in her thirties holding the book at waist height in a bright cafe, shot from a slight low angle, warm window light
a student resting the book on a classroom desk with the cover facing the lens, shot from above, soft overhead light
an older man holding the book toward a camera on a sunny porch, shot at eye level, natural shadows
```

### Meta AI enhancement settings

Check these settings in Ads Manager before every launch.

1. Go to Ad > Creative > Enhancements. [L0865.047]
2. Turn off all Meta AI text and creative variation features. [L0865.047]
3. Click Skip and continue where Meta offers AI-generated text options. Meta then chooses text that is not controlled. [L0865.047]
4. Turn off Overlays, Visual touch-ups and Add music. [L0865.048]
5. Keep Show products on only when the catalogue is optimised. [L0865.048]
6. If you want music, use your own. Otherwise use none, because Meta may add music that does not fit the brand. [L0865.048]

- Automatic AI changes to ads by Meta often hurt results. Check each automatic enhancement and turn it off unless it is proven to help. [L0865.049]

### Quality control and proofing

**Review before publishing**

- Read every AI-generated text and image before it is used. AI output can contain spelling errors and awkward sentences. The proofing tool fixes spelling and typos but does not check meaning or whether a claim is true. [L0794.041]
- Treat AI output as a starting draft only. Verify the content makes sense for your customers, rephrase unclear sections, and apply business judgement. Never use AI output without review and revision. [L0278.046]
- Fact-check product descriptions against the product, because AI output is not always accurate. [L0666.034]
- Review the output to make sure it matches the audience. [L0552.032]
- Check every headline for the unique feature. Ask the tool to rewrite any headline that does not include it, because AI copy often leaves the mechanism out of the headline even when the body copy contains it. [L0516.050]
- Review generated copy against the customer desire, the awareness stage and the principles before publishing. Make sure every claim is one you can actually support. The right structure can still come with weak claims. [L0516.051]
- Ask the AI to check the copy against the frame. [L0646.042]
- Check the line spacing of primary texts and headlines before you publish. [L0348.009]
- Have someone from the target group read the copy to check whether it sounds authentic. [L0353.008]

**Image checks**

- Before asking an AI image tool to recolour a real-world object, check a reference photo of that object, for example with a Google image search. This makes the requested colour match how the object really looks. [L0333.025]
- Playful phrases repeated several times on one cover line can look like too much. For example, "a lot" five times in a row. Review the rendered cover and cut the repetition back to one or two uses. [L0333.027]
- Expect several rounds of refinement for Shopping and Demand Gen images. [L0882.012]
- Refine by naming the specific change. [L0882.013]

**Book scene and batch checks**

- A half-and-half frame, where the book is cut across the picture or split with another image, reads as a 50/50 composition and weakens the photo. Rerun any output where the whole book is not clearly the subject of a full image. [L0794.038]
- A "no image returned" or safety-blocked message means that frame produced no picture. Rerun only that frame with the same input. If it keeps failing, adjust the wording of the prompt. [L0794.039]
- Batch conversion quality check:
  1. Count the outputs against the inputs after the batch finishes. [L0794.040]
  2. Compare each output with its source frame to confirm the right page was generated. [L0794.040]
  3. Rerun any missing or failed frame, changing only that item. [L0794.040]
  4. Skip any frame that is ignored after it was regenerated, and confirm the final set has every page in order before assembling the PDF. [L0794.040]

**Video analysis**

- The AI chat warns that it can make mistakes. A frame-by-frame analysis from Gemini or Claude must be checked against the actual video before you act on it. Treat the output as a hypothesis to verify, not as a finished result. [L0374.048]

### Limits of AI output

**Accuracy and claims**

- AI tools can produce the right structure but not the strongest claims. Review the output before publishing, and do not publish a claim you cannot support. [L0516.051]
- Output is not always accurate. Fact-check before publishing. [L0666.034]
- Using ChatGPT with no product input leads to generic copy. Use the principles and the audience inputs, and check every output. [L0524.060, L0552.033]

**Volume and tool limits**

- Free AI plans have message limits, and long outputs can be cut off, especially on a weak connection. When the output stops early, retry the request or move to a paid plan before the limit is reached. [L0861.034]
- Do not treat a single output as final. Use regeneration for weak outputs and refine each round with specific changes. [L0440.051, L0353.007]

**Adapting templates**

- Replace the original audience of a template with your own avatar and product before generating anything. Otherwise the output will address the template's audience. [L0862.041]

**Image tools**

- Shopping images do not need a prompt, but a prompt enforces the dimensions, the no-text rule and the no-border rule. [L0882.011]

### Working with AI before any output

- Keep one AI chat that already holds the brand guidelines, brand voice and target customer, and send every new copy request into it. The assistant then writes in the brand voice without the brand details being repeated each time. [L0992.024]
- Keep a set of saved ad copy prompts that have already worked, and reuse them on new artboards instead of writing new prompts from scratch. After applying a saved prompt, check that the output still matches the brand voice and the offer. [L0992.025]
- Decide in advance, and define in the training, the answers to questions that need a trained opinion:
  - where a UGC creator stands in the video
  - how long to wait before introducing the product
  - at what point in the script the hook ends

  Do not let the AI guess these from mixed sources. [L1478.008]
- Creative tasks that need a defined training source each need their own proven method: product research, idea generation, static ad creation, B-roll, and choosing UGC creators. Mixed opinions from the web would otherwise shape every one of them. [L1478.017]
- Before you rely on an AI's advice, run the diagnostic prompt below to see which sources it would use. Then decide which proven sources to train it on. [L1478.012]

```
If I asked you to build a system that generates effective Meta ad creative that makes sales, which specific resources would you study to learn what to do? Name each source, explain why you chose it, and state how reliable you think it is. Also say where you are unsure, and name any sources you would reject and why.
```
[L1478.012]

- An agent given a goal creates its own tasks, such as researching problems, gathering features and generating copy. It keeps iterating, evaluates its own output and may suggest A/B tests, then stops when it judges the work finished. [L1427.068]

### Copy prompts: product descriptions and feature blocks

**Product descriptions**

Two variants of the same product description prompt. Both are kept in full.

```
Please act as a direct response copywriter. Write a product description for [PRODUCT NAME and/or PRODUCT URL] using this format: 1) a headline; 2) a one to three sentence description; 3) features and benefits; 4) bullet points. Keep it short, simple and to the point. You can work from the product name or the product URL, or paste the copy you already wrote and have it condensed into this format while keeping all facts. Use only facts that appear in the product name, the URL or the pasted copy, and do not invent specifications, materials, sizes or claims.
```
[L1116.055]

```
Act as a direct response copywriter. Write a product description for [PRODUCT NAME] and/or [PRODUCT URL] in this format: 1) a headline; 2) a description of one to three sentences; 3) features and benefits; 4) bullet points. Keep it short, simple and to the point. If I paste existing product copy instead, condense it into this format and keep every fact it contains. Use only facts that appear in the product name, the URL or the pasted copy, and do not invent specifications, materials, sizes or claims.
```
[L1116.058]

**Feature blocks and problem-solution copy**

```
Using the base product description I provide, write two new feature block variations for [PRODUCT NAME]. Variation 1: a direct, urgent headline and a body of 2 to 3 short sentences that focus on the most concrete benefit in the data. Variation 2: a question-based headline and a body of 2 to 3 short sentences that focus on the buyer's problem. Use only facts from the data I provide, do not add numbers or claims that are not in the data, and give each variation a button label of 2 to 3 words. Output each variation with its headline, body and button label, in clean copy ready to paste.
```

Please write features that lead to benefits from these, one for each feature, explaining why each feature matters to the customer.
