### Copy prompts: ads, headlines and scripts

**Option sets and brand voice**

```
I have attached screenshots of [NUMBER] design artboards from our brand guidelines. Rewrite all of the copy on every artboard so it matches our brand voice, which is [3 adjectives describing the brand voice]. Write for our target consumer: [who they are, their age or life stage, their main problem or desire]. For each text element (headline, subheading, badge, call to action), give me [NUMBER] different options. Keep the offer in every option: [OFFER, e.g. 50% off, limited time]. Keep the length of each text close to the original and avoid generic slogans that could fit any brand. Use the same options structure for every artboard so I can compare them easily.
```
[L0992.013]

- Ask the AI for several options per text element, not one. Each option set gives a choice for every section of the design, and it is usually possible to find a strong option for each section. [L0992.016]
- In one test, three full option sets for one Instagram post gave a choice of headline, subheading and badge for each text slot. Three option sets were enough to find a usable option in every slot. [L0992.027]
- Template text is often written for a different product or style and may use odd formatting, such as all caps. Rewrite all template copy for the brand instead of keeping the defaults, even when you plan to edit it again later. [L0992.015]

**Meta headlines and primary texts**

```
Help me generate 5 Meta headlines and 5 primary texts for this product. Highlight the pain points and the benefits of the product. Use only facts from the landing page text below, and keep each headline short and each primary text clear enough to stand alone as an ad. Product name: [PRODUCT NAME]. Landing page text: [PASTE LANDING PAGE TEXT HERE].
```
[L1193.020]

**Problem-Agitate-Solution (PAS) framework**

Framework brief for an AI assistant. The quoted prompt is:

```
Write an ad using the problem-agitate-solution framework for this audience: [describe the audience and its problem]. Include these elements: [list required elements, e.g. hook, problem, agitation, solution, call to action]. Use the product title and About text and the audience insights from the review analysis.
```

After this, ask for three Facebook video ad scripts based on the copy, and refine them with the AI tool. [L0995.038]

```
I'm going to feed you some Amazon reviews for this product. Here is the product title and description: [title and description]. Digest this message and do nothing but understand it. In the next messages I will send reviews. For each batch, identify the types of target audience in terms of demographics, psychographics, behaviors and underlying needs and motivations, and say who they are, what they do, why they want the product, and what language they use.
```

Repeat this prompt with each new batch of about 30 reviews, and refine the segments. [L0999.040]

```
Based on this target audience: [describe the audience segment]. Write three Facebook video ad scripts using the problem, agitate, solution framework, and include these elements: [list the required elements, such as the hook, the problem, the agitation, the solution, the offer and the call to action]. Here is a direct-response script to model the structure on: [pasted script text]. Refine the scripts after each draft.
```
[L0999.041]

- A text extractor can pull the text from a direct-response video, so it can be given to ChatGPT, which then writes ad scripts from that text. Use this to avoid retyping the copy. [L0999.039]
- ChatGPT can help draft ad scripts. Give it the product, its features and the principles to use, such as social proof, curiosity and authority, and ask for a problem-agitate-solution script. The first draft is not perfect, so iterate by giving feedback and amending the sections you dislike. [L1425.026]

```
I am selling [PRODUCT NAME]. Its key features are [FEATURE 1], [FEATURE 2] and [FEATURE 3]. Explain what each feature does for the customer in one sentence: [FEATURE 1] makes [CUSTOMER RESULT 1], and so on. The problem it solves is [PROBLEM, e.g. pet hair spread across the house], and the customer feels [EMOTION, e.g. embarrassed when guests visit].

Write a problem-agitate-solution ad script for this product. Start with a hook that names the target audience and the problem. Make the problem worse in the agitate part and attach the emotion. Then present the product as the solution, with its features and the benefits they create. Include social proof, a line that creates curiosity, a bit of authority, and a clear call to action. Keep the script short enough for a 30-second video. Mark where each part starts (hook, problem, agitate, solution, social proof, call to action).

After the first draft, I will give feedback on the sections I dislike. Rewrite only those sections and keep the rest unchanged.
```
[L1425.030]

```
Write a short video ad script for [PRODUCT] using the problem-agitate-solution framework. Target audience: [AUDIENCE: age range, location, income, what they struggle with]. Product facts: [FEATURES, INGREDIENTS, SIZE, PRICE]. Problem the product solves: [PROBLEM]. Feeling the problem creates: [FEELING]. Benefit: [BENEFIT]. Desired outcome the buyer wants: [OUTCOME]. Structure the script as: 1) state the problem in one line the viewer recognizes, 2) agitate it by describing the frustration or feeling it causes, 3) present the product as the solution, 4) turn the benefit into the desired outcome and amplify it, 5) add a social proof line, 6) finish with a call to action. Keep each line short and written for speech in a natural tone.
```
[L1427.065]

**Ad copy variants with limits**

```
Write [number] short ad copy variants for [product name] aimed at [target customer, for example women over 35] in [country or region, for example Germany]. Write in [language, for example Swiss German or English]. Highlight these product benefits: [list the benefits]. Do not make health, weight, body or age-related promises. Keep each variant under [character limit] characters.
```
[L1431.033]

- AI tools can produce usable ad copy for a specific product and region, even in dialects such as Swiss German. Review and adapt every output, and build your own copywriting skills, for example by reading a persuasion book such as Influence by Robert Cialdini. [L1431.034]
- copy.ai and ChatGPT can produce ad copy drafts quickly. Every generated text still needs to be tested against real conversion results before it is scaled. [L1184.064]
- AI text tools such as ChatGPT can produce ad copy variations and ad strategy ideas, so a store can test several angles quickly. [L1416.007]
- AI can write hooks and ad scripts based on proven frameworks. This speeds up creative production compared with writing every script from scratch. [L1459.010]
- Use an AI tool to draft ad copy and social posts from the audience research, but feed it the right inputs: the quality of the output depends on the quality of the information given. [L0995.039]
- An AI chat can draft a full video script from a chosen storyline, but only after the angle has been picked from the research sheet. Without research-based angles, the AI output stays generic and weak for testing. [L0902.030]

Give them a [funny] tone that draws in people shopping for a new [niche product, e.g. surfboards]. If humor isn't right for us, replace [funny] with whatever tone fits our marketing.

### Product images: hero and clean product shots

**Hero shot prompt (square, white backdrop)**

```
Create a square picture of the uploaded item on a plain, pure white backdrop. Position the item in the middle of the frame with soft shadows that give it a sense of depth. Because this serves as the primary hero shot, it must be sharp, evenly lit, and contain no text, props, or background scenery.

Product fidelity: reproduce the item's exact form, dimensions, color, texture, and surface finish. Do not add branding or packaging that cannot be seen in the uploaded photo.
```
[L0887.024]

**Lifestyle scene from a product photo**

Procedure for a lifestyle image in ChatGPT:

1. Open the product page of the product and copy its product image.
2. Open ChatGPT and paste the prompt for a lifestyle image, adding the product image to the message.
3. Send the message and wait about 30 seconds while ChatGPT generates the image.
4. ChatGPT removes the white background, creates a transparent background, upscales the product, and places it in the requested scene at the requested square size.
5. If the result is not right, ask for more versions, for example with different backgrounds, and pick the best one.

[L1075.010]

```
Please create a square image of the attached product, exactly 1080 by 1080 pixels. Show the product [describe the scene, e.g. a surfboard on a beach at sunrise, sticking out of the sand], with the product clearly visible in the scene and its shape, colors and proportions kept as they are. Please do not change the text or graphics on the product in any way. Remove the white background from the product photo and place the product naturally into the scene.
```
[L1075.011]

- Square product and lifestyle images are generated at 1080 x 1080 pixels. State this exact pixel size in the prompt. [L1075.012]
- A product photo does not need a transparent PNG to work. A JPG with a white background can be used, because the image generator removes the background itself. This works for any product photo that shows the product clearly. [L1075.013]
- AI-generated product scene images are useful as ad images, remarketing images, email images, extra product page photos, and unique images for About Us or Contact Us pages. Multiple variants can be generated in minutes instead of waiting for designer revisions. [L1075.014]
- A designer creating a custom scene image in Photoshop might need about an hour. An infographic might take two to three hours plus revision rounds. In the lesson's example, ChatGPT generated the infographic text and image in about two minutes. [L1075.015]

**Pixel sizes and placements**

| Use | Size or position | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Square product and lifestyle image | 1080 x 1080 pixels | L1075.012 |
| Banner (example) | 1800 x 600 pixels, text position stated in the prompt | L0972.073 |
| One promo image for several placements | Exact size of a homepage slider, an email section or a social post, with a separate version per placement | L0972.106 |
| Profile picture | 1:1 square | L1476.018, L1475.019 |
| Cover image | 3:1 wide frame | L1476.018, L1475.019 |
| Landscape from a square or portrait source | Generate square or portrait, then reshape to 16:9 in Canva | L0888.025, L0888.015 |

- Specify the exact pixel size of the image in the prompt, and state where the text should sit. This gives more predictable output. [L0972.073]
- One AI-generated promotional image can be made at the exact size of a homepage slider, an email section or a social post. Create a separate version for each placement by stating the target pixel size and text position in the prompt. [L0972.106]

**Changing details after generation (highlight editing)**

Procedure for editing a generated image:

1. Click the generated image.
2. Use the highlight tool to mark the section that needs to change.
3. Describe what to add, remove, or replace in the box, and include the exact new text in quotes.
4. Send the change; only the highlighted section is changed.
5. Repeat for other errors and download the final image by clicking it.

**Background and detail changes with DALL-E**

Procedure for changing the background or details:

1. Upload the image.
2. Click Edit image.
3. Mark the part to change, or remove the background.
4. Write the replacement instruction in text, for example replace the background with a forest.
5. Click Generate and check the result.
6. Refine the text prompt and generate again if the result is weak, since first results are often not usable.

[L1428.013]

**Product image variations with DALL-E**

Procedure for carousel variations:

1. Upload a clear, high-quality photo of the product.
2. Crop the image to the area you want to keep.
3. Click Generate variations.
4. Review the similar versions that are created.
5. Choose the ones suitable for the carousel and save them.

[L1428.011]

- DALL-E variation results are only as good as the uploaded image. Use a clear and well-lit product photo, because blurry or low-quality uploads produce weak variants. [L1428.012]
- DALL-E generates images from text input and can create variations of an uploaded product photo. It is useful for print-on-demand designs, such as art pieces for shirts or cups, and for extra product images when a supplier provides only one picture. [L1428.010]
- AI image generators such as DALL-E can create product-style visuals from a text description, which helps when supplier photos are weak. Check that the output looks realistic and does not misrepresent the product before using it in ads or on the store. [L1260.066]

**Prompt pattern for image variants**

AI image prompts work well when one short text combines three parts: the subject, the art style and the scene. Examples: `a cat, watercolour, reading a book` and `a turtle, pixel art, riding a skateboard`. Changing one part, such as the style, produces a new variant for print-on-demand products like shirts and cups. [L1428.034]

**Runway ML Inpainting**

- Runway ML (runway.ml) has an Inpainting tool that removes distracting elements such as cables, logos or people from a video by brushing over them. The brush size can be adjusted on the right side, and the result is checked with the Preview button. It is useful for cleaning up supplier or marketplace product videos before using them in creatives. [L1428.003]

Procedure:

1. Log in at runway.ml and open the magic AI tools page.
2. Choose Inpainting.
3. Upload the video.
4. Set the brush size on the right side (bigger or smaller).
5. Paint over the object's full silhouette, covering everything that should disappear.
6. Wait for the processing to finish; the result takes a moment to load.
7. Click Preview to check the full video without the object.
8. Repeat the brushing with more care if parts remain, because a fast first pass gives weaker results.

### Avatars, models and characters

**Product photo set with different models**

Procedure for an AI product photo set:

1. In a text chat assistant, ask for one image prompt per photo and state the total count (here eight).
2. List every required photo: five product photos, one homepage hero image, one image for cold mornings, and one image focused on the fleece layer.
3. Require a different setting and a different model in every photo, all designed to appeal to the target consumer in the life she wants.
4. Ask for simple, plain prompts so a photo style can be added afterwards.
5. Review the settings the assistant proposes, for example indoor morning light in a bright living room, an urban but calm coffee room in early morning, a mirror selfie, a hero image, and a fleece detail.
6. Choose the photo style (for example hard flash) or reverse-engineer it from an inspiration image, and keep the style prompt ready.
7. In the image generator, paste the scene prompt, state that the model wears the attached product, attach several product photos as reference, and paste the style prompt.
8. Adjust details that do not fit, for example change a night scene to daylight.
9. Check that every image shows a clearly different model, and regenerate any image that repeats a person.
10. Adjust the model's clothing colors to match the brand palette where possible.

**Fictional spokesperson for a Facebook whitelisting page**

Two versions of the same spokesperson prompt are kept in full.

```
Act as a top-tier brand strategist for a seven-figure online store. Attached are my customer research files and product materials. Within ten minutes, invent a fictional spokesperson for my Facebook whitelisting page and produce the materials I need to set it up.

Phase 1, review the research: identify the product and the problem it fixes; the core buyer's demographics (age, gender, stage of life, income); who that buyer is, what they want, and what they fear; which kinds of people they already put faith in (a peer, a coach, a parental figure, a quiet expert, a former professional); and the main pain the product tackles. Present a three-line recap so I can confirm your grasp. Where the files lack something, state that openly rather than making it up.

Phase 2, select the archetype: choose the persona category that lines up with what the purchaser already believes in. Possible options (the list is not exhaustive) include a coach, trainer or former athlete for fitness, supplements and performance; a mom or dad of a child for babies, parenting and family; a beauty enthusiast or editor for skincare and cosmetics; a wellness advocate with a nurse-like manner for health and self-care; a pet parent or rescue owner for animal products; a home organizer or 'clean-girl' type for home and cleaning; or a retired professional or hobbyist for products tied to identity. Give the chosen archetype on one line and justify it in one sentence. Never design a medical doctor or any persona that suggests medical qualifications.

Phase 3, build the character: provide a complete sheet covering a casual, realistic first name; a page title in the style of 'Coach Sam', 'Mom of 3 Kate' or 'Doc Ellie'; an age range; an ethnicity and physical look kept loose enough for image generators; three to five personality words; a personal backstory of two to three sentences explaining why they entered this field and how they lived the problem themselves; and one sentence on what they help people with.

Phase 4, create the assets:
4a. A copy-ready profile picture prompt for ChatGPT, DALL-E or Midjourney. Specify a headshot-style frame facing the viewer straight on, in a 1:1 square, with age, ethnicity, hair, expression and outfit; a warm, genuine, approachable feel; natural light and a soft, out-of-focus backdrop suited to the archetype. Exclude corporate headshot style, stock-photo polish and over-processed looks. No text overlays, logos or product shots.
4b. A copy-ready cover image prompt. Use a wide 3:1 frame showing a lifestyle setting from the archetype's world (gym, kitchen, park, home office and similar), with a warm, aspirational, editorial mood and a color palette that fits the character's surroundings. The character may appear in the scene or the scene may stand alone. No text, logos or product shots.
4c. A Facebook page bio of 60 to 100 words in first person. Begin with a hook drawn from the backstory, connect it to the product's problem area, and close with what the person shares or helps with. It should read like a real individual rather than a company, with no hashtags, no emojis and no sales language.

Deliver everything in copy-ready form, in this order: the three-line research recap, the archetype choice with its rationale, the profile picture prompt, the cover picture prompt, and the page bio. Start immediately.
```

### Talking-head videos, voice and comic characters

**Frontal character in Midjourney**

- Generate the character as a frontal portrait in Midjourney, because a side view makes the character look odd once animated. Use a portrait prompt with a described shot and lighting, and create the image in square or portrait format. Convert it to 16:9 in Canva instead of generating 16:9 directly, because the direct 16:9 output looked poor. [L0888.015]
- A 16:9 image generated directly in Midjourney did not look good for this use. Generate a square or portrait image and reshape it into the landscape layout in Canva. [L0888.025]

**Script for a spoken video**

```
Write a spoken video script of at most 5000 characters about {TOPIC_OR_PASSAGE} for an audience aged 20 to 30. Make it educational and engaging, in the style of {REFERENCE_CREATOR}, and speak from a neutral perspective. Keep sentences short and easy to listen to, and write the script in {LANGUAGE}. Write every number as words in the spoken language. Write names and foreign or religious terms phonetically, so that a text-to-speech tool pronounces them correctly. Cover only {SPECIFIC_POINT}, and output plain spoken text without headings, titles or stage directions.
```
[L0888.014]

- Use the ChatGPT script prompt with a maximum script length of 5000 characters. This is the requested length of the script and not a limit of the prompt. Specify the target audience of 20 to 30 years old so the wording fits that age group. [L0888.029]
- ElevenLabs reads numbers aloud correctly only in English, not in German or other languages, so digits in a non-English script are mispronounced. Write all numbers out as words in the spoken language before generating the audio. [L0888.022]

**Full workflow: niche to vertical video**

Procedure for a talking-character video:

1. Choose a niche and a specific angle that has little existing content in the target language.
2. Generate a frontal portrait of the character in Midjourney, create variations, pick the best one and download it.
3. Build a 16:9 layout in Canva by placing the portrait on one side, keeping free space for on-screen text and adding a logo.
4. Create a thumbnail in Canva from a template, using the character and the topic or passage.
5. Write the script in ChatGPT using the prompt, have a knowledgeable reviewer check the facts, and polish the language in a document.
6. Spell out all numbers in words and write names and foreign terms phonetically for the text-to-speech tool.
7. Paste the script into ElevenLabs, choose a voice, generate the audio and download the mp3.
8. Upload the portrait and the mp3 to D-ID, generate the talking video and download it.
9. Upload the video to Vide.io, generate subtitles, choose style, size and font, correct errors against the script in a second window, and download the video.
10. Edit in Final Cut Pro: cover the watermarks, add the logo bottom left, add extra clips if needed, and export.
11. Change the project format from YouTube to TikTok, move the character to the left so it stays in frame, export the vertical version and upload it.

[L0888.013]

**Comic character with voice-over**

Procedure:

1. Create a comic-style character image with an AI image tool that relates to the product.
2. Add the image in Canva and place a name or text on it.
3. Write a script of about 300 words in ChatGPT, telling a short story that teaches something related to the product.
4. Turn the script into audio with an AI voice tool.
5. Combine the audio with the character image in an AI lip-sync tool so the character appears to speak.
6. The result is a video of about three minutes that you can test as an ad creative.

### Video ad scripts and angles

- Have a knowledgeable person check every script for factual accuracy before publishing, since ChatGPT output may contain false statements. This is especially important for religious, health or other sensitive content. [L0888.027]
- Write all numbers as words and write names and foreign terms phonetically, so the text-to-speech tool pronounces them correctly. [L0888.022, L0888.013]
- Choose the angle first from the research sheet, then have the AI draft the script around it. [L0902.030]

### Brand naming and character decisions

- Replace the example product in the brand name prompt with your own product and paste the complete brief in step 2. [L0990.009]
- Decisions that need a trained answer, such as UGC creator placement and hook timing, belong in the training, not in the AI's guesses. [L1478.008]

### Quality control and proofing

**Checking generated copy and images**

- Check every important fact in the generated copy and brief before publishing. AI tools like ChatGPT can make mistakes. [L0992.023]
- Check that the offer is visible in the final design. [L0992.014]
- Rewrite template copy for the brand instead of keeping defaults, even when you plan to edit it again later. [L0992.015]
- Check every word of a generated infographic before publishing it. [L1075.024]
- Always check the generated text for correct offers before running it. [L0972.074]
- Check that every image shows a clearly different model, and regenerate any image that repeats a person. [L0884.003]
- Check that the output looks realistic and does not misrepresent the product before using it in ads or on the store. [L1260.066]
- Review and adapt every AI output for a specific product and region before use. [L1431.034]

**Checking subtitles and video text**

- AI subtitles make errors on complex or less common words, because the tool is built around basic vocabulary. Always compare the generated subtitles with the original script in a second window and correct each mistake before export. [L0888.023]

**Testing copy against results**

- Every generated text still needs to be tested against real conversion results before it is scaled. [L1184.064]
- Check that the output still matches the brand voice and the offer after applying a saved prompt. [L0992.025]
- A quick test is the first step. If the test works, send the concept to designers for more variations. [L0972.070]

**Human control**

- AI can handle scale better than a single human, but a human must stay in control and check that the AI is learning from the right sources. Oversight is needed for nuance and final decisions. [L1478.009]
- Use one clean, well-lit product photo as the source. Blurry or low-quality uploads produce weak variants. [L1428.012]
- Spend more time on mask painting for a clean removal. [L1428.005]

### Case: AI presenter ads at scale

**Simple Brand, supplement, US (2025)**

- Starting point: a small brand, Simple Brand, sold a dietary supplement in the US. Its product showed strong sales on Kalodata in summer 2025. [L1479.014]
- What was done: the brand ran a large set of ads that were all AI-generated, with different AI presenters (an AI lady, an AI doctor, an AI man). It launched on July 9, 2025 and had about 71 active ads in Meta Ad Library after roughly one month. [L1479.014]
- The main brand behind the product had about 650 active ads, all AI-generated with avatar variations. [L1479.014]
- Result: the ads kept running for about a month, which indicates that the spend returned enough money to continue. The brand scaled the presenter versions that held up. [L1479.014]

Note on conflicting rules: the case shows an AI doctor presenter performing well, while the persona prompt says never to design a medical doctor or any persona that suggests medical qualifications. The 'Doc Ellie' title example in the same prompt conflicts with that rule. Follow the prompt rule for your own personas. [L1479.014, L1476.018]

Note on conflicting advice on AI people: real users build trust faster early on, while the case scaled AI presenters that held up in tests. Use real people for early trust and AI presenter variants for testing and scaling. [L1225.048, L1479.014]

### Limits of AI output

- AI tools like ChatGPT can make mistakes, so check every important fact in the generated copy and brief before publishing. [L0992.023]
- AI tools work as a virtual assistant rather than a lead. Their output is only as good as the input, and they miss contextual details that a human finds in forums and reviews. [L0999.038]
- Use an AI tool to draft ad copy from audience research, but feed it the right inputs. The quality of the output depends on the quality of the information given. [L0995.039]
- The AI generates text and images from the prompt. Unprompted visual or layout suggestions were weak, so tie image prompts to a specific offer. [L1224.027]
- Image generators return the same person when prompts describe models identically. Describe each model differently. [L0884.011]
- AI-generated infographics can contain small text errors. [L1075.024]
- Generated subtitles make errors on complex or less common words. [L0888.023]
- ElevenLabs reads digits correctly only in English. [L0888.022]
- Realistic-looking AI people build less trust than real users early on. [L1225.048]
- Decisions that need a trained opinion must be defined in the training, not left to the AI. [L1478.008, L1478.017]
- Generated product visuals must be checked for realistic product representation before use. [L1260.066]
- A generated text still needs to be tested against real conversion results before it is scaled. [L1184.064]

### Testing presenter avatars with AI-generated ads

- AI-generated ads let you test many presenter types (avatars) for the same product at low cost. [L1479.015]
- Work in this order: [L1479.015]
  1. Produce several presenter versions of the same product ad.
  2. Run them and find the one that keeps running.
  3. Scale that version.

## Sourcing creatives, creators and outsourcing

### Build or buy: in-house versus outsourced production

- Creatives are often the bottleneck, so the main problem is usually getting winning creatives into the account quickly. Outsourced creatives from freelance marketplaces do not guarantee performance, and building in-house skill takes weeks or months. [L0343.020]
- You do not need to make every creative yourself, but you should learn enough marketing to brief an outsourced designer or editor. A practical approach is to get a first set of creatives live quickly, then build basic copywriting and ad knowledge so you can judge and direct outsourced work. [L0552.048]
- At the test stage, paying someone to film is usually too expensive to justify. Start with self-shot or masked footage, and consider hiring only after a product proves itself. [L1186.015]
- High-quality video ads from outside agencies can cost thousands of dollars per month. Image ads let you test more creatives faster when budget is limited. [L0692.014]
- Video ads can come from four sources: [L0245.071]
  - DIY iPhone-style videos you film yourself
  - Product videos supplied by vendors
  - Web designer animations of your infographics
  - Static image ads, which work equally well and may be preferable for starting
- Creatives should be recorded or sourced from freelancers on Fiverr or Bilo when the owner cannot find the right people in their own circle. [L1184.046]
- Outsource the parts of video production the owner dislikes, such as on-camera recording, editing, scripting or voiceover, especially if the owner feels nervous on camera. Not appearing on camera is fine: product videos and voiceover content work without the owner's face. [L1424.015]
- Email marketing can be outsourced to an agency once it shows revenue. In one example, the outsourced email campaigns were kept because they produced revenue, while Google Ads results were mixed for this product type and most traffic came from organic sources. [L0337.039]

### Sourcing order for a product test

Source and build creatives for a product test in this order: [L0349.011]

1. Look at competitor ads and supplier content for the same product.
2. Shoot your own content in the same style, using a smartphone, if the product allows it.
3. Use a script adapted from the content you saw, with only small changes, and test it for a short period.
4. Edit pictures with a simple tool such as Canva, or a freelancer for Photoshop work.

If the budget allows, the priority order for footage is: [L1377.064]

1. Buy the product, shoot your own video with it, and return the product afterward. This custom content is the top priority.
2. If that is not possible, re-shoot a proven competitor video by keeping its hook, message, vibe and caption, and changing only the setting and optionally the music.
3. If neither works, search TikTok with 5 to 10 product keywords and hashtags and use videos from the last two weeks.
4. Build a creative folder of 5 to 10 or more videos from these sources.

### Own footage as a competitive advantage

- Ordering the product yourself and shooting original video creates a competitive advantage. You become the only seller with custom footage of that product, while competitors are forced to use generic supplier videos. [L0280.020]
- Ordering products for content is not necessary at the start of testing. A sample from a supplier or Amazon can be used and then returned if you need product shots. Reusing existing winning creatives with clip changes saves time and money. [L0637.057]
- Product video demonstrations can be created for dropshipping businesses only if you first obtain a physical sample to film with. Without the product, this proof point is not an option. [L0295.011]
- Ordering the product yourself is the recommended route for reliable supply, though it takes longer. [L0321.034]
- Real customer photos, obtained with permission, can serve as ad creatives and look more professional than staged photos. Asking customers to tag the brand on Instagram gives a steady source of such content. [L1439.021]

### Competitor and supplier footage when no own footage exists

- When no UGC is available, a product test can use YouTube, AliExpress, Alibaba or competitor videos, reshaped into the same 30-45 second structure with a strong hook and a call to action. This is a valid way to test a product before investing in creators. [L0398.051]
- Source product images and videos from AliExpress, Amazon, Google Image Search, Instagram (search by hashtag #product-name), TikTok, or competitor stores. [L0321.034]
- To test without your own designs, take product photos from AliExpress or Alibaba, or ask a manufacturer for pictures, and run ads with them. A test budget of around 200-300 USD is a typical starting point. [L1217.032]
- When no creators are available for a classic product video, stock clips can be sourced from general websites and from marketplaces such as AliExpress and Alibaba. Captions and video structure are then added so the product is not presented as a plain sales pitch. [L1335.051]
- Fashion product videos can be found on TikTok, where people sell products organically, which gives enough material for ad creatives. [L1161.040]
- A Chinese short-video app is a source for new product clips, because fresh product videos often appear there before they reach other markets. Use it together with YouTube Shorts and Instagram when no own footage is available. [L1177.058]

**Freelancer workflow for footage from existing ads**

Use this when the seller cannot shoot their own footage. [L1194.021, L1194.023]

1. Send the freelancer the AliExpress product link and ask them to find the product.
2. They search TikTok and Facebook for existing product videos and clip them.
3. They cut the clips together and remove the original ad copy text.
4. Deliver several variations where the first three to five seconds differ from each other.
5. Share the TikTok Ad Center or an ad library link with the creative editor, so they can study trending ads and how they are built before making variations.

**Mixing hooks from other footage**

- When the seller cannot shoot their own clips, search YouTube Shorts and Instagram for clips, mix hooks from them, or hire a creator on Fiverr for about 20-30 dollars to deliver content in two to three days. [L1177.030]

**Building an ad from sourced footage**

Source footage for an ad: [L1427.059]

1. Write the narrative as a list of scenes.
2. For each scene, search for product or stock footage that matches the emotion.
3. Download each clip and store it in the correct folder.
4. Speed up slow stock clips so they match the ad's pace.

### UGC creators and creator casting

**Casting**

- Use the customer avatar to cast creators for videos. If buyers are women aged 40 and older, use a UGC creator from that group, because they resonate most with the exact audience. [L1158.024]
- When your own appearance does not match the target audience (for example, a Black African creator selling to Gulf or primarily European markets), create two test versions: one with self-made UGC and one with outsourced UGC creators who match the audience's appearance and accent. Run both in parallel and compare conversion rates to see which demographic resonance drives higher sales. [L0308.036]
- For a video ad aimed at a closing audience, the presenter can appear on camera, or a hired person who resembles the customer avatar can deliver the message. Freelance marketplaces such as Upwork were mentioned as a place to find such a speaker. [L1243.033]
- Creators who are building their own presence will often produce content for free product or small payments, which is a useful source of cheap content. Choose creators whose photo quality matches your brand. [L0790.044]
- Creators can supply high-resolution photos and video for your own social channels. Ask micro-influencers to send their photos and reshare the content, which reduces the need for a photographer. [L0790.043]

**Payment**

- Creator payment for video content is $45 to $60 per 60-second clip, or $45-60 for 12 five-second scenes broken down by hook, use case and call-to-action. Request raw clips rather than edited videos, so internal editors can combine scenes into 5-10 different variations. [L0321.016]
- Fiverr creators for short content (see also the table below) can deliver content in two to three days for about 20-30 dollars. [L1177.030]

**Minimum spend and testing philosophy**

- Creators often demand a minimum spend per creative (for example, 3x average order value) to prove the ad works. Media buyers prefer letting the algorithm choose winners without spend minimums. Clarify your testing philosophy upfront and set budget guardrails to prevent mid-campaign conflicts. [L0217.054]

**Ordering UGC for Facebook**

- When ordering UGC for Facebook ads, the video ad type is the usual choice on Billow, since it is built for paid placements. [L1402.019]

### Freelance marketplaces: Fiverr, Upwork and Bilo

**Fiverr for banners and design**

- Fiverr is a freelance platform where graphic designers create web banners at various price points and turnaround times. Use it instead of hiring an in-house designer, since designers deliver multiple banner sizes and formats. *(Older advice, Source B 2021-22.)* [L0288.012]
- To find designers on Fiverr, go to Graphics & Design, then select Web Banners from the subcategory menu. This section shows freelancers who specialise in web banner design. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0288.013]
- When hiring a Fiverr designer, choose someone with at least 50+ completed jobs and a rating between 4.8 and 4.9 stars. Review their portfolio and select a designer whose style matches your brand. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0288.014]
- Alternatively, Fiverr sellers are more cost-effective than agencies for creative production, and most agencies subcontract to Fiverr anyway. Hire Level 2+ sellers who speak English fluently to avoid revisions and quality issues. [L0309.020]

**Commissioning banners on Fiverr** *(older advice, Source B 2021-22)*

1. Provide the designer with your branding guidelines. [L0288.015]
2. Explain what the banner should communicate or convey. [L0288.015]
3. Supply product images if specific products must appear. [L0288.015]
4. The designer creates the banners in multiple sizes. [L0288.015]
5. The designer sends the finished files to you. [L0288.015]
6. Download the files and upload them to Refersion. [L0288.015]

**Affiliate banners** *(older advice, Source B 2021-22)*

1. Determine which offer types you want to promote: business-wide offers or product-specific offers. [L0202.008]
2. Commission banner ad designs on Fiverr matching each offer type. [L0202.008]
3. Upload the completed banner ads to Refersion or your affiliate software. [L0202.008]
4. Make them available for affiliates to download. They can use them independently without further action from you. [L0202.008]

**Hiring ad designers**

- To hire ad designers, post a small test gig on Fiverr, or a job on Upwork, with one ad, and test several designers. Review each portfolio, and send examples of the style you want as inspiration, not copies of existing ads. [L0667.051]
- Bilo job posts usually need two to three days before applications arrive. [L1184.046]

**Testing a copywriter or illustrator**

- Test a sales copywriter's efficiency before hiring. Give each candidate a small project, such as five headlines and five meta descriptions, measure the time, and hire the best one. In one test, candidates took between 2 and 6 hours for the same small task. [L0382.034]
- Custom illustration was budgeted at about $5 per image. Workflow: [L0380.028]
  1. The illustrator delivers an initial sketch.
  2. The owner gives feedback on the sketch.
  3. The illustrator delivers the final design.

### Agencies

- Most agencies subcontract to Fiverr, so a direct Fiverr seller is usually more cost-effective than an agency for creative production. [L0309.020]
- A top outsourced ad creator cost about $3,500 per month. A brand that produced 100 creatives this way got about 3 winners, a hit rate of roughly 3%. Plan for many creative tests rather than a few polished ads, and consider producing creatives in-house to lower the cost per test. [L0995.035, L0999.079]
- Outsourced batches can have low hit rates. In one case, an outsourced batch of 100 creatives produced only 3 winners, about 3%. Budget for a large number of tests rather than a few high-quality pieces. [L0995.056, L0999.079]
- Viral Ecom Ads was described as about $50 per month, which covers a split test of three TikTok videos at about $12 each. Its quality was judged lower than premium production, which can cost thousands of dollars per month. [L1107.020]
- Creators and in-house production should be compared on the same test: create many creatives and test them. An entertaining, educational or value-first approach should be tested by analysing successful brand ads. [L0995.035]

### Copywriting and copy production

**Who writes the copy**

- In the early stage of an e-commerce business, the best-paid copywriters are usually unaffordable, so owners often have to learn to write product descriptions and emails themselves. Copy is a direct sales lever, so building this skill in-house can shortcut the cost of outsourcing it. *(Older advice, Source B 2021-22.)* [L0684.001]
- Product descriptions, sales emails and other sales copy can be written by owners, employees or virtual assistants who learn a tested copywriting method. Delegating copy production to a trained team member is a practical option for small teams. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0684.002]
- Hire a sales copywriter to write headlines and meta descriptions for about $40 to $100 per hour. Large companies often employ people who only write headlines and meta descriptions. [L0382.032]

**Checking a copywriter**

- Excessive fluff and useless sentences often signal that the writer did not research the product. When hiring or testing a copywriter, check a trial text for this, and reject writers whose copy is full of empty language. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0925.012]

**Product descriptions on Upwork** *(older advice, Source A 2020)*

1. Post a job for product descriptions on Upwork. [L0961.074]
2. Hire at least three or four writers. [L0961.074]
3. Give each writer the same test product page to write. [L0961.074]
4. Compare the results and keep the writer who performs best. [L0961.074]

### Stock sources and assets

- Adobe Stock is a paid stock library with a monthly subscription and keyword search. It offers high-quality images, and it is the paid source the course's author uses across several businesses. *(Older advice, Source B 2021-22.)* [L1310.003]
- Unsplash is a free stock image source that works like a keyword search. Other free stock image sites can be found by searching for free stock image sites, but Unsplash is one of the better ones. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L1310.004]
- Canva's subscription includes stock photos, audio and stock videos that would otherwise be paid extras, which makes it a low-cost source of creative assets for a graphic designer. Confirm the current price and licence scope on the Canva site before budgeting, since the lesson's figure was taken at recording time. [L0754.066]
- After store approval, obtain the creative assets for the Meta ads from the designated asset source before setting up the ad account and campaigns. The creative strategy for these assets is covered in the Meta ads module. [L0491.022]

### Customer and brand photos

- Collect real customer product photos in three steps: *(older advice, Source A 2021)* [L0968.096]
  1. Email customers who bought the product.
  2. Ask them to send photos taken with a good camera or a phone.
  3. Offer a payment for usable photos, for example 50 dollars via PayPal, to encourage participation.
- A friend who is a photographer shot the product for about 200. A typical professional shoot can cost about 1,000. Using a network to reduce costs is a practical option early on. [L0492.044]
- A professional product photo shoot with editing costs around 1,000 to 2,000 USD. A low-budget shoot with friends is an alternative for an early-stage store, although picture quality will be lower. [L1439.023]

### Influencers and authorities

Find influencers or authorities connected to your product: [L1267.006]

1. Search Pinterest or Google for influencers, actors, artists, celebrities or doctors who use or fit your product category.
2. Note each person's name.
3. Find and record each person's social media handle.
4. Note whether they already use or have used your products.

### Refreshing and testing creatives

- Freelance marketplaces such as Fiverr can supply replacement ad creatives when the original creatives stop converting. Refresh creatives as soon as CTR drops and CPM rises, because creative fatigue reduces sales over time. [L0660.047]
- Create many creatives and test them. Budget for a large number of creative tests rather than a few high-quality pieces, since hit rates are often low. [L0995.035, L0995.056, L0999.079]
- A seller does not need to make every creative personally, but should be able to judge and direct the outsourced work. [L0552.048]

- In one brand's outsourced batch, 100 creatives produced about 3 winners, a hit rate of roughly 3%. [L0995.056, L0999.079]

### Hiring checklist

- Fiverr designers: at least 50+ completed jobs and a 4.8-4.9 star rating, with a portfolio that matches your brand. [L0288.014] (older advice, Source B 2021-22)
- Fiverr sellers: Level 2+ and fluent English, to avoid revisions and quality issues. [L0309.020]
- Copywriters: test with the same small project, measure the time, and reject copy full of empty language. [L0382.034, L0925.012]
- Product descriptions: test at least three or four writers on the same product page. [L0961.074] (older advice, Source A 2020)

## Creative testing structure

### Why creative testing comes first

- Creative testing is one of the largest parts of scaling paid ads, whether it is done in-house or outsourced. Make many creatives and test them continually, because only a small share will work. [L0999.034]
- A weak creative can make a product look like a failure even when the product works, so test new creatives before deciding that a product is not viable. [L1038.016]
- Structured testing frameworks during the ads phase keep decisions based on results rather than opinion. [L0914.011]
- Testing many creatives early matters more than the size of the budget. For example, test about double the number of creatives on the first day, then add budget only to the creative that looks promising. [L1379.032]
- Creatives are usually tested for the first time around week three. A creative that fails is information about what to change, not a final verdict on the product. [L1445.004]
- Smaller budgets do not give enough data to judge an ad. Decide quickly on what performs early, since waiting for a month of data at 50 per day is not practical for most sellers. [L0950.039]
- Creative testing often requires enough spend for the algorithm to learn. At very low daily budgets such as 5 per day, controlling spend manually gives faster, clearer results. [L1426.041]
- Simple homemade or cropped creatives can outperform professionally shot ones, so appearance is not a reliable predictor of performance. Decide which creative stays by the data and the sales it brings. [L0562.013]
- Unconventional or aesthetically imperfect designs can outperform polished creative. Test unusual aesthetics even when they do not match typical advertising polish. [L0316.044]
- Test across different concepts such as humour, education, before-and-after and shock, and let audience results decide. Launching quickly and iterating on feedback costs less than planning one polished ad and launching it late. [L1077.016]
- Test creatives aimed at different audience types, because it is not possible to know in advance which audience will respond. Find the creative that works, then scale it. [L1016.017]
- Combine educated guesses about why an ad should work with variation tests of different angles, because psychology alone cannot predict results. Buyer context often only becomes clear once an ad is live, so launching and testing usually beats waiting for a perfect creative. [L1348.027]
- Test formats on your own product before committing budget to one type. In one fashion store, image ads generated most of the revenue while video ads did not work. [L1127.028]
- A product that splits its audience can be tested with creative that deliberately provokes a clear reaction. The mix of positive and negative responses shows which buyers lean toward the product. [L1315.053]

### When to start testing

- Start creative testing when click-through rate (CTR) or cost per click (CPC) is poor, since weak CTR signals a need for new creatives immediately. [L0902.003]
- Also start once a product is a consistent seller and has been profitable for more than two to three weeks. [L0902.003]
- Start creative testing only after two weeks of consistent profitable results, with two or three winning audiences. Early in a product test, focus on finding winning audiences first. [L1177.033]
- Before launching a test, have a finished landing page, 4 to 5 creatives (images, videos or carousels) and ready ad copy. [L0648.003]
- Move to hook testing only after you get consistent profitable sales with ripped creatives. At that point you have a validated angle, avatar and product. [L1252.016]
- Hook testing is the step after ripped creatives prove profitable, and its aim is to raise CTR. Starting it earlier mixes the creative variable with the product test. [L1252.017]
- Start creative testing when a product is already a consistent seller, and use the audience stage first to find where it sells. [L0902.003, L1177.033]

### Test structure: audiences first, then creatives

- Stage 1, audience testing for a new product, works as follows. [L0398.025]
  1. Produce three to four videos for the product. [L0398.025]
  2. Run them in an audience testing campaign across several audiences, such as interests, countries and age groups. [L0398.025]
  3. Goal: find two to three winning audiences whose performance shows the product sells and the message reaches the right people. [L0398.025]
  4. Once two to three winners are found, move to the creative testing campaign described below. [L0398.025]
- Creative testing campaign setup, using ABO with the Sales objective. [L1335.023]
  1. Create an ABO campaign (Sales objective) for creative testing. [L1335.023]
  2. Add three ad sets, each targeting a proven winning audience (for example one winning interest, one lookalike winner, one further consistent winner). [L1335.023]
  3. Place the same three video variations in each ad set; the variations differ only in the first 3 to 5 seconds (the hook) while the rest of the video is identical. [L1335.023]
  4. Run the test for 2 to 3 days to collect enough data. [L1335.023]
  5. Choose the winner by ROAS first; if ROAS is equal, use CTR; if CTR is also equal, use average play time. [L1335.023]
  6. Use the winning creative in audience testing campaigns, CBO scaling campaigns, and wherever new audiences are tested, and reuse it for audiences that are dying down. [L1335.023]
- Separate campaigns: run an interest testing campaign (winning creatives, new interests) and a creative testing campaign (winning interest, new creatives), so a new creative gets its own budget. [L0640.026]
- Creative testing in a separate campaign, with a new CBO or ABO campaign. [L1107.022]
  1. Pick two or three interests that currently perform well. [L1107.022]
  2. Place them in a new CBO or ABO test campaign with two ad sets. [L1107.022]
  3. Test three new creatives in each ad set. [L1107.022]
- Duplicate the winning ad set so that its audience and placements stay identical, then test the new creatives in the duplicate. [L1335.054]
  1. Duplicate the winning ad set so its audience and placements stay identical. [L1335.054]
  2. Put the duplicate into a new creative testing campaign. [L1335.054]
  3. Change only the launch date and replace the videos with the new creatives. [L1335.054]
  4. Keep the targeting unchanged, so any performance difference comes from the creative and not the audience. [L1335.054]
  5. Run the test and compare the hook or creative variants inside the same audience. [L1335.054]
- Test new creatives on a winning audience. [L0774.035]
  1. Take the winning ad sets with the best audience, age, gender and interest. [L0774.035]
  2. Create a separate campaign with the new creatives and compare CTR. [L0774.035]
  3. Move the best-performing creatives into the running ad sets. [L0774.035]
  4. Turn off ads that spend 20 to 30 USD without sales and keep the ones that produce sales. [L0774.035]
- Keep new creatives out of ad sets that contain the old winner. Facebook and TikTok send most budget to the creative with the most data, which hides how well new creatives would perform. [L1177.031]
- Facebook creative testing structure. Keep the winning audience and copy, change only one variable at a time (hook, creative or creator), and put each new creative in its own ad set, or put several new creatives together in one ad set to compete. Do not mix them with the old winner. [L1177.032]
- TikTok launch structure. One winning ad set and winning creative can be duplicated into a new campaign, while new creatives are tested in a separate ad set to avoid budget going to the old winner. [L1177.034]
- Standard Pinterest test structure: one campaign, one ad group with stacked interests, and three creatives (ads). Let it run for at least five to seven days, and let the platform optimise. [L1134.025]
- Structure each test as one campaign, one ad group and three creatives, because one creative may be rejected and two others still give a valid test. [L1135.040]
- Creative testing setup based on a winning interest. [L1212.012]
  1. Find the winning interest or audience first. [L1212.012]
  2. Duplicate that ad set (for example three times) with the same interest. [L1212.012]
  3. Keep only one ad (creative) in each ad set. [L1212.012]
  4. Compare which creative has the highest CTR. [L1212.012]
  5. Only increase the budget once a winning audience is found, then scale the winning campaign by raising the budget. [L1212.012]
- Keep each angle in its own column, and do not mix problem types inside one column. Testing angles separately shows which problem drives clicks and purchases, and empty columns are kept for future angles. [L0392.009]
- Full setup for a Meta CBO test ad. [L0348.007]
  1. In the ad set, select Advantage+ creative / ad format Single image or video and leave Multi-advertiser ads unchecked. [L0348.007]
  2. Upload 6 to 10 creatives (a first round of about 9 creatives across ad sets is the target). [L0348.007]
  3. Choose the Facebook Page and the Instagram account. [L0348.007]
  4. Confirm the website URL points to the correct product page for that product. [L0348.007]
  5. Press Next, then use the regenerate option on the primary text and headline generated by Meta to draft copy. [L0348.007]
  6. Paste the copy from your external prompt into the ad primary text and headlines, and check the spacing and line breaks. [L0348.007]
  7. Press Publish. [L0348.007]
- Ads per ad set: keep the number small (about three to four creatives) so that spend per creative is controlled and each result can be read. Facebook is good at choosing the best creative for a specific audience, so several options give more chances to work. [L0646.039]
- Reuse the same set of three to four ads across ad sets with the same goal. Meta then tests them and spends on the best one, so a single ad is never enough. [L0649.032]
- Full setup needs about 13 ads in total across the campaigns. Lead generation and promotions need 3 to 4 each, the goodwill campaign needs one video, and each sandbox test needs two ads. [L0649.038]
- For a clean creative test, place each of four creatives in its own ad set with about 5 to 15 dollars of spend per ad. This costs more but shows which creative wins on CTR and CPC. In one ad set with four ads, one creative can take most of the budget, so the result is harder to read. [L0646.062]
- Do not blindly trust Facebook's spend allocation. If a creative receives little spend, duplicate the ad set into its own ad set and force spend onto it for a test period (for example three days) before deciding it is weak. [L0640.027]
- Standard test per product uses about three creatives: one or two videos and one or two pictures. [L0349.010]
- Test one interest set at a time... see section on budgets for per-ad-set amounts. [L1177.059]
- Test each new creative with about 10 to 20 dollars of spend in its own single-creative ad set to read its performance on its own. Combine creatives in a shared ad set only after each one has shown its results separately. [L1177.059]

### Isolating variables: one change per test

- Test one variable at a time. Start with the hook, because it is the most important variable at the start. Thumbnails, overall style and ad copy come later. [L0398.027]
- Keep each level above the one being tested fixed, so that only one variable changes at a time. [L0902.027]
- Creative testing works as a chain: an ad angle becomes a concept (the storyline), the concept becomes one script, the script gets three hook variations, and those hook variations run as ads. [L0902.027]
- Static ads mean image ads and carousel ads. A concept can be built as either a video or a static ad, because the concept is the angle or script the test is based on, not the format. [L0902.028]
- Keep a control ad with unchanged interest, copy and hook, and change only one element (such as the mid-section), so any lift is attributable to that change. [L0640.025]
- During creative testing, keep the offer and ad copy identical across all ads and change only the video, clip or creator. This makes the creative the only variable. [L1382.074]
- Only change one variable at a time: in creative tests keep the targeting identical to the proven winning audience, so the performance difference comes from the creative and not the audience. [L1335.024]
- Test one variable at a time: keep audience, creative, copy and targets identical and change only the offer, so a conversion uplift can be attributed to the offer. [L1315.026]
