- Allocate at least 15 percent of the weekly advertising budget to creative testing. For example, with 1,000 weekly ad spend, at least 150 goes into testing new creatives. [L1335.025]
- Once a product is working, keep 10 to 20 percent of the budget permanently allocated to creative testing. [L0639.024]
- Run the testing process 2 to 3 times per week at small scale, 10 to 15 times per week at higher scale, and test 3 to 4 creative variations when spending 1,000 to 2,000 per day. [L1335.026]
- Smaller budgets do not give enough data, so judge early and decide quickly. [L0950.039]

### How many creatives to start with

Sources disagree on the starting number. Use the number that fits your budget, product and stage.

| Context | Starting number | IDs |
|---|---|---|
| Three different creatives per new campaign (a video, a picture and a carousel if the product allows it) | 3 | L0562.012 |
| Product needs explanation: two videos and one picture | 3 | L0562.012 |
| Start creative testing with three creatives; add more if results are weak | 3, then more | L1219.027 |
| Each ad group gets three creatives and one ad text | 3 | L1377.013 |
| Launch with 3 creatives per ad set, up to 5 if the budget allows | 3 to 5 | L0648.003 |
| Launch with 3 to 5 creatives per interest | 3 to 5 | L0639.024 |
| Ads per ad set kept small | 3 to 4 | L0646.039 |
| Per-campaign starting set | About 6 to 10, first round about 9 across ad sets | L0348.007 |
| Minimum per product test | 10 (bare minimum), 10 to 15 recommended, high quality | L1193.019 |
| Target per week, testing many concepts | 10 to 15 | L1077.015 |
| Real creatives for testing | 15 to 20 | L1383.031 |

- Concepts per week: identify two or three marketing concepts (angles, such as comfort or sustainability), write one script per concept, and shoot three hook variations per script, giving 6 to 9 videos per week. [L0298.048]
- Test a minimum of three concepts per week. [L0298.048]
- Duplicates count only if they are changed, for example with a different call-to-action button, so five different videos can become ten ad variants. [L1383.031]
- Creative mix per ad set depends on the product. If the product needs a video, use at least two videos plus one picture ad. If it does not need video (such as shoes or fashion), use one carousel, one picture and one slideshow ad. A slideshow ad rotates pictures about every second. [L1212.014]
- More creative variety gives Meta more data to optimise from the start and raises the chance of a strong creative. With a 5 USD ad set budget, 2 to 3 creatives are enough. [L0648.004]
- Use two to three rounds of creative iteration per product at minimum. [L0640.028]
- Test four images of likely winning products: build one ad with a single image, one slideshow, one carousel and one meme ad, and test them all against the interest ad sets to see which has the best CTR. [L0642.030]
- Test several creatives first, then several interests. The creative with the best CTR and the interest that brings sales are the ones to keep. [L0642.031]
- Launch with 3 to 5 creatives per interest from the start. [L0639.024]

### Hook, copy, thumbnail and angle testing

- Each new video should come with about three hook variations, where only the first five seconds differ. Meta then optimises the combinations. [L0398.028]
- Hooks should be tested by making one video with three different first 3 to 5 seconds, keeping the rest identical. Ideas can be taken from what is trending on TikTok. For image ads, make three images around the same marketing angle. [L1335.027]
- Ad copy angle testing: keep the winning video and hook identical and change only the ad copy, so each version speaks to a different motivation within the same winning audiences. [L0398.060]
  - Formula: one copy per audience motivation, with the video held constant. [L0398.060]
  - Example 1: for a camping product, one copy focuses on night-time visibility and another on gadget features. [L0398.060]
  - Example 2: for a fitness product, one copy focuses on saving time and another on feeling confident during workouts. [L0398.060]
- Ad copy matters more once several audiences need different angles. Test ad copy only after spending more than about 1,000 per day on testing, and keep the video and hook identical while you test it. [L0398.033]
- Thumbnails and ad copy are tested separately from the video. [L0902.025]
  1. Keep the same winning video and vary only the thumbnail (thumbnail 1, 2, 3) to find the thumbnail winner, since thumbnails are the first thing customers see and can raise CTR. [L0902.025]
  2. Keep the same video and thumbnail while varying the ad copy (ad copy 1, 2, 3) to find the ad copy winner. [L0902.025]
- Testing a new angle on a video that did not get the expected views. [L0795.016]
  1. Pick a good video idea that did not perform. [L0795.016]
  2. Add a hook that has already worked for you in the past. [L0795.016]
  3. Publish the new version and compare its results with the previous one. [L0795.016]
- Find the strongest marketing angle without a large budget. [L1218.033]
  1. Pick one marketing angle. [L1218.033]
  2. Make a creative for that angle alone, or use only its first 5 to 10 seconds as the hook, and add UGC-style clips. [L1218.033]
  3. Test each angle's creative separately on Facebook. [L1218.033]
  4. Once one angle clearly wins, add a landing page section for it and move the other sections down. [L1218.033]
- Creative testing by splitting a winning ad. [L1315.045]
  1. Split a winning ad into separate features or benefits, one per creative. [L1315.045]
  2. Run them for a few days. [L1315.045]
  3. Pick the best-performing problem or angle. [L1315.045]
  4. Create new creatives around that problem. [L1315.045]
  5. Keep iterating on existing ads and test new concepts continually. [L1315.045]
- Creative testing as a test of four creative types against interest audiences. [L0642.030]
- A winning angle is tested in video before it is scaled. Launch VSL (video sales letter) ads first and static image ads afterwards, because VSLs convert better and test the full message. The winning angle then gets iterated into static image ads. [L1019.038]
- Replace a Google text ad's single element with one change at a time. Iterative text ad testing isolates single variable changes to identify which specific word or phrase your audience prefers. Only one element varies while all other copy remains identical; performance shifts directly show what caused them. Examples: Join the Community versus Become a Member (different verb, same offer), or Learn More versus Discover More (same action, different tone). [L0085.006]
- Evolutionary text ad testing uses fundamentally different messaging frames, such as leading with a customer pain point versus leading with the solution benefit, to discover which overall approach converts best. Examples: Tired of Back Pain (pain-point focus) versus Professional Spinal Support (solution-forward), or Don't Get Left Behind (urgency) versus Trust the Industry Leader (authority and quality). [L0085.007]
- Iterative testing changes only one element per test and keeps everything else identical, for example changing the call to action from Buy now to Shop now. It is worth doing, but it produces only small differences. [L1401.007]
- Evolutionary testing compares two very different ad styles, such as a question (Struggling with acne?) against a direct statement (The acne solution). On Google text ads, evolutionary tests usually produce bigger gains than tweaking single words, so new concepts should be tested more often. [L1401.008]
- Test sales copy on real members of the target market before launch. [L0340.077]
  1. Give the copy to 3 to 5 people who fit the buyer profile and do not know the product. [L0340.077]
  2. Ask each reader to say in their own words what the product does and what they should do next. [L0340.077]
  3. Mark every sentence where the reader hesitates, misreads, or asks a question, and rewrite those sentences with simpler words and one claim each. [L0340.077]
- Free pretest for a sales letter, in order. [L1370.058]
  1. Read the letter aloud and fix any tongue twisters or awkward phrases. [L1370.058]
  2. Read it to several people who match the target customer, possibly in a casual setting, and watch whether they ask how to buy, which signals that the approach works. [L1370.058]
  3. Have a young reader read it aloud and change any words or phrases they struggle with. [L1370.058]
  4. Check whether typical customers have questions the letter leaves unanswered, and if so add a page that answers them. [L1370.058]
- Testing a voiceover against text-only overlays before committing. A voiceover reaches people who cannot read the screen, and text reaches people who cannot hear, and many text-only ads perform well. [L1427.051]
- Case: a text-only ad with rain overlays and heavy effects reached about 2.5 ROAS and was treated as a failure. A simple UGC-style ad with plain text overlays and a voiceover reached 4 to 6 ROAS. [L1427.052]
- Subtitles: when a video from abroad is strong but not in the local language, add subtitles if the creative is good; otherwise create or hire a similar one. Image ads were the main format used for testing new products. [L1108.020]
- Testing AI presenters for a proven product. [L1479.016]
  1. Take an ad angle and offer from a brand whose ads have run for a long time. [L1479.016]
  2. Create AI presenter versions of the same ad, each with a different avatar type (for example a doctor, an everyday woman, a man). [L1479.016]
  3. Keep the product, script and offer identical so that only the presenter changes. [L1479.016]
  4. Let the versions run and compare their results. [L1479.016]
  5. Scale the avatar that performs best and stop the rest. [L1479.016]
- Test platform-specific hooks: write two or more strong hooks, titles or captions for the same video and publish each variant on a different platform. [L0784.017]
  1. Write two or more strong hooks, titles, or captions for the same video. [L0784.017]
  2. Publish each variant on a different platform, for example variant A on TikTok, variant B on Instagram, and a third variant on YouTube. [L0784.017]
  3. Compare the results per platform. [L0784.017]
  4. Adjust the messaging for each platform based on what performed best there. [L0784.017]

### Offer testing

- Keep the offer out of the ad creatives while testing, because the offer changes often. Once a winning offer is found, add it to the ads; every offer change then requires updating the ads as well. [L0502.025]
- Test offers with simple static creatives, such as buy one get one free, a free gift or 40 percent off, to see which offer responds best across markets and products. [L0341.022]
- Image creatives can be built fast from templates and tested before video creatives are made. [L0343.002]

### Format choice: static before video

- Video takes longer to produce, so use it once a static layout has shown it converts. [L0343.002]
- When product footage is limited, run quick image ads first to see which market responds, and only then produce a full video for the winning market. If footage is good enough for a clear narrative, use it, but the hook and offer come first. [L0344.014]
- Use simple image ads with product imagery in an AI tool, Photoshop, or a freelance graphic designer to test quickly before committing to video. [L0950.052]
- Test formats on your own product before committing budget to one type. [L1127.028]
- Swipe file creatives: the full testing workflow. [L0343.040]
  1. Choose a product and find a matching swipe file layout, such as Them vs Us, testimonial, benefit callout, meme or offer. [L0343.040]
  2. Replace the text with your branding, product benefits and offer. [L0343.040]
  3. Swap in your product cut-out and adjust colours and gradients. [L0343.040]
  4. Publish the variants as ads and compare which layout performs best for each product. [L0343.040]
  5. Scale the winning layout and build video versions only after the static test shows a clear winner. [L0343.040]
- Concepts that do not show the product at all, such as a close-up of two faces contrasting a problem and a solution, can be tested when competitors use this style successfully in search. Test such images against product-visible versions rather than replacing them. [L0882.015]
- Replacing the image of a working Shopping listing without a split test can lose performance that was already earned. Duplicate the listing first so the new image competes against the original. [L0882.032]
- Study competitors' ads in the Meta Ad Library and note recurring hooks, ad copy and story structure. [L0639.024]
- Reused TikTok-style video pins on Pinterest held a CTR of roughly 3 to 4 percent for about a month, which is well above the 1 percent day-three minimum used as a go or no-go gate. [L1135.061]
- Simple video formats: a new Spark Ad test on a new account. [L1381.028]
  1. Choose the best organic video. [L1381.028]
  2. Use no interest targeting, only an age range such as 18 to 45 depending on the product. [L1381.028]
  3. Let about 20 dollars of spend run completely. [L1381.028]
  4. Do not reopen Ads Manager for the account afterward, since the account was seen to get an organic boost once the spend finished. [L1381.028]
- Creative testing: find the strongest format. Testing many creatives early (for example an image test and a video test in one ad set) lets the platform tell you which format responds. [L1379.032]

### Pre-launch checks

- Before launching, have a finished landing page, 4 to 5 creatives, and ready ad copy. [L0648.003]
- Check the spacing and line breaks of ad copy before publishing. [L0348.007]
- Check that the website URL points to the correct product page for that product. [L0348.007]

### Thresholds and stop rules

- A clear winner is a video creative with at least 3 sales and a positive ROAS above break-even. One sale can be luck, so wait for more data before calling a creative a winner. [L0398.030]
- To pick a winning creative, read hard metrics such as purchases once the ad has spent around its target cost per acquisition. If it has not yet spent that much, use softer signals such as attention and CTR to decide which ad deserves more budget. [L0646.059]
- A reused creative with 3 to 4 percent CTR above a 1 percent day-three minimum passed the go or no-go gate. [L1135.061]
- Turn off ads that spend 20 to 30 USD without sales and keep the ones that produce sales. [L0774.035]
- Stop a product if metrics do not show promise after break-even spend. [L0640.028]
- A hook and creative combination counts as a clear winner only when it performs best in every ad set of the test, not just one. A result that wins in one audience but loses in the others should be retested before it is scaled. [L1335.052]
- Start creative testing when CTR or CPC is poor. [L0902.003]

### Declaring winners

- Choose the winner by ROAS first; if ROAS is equal, use CTR; if CTR is equal, use average play time. [L1335.023]
- A winner must perform best in every ad set of the test. [L1335.052]
- Decide on the winner with the hard metric once the spend passes the target cost per acquisition; before that, use CTR and attention. [L0646.059]
- Once one angle clearly wins, add a landing page section for it and move the other sections down. [L1218.033]
- Keep the three best performers after the test. [L1219.028]
- Compare the highest CTR creative in each ad set. [L1212.012]
- Scale the winning layout and video version only after the static test shows a clear winner. [L0343.040]
- Decide which creative stays by the data and the sales it brings, not by how polished it looks. [L0562.013]
- Let the platform decide which performs best, then turn off the weak ones. [L0562.012]
- Decide quickly on what performs early; waiting a month at 50 per day is not practical for most sellers. [L0950.039]
- Keep creative testing going: the winning creative is reused in audience testing campaigns, CBO scaling campaigns, and new audience tests. [L1335.023]

### Batch naming and benchmarks

- Testing creatives in batches works by naming ads by batch number, not by individual creative number. The best-performing creative becomes the benchmark, and each new variation is tested against it. Any variation that beats the benchmark moves into a scaling campaign. [L0819.006]
  - Example pattern: Batch 12, Creative B vs Batch 11 benchmark: move to scaling if it beats the benchmark's cost per purchase. [L0819.006]
  - Second example: Batch 7, skit hook vs Batch 6 benchmark: scale only if it beats benchmark ROAS for three days. [L0819.006]

### Testing cadence and weekly planning

- Testing creatives is a weekly job: plan 6 to 9 videos per week from 2 to 3 concepts, and test a minimum of three concepts per week. [L0298.048]
- Creative testing frequency: 2 to 3 times per week at small scale, 10 to 15 times per week at higher scale. [L1335.026]
- Angle tests are cycled: after a winning angle is found, keep testing new concepts continually while iterating on existing ads. [L1315.045]
- A creative test that starts with a lot of spend will show a high CPM at first. [L0298.029]
- For new creative tests, expect initially high CPM regardless of creative quality, because new ads lack social proof. CPM reduces as real user engagement accumulates. [L0298.029]
- Creative testing begins on a small budget of about 5 per day per ad set to see whether an audience responds. [L1077.015]

### Common mistakes

- Changing many things at once makes results unreadable. Keep a control ad and change one element. [L0640.025]
- A single creative inside a shared ad set can absorb most of the budget. Test each new creative in its own ad set first. [L0646.062, L1177.059]
- Forgetting to test a new creative separately lets the winning creative hide new results. [L1177.031]
- Judging an ad before it has spent enough. Wait for the target spend before reading hard metrics. [L0646.059, L0640.027]
- Launching a single polished ad late. Launch many creatives quickly and iterate. [L1077.016]
- Changing the offer and the creative in the same test. Keep the offer fixed while testing creatives. [L0502.025, L1382.074]
- Starting hook testing before ripped creatives have proven profitable. [L1252.016, L1252.017]
- Blindly trusting platform budget allocation. Force spend onto a creative before calling it weak. [L0640.027]
- Declaring a product dead after a weak creative. Test new creatives first. [L1038.016]

#### Further details

- Test ads for a product in the US first, but if CTR stays low with the same product, test it in another market such as Canada or Australia. Australia is named as a good test market. [L0513.032]

- Keep testing ad creative and the wording of customer messages, because small changes in phrasing can have large effects on sales. Spending money on testing was a core part of this seller's approach. [L1437.019]

## Reading results, iterating and scaling creatives

### Read the data and the creative together

1. Review the ad performance data. [L0008.004]
2. Examine the creative assets: visuals, headline, body copy and hooks. [L0008.004]
3. List hypotheses about why performance is what it is, based on both the data and the creatives. [L0008.004]

Full troubleshooting order when an ad underperforms:

1. Review ad performance metrics to find the weak point in the funnel: attention, interest, desire or action. [L0067.018]
2. Open the ads in creative view. [L0067.018]
3. Watch the ad journey and identify where it could improve. [L0067.018]
4. Go through the creative review checklist below. [L0067.018]
5. List all hypotheses about why the ad is underperforming. [L0067.018]
6. Prioritize the most important hypothesis. [L0067.018]
7. Create variations: some as iterations of the working ad, some as brand-new concepts. [L0067.018]
8. Run the new ads and test them. [L0067.018]

Creative review checklist:

| Check | Source |
|---|---|
| Attention-grabbing hook that is relevant to the target audience | [L0067.019] |
| Clear problem statement or main benefit highlighted | [L0067.019] |
| Compelling offer presented | [L0067.019] |
| Clear call to action: tell people what to do and where to go | [L0067.019] |
| Benefits-focused copy, not just features | [L0067.019] |
| Social proof: testimonials, reviews, case studies, customer results | [L0067.019] |
| Scarcity or urgency: limited stock, end date | [L0067.019] |
| High-quality visuals that illustrate the point | [L0067.019] |
| Educational or entertaining content | [L0067.019] |
| Builds curiosity without being unclear | [L0067.019] |
| Problem-Agitate-Solution framework: outline the problem, make it worse, present the solution | [L0067.019] |

Creative review procedure:

1. Look at the ad data to find where the funnel falls. [L0640.021]
2. Open the creative and identify which ads worked and which did not. [L0640.021]
3. Check the middle section of the ad for where it loses viewers. [L0640.021]
4. List all hypotheses for why it falls down. [L0640.021]
5. Pick the most important hypothesis and test it. [L0640.021]

Creative review after every ad set test:

1. Use the data and visual analysis to work out why each ad performed as it did. [L0652.014]
2. Write down why the winning ads worked and why the losing ads did not. [L0652.014]
3. Create three new ads that build on the analysis, iterating on the tested ads with new ideas expected to improve them. [L0652.014]
4. Test a whole new creative concept alongside the iterations. [L0652.014]

After scoring the ads, list which hook styles, message angles, formats and talent types appear among the winners and which among the losers. Turn these patterns into the direction for the next creative round. [L0613.070]

### Diagnose weak funnel stages from metrics

**Soft metrics point to the stage**

- Use attention rate and CTR to diagnose a creative. Low attention points to the hook. Low CTR points to the middle content. No sales point to the offer. Optimize the weakest stage rather than changing everything at once. [L0639.031]
- Poor hook rate with good interest and desire means the opening needs better hooks. Good hook rate with poor CTR means the middle messaging is not generating interest, and the hook may be attracting the wrong audience. Strong hook and CTR with weak sales point to the offer or page rather than the creative. [L0652.013]
- Read hook rate and hold rate together. A strong hook with a weak hold means the opening works but the rest of the video loses viewers. A strong hold with a weak hook means the rest of the video works and only the opening needs a rewrite. Reuse the strong part in new creatives. [L1024.033]
- Judge creatives by consistency across several days, not one sale. A low hook rate or low CTR points to the creative's opening. A low conversion rate points to the page. [L1315.046]
- Judge a product's soft metrics on the same budget over several days, not on one day. A single day of poor results is not a reason to cut a product that is still in its learning phase. [L1030.025]
- Engagement rate ranking, quality ranking and conversion rate ranking rate an ad against other advertisers aiming at the same audience. Use them as optional diagnostics for engagement, content quality and conversion quality. [L1024.044]
- Ad ranking order: ROAS first, then CTR, then average play time. Some ads have lower CTR but strong conversion, so ROAS takes priority when it is clearly positive. [L0398.031]
- If two or more creatives have similar ROAS, use CTR to choose between them. If CTR is also similar, use average play time. Give a creative with a large CTR gap more time to collect data before deciding. [L0398.032]
- Judge a creative on hook rate, click-through rate and conversion rate after launch. [L0950.078]

**Video retention, in detail**

- Build extra custom metrics for 25%, 50% and 75% video views, each divided by impressions. With high traffic these show exactly where viewers drop off, so you know which part to fix. [L0644.004]
- Video length matters for hook analysis. A 15-second video that averages 8 seconds of watch time means many viewers drop out in the middle. Check this alongside the hook rate. [L0950.041]
- Hook-first diagnostic:
  1. Test many hooks for the first seconds of the video. [L1426.017]
  2. Check the video attention rate. If it is low, keep testing hooks. [L1426.017]
  3. Check the click-through rate. If it is low, improve the middle of the ad: story, offer timing, engagement. [L1426.017]
  4. Check add-to-carts and purchases to confirm the funnel works. [L1426.017]
  5. Keep the hook messaging consistent with the landing page copy. [L1426.017]
- Test better 3-second hooks to raise CTR and lower CPC. Weak CPC, CPM and CTR usually point to the creative, so the first seconds must capture attention and the ad must look high quality. [L0874.012]

**The four numbers, read together**

1. Check the video attention rate to judge how well the opening hook holds viewers. [L0644.005]
2. Check the click-through rate to judge whether the middle and offer make people click. [L0644.005]
3. Check content views and add-to-carts as extra signals, since Facebook may not record every event. [L0644.005]
4. Check purchases as the final result. Read the four numbers together, not one alone. [L0644.005]

| Symptom | Likely cause | Action | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Low video attention | Weak opening seconds | Test several new hooks in front of the same video body | [L0644.006] |
| Good attention, low CTR | Weak middle, offer shown too late, or irrelevant viewers | Strengthen the middle, show the offer sooner, make the message more specific | [L0644.006] |
| Content views but few add-to-carts | Landing page does not match the ad | Fix relevance and copy on the landing page | [L0644.006] |
| Add-to-carts but no purchases | Checkout problem | Test the checkout, then rerun the original ad to compare | [L0644.006] |

**Functional problems come before creative**

- Troubleshooting order by funnel stage:
  1. Check the funnel stage with the biggest drop: attention, interest, desire or action. [L0640.018]
  2. For weak desire or action with good attention and interest, check functional problems first: broken checkout, wrong currencies, shipping charged by mistake, missing add-to-cart button, wrong pricing display. [L0640.018]
  3. Then check price shock, poor product page, lack of trust, an unclear ad that misleads, and whether the offer is good enough. [L0640.018]
  4. For poor attention with good interest and desire, test better hooks aimed at the right audience. [L0640.018]
  5. For good attention with poor interest, test better messaging and the middle section of the ad. [L0640.018]
- Clicks and add-to-carts but no sales: check the checkout first. Then rerun the original ad to find out whether the ad or the checkout caused the problem. Either sales return because the checkout is fixed, or the test shows the ad was less targeted than the current one. [L0644.011]
- Zero add-to-carts after a large spend may mean customers do not care about the product, which is the real reason. Creative changes alone rarely fix a product that generates no add-to-carts. [L0361.029]
- Make sure the creative, meaning the video and product pictures, is strong before adjusting the offer. While CTR is good, focus on making the offer convert. [L0549.030]
- A strong creative and a strong offer allow more spend per customer acquisition, because more qualified people enter the funnel and average order value rises through upsells and cross-sells. Scaling then depends on the quality of the funnel rather than on tricks. [L0646.033]
- A high view count from an organic video does not guarantee sales. A viral toy-type product with 1.8 million views produced only 2 orders in the observed period, so check organic reach against real order numbers. [L0655.002]
- Comments such as "I'll buy because you're honest" are not reliable purchase signals. Place a real test order and check the confirmation or order number to verify whether the audience converts. [L0655.003]
- Use CTR as a sign of interest in the product. If no one clicks, the product is not appealing enough. Keep the ad running only if CTR holds up over the test budget. [L0661.039]
- Judge advertising only by whether it makes people act: ordering, requesting information or paying. An ad that people merely admire and forget has failed its purpose. [L0340.001]
- The purpose of a Facebook ad is to drive traffic to the store. The store must then convert visitors into customers, so the website offer deserves improvement if ads are performing. [L1212.045]
- Measure readership by how many people actually travel through the full copy, not by circulation or impressions. Only readers who go through the copy can buy, so an ad with a large audience that reads little is weak. [L1366.007]
- Plan for delayed responses. Some readers clip an ad and act months later when the need appears, so a good ad can produce sales long after it stops running. [L1366.096]
- Formula: readers x response rate = responses. Example: if 50 percent of 100 tear-sheet recipients read it and 10 percent of readers respond, you get 5 responses per 100 pieces. A standard letter that starts at 10 percent reading would need 50 percent of its readers to respond to match that. [L1370.037]

### Benchmarks and thresholds

Several sources give different values for the same metric. Each value is listed with the condition it applies to.

| Metric | Value | When it applies | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| CTR | Below 0.7% | Replace the creative, because the video is not stopping viewers | [L1377.016] |
| CTR | Below 1% | Creative is failing; fix the hook or creative and iterate once | [L0398.040] |
| CTR | About 1% or higher | Creative works and the funnel can keep running | [L1377.016] |
| CTR | 1 to 1.5% | Workable only with a cheap CPM and CPC; otherwise it means paying more per visitor and fewer conversions. Below this range the creative has clear room for improvement | [L1177.023] |
| CTR | 1.5% (minimum acceptable, Facebook) | General floor | [L1177.021] |
| CTR | 2% or more | Excellent | [L1177.021] |
| CTR | Above 2% | Keep iterating if the landing page can be improved | [L0640.029] |
| CTR | About 3% | Judged strong on a winning creative | [L1177.024] |
| CPC | Below $1.5 | Good | [L0398.040] |
| CPC | Below $1.4 to $1.5 (US) | Acceptable. The source notes costs are rising, so $1.5 is the current industry benchmark | [L1177.022] |
| CPC | Above $1, combined with CPM above $10 and CTR below 1.5% | Ads are not attracting interest; test new, more engaging creatives rather than touching the store | [L1375.009] |
| CPM | Above about $30 (sometimes about $35) | Suggests a competitive audience or weak creative that forces people to see the ad | [L0398.040] |
| CPM | Above $10, combined with CPC above $1 and CTR below 1.5% | Creative problem, see above | [L1375.009] |

- Rough diagnostic: a creative with a CTR of 1 percent and a cost per link click of $1.52 was judged weak. A CTR of about 3 percent on a winning creative was judged strong. [L1177.024]
- Low CTR with cheap CPM and CPC can stay profitable. A CTR of 1 to 1.5 percent must be paired with cheap CPM and CPC to remain profitable. [L1177.023]
- If CTR is above 1% but CPC or CPM is high, simplify the campaign structure. Reduce the number of ad groups per campaign, for example from 4-5 down to fewer, because more complexity tends to increase CPM. [L0363.045]
- If CTR is poor on day 1, the ads will not improve on day 2 or 3. Test new creatives. A bad first-day CTR is a signal to change the creative, not to wait. [L0363.044]
- Use the click-through rate of an ad as a sign of interest. Keep the ad running only if CTR holds up over the test budget. [L0661.039]
- Diagnose a campaign that is not converting, in this order:
  1. Check CTR first. If CTR is below 1%, the creative is failing; fix the hook or creative and iterate once. [L0398.040]
  2. Check CPC next. A CPC below $1.5 is good. [L0398.040]
  3. Check CPM. A CPM above about $30 (sometimes about $35) suggests a competitive audience or weak creative that forces people to see the ad. [L0398.040]
  4. If CTR is good but CPM is high, rework the creative anyway, because Meta penalizes weak ads with higher costs. [L0398.040]
  5. If the creative still fails after one iteration, switch to the next product instead of pushing more budget into it. [L0398.040]
- Peak-CPM fix for high CPM: improve creative quality and engagement ranking. Add social proof by manually posting customer reviews and comments on ads, such as 5-star reviews and user photos. Test different interest targeting to find less-competitive audiences. Let engagement such as likes and comments accumulate naturally. CPM typically drops from 35-40 to 20-23 within 3-4 days as engagement builds. [L0298.028]
- Creatives are the main deciding factor once a product is performing. The coach's estimate is around 90-95% of results. Test more creatives when the low-performing metric is CTR or cost-per-click is high, since better creatives lift conversion across the funnel. [L0363.046]
- For the first 1-2 weeks, normal creatives are enough to see whether a product sells. Better creatives are needed once you want to scale the product further. [L0363.047]

### Kill, keep and wait decisions

- Kill criteria: stop an ad or product if you have spent at least the break-even cost per purchase and the metrics (sales, add-to-cart, attention, CTR) show no promise. Keep iterating if attention is above 40% or CTR is above 2% and the landing page can be improved. [L0640.029]
- Once a product fails after one creative iteration, switch to the next product rather than adding budget. [L0398.040]
- Do not switch off an ad that makes revenue only because its CTR is low, if it at least breaks even. Improve the middle section of the ad to raise CTR while keeping sales coming in. [L0644.010]
- Keep a winning ad running as long as it delivers a good return on ad spend. Test new creatives in parallel with a new angle to prevent ad fatigue. [L0519.029]
- Turning off campaigns too soon, before enough frequency, is a common mistake. Mere exposure effect requires about 21 impressions before a brand is remembered. Do not turn off ads before they have built the repeated exposure needed to make an impression. [L0196.059]
- Stay on message repeatedly and consistently. Use retargeting with increased frequency on individual ads, and do not turn them off too soon. Be the familiar barista your audience knows and prefers. [L0196.034]
- Facebook ads with near-zero sales (older, 2022): check reach in Facebook Business Manager reporting. If the audience is small, the sample is too small to judge. If the audience is large and sees ads but does not buy, test different ad copy. [L0665.074]
- Pinterest and other secondary platforms (older, 2022): judge by return on ad spend, not just cost per click. If traffic is high and sales are low, the page or offer needs work. If traffic is low and sales are still low, the account has a bigger structural problem. [L0665.073]

### Iteration loops

- Test new creatives in an iterative loop: take an ad that performed well earlier, make variations, relaunch, and keep the ones that hold their results. [L0950.038]
- A winning ad keeps getting sales because it sends the right message to the right audience. Keep testing new creatives and iterate on the ones that previously worked, rather than assuming the cause of a performance drop is known. [L0950.037]
- Build a new test set after a creative review:
  1. Create three new ads based on the analysis. [L0640.050]
  2. Make some of them iterations of the best-performing ad. [L0640.050]
  3. Make the rest brand-new concepts. [L0640.050]
- Creative testing is central to scaling. A good message and creative attract the right audience, and small spend on each ad helps identify winners quickly. Small, controlled tweaks to a creative can improve results and should not be skipped because they feel dull. [L0646.052]
- Set up new creatives in the existing testing campaign. When relaunching a product with new ad copy, copy your best-performing ads into the existing testing campaign and run the new copy variations on them. Do not start a fresh campaign for each copy change. [L1215.028]
- Loop for turning a winning message into new concepts:
  1. In Ads Manager, find the creative with the highest website purchases in your CBO. [L1195.036]
  2. In Google AI Studio (Gemini), upload the winning video and transcribe its messaging, plus the primary text and headline from the ad. [L1195.036]
  3. In Claude, hand over the transcript and rebuild the messaging: the angle, the promise, and the objection it handles. [L1195.036]
  4. Turn the winning message into new concepts in different formats, such as podcast, conference, seminar, claymation, cartoon, or UGC AI ads. [L1195.036]
  5. Launch each concept for 3 days in CBO 2 or CBO 3, then read website purchases and ROAS to see whether it resonates. [L1195.036]
  6. Fold the winners back into the main CBO and repeat the loop. [L1195.036]
- Process for a new product on a proven layout:
  1. Keep a file of ad creatives that have produced sales. [L0950.078]
  2. For a new product, replace only the product imagery in a proven ad layout instead of building new creatives from scratch. [L0950.078]
  3. Write or check the core benefits and the offer in the copy yourself before launch, rather than handing this to a freelancer. [L0950.078]
  4. Launch the ad and judge it by hook rate, click-through rate and conversion rate. [L0950.078]
- Case (informational test): a test used a knee anatomy image. The first output was a 3D render. A follow-up asked for two cross-sectional drawings instead, one profile view facing left and one front-facing view. The second version was closer to the target because it looked like a textbook illustration. [L0882.026]
- Pattern to watch: a creative is a likely winner only when it has the best CTR consistently across all winning audiences, not just in one. Replace the older creative with it once that pattern is confirmed. [L0648.058]
- Before scaling an audience, build a winning combination of the audience and two of the best creatives, selected for strong CTR and CPM. [L0646.017]

### Creative fatigue and rotation

- Ads on a single audience can lose performance over time, so new creatives keep the reach alive. Test alongside the winner rather than as a replacement for it. [L0519.030]
- Advertising styles wear out. Verse, narrative confessions and comic-strip stories each lost believability as they became familiar. Keep the strategy and rotate the style when it grows stale. [L0330.065]
- Ad creatives need regular refreshing because customers get used to the same ads. Produce new photos and videos as the previous ones lose effect. [L1439.022]
- TikTok account-level fatigue: the same material can stop an entire account from performing after roughly three to four weeks. Pausing the account for about a week and then restarting was reported to restore reach. Rotate new content in before results decline. [L0819.007]
- TikTok single-creative lifespan: a creative rarely holds more than about a week. Copied creatives often perform poorly after a few days, sometimes within one day in the US. [L1177.025]
- The two TikTok values in [L0819.007] and [L1177.025] describe different scopes: one creative versus the whole account. Both apply.
- Pinterest creatives saturate much more slowly than TikTok creatives. A video can run for six to seven months and older videos still work, so TikTok winners can be reused directly there. [L1135.042]
- Video age in paid tests: a video that is 2 to 3 months old has usually been seen by many people in the target market. This tends to lower CTR and raise CPM. Prefer creatives posted within about the last two weeks, and treat older videos as a weaker option for paid tests. [L1377.067]
- Viral video reuse: a creative running for more than about 15 to 30 days after going viral may already be known to TikTok's algorithm, so reuse gives less reach. A video with views in the 20,000 to 30,000 range three days after posting may still have room to scale. [L1382.023]
- Run length as a performance sign: ads that ran for 68 and 79 days were winners, so keep them and reuse their hooks and structure. [L0871.064]

### Scaling winners

- Scale by combining winners. Find the winning hook, video, concept, thumbnail and ad copy through the separate tests, then combine the best assets in the scaling campaigns. [L0902.026]
- Only shift the best-performing ads into one ad set and let Facebook optimise once the separate tests have shown which ads and countries work. [L1426.030]
- Prepare multiple creatives in advance when scaling, so you can quickly test whether a new video or picture beats the current winner. [L1212.015]
- Scaling through new creatives on TikTok: create new creatives every week, even if older ones stop working. Duplicate a working ad set and put in four new creatives each week to double its effective budget without raising the budget. [L1374.021]
- Once a product shows steady sales for one to two weeks, switch to UGC or TikTok-style creative as soon as possible, since this can multiply results. Start UGC production in parallel with the first winning ads. [L0398.056]
- Use a winning ad's CTR, CPM and ROAS, not impressions, as the basis for scaling decisions. [L0646.017, L0648.058]
- Judge a creative in the scaling phase by its ROAS first, then CTR. [L0398.031]

### Repurposing winning creatives

**Same-platform and cross-platform reuse**

- Repurposing on the same platform can test a different angle on a previous video, such as a new hook, a new voice or a new call to action. [L0795.007]
- Ways to build more videos from a winning video:
  1. Make variants that change the hook. [L0795.023]
  2. Shorten the duration without cutting key points, for example from 15 seconds to 11 seconds. [L0795.023]
  3. Recreate the same video with a different product variant, such as a red version after a blue one went viral. [L0795.023]
- Turning a proven organic video into a paid ad: take the top organic videos that performed well, keep the core content, and make small adjustments to fit the ad platform. Add a call to action and scarcity. [L0820.011]
- Hook-led rebuild of a winning ad:
  1. Record a set of scenes covering the hook, the use case, the relief and the result, about 12 scenes in total. [L0871.066]
  2. Find the hook that is running longest and keep the best-performing clip for it. [L0871.066]
  3. Build new ads by pairing the winning hook with different body clips. [L0871.066]
  4. Keep the voice and action the same and change only the camera angle or opening clip for each new version. [L0871.066]
  5. Track how long each ad runs and keep the ones that run past 60 days. [L0871.066]
- Reuse user-generated video by recutting the footage, changing the narrative, cropping out unwanted text, and adding simple transitions. Basic editing skills are enough. [L1426.022]
- Use one creative for different audiences by changing only the caption, for example one caption for a girlfriend, another for a boyfriend, and another for family members. [L1469.027]
- Recycle good product visuals by reposting them every couple of months on social media. This keeps accounts active without needing new material each time (source undated). [L0921.033]
- Save finished ad assets such as images and videos so you can reuse them across campaigns and change only the text (older, 2021-22). Recognizable creative helps shoppers identify the event quickly. [L0799.010]

### Seasonal planning

- Check seasonal buying patterns before planning creatives. Determine whether customers buy your product only in certain seasons or all year round. The answer determines when ads and creative themes should run. [L1267.007]
- A seasonal angle lets a seasonal product sell where the weather is not yet right. A pre-summer sale, for example, lets summer dresses sell in countries where the weather is not yet warm. [L1171.042]
- For a holiday, start organic testing early. For example, begin on January 1 for Valentine's Day. Test many different hooks before the peak period begins. [L1469.028]
- Holiday remarketing (older, 2019): use a gift-related image, such as gift boxes, with the current offer printed on the image. The link should go to the holiday collection page. [L0467.063]
- Stop running Christmas ads from mid-December, because products ordered then will not arrive before Christmas and customers will be disappointed. [L0780.009]
- Reuse Black Friday ads that still perform by changing the headline and ad copy and launching them as a new Christmas ad. Test new ads only if they stop performing. [L1225.049]

### Peak CPM seasons and Black Friday / Cyber Monday

**Managing peak cost**

- During BFCM, when CPM is high, do not create many new creatives. Scale existing winning creatives by adding offer banners and testing those variations. [L0298.045]
- Reducing ad cost during peak CPM seasons:
  1. Test better creatives, with new ones in parallel at small budgets. [L0298.046]
  2. Add offer banners to existing winning creatives, for example "Early BFCM Sale" or "Halloween Sale Ongoing". [L0298.046]
  3. Banners can be static images, animations, or continuous slideshows. [L0298.046]
  4. Focus scaling spend on banner-enhanced versions of proven creatives, not on building entirely new creative. [L0298.046]
- For Black Friday, test one or two dedicated creatives that clearly show the offer, for example with a banner, rather than producing complex productions. Keep the message simple: the offer itself is usually enough. [L0692.037]
- Use dedicated Black Friday creatives in these formats:
  - Square image ad: black background with a sales banner, three product images below, headline "Black Friday sale is now on", and text "Get up to 50% off, get yours now". Stories ad: the 9×16 portrait version of the same. [L0308.010]
  - Overlay method on proven video creatives:
    1. Take existing winning video creatives. [L0308.013]
    2. Import them into Canva. [L0308.013]
    3. Resize to 4:5 ratio (1350×1920px). [L0308.013]
    4. Add a black banner at the top: "Black Friday event now on". [L0308.013]
    5. Add a black banner at the bottom: "Get up to 50% off". [L0308.013]
    6. Export and run as a video ad. This overlay method works extremely well on proven winning creatives. [L0308.013]
  - Note: 1350×1920 px is a ratio of about 0.70, not 4:5 (which is 0.80, for example 1080×1350). Check the export size before upload. [L0308.013]
- Black Friday approach used in the course example: take the best-performing existing creatives, add a Black Friday sale banner or overlay with "up to 60% off" and the end date, and export in both 9:16 (Stories, Reels) and 1:1 square (Facebook feed). Videos were cut to 4:5 for the Facebook feed with a top and bottom banner. [L1363.046]
- Save finished BFCM assets so they can be reused across campaigns. Only the text changes, and recognizable creative helps shoppers identify the event quickly. [L0799.010]

## Store, email and organic content copy

### Product page copy: persuasion order

- Work through product copy in this order:
  1. List the problems and pains the product solves, and the problems current and potential customers feel now, which may have brought them to the page. [L1157.007]
  2. For each problem, identify the opposite desire: the pleasurable outcome the buyer wants. [L1157.007]
  3. Describe the end result the product delivers in the buyer's life, for example at home, in the car, or wherever they use it. The product itself is not the ultimate pleasure; the result it creates is. [L1157.007]
  4. Write the copy so it shows that you understand the buyer's pain and that the product delivers the pleasure they seek. [L1157.007]
- Marketing means educating the market that a business can solve problems, fill gaps or achieve goals better than any other business. Product copy has the same purpose: show the buyer that this product solves their problem in a way no other product does. (older, 2021-22) [L1157.005]
- The ultimate pleasure for a buyer is not owning the product but what the product does for them. Describe this outcome rather than the ownership itself. (older, 2021-22) [L1157.008]
- Use this order for product copy (older, 2021-22):
  1. Name the customer's pain or problem back to them so they start to feel the negative emotion it causes. [L0611.004]
  2. Paint a picture of the pleasure and positive end result the product brings, so they feel the emotion they would have when the product is working for them. [L0611.004]
  3. Tell a story that makes the reader imagine the situation and feel something, to create emotion and a sense of connection. [L0611.004]
  4. Show proof, either through demonstration or through testimonials from customers who describe what they loved about the product. [L0611.004]
  5. Only then give logical support: features and specifications such as size, weight, speed and colour options, plus manuals or other documents and social proof such as reviews. [L0611.004]
- Use pain before pleasure and pleasure before features. Talking about pain alone produces negative emotions, so follow it with the positive outcome the product delivers. (older, 2021-22) [L0611.005]
- Emotion-before-logic pattern (older, 2021-22): open with a pain point, move to the desired outcome, support it with a short story or proof, then close with specs and reviews that justify the choice. [L0611.006]
  - Kitchen knife, pain and pleasure: "Tired of slicing dinner into uneven chunks every night? Imagine prepping in half the time with a blade that glides through tomatoes like butter." Then add: "A 20 cm forged steel blade, 180 g, with a 5-star rating from 2,300 buyers." [L0611.006]
  - Dog harness, pain and pleasure: "Walks that end with a yanked neck and a frustrated owner? Picture every walk calm and enjoyable, like the one Maria shared after a week with her rescue dog." Then add: "Padded chest strap, reflective stitching, sizes XS to XL in four colours." [L0611.006]
- A story in product copy does not have to be fiction. A real-sounding scenario the buyer can picture creates emotion and a sense of connection with the brand, and makes the benefit feel real rather than abstract. (older, 2021-22) [L0611.007]
- Product copy should open with emotional hooks (unique mechanism, power bullets, benefits) before proof points. Proof confirms an emotional decision with logic; it does not start the persuasion. (older, 2021-22) [L0295.002]
- Product copy should lead with how the product makes the customer feel and how it fits into their life, not with generic claims such as high quality or shipping in two days. [L0774.022]
  - Pattern: name the situation the buyer cares about (a family gathering, a gift moment), show the outcome they want, then give one concrete benefit. [L0774.022]
  - Example one: 'Make your next family dinner easier and bring everyone together with this product.' [L0774.022]
  - Example two: 'Give your partner a gift that feels personal and arrives ready to use this week.' [L0774.022]
- Common elements developed for product page copy (benefits, unique mechanisms, problem statements) can be reused directly in emails and ads without rewriting from scratch. (older, 2021-22) [L0241.003]
- Before writing ad copy from scratch, audit the website's existing copy for benefit-driven lines, bold headlines and strong claims. Adapt these proven elements for Facebook and TikTok ads so the language already resonates with the audience. [L0204.019]

### Product page copy: headlines and claims

- Primary promise formula (the opening headline of a product description): [verb promising an outcome] + [everyday benefit] + [in the setting where the customer lives] + [superlative claim for the category]. It names the desire directly; the superlative hooks the reader but creates a claim the rest of the copy must prove. (older, 2021-22) [L0396.017]
  - Example 1: 'Keep your coffee hot all morning with the most leak-proof travel mug available at this price.' [L0396.017]
  - Example 2: 'Sleep cool every summer night with the most breathable cotton bedding in its price range.' [L0396.017]
- Desire headline: name the outcome the buyer wants, using the words from your customer research, and tie it to the product's use. [L0567.022]
  - Example: 'Gear that keeps your longest weekend ride comfortable' [L0567.022]
  - Example: 'Stylish kit that holds up on every climb' [L0567.022]
- Scarcity lines: name what the shopper loses if they leave, such as stock running low or a price ending. Use one only if it is true. [L0567.024]
  - Example: 'Only a few units left in your size' [L0567.024]
  - Example: 'This colourway is sold out soon, so hold it now' [L0567.024]
- Shipping claims: do not include 'Free Shipping' in product page copy if Google Merchant Center flags it as redundant. Put the shipping offer in the meta description instead, or rely on Shopify free shipping settings. (2023) [L0274.054]

### Product page structure

- Source E pattern, product description in three blocks (2025-26):
  - 'What it is' paragraph: material, use case, colours, size range. [L1331.018]
  - 'How it works' list: three features, each tied to a function. [L1331.018]
  - 'What you will feel' list: short sensory benefits. [L1331.018]
  - Why it works: it sells the product at the top, keeps the buy button high, and keeps the details easy to scan. [L1331.018]
  - Example pattern: 'Water-resistant upper' followed by 'helps keep damp floors out'; 'Foam insole' followed by 'steps feel softer by the door'. [L1331.018]
- Structure that worked in one Source B example (older, 2021-22):
  1. Unique mechanism.
  2. A bridging paragraph that introduces the extra benefits.
  3. A bulleted list of extra features, with each benefit shown as a short paragraph.
  4. The call-to-action paragraph.
  - The primary promise may be replaced by a convenience-based promise when a product is health-related and a health promise is restricted. [L0461.010]
- Use a clear visual difference between the bridging paragraph and the feature list, such as an optional features heading, if it helps readability. Headings are optional. (older, 2021-22) [L0461.016]
- Product page conversion depends on a clear, irresistible offer and on a product with real demand. A great product page cannot save a product with no demand or heavy competition. [L0690.033]
- Study high-performing brand product pages (for example Blendjet and hoodie brands) to see how they structure copy, and compare them with weak product pages. Frameworks such as AIDA are a starting point. [L0690.034]

### Product page proof and reviews

- Include 3 to 5 customer reviews directly within the product page copy, at the proof section. Extract them from review widgets and place them into the sales copy. (older, 2021-22) [L0295.003]
- Reviews can be embedded as text, images or video. Select reviews from existing review widgets and integrate them into the copy. (older, 2021-22) [L0295.004]
- A video walkthrough showing the product in actual use demonstrates the claimed functionality and works as proof where features can be shown visually. It is not viable for every product type. (older, 2021-22) [L0295.005]
- Reference media coverage when a product has been featured in recognised outlets: news, magazines, newspapers, current affairs shows, reality-based TV shows, blogs or online publications such as Buzzfeed. Include optional links to the original coverage, because audiences perceive media-featured products as high quality. (older, 2021-22) [L0295.009]
- Pair proof for claims with the product page. Testimonials, clinical studies and statistics used in abandoned cart emails should stay accessible from the product page or a pop-up, not be linked externally, because external links break the purchase flow. [L0261.022]
- Authorised retailer badges, procedure (2024):
  1. Add brand logos or text to the home page as a 'Brands We Carry' section. [L0253.044]
  2. Add 'Authorized Retailer for [Brand Name]' text to product descriptions. [L0253.044]
  3. Create a 6th product image in Canva showing an 'Authorized Dealer' badge. [L0253.044]
  4. Place this image at the end of the product image gallery, after images 1-5. [L0253.044]
  5. This works across the home page, collection pages and product pages. [L0253.044]

### Product descriptions at catalogue scale

- Run the product description prompt product by product for the whole catalogue. A short, fixed format keeps the work fast and avoids outsourcing product copy. (2025) [L1116.056]
- If a supplier has no product description, write one before the product goes live. Writing many descriptions by hand takes a long time; for example, 500 products require a large amount of focus, so outsourcing is an option. (older, 2021-22) [L1163.021]
- Prioritise unique product descriptions by traffic (2021):
  1. Pull a monthly report in Google Analytics. [L0671.268]
  2. Open the Content section. [L0671.268]
  3. Sort pages by traffic. [L0671.268]
  4. Add unique copy to the highest-traffic pages first, then work down the list. [L0671.268]
- Beat Amazon with unique, benefit-led product descriptions rather than generic supplier text. Amazon's own descriptions are short, so a longer, story-driven description with a call to action is a clear advantage. [L1293.021]
- For product page images and copy, reuse supplier assets when they are allowed. Logos, product images and descriptions from the supplier can be used directly if no restrictions apply. Customise only for SEO where needed. (older, 2022) [L0272.040]
- Add GIFs cut from the product video to the product page and ad creatives as a low-effort test of a richer description. Test them against the current description. [L1173.014]
- Source E pattern for organic product posts is covered under social content; for product page copy use the structure above. [L1331.018]

#### Product description prompts

Direct-response copywriter prompt, use with the product name or URL filled in (2024):

```
Adopt the persona of a direct-response copywriter and draft a product description for [product name and/or URL] following this arrangement: a headline, a short description of one to three sentences, a features-and-benefits block, and bulleted points. Base everything solely on the supplied product information and avoid fabricating specs, measurements, materials, or assertions. Before release, reword the draft into a natural, human-sounding voice while keeping the same arrangement.
```

[L0471.064]

Benefit-driven description prompt, with placeholders filled in (Source C):

```
Write a benefit-driven product description for [PRODUCT] aimed at [TARGET CUSTOMER]. Focus on the feelings and benefits the customer, and their [PET or other user] if relevant, will experience after receiving the product. Then turn the same content into bullet points for the first section of the product page, and write a short four-line paragraph for each of these features: [FEATURE 1], [FEATURE 2]. Keep the same topic throughout and set the tone to [TONE, e.g. emotional or funny].
```

[L0605.012]

### Product videos and media

- Add videos to product pages only if the supplier provides high-quality video assets that genuinely demonstrate the product. Do not source or create videos for every product. If the supplier sends videos, embed them from YouTube rather than uploading them directly to Shopify. (older, 2022) [L0272.068]
- Short product videos placed directly at the point of sale can answer the buyer's last questions, such as unboxings, ease of use, education and common FAQs. They work in place of or alongside a written description, so the shopper gets the answer without leaving the purchase decision. (2025-26) [L0951.003]
- Short product videos of 15 to 30 seconds, modelled on the style used by Zappos, can be made for each product even without access to the physical item. [L1293.024]
  - Show the product, state the top benefits (such as easy-adjust knobs or easy to clean), add a call to action such as 'Buy today', and mention authorised dealer status if it applies. [L1293.024]
  - Example: a 20-second video for a best-selling product, where a presenter says the three strongest benefits and ends with 'Buy today'. [L1293.024]
  - Example: a green-screen clip of a presenter describing a kitchen gadget's ease of use and ending with 'Order now'. [L1293.024]
- To reuse supplier product videos on a store YouTube channel, follow these steps in order (2025):
  1. Ask the brand for permission to upload its product videos to your own channel. [L0667.089]
  2. Create a YouTube channel for the store. [L0667.089]
  3. Upload each supplier video with a correct file name and the right tags. [L0667.089]
  4. In each video description, add a link to the matching product page on the store. [L0667.089]
  5. Embed each video on its matching product page. [L0667.089]
- Asking viewers a question in a YouTube description can prompt replies and engagement, which can help the algorithm and conversion. Choose questions that push the viewer to respond. [L0655.010]
- Customer videos and photos are valuable user-generated content. Use them as social proof on the site and in ads, and repost them on YouTube, where they can rank in Google because Google often places video results above other organic results. (older, 2021-22) [L1012.019]

### Store structure and landing pages

- Traffic distribution for ecommerce stores: send 90 to 95 percent of traffic to the product page and only 5 to 10 percent to the home and collection pages. Optimise the product page first; home and collection pages need minimal attention. [L0321.014]
- When a store sells several items in a niche with a similar theme, a home page featuring all products together can work. Each product should still link to a dedicated product page. Keep visitors on the landing page where possible and include add-to-cart options directly on it. [L0918.020]
- Hero section principle: above the fold, a landing page hero should carry a big benefit call-out, striking visuals, trust, social proof and risk reduction, so the visitor understands the offer without scrolling far. [L0353.010]
- Hero section workflow with AI:
  1. Know the hero section's job: visitors should immediately see what the product is, what the offer is and how it helps them. [L0353.009]
  2. Give the AI the product and the problem it solves, then ask for a big benefit statement. [L0353.009]
  3. Ask for trust elements such as social proof and authority. [L0353.009]
  4. Ask for copy that reduces risk, such as guarantees. [L0353.009]
  5. Combine the outputs into the hero section. [L0353.009]

### Post-purchase and packaging

- Branded insert cards can serve as a built-in upsell channel. They include a personal thank-you message, the brand logo, a preview of upcoming products and a discount code for the next purchase, which turns the package into a re-engagement tool. [L0403.018]
- Shopify order confirmation for returning customers, to be used as written with the placeholders in square brackets replaced (2024):

```
Thank you for placing your order with [YOUR STORE NAME]! Did you know we also offer [NICHE] products at [NICHE STORE NAME]? As a thank you, all of our returning customers save [10 percent] for the next 7 days, so don't wait. Enter coupon code [GRATITUDE] at checkout to redeem your savings. Your coupon code works at [NICHE STORE URL] for the next 7 days.
```

[L0923.014]

### Email: role, length and format

- Email copy and website copy have different jobs. The email's main job is to get the reader to click through to the website, not to make the full sale. The sales pitch belongs on the product page or destination page. (older, 2021-22) [L0568.001]
- Inbox attention spans are short, and readers receive more emails per day than they did five or ten years ago, so an email has very little time to hold a reader. Keep it brief rather than covering every selling point. (older, 2021-22) [L0568.002]
- Long copy in an email is often not read. Product images, videos, full copy, price and the complete sales argument work better on the website, which presents them far better than an email can. (older, 2021-22) [L0568.003]
- When an email links to a blog post, it does not need to prove the post's merits. It only needs to make the reader click the link, so it should not try to prove the post is great. (older, 2021-22) [L0568.004]
- Image-heavy emails are more likely to land in the Promotions or Spam tab. Simple text emails that use a name and read like a normal message tend to reach the inbox and get opened more. Split test plain text against image plus text. [L0605.015]
- Promo block for a time-limited sale, as a reusable structure. Keep the same structure for every promo so readers learn where to look (2025-26):
  - A headline with the sale name, for example 'Flash deals'.
  - A time window line, for example '24-hour flash deals'.
  - An extra discount on sale items, for example 'Extra 15% off sale items'.
  - One or two sentences that tell the reader why the sale matters.
  - A SHOP NOW call-to-action button.
  - Full block as a reusable structure:

```
Email newsletter promo block for a time-limited sale, as a reusable structure: a headline with the sale name (for example 'Flash deals'), a time window line (for example '24-hour flash deals'), an extra discount on sale items (for example 'Extra 15% off sale items'), one or two sentences that tell the reader why the sale matters, and a SHOP NOW call to action button. Keep the same structure for every promo so readers learn where to look.
```

[L0992.020]

- Pain-point email pattern (2025-26): open with the frustration the customer has when the product fails, phrased as a question. Then show you understand it, say how the product removes it, and give the CTA. [L0567.023]
  - Example: 'Tired of shoes that pinch by mile three?' [L0567.023]
  - Example: 'Sore wrists after every typing day? Fix that today.' [L0567.023]

### Email: subject lines and sign-up

- Problem-focused subject and teaser formula (Source C):
  - '[Emotion word] because [common problem]'
  - 'Entrepreneurs: [time-based guilt problem]'
  - 'Students: [achievement-limiting problem]'
  - Example: 'Guilty because you don't spend time with family?' (problem exposure), followed by 'World of distractions makes it impossible. We fixed this.' (solution claim) [L0307.029]
  - Example: 'Can't stay focused at work?' (problem), followed by 'Entrepreneurs are losing 10+ hours weekly to distractions.' (severity), followed by 'New focus solution reduces distraction by 90% in 7 days.' (outcome) [L0307.029]
- Sign-up headline: name the discount and the condition of the first purchase, phrased as a question or an invitation. Stating the reward up front makes the email exchange worth it. [L0607.013]
  - Example: 'Want 15 percent off your first order?' [L0607.013]
  - Example: 'Get a free gift with your first order when you join today.' [L0607.013]
- Sign-up button: use a verb that describes what the visitor receives, such as unlock or reveal, so the button promises the reward instead of asking for a submission. [L0607.014]
  - Examples: 'Unlock my 15 percent off' and 'Send me my code.' [L0607.014]
- Decline link: write the opt-out as a short, friendly statement that keeps the visitor's dignity and makes the choice feel deliberate. [L0607.015]
  - Examples: 'No thanks, I will skip the savings' and 'Not right now, I will pay regular price.' [L0607.015]
- Exit-intent popup copy (Source A):

```
Use this copy for your exit-intent email popup: Headline: 'wait, don't leave us'. Body: 'enter your email below to receive a special discount from [Store-Name]'. Button: 'send me the discounts'.
```

[L0201.006]

You are eligible for a refund of your purchase. The only thing I need from you is a testimonial. ### Abandoned cart and recovery messages

- Second abandoned checkout email: write the draft directly in Shopify, copy the complete text, paste it into ChatGPT or another AI tool, request improved clarity and tone, then replace the original draft in Shopify with the AI-improved version. [L0149.010]
- Proof belongs on the product page, not in the cart email. See the proof rule above. [L0261.022]
- Cart-recovery email prompt, Gary Bencivenga style (Source E, 2025-26). Use with the brand name filled in:

```
Write a cart-recovery email for [brand] that reads like a Gary Bencivenga piece. It should bring a shopper back to checkout by speaking to the strongest want they have. Keep the voice chatty, as if one person is talking to another, and take tone, values and word choice from the brand profile supplied earlier in this chat. This is the first message this shopper receives from us, so leave out the subject line and preview text, and offer no discount. Sell only what finishing the order gives them. Structure: (1) a brief, punchy headline naming our single most valuable selling point, preferably one that also answers a common hesitation, such as fast delivery, a 30-day guarantee, or Australian-owned. (2) A sub-headline built on their desire. (3) Wording in the target market's own language that says 'you left this behind'. (4) A picture of the items they abandoned. (5) A short call to action reading either 'Complete Your Order' or 'Return to Cart'. (6) A scarcity or urgency line suited to the audience, invented fresh rather than borrowed from any example, such as one about low stock after a viral moment. (7) A short opening centred on their desire that invites them back to the cart. (8) Persuasive answers to the three most common customer reservations, never using the word 'objection'. (9) A line saying help is available at [email]. (10) A strong closing call to action. (11) A sign-off. Aim for high burstiness and perplexity: original phrasing, varied sentence length, emotional pull. Adapt language to the target market. Keep it short enough to scan, put spacing between every block, and never repeat the same claim in two blocks.
```

[L0567.040]

- Subject line prompt for the email above (2025-26). Use after the cart-recovery email exists:

```
Write several subject line options for the email above, drawing on that email's own subject and preview content. Give each option its own preview text. Each option takes a different angle: the main selling point, the shopper's core desire, or the item left in the cart. Keep every subject short enough to display in full on a phone screen. Present the output as a list, with the subject first and its preview text directly beneath it.
```

[L0567.041]

- Messenger cart reminder formula: name the item, state that it is still in the cart, and add one clear link with no pressure. The tone can be casual, with an emoji or light personality, because Messenger feels like a text from a friend. [L1243.021]
  - Example 1: 'Hey {first name}, the {product name} you picked is still waiting in your cart: {link}' [L1243.021]
  - Example 2: 'Still deciding? Your {product name} is saved and ready whenever you are: {link}' [L1243.021]
- Day 3 to 4 Messenger offer. Add a cheerful closing line when it fits the brand, and keep the sender personal:

```
Messenger message for the day 3 to 4 offer: "Hey {first name}, your {product name} is still waiting for you. Here is a code for {free shipping or 10% off}: {code}. Go straight back to the store here: {link}"
```

[L1243.028]

- Day 7 Messenger offer with a deadline. Replace the 12 hours and 15% with the real offer, and keep the deadline visible:

```
Day 7 offer message with deadline: "Last chance, {first name}. You have 12 hours to use this 15% off code: {code}. This is the best offer we can give you. Go back to your cart here: {link}"
```

[L1243.032]

- Pre-sale content should engage cold users first, then move them closer to the product with more commercial content at each retargeting step. Early pieces are educational; later ones compare or explain products the store sells. [L1203.034]
- Make the remarketing ad headline match the email subject line sent at the same time, so the same people see a consistent message across email and ads. (2024) [L1285.095]
- Use past subject lines and ad headlines that performed best on opens, clicks and sales as a starting point for Q4 messaging. Model new ones on them rather than reusing them word for word. (2024) [L1285.096]
- Create ad copy from the approved email sequence, not from scratch. Each ad should match the message of the email sent on the same day, so the audience hears one consistent offer. (2025) [L1287.051]
