### Lead magnet ebooks

- Lead magnet offer formula: '[Product category benefit] solved with [number] proven [format] in [time]. [Social proof or scarcity]. Normally [original price], get it free. [Scarcity limiter, e.g. only 100 copies available].' This frames free content as premium while creating urgency. [L0307.015]
  - Example: 'Seven best relaxation techniques to relax at home in less than 5 minutes. Usually $19.99, download free. Only 100 copies available.' [L0307.015]
  - Example: 'Five energy-boosting rituals for busy entrepreneurs in under 10 minutes. Usually $29, free today only. Limited to first 50 subscribers.' [L0307.015]
- Ebook cover line pattern: a named brand or expert presenting a solution, followed by the author's name, for example 'Your mentor presents [solution], written by [author name]'. This makes the cover read as a credible guide to a specific problem. [L0513.049]
- Ebook title formula: a number or timeframe, a concrete promised result, and the topic or audience. The title should promise a clear, specific outcome that matches the product. (2026) [L0860.025]
  - Example 1: '5 Desk Stretches To Ease Stiff Shoulders' [L0860.025]
  - Example 2: '30-Day Starter Plan For Beginner Runners' [L0860.025]
- AI chat tools can contain factual or wording mistakes, so review the full ebook text before publishing it to customers. Health-related guides should carry a short educational disclaimer and point to a qualified professional. (2026) [L0861.033]
- An ebook used as a free gift should be 15 to 25 pages with 4 to 6 chapters. The product is mentioned only in the closing section. The ebook gives real value first and supports the product second. (2026) [L0861.035]
- Creating a free ebook gift with AI (2026):
  1. Use the ebook prompt, replacing the target audience, the product name and the problem with your own. [L0862.027]
  2. Check the generated text for placeholder text and for any leftover call-to-action placeholders. [L0862.027]
  3. Ask the AI to turn the text into a stylish, complete HTML file with the product name, and ignore the CTA link. [L0862.027]
  4. Review the HTML and the design notes. [L0862.027]
  5. Ask the AI to convert the HTML into a PDF. [L0862.027]
  6. Download the PDF and upload it to the Digital Downloads app as an asset. [L0862.027]
  7. Attach the e-book product to the gift position in the bundle. [L0862.027]
- Structure of a free-gift ebook, in order (2026):
  1. Title and subtitle. [L0862.028]
  2. Welcome note or short author intro that explains what the reader will get. [L0862.028]
  3. Four to six chapters, each with real, practical content, subheadings, short paragraphs and bullet points. [L0862.028]
  4. An actionable exercise in the chapter where it fits. [L0862.028]
  5. A closing section with a single soft next step. [L0862.028]
  6. An educational disclaimer at the end. [L0862.028]
- Example of an actionable exercise: a 30-second self-check at night with a flashlight and a mirror, followed by a single simple observation. It gives readers a concrete task without asking them to change their routine. (2026) [L0862.029]
- Choosing a lead magnet topic (Source A):
  1. Pick the sites, communities or influencers where you want to advertise. [L1076.007]
  2. Look at their homepage, feature articles and what is trending or popular there. [L1076.007]
  3. Check which books or resources on the topic sell best. [L1076.007]
  4. Create your own related version of the most popular idea and offer it as the free item. [L1076.007]
- Design the lead magnet PDF as a brochure. The first page introduces the company and why it is in business. Every page footer carries an offer and a link to the store. The conclusion explains why to buy. Save it as a PDF with clickable links so readers can act from their device. [L1076.015]
- Outsource lead magnet ebook design on Fiverr or Upwork for about 20 to 50 dollars, after you have written the content yourself in a Google Doc. Only the footers, logos and backgrounds need a designer. [L1076.020]

### Blog and SEO content

- Create one custom image per blog article that contains the target keyword and matches the brand. Most competitors skip this step, so it helps you stand out. [L0380.027]
- Google Docs article template, kept in one document so there are no multiple file versions:
  1. The keyword at the top. [L0382.024]
  2. The article draft. [L0382.024]
  3. The edited version, in the same document. [L0382.024]
  4. Meta descriptions and headlines. [L0382.024]
  5. Images and anything else related to the article. [L0382.024]
  6. A content suggestion section, filled by the data entry assistant with what the top 10 results contain. [L0382.024]
- Optimise existing articles first. Use a sales copywriter to improve headlines and meta descriptions for articles that already exist, because this is the highest-leverage step for traffic that already comes in. Old-article optimisation can be tested before new articles are written. [L0382.035]
- Create custom images for articles to keep a consistent brand look, and put the target keyword in the image alt tag so search engines understand the image. [L0382.036]
- Content is a versatile asset. It supports organic search, Google search text and display ads, YouTube ads and organic traffic, LinkedIn for B2B, Google remarketing, Facebook and Instagram retargeting, and cold social traffic on Pinterest, Facebook and Instagram. It also improves conversion rate and makes email marketing easier. (older, 2021-22) [L0414.021]
- Four-step content marketing process (older, 2021-22):
  1. Plan: write 12 content ideas that answer the customer's most common problems and pain points in as much detail as possible. Start with easy, low-hanging topics and move to research-based topics later. Twelve pieces give roughly three to six months of content. [L0414.023]
  2. Produce: write it yourself or outsource it to a freelance writer, which makes consistent output more likely. A freelance job can be posted on ProBlogger (problogger.com) via its jobs board. [L0414.023]
  3. Post: publish two new pieces of quality content per month for 12 months. [L0414.023]
  4. Promote: actively promote each piece across traffic channels, since posting alone does not grow traffic. [L0414.023]
- Affiliate blog post for an information product (Source A):
  1. Find the information product on ClickBank or in your niche's resources, communities or forums. [L0923.029]
  2. Watch reviews or unboxing videos of the product so you understand what it is, without buying it. [L0923.029]
  3. Write a blog post on your Shopify blog that gives useful information about the product and explains why you recommend it. [L0923.029]
  4. Close the post with a call to action and your affiliate link, for example a link to join the program. [L0923.029]
  5. Retarget visitors of the blog post with Facebook ads. [L0923.029]

### Organic social: cadence and content

- Post one to two times per week on both Facebook and Instagram, without exception. Inactive pages whose most recent post is months or years old signal to customers that the business may no longer be operating. [L0157.002]
- Basic organic posts, about a couple per week, add credibility but do not drive early revenue. Posts can be scheduled weeks or months ahead, and AI can help draft them. (2025) [L0972.101]
- For a brand that posts organic content, publishing a higher volume of posts showing the product in use supports reach and virality. Choose posts that show the product in use rather than giveaways, because they attract people more likely to buy. (2025-26) [L1016.075]
- Test organic posts first, then move the best performers into paid ads. Running organic posts as ads without adjustment produced no sales in one brand's test over three months. (2025-26) [L1225.055]
- Share the product images and pins you create for Pinterest on Facebook and other social networks too. Visual content performs well there, so one set of images can serve both platforms. [L1136.035]
- Keep most reels evergreen, meaning still relevant months later. A common split is about 70 percent evergreen content and about 30 percent trend-based content. (2025-26) [L0796.021]
- Keep posts professional and straightforward rather than chasing viral content. Announce new authorised supplier relationships, highlight specific products you recommend, or create product spotlights that explain one to three key reasons why customers should benefit from each item. [L0157.003]
- Use AI to generate 30 weeks of weekly content ideas if you need guidance on post themes. Keep the focus on posts that build business credibility rather than chase viral engagement. [L0157.016]
- Start with easy wins in your niche. Example: home grilling for a grilling brand. [L0237.007]
  1. Create a Facebook Business Page.
  2. Create an Instagram account.
  3. Post memes related to your niche.
  - Steps 1 to 3 in the order given. [L0237.007]
- Share diverse content types that resonate with your audience: blogs, recipes, stories, photos, videos and memes. [L0237.008]
- Start with content that is funny or educational, because humour is the easiest way to earn engagement early. Test formats until one earns shares, and keep making content people want to share. [L0487.039]
- Post content people are proud to share, because sharing should raise their social standing with friends by making them look funny or informed. Ask whether a friend who shares the post will look good for doing so. [L0487.040]
- Meme-style audience-building pattern: set two contrasting options that the niche cares about, such as a premium version against a mass-produced one. End with a short request to like and share if the reader agrees. People who identify with one side engage quickly and invite friends to join. [L0487.041]
  - Example: 'Hand-ground coffee versus the instant stuff: which side are you on? Like and share if you agree.' [L0487.041]
  - Example: 'Hand-rolled pasta versus the boxed kind: tag the friend who still buys boxed.' [L0487.041]
- Blanket statements that could describe any brand get no engagement, because people see many similar posts every day. Content has to be specific to the niche and stand out from competing posts. [L0487.042]
- Product post captions for organic social use three parts: a short everyday moment or season the product fits, the product photo, and one light call to action such as a new arrival, a restock or a link to browse. The mood line makes the post relatable without pushing a price. [L0653.023]
  - Example 1: 'Mornings start easier with our new travel bottle. Back in stock, link in bio.' [L0653.023]
  - Example 2: 'Rain outside, warm drinks inside. Our insulated mugs now come in three new colours, see the collection.' [L0653.023]
- News-based posts: ask the AI for recent news in a niche and for post ideas that tie the brand into it. Web search in the tool may return only a few results, so verify the news before posting. [L0353.048]
  - Template:

```
Ask for the latest news in [niche], explain that you sell [product], and request news items that could serve as material for social posts linking your brand to them.
```

  [L0353.049]
- Organic videos should be entertaining and show the product in use, not list ingredients or specifications, because informational talk reduces watch time. [L0820.008]
- Overly polished, brand-heavy content lowers performance on short video. Aim for authentic, watchable content with a clean background and good camera quality rather than heavy branding. [L0820.009]
- Organic videos should avoid explicit buy or shop calls to action. Paid ads should include a clear call to action and a scarcity element. [L0820.010]
- Mistake to avoid: blanket content is ignored; see the niche-specific rule above. [L0487.042]

### Organic social: captions, polls and interaction

- Write the way you would text a friend, in captions and replies. Humour, voice notes and voiceover make content feel real, and the more casual the tone, the better it resonates. (2025-26) [L0576.004]
- Questions in captions invite comments and act as free market research, showing what the audience thinks and wants. They also make followers feel more connected to the brand. (2025-26) [L0576.005]
- Question-and-reply procedure:
  1. End the post caption with an open question that invites an opinion or a verdict. [L0576.006]
  2. Check the comments on the post. [L0576.006]
  3. Reply to each answer, ideally with a follow-up question about what the commenter meant. [L0576.006]
  4. Keep the dialogue open for as long as people keep responding. [L0576.006]
- Caption question pattern: end with a short, open question that asks for a verdict, an opinion or a shared experience. It gives people a reason to respond and turns the post into a conversation. [L0576.007]
  - Example 1 for a kitchen gadget: 'Did this actually save you time, or is it just a gimmick?' [L0576.007]
  - Example 2 for a skincare brand: 'Have you ever had a breakout before a big event? What helped you?' [L0576.007]
- Asking a question and then not replying to the answers wastes the engagement the question created. Reply to comments so people see the brand is listening. [L0576.008]
- Instagram's polls-in-captions feature is newer and actively promoted by the platform, and creators use it to boost engagement. Newer features a platform pushes are generally worth adopting early. (2025-26) [L0576.009]
- Polls in captions: write the caption first, then add a poll below it. Viewers can vote while they watch the reel, without leaving the caption or writing a comment. (2025-26) [L0576.010]
- Two-option poll pattern: pose a light, fun question about what the audience prefers next, such as behind-the-scenes content against a tutorial. Keep it quick to answer, so people vote in seconds. A single tap is an easy ask, and the result shows which content the audience wants more of. [L0576.011]
  - Example 1: 'Coffee at home or at the café?' [L0576.011]
  - Example 2: 'Morning routine or packing hacks next?' [L0576.011]
- Polls can also use emoji voting, where each choice is represented by an emoji. Low-effort formats like polls and emoji votes are the easiest way to start audience engagement. (2025-26) [L0576.012]
- Instagram Stories interactive stickers include polls, question boxes and quizzes. Use them repeatedly in a recurring series so the audience expects them and returns to the same format. (2025-26) [L0576.013]
- Emoji sticker on Instagram Stories: place a heart (or another emoji) sticker with a short prompt, for example asking viewers to tap it if they have been following for a while. Tapping sends an immediate reaction back to the story, a one-tap way to take part. [L0576.014]
- Offer low-barrier ways to take part, such as tapping a sticker, double tapping or dropping one emoji, instead of asking for a full comment or direct message. Lower effort brings more participation. (2025-26) [L0576.015]
- Add new interactive elements to content followers already know and love, such as the regular weekly stories, so engagement becomes part of an existing habit. [L0576.016]
- Polls in Instagram captions help the algorithm and give the brand insight into what its audience wants. A poll below the caption is a quick way to get engagement and feedback from the same post. (2025-26) [L0576.027]
- Pair a quick poll with an open question. Use the poll for a one-tap yes-or-no or either-or choice. Ask a more in-depth open question in the comments for people who want to write more. Low-effort and high-effort participants then have separate ways to respond to the same post. (2025-26) [L0576.028]

### Viral follow-up and organic-to-paid

- Organic video conversion rules differ by stage. Two values apply to two situations:
  - Default organic videos: no explicit buy or shop call to action [L0820.010].
  - After a viral video: the next video can be more product-focused, with a clear call to action and a direct offer, because converting viewers often needs an offer more than entertainment [L0706.044]. Follow-up videos can be more toned down and professional, with more calls to action and some traditional ad tactics [L1077.019].
- Once one organic video goes viral, the next should be more toned down and professional. Viewers who come from the viral video then see a calmer follow-up, which builds credibility and encourages them to visit the store and buy. [L1077.019]
- Extend a viral video's effect and turn views into sales:
  1. Upload four to five good-quality videos while the viral effect is still active, spaced about two hours apart. [L0706.045]
  2. Once the viral effect slows, boost the video with TikTok coins. [L0706.045]
  3. Alternatively, run Spark Ads on the video to reach more viewers. [L0706.045]
  4. Use an urgency call to action at the end of new videos to convert viewers. [L0706.045]
- Case: a slip-resistant slipper product went viral with a video of about 44 million views, posted September 14, with no paid ads. The video quality and audio were poor, but the clip opened with a slipping risk, showed the slippers solving that problem, and repeated the demonstration. The account had uploaded several times a day, and this one video drove most of the result. The store was later no longer available. [L0657.030]
- Organic-only success can be judged by the absence of repeated ad-style videos or paid-boost patterns on the account. The hosts believed the slipper account was fully organic because no other video showed signs of paid promotion. [L0657.031]

### Images and alt text

- Image alt text describes what an image shows. It helps visually impaired users and lets Google understand the images, including their appearance in Google Images. Editing alt text in bulk saves time when a store has many product images. [L1337.005]
- Blog article images and alt tags: see the blog section above, which covers one custom image per article with the target keyword [L0380.027] and the keyword in the alt tag [L0382.036].
- One set of images can serve Pinterest and Facebook alike [L1136.035].

### Sales copy inputs from the customer and the store

- Desire, pain and scarcity lines should be built from real customer words and real stock situations. Use the customer research as the source of wording [L0567.022], and use scarcity only when it is true [L0567.024].
- Lead with the feelings and situation, then one concrete benefit, rather than generic claims [L0774.022].

### Organic Instagram features

- Instagram's Replace Audio, launched July 21, lets you swap the music on already published public feed posts and carousels without losing likes or reach. Changing the track does not reset the engagement the post has already earned. [L1338.001]
- Replace Audio is useful for older posts that unexpectedly go viral months or years later. Switching their sound to a track that is trending now can help the post reach the new audience it is being shown to. [L1338.002]
- Instants is a separate Instagram app that also appears as a plug-in in the Instagram DM tab. It added video recording, so users can send short disappearing clips to close friends, not only photos. [L1338.003]
- Brands can use Instants for spontaneous behind-the-scenes clips, such as a quick video while packing orders in the warehouse or during a product photo shoot. The goal is to give followers an inside look. [L1338.004]
- On Instagram carousel posts, you can write a different caption for each slide instead of one caption for the whole post. A five-slide educational carousel should get five unique captions. [L1338.005]
- Per-slide captions make a carousel more interactive and give viewers a reason to keep swiping and spend longer on the post. They also let you share more information without overloading one caption. [L1338.006]
- Instagram is expanding screenshot alerts to Stories, so creators get notified when someone screenshots their Story. The creator in the lesson believed this applies only to subscription and close friends Stories, and this was not yet confirmed. [L1338.007]

### Trend-driven organic content

- Jimothy the Raccoon is a raccoon in Seattle with a very distinctive body shape who became a viral internet meme, with fan pages and people posting his sightings. Some brands tied him into their content, such as a bakery that etched his image into a sourdough loaf, and the trend can be searched on TikTok for inspiration. [L1338.008]
- Tying a viral trend into one piece of content while it is peaking is a low-cost way to plan organic reach. It works best when the trend is used in the same week it is popular. [L1338.009]
- Reposting content you already have to Snapchat takes almost no effort and can help reach a new audience. Founder-led stories are a stronger option if you want to build a more personal presence there. [L1338.018]

### Testing new Instagram features

- Test the new Instagram features on your own account to see whether they give a reach boost. [L1338.022]

  1. Replace the audio on older carousel posts that have gained traction.
  2. Write a unique caption for each slide in new carousels.
  3. Post a short video via Instants, such as a warehouse or photo shoot clip.
  4. Compare reach and engagement before deciding which features to keep using.

### Viral Reels production and posting

- Produce and post viral Instagram content for a product. [L1367.009]

  1. Order the product from Amazon to your own address so you can check it firsthand.
  2. Do not post any reels until you have produced 3 weeks' worth of content.
  3. Study the largest pages and videos that made content for your product.
  4. Copy their video style, change elements based on comment feedback, and add something dramatic or crazy.
  5. Produce 2 to 3 videos per day. Make the full 3 weeks of content before posting. After 1 to 2 weeks, raise the daily count by 1 to 2 videos to avoid shadow bans for spam.
  6. Once all 3 weeks of content are ready, move on to the posting routine.
  7. Post on a strict schedule of 2 to 3 times a day for 3 weeks, for example at 2 pm EST, 6 pm EST and 10 pm EST.
  8. After 1 week, change posting times if you spot time-of-day trends.
  9. Post content immediately, sticking to your content strategy.
  10. Use the hashtags with the highest volume and those your competitors use. Write hashtags inside short sentences that describe the audience and the look, for example a shark slides product tagged with a university students group and a fashionable look.
  11. Read the feedback and comments on every video and look for recurring comment themes.
  12. Reply to as many comments on your videos as possible.
  13. Aim for 10k views in the first 5 days to build momentum.
  14. Use boost post on early content to add initial momentum to your account or to gain followers.

- Target 2 to 3 videos per day on Instagram, with 3 weeks of content finished before the first post, and a posting schedule of 2 to 3 times daily for 3 weeks. [L1367.010]
- Ramp up daily video output gradually: after 1 to 2 weeks, add 1 to 2 more videos per day, so the account does not look like spam and risk a shadow ban. [L1367.011]
- Posting reels before 3 weeks of content is ready, or posting identical clips without changes, makes the account look like spam and can lead to shadow bans. [L1367.012]
- One Reels video reached 18,000 views on day one and about 3.5 million total, so Reels can drive large view counts even for products that will not sell well on them. Cross-post proven TikTok content to Reels once TikTok sales appear. [L1429.033]

### Profile redirect to the Instagram shop

- Use a bio and comment redirect text such as "Check our IG" or "shop is in IG", shown with an upward-pointing finger and a gift bag emoji to point viewers to the Instagram shop. Adapt the wording to the brand and keep the pointer and gift bag as the visual cue. [L1381.025]

```
Check our IG ☝️🛍️
```

```
shop is in IG ☝️🛍️
```

### Comment-driven engagement and calls to action

- Use a call to comment: the video shows a short clip with a clear reason to act, and the caption asks viewers to comment one keyword to receive a link. The automatic message then delivers the link, which raises comment volume and engagement. Example: a 30-second clip of a product being built, with the caption asking for a comment of one word to get the download link. [L1457.019]
- Posting organic Instagram content three times per week using AI-generated images and copy had a goal of 5x monthly engagement, starting from 100 engagements per month. [L1509.011]

### Landing pages

- The hero section (top of the page) of a landing page carries most of the conversion weight, so it must answer the buyer's questions immediately: what they get, the main benefit or desired outcome, why trust them, reduced risk, the offer, and a call to action. The rest of the page is for visitors who still need more information. [L1363.001]

### Email and SMS copy

- Email copy and ad copy use the same persuasion mechanisms as product copy, but they are formatted differently. Writers should apply the same building blocks to these formats, adapting length and layout to each. (older, 2021-22) [L1420.010]
- For welcome emails, the offer must be clear and easy to understand, because strong products sell themselves and a simple discount drives the click. Long product copy is less important than a clear offer line. [L1470.019]
- Welcome email prompt (use with the placeholders filled in): [L1470.018]

```
You are an ecommerce email copywriter. Write a welcome email for {BRAND_NAME}, sent to new subscribers who signed up through {SIGNUP_OFFER}. Include a warm greeting, one short sentence about the brand, the offer {OFFER_DETAILS} stated clearly, and one call-to-action button text. Keep the entire email under 200 words, use plain and concise language that is easy to understand, and focus on the offer rather than long product descriptions.
```

### Content mix and formats

- Content should be produced in a mix of content types rather than one format, and the format itself is not fixed: the same idea can be a blog post or a video. Six types are the core of a content production system: how-to, listicle, ultimate guide, best of the interwebs, expert roundup and controversial content. Other formats are allowed when they serve a clear purpose. (older, 2021-22) [L1421.001]
- Controversial content works because people engage strongly with it. Taking a clear opinion may push some people away, but it ties the rest closer to the brand; staying in the middle makes a brand boring and unnoticed. (older, 2021-22) [L1461.018]

### Video content for stores

- Video content for an online store works best when it is evergreen, meaning it keeps delivering traffic for years after publishing, rather than being posted only for a short social media feed where the algorithm stops showing it after a while. Evergreen value depends more on how the video is used and distributed than on how it is produced. (older, 2021-22) [L1424.001]
- Video formats that suit a store include unboxings, how-to videos, listicles, product reviews, customer video reviews and FAQ videos. Unboxing videos filmed from above are a simple format that can attract searches for a popular product. (older, 2021-22) [L1424.005]
- A reusable content strategy is to write a blog post first and then turn the same content into a video by recording narration that reads the post aloud, publishing the video on the store's content page and on YouTube so both the text and the video can rank and bring traffic. This is a low-effort entry point for a store that already produces written content. (older, 2021-22) [L1424.006]
- Production quality matters less than openness, honesty and helpfulness for content videos, while the same is not true for video ads. A video should move quickly, skip padding, open with a clear introduction that says what the viewer will learn, and be concise. (older, 2021-22) [L1424.007]
- A strong introduction tells the viewer what they will get from the video in the first moments, because YouTube rewards videos that viewers watch for a long time. Viewers who leave early lower the ranking of a video, so an intro that explains why to watch to the end matters more than a fast start. (older, 2021-22) [L1424.008]
- Simple video production workflow for a store owner: (older, 2021-22) [L1424.009]

  1. Record the raw video or audio without worrying about mistakes, since retakes and bloopers can stay in.
  2. Send the raw files, for example from the phone via cloud storage, to a freelance editor.
  3. The editor cuts out mistakes and pauses and assembles the final video so it flows.
  4. Publish the edited video.

- LED Grow Lights Depot is a reseller drop-shipping store selling grow lights from many brands and does not hold or produce its products. Its YouTube channel had about 22,000 subscribers after roughly two years, with videos earning between about 21,000 and 35,000 views each, and it produced reviews, buyer's guides and top-7 lists. Its videos are often slideshows or product walk-throughs with recorded voiceover, and the descriptions link to products, so the videos drive traffic back to its store. The channel shows that simple, low-budget videos can attract engagement and traffic without expensive equipment. (older, 2021-22) [L1424.027]
- Video content for a drop-shipping store can be made by a slideshow of product images with recorded narration, which gives a list or guide style video at very low production cost. Descriptions should link to the products shown and to related pages on the store. (older, 2021-22) [L1424.028]
- Content videos do not need professional production to work. A creator with no prior video experience can start immediately and get better by making videos regularly. (older, 2021-22) [L1424.035]
- Opening line for a video, said in the first moments before the main content: (older, 2021-22) [L1424.036]

```
In this video you are going to learn [the specific outcome the viewer gets] and why [the reason it matters to them].
```

### Product review videos

- Structure of a product review video for a store: (older, 2021-22) [L1424.030]

  1. Show the product and list its features.
  2. Explain its benefits, what it does for the viewer and how it does it.
  3. Say why the viewer should buy it.
  4. Mention drawbacks honestly if there are any.

- For product review videos, choose a popular product that the store sells as the subject. Reviewing a product people already search for makes the video easier to find. (older, 2021-22) [L1424.031]

## Claims, compliance and legal risk

### Ground rules for every claim

- Never publish a statement without backing it with proof. If you claim "lose three kilos in a week," include a customer testimonial or a data point from a clinical trial. If you cite dosage or effectiveness, link to or reference the study. Provide evidence before asking for the purchase. [L0261.013]
- Check every claim for truth and relevance before publication. Readers who doubt a claim or cannot see how it relates to them stop reading. [L1366.069, L1366.095]
- Ad creative must reflect the product's real ingredients and results. You may copy a winning structure in format, but the claims must be true for your product, or the ad will fail platform review and lose customer trust. [L0707.021]
- The reframe, the proof and the call to action must match the actual offer. A script that promises more than the product delivers makes buyers feel misled after the click. [L1140.026]
- Advertise the product accurately, so that buyers who purchase it are the ones who want to keep it. Accurate imagery and descriptions help reduce returns. [L1438.028]
- Imitate the form and structure of researched ads, never their exact wording. Copying ad text word-for-word is plagiarism and illegal copyright infringement. [L0196.061]
- Raise stakes with real, serious risks, not with very unlikely risks presented as likely. Fear-mongering without substance is manipulative and ethically questionable. [L0196.062]
- Review AI-generated ad copy against Google Ads policies before enabling any ad. Google enforces strict rules on health claims, personalised content and protected categories. Non-compliant ads are disapproved or suspended. [L0220.010]
- Platforms also review the landing page that the ad sends traffic to, not only the ad. Health or financial result promises on that page can lead to disapproval or suspension of the ad account. [L0416.015]
- Any claim about tax deductibility needs a note that tells the reader to consult a tax advisor. Keep the claim qualified and never promise a specific tax result. [L0340.071]

### Health, finance and regulated claims

- Never make health, finance or general life-quality claims in ads, such as "earn more money," "improve your health" or "make your life better." Ad networks flag these as potentially misleading, unsupported or misaligned with the landing page, and they regularly lead to account suspension.
  - *Older advice (2021-22):* [L0241.009]
- Claims that get health or finance products into trouble include stating that a product cures a serious disease, or guaranteeing a specific income within a set time. Both are result promises that platforms and regulators review.
  - *Older advice (2021-22):* [L0416.016]
- A health promise with a fixed timeframe, such as "lose 10 pounds in 8 weeks," is high risk unless a peer-reviewed scientific study proves that exact result. Such a study is very unlikely for most small product brands.
  - *Older advice (2021-22):* [L0416.017]
- For products where health claims are not allowed, such as an infrared sauna, do not make health claims in the copy. Let the reader draw health conclusions personally. The aim is to send paid traffic to the page, not to educate on health benefits there.
  - *Older advice (2021-22):* [L0580.014]
- Health or ingredient-harm claims need a verifiable source before launch and must be checked against Meta's ad policies. Claims about attraction, status or body image also carry policy risk. Test them cautiously and keep a proof file for each claim. [L0524.072]
- Avoid large claims about health or prevention that tests do not support. Keep the primary headline on benefits readers already want. Errors in health claims can lead to rejection by media and damage trust. [L1261.083]
- For health-adjacent food products (low-calorie, keto, diabetic-friendly), do not make medical claims about treating diabetes or obesity, and do not promise guaranteed weight loss. Use lifestyle wording instead, such as "supports fitness goals," "macro-friendly" or "low-calorie alternative." [L0876.009]
- When copy compares a product reading against a recommended limit (for example, an electromagnetic field of 1 mg against a recommended maximum of 3 mg), the figures must come from the manufacturer's testing and be stated as that source's data. Do not turn the comparison into a promise of health or safety outcomes. [L0416.028]
  - *Older advice (2021-22):* [L0416.028]
- For products outside health and finance, the promise can describe what the product actually does for the buyer. It must be specific: write the how into the promise instead of vague phrases such as "improves your life."
  - *Older advice (2021-22):* [L0416.019]
- An expert presenter with a stated credential, such as a coach or clinician, makes a claim easier to accept. Name the credential early in the ad, but use only credentials that are real and relevant to the claim. [L0524.073]
- Tax claims: see the ground rule above. Do not write tax results as promises. [L0340.071]

### Superlatives, hype and numeric claims

| Claim type | Avoid | Use instead | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unsupported superlatives | "number one," "highest quality" | A best or highest-rated claim only with a measurable proof point next to it, such as the number of reviews | [L0411.030] (older, 2021-22) |
| Hype | "multiply your life by ten," "ten thousand percent better than everything on the market" | Specific, checkable facts | [L0416.012] (older, 2021-22) |
| Generic superlatives | "best in the world," "lowest price" | Specific facts that can be checked | [L1261.076] |
| Numeric certainty | "100% certain," especially in niches where it is implausible (for example the stock market) | A specific figure such as 93%, kept legally defensible | [L1356.014] |

- Generic and superlative statements are discounted by readers and suggest exaggeration. [L1261.076]
- A 100% claim reads as unbelievable in many niches and increases skepticism. [L1356.014]

### Urgency, scarcity and sale timing

- Fake urgency must never appear in a call to action. Fake sales, fake countdown timers and false stock levels (for example, showing 5 left while 1,000 sit in the warehouse) are dishonest and deceive customers.
  - *Older advice (2021-22):* [L0461.004]
- Repeating a 10% off sale that ends on Sunday and is replaced by another 10% off sale on Monday is effectively a lie, not real urgency. Habitually deceiving customers also tends to spread into other areas of the business.
  - *Older advice (2021-22):* [L0461.005]
- Black Friday: keep creatives and sale banners running for a week or more after the sale ends, so the offer still appears active. The source frames this as slightly shady. Treat it as a judgement call and avoid misleading claims. [L1363.047]
  - *Conflict:* [L0461.005] calls a sale that is repeated back-to-back a lie. [L1363.047] allows banners to stay up a week after a sale ends. Keep the banner only if the offer genuinely remains available, and never present it as a new deadline.
- Aggressive "breakthrough" claims combined with urgency can get ads and offers banned by ad networks. One source reports that a cryptocurrency offer written this way brought in over 100,000 new paid names before Google and other networks banned it. Check each network's policies and keep claims defensible before launch. [L1365.050]

### Proof, reviews and credentials

- Use only product reviews that the supplier has given you permission to use. Never import reviews from other websites or from Amazon.
  - *Older advice (2021):* [L0671.184]
- Amazon reviews must not be copied and pasted into ads. Amazon treats them as genuine customer reviews and may penalise sellers who misuse them. A copied review can also send viewers to Amazon, where the product is often cheaper. [L1348.019]
- Ads with fake comment screenshots carry a risk of being caught by platforms or competitors, with consequences. A lower probability of detection does not make such practices risk-free. Using copyrighted footage or others' ads as hooks can also lead to takedown demands or legal claims. [L1348.020]
- Celebrity or famous-name mentions (for example, "used by a famous person" or "an expert credited the product for results") draw attention. Check that the link is real and that the product is genuinely connected to the person or event. [L1370.028]
- Never take another person's creative work, such as ad copy, videos, images or store text, and present it as your own. Create original material, or adapt it with clear permission. [L0534.002]
- Tools for seeded reviews: the source's paste-ready template for fake reviews in the ad comment section is not reproduced here, because it is a format for invented testimonials. Its structure, for reference only, is:
  - a quoted testimonial about one specific benefit, in plain language;
  - a five-star rating, a first name, a city or state, and "USA";
  - a photo of the product or a customer using it;
  - two or three similar comments with different names and testimonials, so the ad does not look artificial.
  - Presenting invented comments as real customer proof is deceptive and is not permitted. [L0645.029]

### Copying competitors and third-party content

**Legal and platform risks**

- Copying competitor ads that use their own branding or custom content can get the video taken down or the product shut down. [L0363.049]
- Competitor video content should not be copied directly. The competitor can file a copyright complaint and have the videos removed. Short-term testing with adapted scripts and a shoot-your-own approach is safer. Supplier videos can be a base, but re-edit them with your own captions. [L0349.012]
- Reusing footage or layouts from other creators carries legal and platform risk. Make the decision to use third-party content deliberately. Creating original footage or licensing content avoids the risk. [L0343.024]
- Drop shippers may send legal notices that can shut down a domain. Take inspiration from competitor stores, but do not copy their pages exactly. Rewrite all copy in your own words, for example with ChatGPT. [L1345.092]
- Do not copy the layout or wording of another ad so closely that it could be mistaken for theirs. A close copy violates the rights of the original writer. [L1366.053]
- Do not copy competitors' product images, even when a competing listing shows good ideas. Create your own images that show the same benefits in your own way. [L1346.032]
- Copying a competitor's product images directly can lead to a DMCA takedown of the Shopify store. Use your own or substantially edited images. [L0660.030]
- Big brands have legal teams and can pursue action beyond DMCA notices. Avoid copying their content. [L1218.024]
- TikTok competitor content: avoid big brands such as Adidas and Gymshark, because they enforce DMCA takedowns within one to two weeks. Use recent content (less than one to two months old) rather than outdated videos. Do not claim celebrity endorsements or false associations. [L0321.015]
- Do not copy videos from large brands. Skip any video in which the product or brand logo is clearly visible. Copying is limited to short tests of content not owned by a major brand. [L1377.023]
- Once a dropshipping brand has proof of concept and sales, replace copied content with original content and build a distinct brand. A large, known brand that gets caught copying faces more reputational damage. [L1348.021]
- Original footage separates your brand from competitors and makes copying harder. Copycats are a common problem once an ad performs well. [L1427.063]

**Test windows for competitor and third-party content**

Sources give different windows. Use the one that matches the situation.

| Content | Window or rule | When it applies | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Competitor or shared video | 3-4 days in testing | Only if many people are already using the same content | [L0321.015] |
| Competitor video | About one to two weeks, then switch to custom content | Standard short test; longer runs raise takedown risk that can remove the landing page or ads | [L1377.022] |
| Competitor logo, product name or shot content | One to two weeks at most in testing | Best avoided altogether | [L0361.026] |
| Another store's video or an Instagram photo | Test only; replace with your own creator content within one or two days | Any use outside a test is not permitted | [L1345.086] |
| Brand face, hired model or custom content | DMCA notice or ad ban within about seven to eight days | The risk appears within this time | [L1218.026] |

- Check whether a supplier photo is generic or custom before using it. [L1218.034]
  1. Run a Google image search on the photo.
  2. If the same photo appears on many stores and on AliExpress or Alibaba, treat it as a generic supplier image.
  3. If other stores do not use it, or your version differs from the supplier listing, someone probably made it custom, so do not use it.
- Using a supplier or competitor product image without edits can lead to a DMCA notice even after months of use, and the site can go down for an hour or two. Remove the image and republish the site to bring it back online. [L1218.025]
- Using a brand's face, hired model or custom content in your ads or store risks a DMCA notice or ad ban within about seven to eight days. [L1218.026]

### Images and product photos

- Google Ads can reject or hide images that contain text. Text overlays on product images are not a ban, but Google may stop showing that image and show other images instead. [L0353.040]
- The store must not depend on images with text only. Check the text on each image against Google's policies. [L0353.050]
- Only upload display ad images you have the legal rights to distribute. Google asks advertisers to confirm this before uploading.
  - *Older advice (2021-22):* [L1342.023]
- Images that require attribution need a credit line. Shopify product pages have no built-in place for image credits. Check each image's licence terms before using it on a store. [L0934.047]
- Do not copy product images from other websites or from general Google results. Use only images that are explicitly labelled as allowed for reuse.
  - *Older advice (2019):* [L0960.046]
- Using a competitor's logo, product name or shot content in ads carries a copyright strike risk against your ad account. Avoid these creatives, or use them for one to two weeks at most in testing. [L0361.026]
- Reusing a competitor's logo and product name can make customers distrust your store when the landing page shows a different brand. Replacing the logo and product name is quick and reduces that mismatch. [L0361.027]
- Copying a competitor's logo, brand name, trademark or text branding into a remapped ad is a legal and brand risk. Recreate only the layout, composition and visual arrangement, and replace every branded element with your own. [L0794.022]

### Reused video and platform detection

**Methods that change metadata**

- Changing a video's playback speed (for example, between 1.02x and 1.05x) changes its metadata without a visible change. The source uses this method, but it goes against the spirit of platform rules on duplicate content and carries a risk of penalties. [L0637.052]
- Changing playback speed or clips alters metadata, which can reduce the chance that Facebook detects reused content. This applies only to short tests, not to long-term use. [L1345.084]
  - *Conflict:* [L0637.052] treats speed changes as a penalty risk. [L1345.084] treats them as a test-only tactic. Use neither for ongoing campaigns.
- Video editing apps such as CapCut or Filmora can change a video's file metadata and aspect ratio. This is a practical workaround that has worked for some sellers, not a guaranteed method, because platforms can still detect reused video. [L0638.052]
- For tests, short clips under five seconds from supplier or stock sources such as AliExpress, Alibaba or Fiverr are considered lower risk. TikTok content can also be used cross-platform in tests because Facebook cannot check TikTok data. [L1345.085]

**Rules on identical or reused content**

- Do not copy-paste the same video from another store into your ad account. Identical reused videos can cause problems with the ad account. Download several creatives and edit them so each is clearly different. [L1216.020]
- TikTok penalises accounts that run identical copies of the same video. Ripping a competitor's content is more likely to fail quickly in the US market than in Europe. [L1177.026]
- Controversial or offensive jokes can lead TikTok to report and remove an account. Indirect wording and clearly signalled humour lower the risk. Avoid direct jokes on sensitive topics. [L0372.037]

### Music, trademarks and branding

- Music taken from a TikTok sound list is a risky choice for a paid ad, because its rights may not cover advertising. Use music you have the rights to, such as licensed library tracks. [L1427.076]
- Trademark and branded elements: see the logo and branding rules above. Only layout, composition and visual arrangement may be recreated. [L0794.022]

### Mailings and offline tactics

These tactics appear in the source as known techniques. They are listed here so that you know the compliance requirements, not as recommended methods.

- Official-looking imprints, such as verified or audited delivery wording, or seal-style labels about enclosed important documents, are used to get past postal workers and company gatekeepers. The source says they work best in political, fundraising and business-to-business mailings. Using them to imply an official or priority item that is not one is deceptive. [L1370.013]
- Tear-sheet mailings and sneak-up tactics must be cleared with a printer and mailing house that know the laws governing them. Some large users print the word "Advertisement" in small type on both the sticky note and the tear sheet, with no measurable loss of response. The sender must not use real publication names, logos or trademarks. [L1370.038]

### Pre-launch compliance check

1. Confirm that every claim has a proof file, and that health claims have a verifiable source checked against the relevant platform policy. [L0261.013, L0524.072]
2. Read the landing page as the reviewer does, because it is reviewed together with the ad. [L0416.015]
3. Check each image for text overlays and confirm the text meets Google's policies. [L0353.040, L0353.050]
4. Confirm the rights to every image, video and piece of music, and the attribution requirements. [L1342.023, L0934.047, L1427.076]
5. Confirm that no competitor logo, product name, trademark or custom content appears, and that third-party videos stay within their test window. [L0361.026, L1377.023]
6. Confirm that urgency and sale timing are true, and that any tax reference includes the advisor note. [L0461.004, L1363.047, L0340.071]
7. Check the policies of each network (Google, Meta, TikTok) before launch, since a rule set can differ by platform. [L0220.010, L1365.050]

## Other details

### Setup and onboarding

- Build five reference files for your project: Voice Guide, Structure Library, Banned List, Avatar, and Psychology Lens. Upload each as a separate file into your Claude or ChatGPT project knowledge once created. [L0039.017]
- Complete the business onboarding form in full and answer every question before you create any ad creatives, because those answers determine the direction of all creative and marketing decisions. [L1267.001]

### Naming a new store

Use this prompt for brand name ideas:

```
Suggest 10 brand name ideas for a new online store in the [NICHE] niche. Mix two relevant words where it helps, keep the names short and easy to remember, and note that the exact domain may not be available so combinations should be checked. Use the same conversation thread for follow-up requests such as more playful names.
```

[L0605.013]

### Store readiness before traffic

- Traffic is brought in only after the site is optimized and has real products, so that visitors who arrive are able to buy. [L0506.010]
- A store should carry at least 50 products; with only 10 products, the chance that a visitor buys one of them is too low. [L1293.004]

### Scope of ad copy by business model

- Ecommerce ad copy formulas differ from ads for digital courses, consulting services, or other online business models. Advice about online advertising may not apply to product promotion, as the copy structure and persuasion strategy are fundamentally different. [L0241.002]
  - *Older advice (2021-2022).*

### Coupons and reviews

- YouTube product reviews with embedded coupon codes should appear in top search results alongside your product name; these become your most-used coupon codes after the first-email offer. [L0041.004]

### Delivery tiers for large or heavy products

When the product is large or heavy and requires freight shipping, offer two delivery tiers:

1. **Standard:** free or freight shipping to curbside; the customer unboxes and sets up. [L0245.068]
2. **Premium:** upcharge; professional installation and setup included. [L0245.068]

- *Older advice (2020).*

### Outreach to website owners about broken links

Use this outreach email and follow-up:

```
Subject: Broken link on [page title]

Hi [first name],

While reading your page [URL of their page], I noticed the link to [name of the resource] now returns an error (404). I thought you would want to know, since it is a great resource and the broken link could frustrate your readers.

If you want to replace it, I have a page on [topic of the resource] that fits the same spot: [your URL]. Feel free to use it. If not, no problem at all, I just wanted to help.

Best,
[your name]

---

Follow-up (send a few days later):

Subject: Re: Broken link on [page title]

Hi [first name],

I wanted to follow up on my note about the broken link on [URL of their page]. If [your URL] fits, it is yours to use; if not, I will leave it there.

Best,
[your name]
```

[L0332.019]
- *Older advice (2021-2022).*

### Door-to-door sampling

Use this script for a trial approach:

```
"Hello, I am visiting you today to offer you a free sample of [PRODUCT_NAME]. I have [NUMBER_OF_OPTIONS] options here, so please choose the one you like best. There is no charge and no obligation to buy. I will come back in [NUMBER_OF_DAYS] days to hear how you liked it, and you can tell me what you think of it at that time."
Do not ask for an order at the first visit. Let the sample carry the claims, and only return to hear the response.
```

[L1261.084]

### Focus rule

- Choose one idea and push for it. Before a meeting, choose the one outcome you want. At a networking event, choose the one person and the one thing to say to them. This focus usually produces a result more often than covering many goals at once. [L0756.061]

### Learning copywriting

- Beginners find it very hard to design ads from a blank canvas, so start by imitating well-made examples found on YouTube and social media. Imitating an existing principle is a practical way to learn motion graphics and layout before creating original work. [L1348.033]
- Breakthrough Advertising by Eugene Schwartz is a recommended read for beginners learning copywriting for ads, and 100 Million Dollar Offers and Dotcom Secrets are commonly suggested for offer and funnel thinking. Taking notes while reading and turning them into concrete ideas for the store is what makes these books useful. [L1347.039]
- For anyone who wants to study copywriting in depth, Breakthrough Advertising by Eugene Schwartz is the first book to read. It is widely regarded as the core reference for writing good copy and marketing. [L1523.003]
  - *Older advice (2021-2022).*
- Avoid buying used copies of Breakthrough Advertising by Eugene Schwartz on Amazon, because sellers often charge far more than the normal price. The book is not cheap even new, so buy it from a legitimate new-book source. [L1523.004]
  - *Older advice (2021-2022).*
- Breakthrough Advertising by Eugene Schwartz was out of print for a long time and has been republished recently. The new edition can be ordered through a site linked to Brian Kurtz, a longtime marketing figure. [L1523.005]
  - *Older advice (2021-2022).*

### Copywriting case studies

**Video sales letter method (Eugene Schwartz-style copy system, as described by its author)**

- *Starting point:* Before adopting the method, the author averaged $2 to 3 million in sales per year, with a hit ratio of 20 to 40 percent, meaning only one or two of every five sales letters worked. [L1365.045]
- *First use:* In early 2017 he used the method for the first time in a video sales letter that went live in July 2017, and sales started coming in within an hour; that one letter generated more than $30 million. [L1365.045]
- *Scaling:* He then applied the method to every project, and his copy generated over $120 million in about two years across different offers and products, with his hit ratio rising to 60 to 80 percent. [L1365.045]
- *Output:* His output also doubled, from one full package every two months to one new sales letter per month, and some full packages were finished in as little as two weeks. [L1365.045]
- *Other results:* A crypto offer built on the method brought in over 100,000 new paid names before the platforms banned it. Mentored copywriters also reached multi-million-dollar sales, with one mentee's first letter generating over $5 million in five months. [L1365.045]

**Industrial parts seller (direct mail)**

- A dull industrial parts seller sent 100 pink-and-red letters with the headline about 69 things to do after work when parts arrive on time, plus a catalogue with a sticker reading "BORING BUT NECESSARY". [L1370.054]
- The mailing produced 22 phone calls and 18 first-time orders, all of which became long-term accounts, worth more than $200,000 in new business that year. [L1370.054]

**Health charity telethon (sponsorship letter)**

- *Starting point:* a local chapter of a health charity needed corporate sponsors for its annual telethon. Typical nonprofit letters to companies described the charity's own needs. [L1370.116]
- *Rebuild:* The writer rebuilt the letter around three donor questions: what benefit justifies the cost, who else already chose this cause, and where the money would come from in the budget. [L1370.116]
- *Offer:* The letter offered sponsorships that required little or no company cash because staff events and customer promotions would raise the funds. [L1370.116]
- *Results:* One employee promotion raised over $50,000 and a small company's bowl-a-thon raised $5,000. [L1370.116]
- *Response:* Experts had predicted the letter would fail, and the response rate was only 0.5 percent, but the responders were important new donors. One of them gave $13,000, which covered about half of the local telethon's costs that year, and the campaign was the chapter's most successful fundraising effort by return on investment. [L1370.116]

**Mortgage broker (first sales letter)**

- *Starting point:* A newly independent mortgage broker, who had recently left a loan officer job, wrote his first sales letter after using a copywriting book and seminar kit. [L1370.117]
- *Mailing:* He mailed an eight-page illustrated booklet with black text on white paper and handwritten notes in blue ink, at a cost of $1.00 per piece, or $5,000 for 5,000 pieces, and paid for the first mailing with a credit card. [L1370.117]
- *Results:* Within the first 30 days it brought in $40,000 in fee income from funded loans, and within 60 days the total reached over $75,000, which he reported as a return of 15 times the cost. [L1370.117]
- *Follow-through:* He kept mailing the same letter, and after four months his bank balance had grown substantially, which he credited to the letter as the foundation of his business. [L1370.117]

**Wartime candy (product-led insight)**

- Forrest Mars spotted a chocolate pellet in a candy shell in soldiers' field kits during the Spanish Civil War, and he patented his own version in 1941. [L0756.069]
- The candy entered wartime rations and then reached the general public after the war. [L0756.069]
- Mars then hired a copywriter for television advertising, and the key insight came from the product itself: it melts in your mouth, not in your hands. [L0756.069]
- Within four years, Mars was selling one million pounds of the candy per week. [L0756.069]

### Platform updates (Source E, 2026)

**Instagram**

- Instagram's new handwritten fonts were built from real creator handwriting and were scheduled to launch on 30 June 2026 for Reels and Stories. They were released in partnership with creators, so testing them can make videos look more native and personal. [L1504.003]
- Instagram was testing auto-generated text overlays for Stories, called Captions, to improve accessibility and reach. Creators can use these to add readable text without typing it manually. [L1504.004]
- Instagram's Edits app includes Reels "Suggested Fixes", an AI feature that proposes in-app edits to improve retention and watch time on underperforming Reels. It was rolling out at the time of the update. [L1504.006]
- Instagram photo dumps now allow a separate caption for each individual photo in the set. Creators use this to add context to each image instead of one caption for the whole post. [L1504.007]

**Snapchat Spotlight**

- Since the week of 29 June 2026, photo posts on Snapchat Spotlight must include a song. The photo is shown as a roughly 15-second still video with the audio, which is meant to improve discoverability and reduce silent image posts. [L1504.014]
- To post a still photo on Snapchat Spotlight:
  1. Add a song so the photo plays as a 15-second video. [L1504.015]
  2. Add a short caption and a currently popular track so it is served like a regular Spotlight video. [L1504.015]
- The update commentary suggested adding a short black-bar caption and a popular track so the post is served more like a regular Spotlight video. This was advice from the commentary, not a rule confirmed by Snapchat. [L1504.028]
- Snapchat Topic Chats, in testing in the US, Canada and New Zealand, work like hashtags that group community conversations around shared interests. Adding a topic to a post places it in that conversation. [L1504.020]

# 13. Influencers and UGC

## Role of Influencers, Creators and UGC in the Business Model

### Role of Influencers, Creators and UGC in the Business Model

#### Where Influencer Marketing Fits

- Influencer marketing is an advanced lever for later stages of a business, not a starting tactic for a new store. [L0544.012]
- Influencers are one of the core traffic sources in this model and are used alongside SEO and paid search, not instead of them. [L0759.005]
- Consistent revenue comes from paid ads, while influencers add brand and social proof. [L0661.059]
- Influencer marketing is a long-term channel that requires patience, consistency and admin work. Over time it tends to be more profitable, consistent and reliable than relying on paid traffic alone. [L1251.016]
- Affiliates, influencers and high-authority blogs rarely send meaningful sales early on. Focus first on Google Ads and Meta remarketing. Once the business has momentum, use paid affiliate deals and a referral program. [L0804.057]

#### When to Start (Stage-of-Business Timing)

- Validate the product with Facebook ads before investing in influencers. Then choose influencers with an engaged audience. Influencer work is best used to build social proof and brand awareness once sales exist. [L0661.057]
- Start commissioning UGC after a product is validated, meaning ads on Facebook or TikTok already bring real buyers and the goal is to improve conversion rate and prepare for scaling. [L1402.002]
- When building a brand with purchased stock instead of dropshipping, hire creators from the start to make authentic videos that connect people with the brand faster. [L1402.003]
- Early growth was built by finding the most ideal customer, growing an Instagram page organically, and getting people and influencers to promote the brand. This worked well only in the earlier social media environment. [L1438.042]
- Influencer marketing and referral marketing suit later stages, after validation, when sales already exist. [L0544.012, L0661.057, L0804.057]

#### Why Influencers Work

- Influencer marketing transfers the trust an influencer already has with followers to a brand. Recommendations often feel more genuine than traditional advertising. [L0479.017, L0480.001]
- Influencer marketing is a useful way to reach a new audience and bridge the gap to consumers, especially for new brands, because the creator already has an established audience and the content feels authentic. [L0630.011]
- Influencer marketing suits new brands because influencers already have an audience, which helps bridge the gap between a new brand and its customers. Its authentic, relatable content tends to build brand awareness and visibility, though its effect must still be measured. [L0786.014]
- Influencer partnerships drive brand growth mainly because they put a recognizable face behind the brand, which raises visibility and credibility. [L0505.001]
- Shoppers often check a brand's social profiles to confirm it is legitimate and to see real people who have used the product. [L0505.001]
- Content posted on the creator's own page carries more trust than content they only deliver for paid media, because it uses the audience relationship the creator has built. [L0505.001]
- An influencer's large reach can expand brand awareness and visibility on social platforms, bringing the product in front of people who would not otherwise see it. [L0480.003]

#### Creative Reuse

- Influencer collaborations give brands access to creative content that already resonates with an audience. That content can be reused as shareable material to amplify the brand's message. [L0479.018]
- Influencers are skilled at making content that resonates with their audience. Brands can reuse that content as shareable, compelling material to amplify their message. [L0480.004]

#### Expected Returns and Volatility

- Influencer marketing has high ROI potential if successful. When it works, the return can exceed any other paid platform. Success is not guaranteed and requires strong research skills. [L0296.027]
- Influencer marketing gets traction more cheaply and quickly than paid ads. [L0561.038]
- Influencer sales come in spikes and are hard to predict, so they are a gamble for direct sales. [L0661.059]
- Influencer-driven sales are volatile and come in spikes. Do not expect steady daily revenue from influencers alone. [L1440.040]
- Example: an influencer-led store sold about 16,000 euros in one day with a 50% profit margin on a one-day spike. The sales came from influencer marketing only, with no other ads running. This is one case and a spike, not a steady baseline. [L1440.039, L1440.040]
- A survey figure cited for influencer marketing states that 86% of people who use it effectively report an immediate or long-term effect on their brand. No survey source is named. Use it only as a rough indication and verify it before relying on it in a plan or report. [L0630.012]
- About 50% of consumers look for recommendations from others before they buy, so influencer content works best high in the sales funnel to bring in qualified traffic. [L0790.091]

#### Trends by Period

- Influencer marketing was described as regaining strength in 2023 after a weaker period in 2021 and 2022, so it was treated as a channel to test again. Check the current market before relying on older assumptions about any channel. [L1214.060]
- Older advice from 2019 to 2022 on influencer effectiveness should be treated as dated; the 2023 recovery means it must be re-tested rather than assumed. [L1214.060]

#### Brand-Image Tradeoffs

- Influencer marketing gets traction more cheaply and quickly than paid ads, but may devalue the brand image. Paid ads give more control over how the brand is perceived. [L0561.038]
- Celebrity endorsements paid for across many unrelated products have damaged the credibility of testimonials. Prefer ordinary customers describing their own experience over famous names praising products they have not truly used. [L1369.038]

| Channel | Speed to traction | Cost profile | Brand control | Revenue pattern |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Influencer marketing | Faster, cheaper traction | Lower entry cost | Lower; may devalue brand image | Spiky, hard to predict [L0561.038, L0661.059] |
| Paid ads | Slower to start | Ongoing spend | Higher control over perception | Consistent revenue [L0561.038, L0661.059] |

#### Affiliates and Referral Partnerships

- Affiliate partnerships with blogs and creators can bring traffic and sales. They are a useful growth channel once a product is validated. [L0661.060]
- Once the business has momentum, use paid affiliate deals and a referral program. [L0804.057]

#### Testing Influencer Traffic

- When paid ads produce few add-to-carts, influencer content can be tested as an alternative source of traffic. In the discussed case it generated more add-to-carts and at least one purchase. [L0361.030]

#### Seeding and Budget Split

- In a first year with almost no money, one brand split its marketing budget 75% to influencer seeding and 25% to remarketing. The reasoning was that traffic it paid for had to be captured again. This is one brand's choice in a low-budget situation, not a general rule. [L0790.088]

#### Choosing Influencers by Niche

- Influencers are useful for a print-on-demand niche only when the niche is open to influencer marketing and the influencers are not too large (not macro). Choose influencers whose audience fits the niche. [L1438.041]

#### Digital Products

- Digital products such as eBooks can be promoted through influencers instead of paid ads. This approach was planned but not yet tested. [L1431.048]

#### UGC Practice

- User-generated content builds trust because prospects believe other buyers' experiences more than polished brand ads. In dropshipping, raw clips from real people often move a viewer to the next step faster than traditional advertising. [L1402.001]
- For UGC after validation: give the creator the product and let them name the store in the video to build more trust. [L1402.002]

#### Common Mistake

- Celebrity endorsements paid for across many unrelated products have damaged the credibility of testimonials. [L1369.038]

#### Further details

- For holiday campaigns, influencer marketing on TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and Twitter was described as the most profitable approach, ahead of paid ads. Twitter ads and influencers were described as especially strong. [L1214.036]

## Setting Objectives and Choosing Platforms

### Setting One Campaign Objective

- Define one specific objective before starting an influencer campaign, such as launching a new product, promoting an upcoming sale or building brand awareness. Tell the influencer this objective so both sides work toward the same goal. [L0787.001]
- Set the campaign objective before choosing an influencer, because brand awareness, engagement and conversions each require a different kind of influencer. [L0479.008]

| Objective | Influencer to look for | Reason | Source ids |
|---|---|---|---|
| Brand awareness | Broad reach and a large, diverse audience | A high-profile influencer can introduce the brand to many new potential customers. | [L0479.009] |
| Engagement | An active audience whose followers regularly comment, like, share and re-post | This audience may be smaller than a broad-reach audience but is more involved. | [L0479.010] |
| Sales and conversions | A track record of shaping purchase decisions, such as in-depth product reviews, product usage demonstrations or exclusive discounts for followers | Purchase decisions are the target. | [L0479.011] |
| New product launch | An influencer who has previously introduced new products to their audience | Consider a promotion or giveaway with them. | [L0479.012] |

- For awareness, a high-level influencer may still be worth it when you need impressions, brand recognition and press. Press features and backlinks from these collaborations can also drive traffic and improve search visibility. [L0790.050]
- Creators match different objectives. A creator with a highly engaged community who starts conversations on most posts suits community engagement. A creator who dedicates videos to product reviews suits driving sales conversions. [L0505.008]

### Defining the Target Audience First

- Define the target audience's demographics, interests and behaviour before searching for influencers, because these determine which influencer will resonate most with your customers. [L0479.002]
- Examples of audience-first matching:
  - A fitness brand targeting health-minded young adults should look for a fitness, nutrition or wellness influencer whose followers already share that interest, not only an influencer with a large following. The influencer then aligns with the brand's values, and their followers are more likely to share the buyer's interests. [L0479.003, L0480.024]
  - A tech brand should look for an influencer who does gadget reviews, tech tips and gaming content, or who regularly publishes product reviews and covers the latest gadgets. That audience is tech-savvy and more likely to be interested in technology products. [L0479.004, L0480.025]
  - A fashion brand with bold, edgy designs aimed at young buyers should look for a streetwear or experimental fashion influencer whose aesthetic matches the brand. That style fits the brand's look and can attract new customers who match its designs. [L0479.005, L0480.026]
- The right influencer depends on the brand's niche and region. A kitchenware brand may work with food bloggers, while a wellness brand may work with fitness coaches or lifestyle creators. There is no universal list of influencers for every brand. [L0505.018]
- Start with micro-influencers, and test at least five different influencer categories before choosing a focus. Categories can include fashion, beauty, fitness, pets, mommy bloggers and photographers. [L0790.047]

### Influencer Selection Procedure

Follow these five steps in this order:

1. Define the target audience by demographics, interests and behaviour. [L0479.001, L0480.023]
2. Set a clear campaign goal: brand awareness, engagement, conversions or another specific objective. [L0479.001, L0480.023]
3. Use an influencer marketing platform to search for candidates that fit the audience and goal. [L0479.001, L0480.023]
4. Check each candidate's social media channels on every platform they use, and check whether their content style suits your audience. [L0479.001, L0480.023]
5. Analyze the influencer's engagement metrics before collaborating. [L0479.001, L0480.023]

- The influencer marketing platforms in step 3 are search tools for finding creators. They are a different thing from the social platforms covered in the next sections. [L0479.001, L0480.023]

### Platform First or Influencer First

- Audiences differ significantly by platform, so a creator's audience on TikTok, Instagram, Snapchat or YouTube should be evaluated separately. Choose the platform for the campaign first, then find creators present on it. [L0505.010]
- Start influencer work by choosing the social platforms your brand will use, and complete your research on those platforms first. Only after that, identify potential influencers who are active on them. Then evaluate each candidate on content, engagement and past collaborations. [L0782.014]
- These two rules agree on the order of platform and creator. The selection procedure above uses "platform" for influencer search tools, so keep the two meanings apart when briefing your team. [L0505.010, L0782.014, L0479.001]

### Instagram

- Instagram skews toward millennials and young adults aged 18 to 34 and is strongly visual. [L0479.019, L0480.014]
- Instagram works well for photos, very short videos, Stories and links in Stories. It is a strong choice when you want high engagement. [L0479.019, L0480.014]
- Instagram has a shop feature. A shop can be attached to the account so products can be sold directly from the platform, and influencer content can drive direct product sales. [L0479.020, L0480.015]
- Instagram's "Your Algorithm" control accepts plain-language requests about the content a user wants to see. A baby-product brand could ask for parenting advice, baby care and children's DIY videos, which surfaces creators whose audiences match its target customers. [L1504.026]
- Instagram remains the largest audience for most influencers, even when they also post on TikTok. [L0789.018]

### YouTube

- YouTube has a broader audience and favours long-form content such as tutorials, reviews and entertainment. [L0479.021, L0480.016]
- Viewers who watch a full video are more likely to buy, so YouTube has a high conversion rate. [L0479.021, L0480.016]
- YouTube viewers often arrive with search intent, looking for a specific product or solution. This high purchase intent gives YouTube influencer content strong conversion potential, which is why YouTube suits product-focused influencer content. [L0479.033, L0480.028]
- YouTube is sometimes used as an SEO platform, and YouTube videos can support SEO. [L0479.021, L0480.016, L0480.028]
- A YouTube creator with large view counts can still underperform for a physical product if the audience is young and often lacks its own payment method. Check the buyer age before paying for a YouTube collaboration. [L0790.096]

### TikTok

- TikTok's core audience is Gen Z. Its short-form content spreads trends quickly and favours very short, fast content. [L0479.022, L0480.017]
- TikTok's perceived authenticity is high, and users often buy directly from authentic creators. [L0479.022, L0480.017]
- TikTok Shop allows a shop to be attached to a TikTok account. It is a newer function, and it has shown strong sales results and growth. [L0479.023, L0480.017]
- TikTok influencers can deliver about three times the results of an Instagram influencer at about half the price. Once they have a following, they start receiving sponsorship offers themselves. [L1440.038]
- TikTok creators can be cheaper than Instagram creators, so a TikTok-focused campaign can be proposed as an alternative to Instagram. [L0789.018]
- The two figures above come from different sources and make different claims. The first is a results and price claim. The second is a cost and reach comparison. The units do not state a measurement basis for either, so test with your own data before relying on them. [L1440.038, L0789.018]

### Snapchat and Pinterest

- Snapchat and Pinterest also exist but were left out of the main comparison. Instagram, YouTube and TikTok were chosen for their engagement, sales and conversion results. [L0480.019]
- Snapchat and Pinterest are additional social channels. For influencer vetting, check Instagram, YouTube and TikTok first, and add other channels only when the target audience clearly uses them. [L0479.034, L0480.019]
- For a fashion sunglasses brand, Pinterest was used only as a repost channel and Snapchat was hard to penetrate, so the paid focus went to Facebook and Instagram. [L0790.095]
- Pinterest group boards have more than one contributor and are marked by a multi-person icon in the corner. Some have thousands to over 100,000 followers, so getting pins onto them can reach a much larger audience than your own profile. [L1136.024]
- To move existing audiences onto Pinterest, post a message on your other social accounts, such as Twitter or Facebook, inviting followers to follow your Pinterest profile or a new board. [L1136.036]

### Matching Content Style to Platform

- Match the platform to the content style and the audience. TikTok suits quick, short-form, entertaining content for a younger, trend-driven audience. Instagram suits visually appealing images, videos and Stories. [L0479.024, L0480.018]
- Let the chosen platform shape the influencer brief, so the format delivered fits how the audience on that platform consumes content. [L0479.025]
- For influencer marketing of clothing, try-on hauls perform best, followed by unboxing content, which can be used as reels and Stories. [L0779.016]

### Brand's Own Channels

- The platforms used to vet influencers, Instagram, YouTube and TikTok, can also serve the brand's own presence. Plan the brand's own channels alongside influencer partnerships. Each platform's format and audience should guide what the brand posts there. [L0479.031]

## The Dream 100 Partner Strategy

### The Dream 100 Concept

- The Dream 100 strategy identifies the top players already established in your niche, such as celebrities, websites, blogs, YouTubers, course creators, events, Instagram accounts, podcasters and associations. You form relationships with them so they send their traffic to your store, instead of competing with them for the same audience. This traffic source is relationship-driven and requires constant nurturing and tweaking, but it can generate consistent revenue as a gold mine channel. [L0183.001]
