- The approach means identifying people, businesses or organizations that already have an engaged audience of your target customers, then building relationships with them. This lets you gain some of the reach and trust of their audience while growing your own. [L0412.003] (older, 2021-22)
- Partnerships with influencers work because target customers trust, respect and listen to that person. The "influencer" label describes this narrowly. Think of it as borrowing an existing audience's trust. [L0412.004] (older, 2021-22)
- The concept has been described in sales and marketing literature for a long time and is a common way many businesses grow through relationships with others who serve the same target customer. It is used less in e-commerce than it should be, but it is a well-tested process. [L0412.006] (older, 2021-22)

### The Four-Step Process

(older, 2021-22) [L0412.009]

1. **Research:** Identify the people, businesses or organizations that already have an engaged audience of your target customers.
2. **Follow and contact:** Follow them and make contact with them.
3. **Build a relationship:** Build a relationship with them.
4. **Explore collaboration:** Explore collaboration options with them.

### Building the Dream 100 List

- A Dream 100 list is the top 100 people and entities in your industry that already reach your ideal customers. It works like a master supplier list, but for influencers and referral partners. Blogs, companies and communities count as well as individuals. [L0528.004]
- The method builds a fixed list of about 100 high-reach partners in a niche, such as influencers, community administrators or companies. You then approach them for partnerships, instead of sending individual cold emails or posting ads directly in their communities. [L0837.067]
- Any online place where your target audience already spends time belongs on the list. [L0528.005]

### Partner Types

- Dream 100 partners can be celebrities, websites, blogs, YouTubers, course creators, industry events, Instagram accounts, podcasts, online stores that are not direct competitors, and associations or online communities centered on your niche. [L0528.005, L0183.001]

| Partner type | How to find or approach it | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Course creators | Teachers of your niche on learning platforms such as Udemy. Search the platform for niche courses. [L0528.006] | L0528.006 |
| Niche competitions and industry events | Valid partner types for your list. [L0528.006] | L0528.006 |
| Communities (Facebook groups, Reddit communities) | Where a whole segment already gathers, such as interior designers. Approach the group administrators, not the group. [L0837.003] | L0837.003 |
| Blogs and YouTube channels | Approach the owners of the channel or blog about a partnership. [L0837.003] | L0837.003 |
| Instagram pages | Approach the owner of the page about a partnership. [L0837.003] | L0837.003 |
| Associations | Find them by searching Google for your niche name plus "association." (older, 2018) [L1274.083] | L1274.083 |

- To reach a whole segment at once, such as interior designers, find the communities where they already gather: Facebook groups, Reddit communities, blogs and YouTube channels. [L0837.003]

### Partnership Forms

- Free relationships require no upfront payment. They include guest podcast appearances, guest blog posts, speaking at industry events while representing your store, and affiliate deals where the partner earns a commission. [L0528.010, L0183.002]
- Paid relationships mean putting money or product in upfront. They include sponsored YouTube videos, Instagram posts, event sponsorships, celebrity video collaborations, and paying a creator for a recorded video. [L0528.010, L0183.002]

### Association Partnership Procedure

(older, 2018) [L1274.083]

1. Search Google for your niche name plus the word "association."
2. Contact each association by email or phone. Introduce yourself and say where you are calling from.
3. Offer the association's members a bonus gift or a discount on your products.
4. Ask the partner to add a link to your store, with your promo code, on their website.

The link brings customers from the partner and gives you a backlink for SEO. This works whatever you sell. [L1274.083]

### Why Relationships Beat Cold Outreach

- Partner credibility transfers into purchase decisions because customers recognize the name and face of a partner they trust. The partner's endorsement can move buyers who would not find the store through search alone. [L0528.016]
- One-to-one cold emails to individual companies are manual and require long back-and-forth conversations. Partnership-based one-to-many outreach is usually more efficient, because many inbound cold emails get ignored. [L0837.004]
- Posting ads directly in groups usually gets them removed. Approach the group administrators and the owners of channels or Instagram pages about a partnership instead. [L0837.003]

### Approaches to Avoid

- Do not reach out to media or as-seen-on companies proactively, because the cost is high and the benefit is small. (older, 2022) [L1281.114]
- If a company asks for free products in exchange for a credit, offer the products at wholesale cost instead of giving them away. (older, 2022) [L1281.114]

## Building and Qualifying the Prospect List

### Setting Up the Tracker and Channel Mix

Follow these steps to set up the tracker. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0202.001]

1. Create a tracker document to organize Dream 100 prospects.
2. Identify prospects across multiple channels (social media, email, communities, forums).
3. Follow them on their platforms.
4. Subscribe to their email newsletters.
5. Join their Facebook groups and online forums.

- Target platforms for Dream 100 are blogs and websites, online forums (including the forum and its owners or moderators), Facebook groups, Instagram, YouTube, and LinkedIn for B2B businesses only. Other channels relevant to a niche, such as Pinterest for interior design, can be added. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.008]
- Facebook pages with large followings are excluded from Dream 100 targets, because page posts reach under 10% of followers and page audiences are largely unengaged unless you run ads. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.009]
- Facebook group admins are valid targets, because their posts reach at least around 50% of members as notifications. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.009]
- A creator who posts on several platforms can be entered more than once, and a single person can have several entries. Some niches only have YouTube, Instagram and Facebook groups, which is acceptable. Aim for a reasonably balanced spread across channels when the market allows it. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.010]
- Instagram reach is moving closer to Facebook reach but is still much better than Facebook pages. LinkedIn and YouTube also reach more of their followers than Facebook pages, so an active creator on these platforms is more valuable. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.026]
- A large forum can be split into subsections. When one section matches your target market better than the whole forum, enter that subsection as its own tracker row next to the parent forum. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.023]

### Pure Creators and Sources Without a Website

- Pure creators with no website or other online presence usually earn from ad revenue, sponsorships, viewer donations or membership platforms. They typically form a single entry in the matrix with only a YouTube or podcast property. This is acceptable, because the entry still shows where your buyers watch. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0478.033]

### Sourcing Experts and Creators

- Experts in a niche include anyone with a large audience there, such as large YouTube channels, large blogs, or pro athletes with big followings. Identifying them is useful for ad targeting and for partnership opportunities. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0872.021]
- Example: a seller of running shoes would search Google for the top runners with large followings, look up lists of experts in the running niche, and search YouTube for running channels that have many followers. The creators found this way go into the Experts Followed field. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0872.022]
- Build a list of potential influencer and authority partners:
  1. Search Pinterest or Google for people already using or showing your product.
  2. Note each person's name and category, such as social media influencer, actor, artist, celebrity or doctor.
  3. Record each person's social media handle next to their name.

  [L1268.009]
- Creator discovery and contact procedure:
  1. Find one well-known creator in your niche as a starting point.
  2. Study the accounts that like and comment on that creator's posts to find more creators with the same audience.
  3. Search Google for the creator's name plus email to find contact details.
  4. If the bio has no email, send a direct message; keep the first message short and specific because high-profile creators receive many messages.
  5. Use sales CRM tools that scrape contact information as a supplement to manual search.
  6. For high-level creators, contact their manager or agency.

  [L0790.062]

### Target List Size and Thresholds

| Check | Threshold | Conditions | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Target list size | 50 to 80 influencers | Build before starting outreach | [L0788.004] |
| Instagram engagement rate | At least 3% | Required for a creator to be selected | [L0788.004] |
| Website monthly visits | More than 10,000 | Safe level, checked with a domain traffic tool. *Older advice, 2021-22.* | [L0527.016] |
| YouTube upload frequency | Weekly is ideal | Roughly monthly can still be valid if recent videos keep consistent view counts. *Older advice, 2021-22.* | [L0527.027] |

### YouTube Checks

1. Open the Videos tab and check upload dates to confirm regular posting.
2. Check the view counts and comments on recent videos.
3. Open the About section for the creator's name, website, email and social links.
4. Note the channel's subscriber count and whether it is focused on your niche.

*Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.014]

- Quick credibility check on the About page: note the join date and the lifetime view count in the Stats section. Combine these with the subscriber count and recent video views before adding the channel to the tracker. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.028]
- Upload frequency: the ideal is weekly uploads. A channel that uploads roughly monthly can still be a valid target if its recent videos keep consistent view counts. Check the upload dates on the Videos tab to judge this. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.027]

### Forum and Website Checks

- Judge engagement by checking whether recent posts receive answers and views. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.016]
- A blog with many posts but no comments generally has a weak audience. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.016]
- Check monthly traffic with a domain tool. Aim for more than 10,000 visits per month as a safe level. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.016]
- Domain traffic tools for checking a website's monthly visits when researching Dream 100 targets:
  - Ubersuggest
  - Ahrefs
  - Semrush

  *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.017]
- A Dream 100 target who is a moderator or owner of a forum or Facebook group is often only visible after joining, so the admin's name can be filled in later. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.019]

### Facebook Group Checks

- Facebook group search results show whether a group is Public or Private, its member count, and its posts per day.
- In a private group you cannot see the discussion before joining. Read the group rules and judge activity from the listing stats first. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.021]

### Finding Contact Details and Advertising Pages

- For a blog or website, look for the owner's name on the About Us page and any contact details on the Contact page, then record them in the tracker. If the site has no about or contact information, the name can be left blank for now. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.024]
- On a blog or media site's contact page, look for a separate podcast, media, advertising or partnership email before using the general contact address. Send guest and partnership pitches to that role-specific address, because it usually reaches the person who handles those requests. [L0528.048]
- Look for advertising pages on websites and forums, labelled such as *Advertise* or *Advertise with us*. They often list banner ads, sponsored listings or business listings. Record the advertising page URL in the tracker, because advertising can be a future traffic source alongside the relationship. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.018]
- Forums and websites often have an advertise page listing:
  - banner ads
  - single product listings
  - affiliate or multi-product store listings
  - spot or location pages
  - business listings

  Record the advertising page link and the types of placements offered in the tracker. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0527.022]

### Verifying AI-Generated Lists

- AI-generated partner lists can contain broken websites, wrong or missing emails, and names that do not match. Every entry must be verified manually before outreach. [L0528.024]
- One AI run returned only 30 rows, and a rerun asking for 100 rows returned 42. If the output is short, keep the usable rows and build the rest through manual research. [L0528.025]
- Prompt for generating the list:

```text
As the proprietor of [STORENAME], you are assembling a list of 100 potential partnership targets: public figures, media properties, independent publishers, video creators, course developers, industry events, social media personalities, podcast producers, and professional organizations whose audiences overlap with your [PRODUCTS] customer base. Record this list in a spreadsheet with four columns: (A) the category describing the partner type (Public Figure, Media Property, Writer, Video Creator, Course Developer, Event, Social Media Creator, Podcaster, or Professional Group), (B) the person's or organization's name, (C) their web presence address if available, and (D) their contact email if obtainable. Complete the list with 100 entries.
```

[L0183.005]

- Verification procedure for each AI-listed entry:
  1. Open each URL the AI listed. If the site is broken or flagged unsafe, search the person or business name to find the working site.
  2. Confirm the site matches the name and note the audience location, for example a site based in one country with a US audience.
  3. Find the contact page or email, using Cmd+F (Ctrl+F on Windows) to search the page for *contact*.
  4. If there is no email address, record the contact form or an Instagram account for direct messages.
  5. Check blog posts for named outside authors. If none appear across several posts, mark guest posts as no.
  6. Check the sidebar, footer and blog for current ads. If none are running, mark paid ads as NA and note any empty ad space.
  7. Look for an advertising or media section and for emails shown as images, which AI tools cannot read. Copy those addresses manually.
  8. Enter the contact details, dates and notes in the sheet.

  [L0528.023]

### Expanding the List and Qualifying Partners

- Before outreach, open the partner's about or partners page and look for other companies they already work with. Add those linked companies to the list as new rows, since they are likely to be relevant to your niche too. [L0528.047]
- If a prospect gets annoyed when you respectfully disagree with a specific point in their content, treat that as a sign they may be a poor long-term partner. Creators who care about delivering value to their audience usually welcome honest, constructive feedback. *Older advice, 2021-22.* [L0453.021]

## Finding Influencers and Creators

### Choosing a Discovery Method

- Start with manual search on native platforms. It is the primary method because it lets you review each creator's engagement and the conversation around them directly on the platform. [L0505.012, L0505.013]
- Use third-party tools as a secondary option, mainly when time is short. [L0505.013]
- Once you find one suitable influencer, find more through the creators they collaborate with and the accounts the platform suggests on their profile. This builds a chain of relevant creators. [L0505.012, L0505.017]
- AI-generated lists are only one source. Also search Google, YouTube and Instagram for your niche terms and check which sites, channels and accounts already publish for your audience. This shows real web presence and quality that an AI list cannot reveal. [L0528.049]
- Start with your own network. Use your local contacts to reach creators in the target market and ask them to promote the product there. [L0549.042]

### Building the Long List

Source A's outreach procedure (2021 material, older; the approach still applies):

1. Search keywords around your niche, for example "best kayak accessories", "kayak reviews" or "how to choose a kayak". [L0226.002]
2. Identify bloggers, YouTubers, Instagram creators and Twitter users who discuss your products. [L0226.002]
3. Create a large list of potential influencers. Expect rejection from most of them. [L0226.002]
4. Contact 20 to 30 influencers with personalized outreach by email, Twitter or Instagram. [L0226.002]
5. Assess each influencer's content quality, follower engagement, posting frequency and audience relevance, using Alexa.com or similar tools. [L0226.002]

If a few channels dominate the results for a keyword, rerun the YouTube search with variations. For example, add "advanced" to a beginner term. This removes generic tutorial videos and surfaces more creators in the niche. (Source B 2021-22 material, older.) [L0527.020]

Only contact influencers in a niche you understand. You must be able to judge the product and provide real value, so avoid chasing unrelated niches. [L0789.009]

### Native Platform Search

**Instagram hashtag search (free)**

1. On Instagram, search for a specific hashtag in your niche, such as hair, nails or acne. [L1213.043]
2. Choose hashtags with about 50K to 100K posts. [L1213.043]
3. Open the Top posts tab, not Recent posts, to see the most engaged creators. [L1213.043]
4. Check each creator's profile and avoid those who promote many products. [L1213.043]
5. Check the engagement rate and the comments before shortlisting. [L1213.043]

**Instagram hashtag research without paid tools**

1. Search hashtags related to your product. [L0788.002]
2. Open the top results and note the creators or posts that appear. [L0788.002]
3. Check each creator's profile and calculate their engagement rate with free online tools. [L0788.002]
4. Keep only creators with an engagement rate of at least 3%. [L0788.002]
5. Read the comment section to spot bought likes and generic or fake comments. [L0788.002]

**TikTok**

- Searching a product name on TikTok shows which brands are driving trends. Other examples cited include chlorophyll drops added to water in health and wellness, and a candida cleanse product that prompted many creators to post about lifestyle changes. [L0505.006]
- The product detail page in the TikTok Shop explorer lists the creators who promote a product, with their revenue, sales and video output over the last 30 days. It also shows the highest-revenue videos for that product. [L0892.012]

**Instagram Explore, TikTok Discover and YouTube Search** are the native tools for the manual method. [L0505.012]

### YouTube Research

**Keyword-based channel research**

1. Compile 40 to 50 keywords covering your niche, the problem your product solves and what your target audience searches for. [L0788.010]
2. Search each keyword and filter the results to show channels only, not videos. [L0788.010]
3. Keep channels with between 10,000 and 100,000 subscribers. [L0788.010]
4. Check upload frequency. A channel should post at least two videos per month, and weekly or daily posting is better. [L0788.010]
5. Check the view rate. Recent videos should reach at least 15% to 20% of the subscriber count, and 50% or more is a strong sign. [L0788.010]
6. Check the comments. A video with around 50,000 views should have at least 2% comment rate, roughly 100 to 200 comments, and they should be genuine. [L0788.010]
7. Find the contact in the About section, where an email or a linked Instagram or TikTok account is often listed. [L0788.010]

Note on the comment figures: at 50,000 views, a 2% comment rate would be about 1,000 comments, not 100 to 200. The source gives both values without reconciling them. Use the 2% rate as the stricter check and treat 100 to 200 as the floor that the source states for that view count. [L0788.010]

**Channel size.** Sources give different thresholds:

- Step 3 above uses 10,000 to 100,000 subscribers. [L0788.010]
- Another source considers YouTube creators to be up to roughly 100,000 subscribers, and sometimes above that. [L0788.008]

**VidIQ** is a free tool to check YouTube channel engagement and trending videos. Use it during YouTube research. [L0788.011]

### Free and Low-Cost Tools

| Tool | Type | Cost | Notes | Ids |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Shopify Collabs (also written Shopify Collab) | Shopify app for finding, checking and managing creators | Free | Used as an alternative to paid research tools; checks engagement rate | [L0788.003, L1213.042] |
| TikTok Creator Marketplace | Creator search across TikTok | Free with a TikTok business account | Searches multiple creators in one place | [L0788.009] |
| VidIQ | YouTube engagement and trend check | Free | Used during YouTube research | [L0788.011] |
| Linker | Shopify app for identifying and managing micro-influencers | Not stated | Speeds up building a large prospect list; manual outreach via Google, Twitter and Instagram still works | [L0226.042] |
| BoardDeckHQ.com | Directory of Pinterest group boards | Not stated | Finds group boards in your niche and their owners, replacing manual board search | [L1136.025] |
| Karo (influencer partnerships) | Shopify-connected partnership tool | Minimum setup is recommended first (cost not stated) | See the existing-customers section below | [L0869.002, L0869.013] |

### Paid Influencer Platforms and Tools

- **Modash.io** is a paid tool for finding Instagram influencers. It gives detailed analytics and engagement data for each creator and is considered accurate. [L0788.001]
- **Modash** is a paid influencer search tool with good results. [L1213.042]
- **Influencity, AspireIQ and Tracker** are influencer marketing platforms. They connect brands with influencers and show performance data, audience demographics and engagement rates. [L0479.013, L0480.011]
- These platforms list hundreds of thousands of influencers, so searching with defined criteria is much faster than finding candidates manually. [L0479.015, L0480.011]
- These platforms are most useful at the start of an influencer search, because they allow data-driven filtering and comparison of many influencers instead of manual searching. They are especially useful for brands that are just starting with influencer marketing. [L0479.014, L0480.011]
- **Influencer databases** with filters: Upfluence, Aspire and Traackr. They are useful when time is short, but they only show creators who have signed up to the tool. [L0505.012]
- **Social listening tools**: Hootsuite, Sprout Social or Brandwatch. Use them to monitor conversations about relevant topics and identify creators already engaging with your topics or with your brand. [L0505.012]
- **Fiverr** can be used to hire someone who sources influencer lists to a specific brief covering country, niche, follower range and minimum engagement rate. Check any list from any source against a second analytics tool. [L0789.007]

**Working with a platform, in order**

1. Sign up and create an account. [L0479.016, L0480.012]
2. Define your search criteria. [L0479.016, L0480.012]
3. Search for influencers that match the target audience. [L0479.016, L0480.012]
4. Review the platform profile of each candidate. [L0479.016, L0480.012]
5. Reach out and connect with the influencer. [L0479.016, L0480.012]
6. Negotiate the deal. [L0479.016, L0480.012]
7. Track the campaign performance. [L0479.016, L0480.012]

### Influencer Directories

- **Collabstar** is an influencer directory. Use it to find people, then contact and pay creators directly instead of through the directory. [L1214.044]
- **InfluSpine** is a French influencer database. It requires a paid plan, reported at about €40 per month, and works best with a translation tool for non-English profiles. [L1214.045]
- **InfoSpy** is a French influencer-discovery tool. It shows placement history, follower growth, engagement rate and audience demographics. Its paid version unlocks country, follower and language filters, audience breakdowns and contact email addresses. [L0789.006]

### Existing Customers With an Audience

Karo's influencer side can scan your existing customers. The following steps are from Source B's 2021-22 material (older):

1. Sign up for the influencer partnership side. This is the minimum recommended setup. [L0869.002]
2. Click "Get Started" and follow the setup wizard. [L0869.002]
3. Connect your Shopify account. [L0869.002]
4. Let Karo scan your existing customers and, optionally, feed in your email list through an email tool such as Klaviyo. [L0869.002, L0869.013]
5. Review the flagged customers who have an audience and check whether they are relevant for your Dream 100 list. [L0869.002]
6. Contact them directly, because they already know and bought your product. [L0869.002]

Why this works:

- Customers who have an audience are a good starting point, since they have already had a good experience and own the product. [L0869.003]
- Influencers already in your customer base or email list are a shortcut in a Dream 100 process, because they already have your product and are easy to approach. Sort them into the Dream 100 list after you discover them. [L0869.015]
- Karo's influencer side also covers creators and press or media who like your brand, not only social media influencers. A customer who runs a blog, podcast or publication can be approached through the same process. [L0869.020]
- Karo's Shopify integration can read email lists from tools such as Klaviyo, so both your customer base and your email subscribers can be screened. [L0869.013]

Outreach pattern for existing customers (Source B 2021-22 material, older). Approach them as a warm lead: thank them as a customer, point out that you noticed their audience, and propose exploring a way to promote your products to it.

```text
Thanks for being one of our customers. We noticed you have a following that fits our brand. Would you be open to talking about a partnership where you share our products with your audience?
```
[L0869.003]

Limits of this method:

- For a young store with few customers, Karo's discovery may find nothing. It is still worth setting up early, because the next sale could come from an influencer. [L0869.005]
- A store with many sales can still have no customers with an audience, so the free test is the only way to know. [L0869.005]
- Karo's network figures were recorded in 2021 to 2022 and are a rough scale reference only, not current figures: about 33,598 brands, 1,098,986 products, 6,853,585 influencers and 170 countries. [L0869.018]

### Trend Discovery and Competitor Check

- Searching a product name on TikTok shows which brands drive a trend. [L0505.006]
- The TikTok Shop explorer product page shows which creators promote a product and their 30-day revenue, sales and video output. [L0892.012]
- Competitor-comparison videos performed reasonably well in one case. [L1379.049]

### Agencies and Management

- **Avoid agencies that represent influencers for a fee.** Agencies often place many brands in front of the same audience, which causes burnout. Find hidden opportunities manually instead. (Source A 2021 material, older.) [L0671.101, L0671.238]
- High-level influencers usually go through their management or an agency, so you may never speak to the person directly. Mid-level and micro-influencers are usually reached directly or through an assistant, which allows a closer one-to-one relationship. [L0790.051]

The two rules are compatible: the avoidance rule concerns fee-based agencies representing creators, while the second rule describes how to reach top-tier creators who sit behind management. [L0671.101, L0790.051]

### Creator Size

The sources disagree on the right size. Use each figure for the situation it describes.

- **Under 50,000 followers, one country or language.** These creators are easier to work with and usually have an audience but no own product or paid-placement income yet. Avoid influencers who already sell their own course, product or brand. [L0789.001]
- **Micro-influencers near the target market.** When the market is a specific country, find a micro-influencer near it and have them film the video, so the accent and context fit the audience. A creator from a different country can reduce trust among local customers. [L1439.026]
- **Big influencers outside the US.** For influencer marketing, target big influencers in countries other than the US, such as Germany, France, the Netherlands and Sweden. [L1440.037]
- **Example range.** A specific niche, for example beauty influencers in Germany with 50,000 to 200,000 followers, makes the search more precise. [L0789.008]

The sources do not state a rule for choosing between small and big creators beyond the market context: small creators fit one country or language, while the big-creator guidance applies to markets outside the US. [L0789.001, L1439.026, L1440.037, L0789.008]

### Regional and Non-English Markets

**Choosing the market**

- Focus on one country or language and one niche when searching. Non-English markets such as Spanish, German or Dutch face less competition than English. [L0789.008]
- Untapped markets, such as certain European countries, Australia and New Zealand, are often better for influencer launches than the US, where beauty products are already widely seen. [L1213.041]
- Strong influencer markets were listed as the UK, France, the Netherlands, Germany, Canada and Australia. In Europe, the Netherlands, Germany and France were ranked strongest, with Belgium acceptable. [L1214.041]

**Working in a non-English market**

- For creators in non-English countries, the influencer's posts and your website must both be in their native language. Use a human translator for the website. [L1214.043]
- Message the influencer on the platform where they are most active. [L1440.037]
- If TikTok is blocked or restricted in your own country, hire creators in other countries to shoot content and manage your TikTok accounts. The course operator used this approach for brands that could not access TikTok locally. [L1377.069]

**Tools for non-English discovery:** InfoSpy for French creators and InfluSpine for French profiles, with a translation tool for non-English profiles. [L0789.006, L1214.045]

### Creator Outreach Case: Thomason

Thomason is a platform connecting sellers with lifestyle bloggers who write reviews and promote products across their blog, Facebook, Instagram and Twitter.

- Offering free products, or charging $197 for a $40 product, drew backlash from the community. [L0228.034]
- Even charging $2 per blogger produced 50% non-completion rates. A real review needed $100 to $300 per quality blogger. [L0228.034]
- ROI was poor and the time investment was not worth it. The seller abandoned the platform in favor of Feedback Genius email automation and organic, sales-driven reviews. [L0228.034]

### Product-Specific Case: Teddy Bear Product

A seller testing a teddy bear product found it hard to crack with ads and turned to influencers.

1. Target accounts that post videos with kids, and check the audiences of those accounts. [L1379.049]
2. Reach out to moms through those accounts. [L1379.049]
3. Share a demo video of the product with a child reacting. Moms who saw it were more willing to promote it. [L1379.049]
4. Comparison videos against a known competitor also performed reasonably well. [L1379.049]

## Vetting Influencers and Spotting Fakes

### Choosing Influencer Tiers and Follower Ranges

#### Tier definitions

- Micro-influencers generally have 1 to 100,000 followers. On TikTok, where follower counts run higher, a large following is worth less per follower than on Instagram. [L0505.014]
- Macro-influencers have 100,000 to 1 million followers and offer a broader reach. [L0505.015]
- Celebrity influencers, such as Kim Kardashian, usually produce lower engagement but add strong reputational credibility to a brand. [L0505.016]
- The follower ranges for micro (1 to 100,000) and macro (100,000 to 1 million) influencers are a working convention, not an industry standard. Platform matters: the same follower count carries less value on TikTok than on Instagram. [L0505.020]
- Mid-level influencers were grouped at roughly 100,000 to 600,000 followers, and they usually expect payment rather than free product. [L0790.089]
- Older advice (Source A, 2020 to 2022 material, as labelled in the source): the ranges above differ from the creator's own grouping, so use them only as orientation. [L0790.089]

#### Tier comparison

| Tier | Followers (source values) | Typical behaviour | Source ids |
|---|---|---|---|
| Micro | 1 to 100,000 | Engaged audience, accessible, often free product | L0505.014, L0226.001 |
| Mid-level | ~100,000 to 600,000 | Usually expects payment | L0790.089 |
| Macro | 100,000 to 1 million | Broader reach | L0505.015 |
| Celebrity | No range given | Lower engagement, strong reputational credibility | L0505.016 |

#### Where the sweet spot lies

- Influencer sweet spot is 20,000 to 50,000 followers: they have an audience but are not yet demanding. [L0789.017]
- Between 50,000 and 80,000 followers influencers know their value and may need extra cash up front. [L0789.017]
- Above 100,000 followers deals usually require substantial cash flow and the influencer often has managers or agencies. [L0789.017]
- Target influencers with about 10K to 50K followers, since they usually charge less and often have loyal audiences. Verify their engagement rather than judging by follower count. [L1213.046]
- Newer creators who have just seen success often produce the most sales per dollar spent. Large celebrity deals were reported to give poor returns. [L1214.039]
- Instagram creators under about 30,000 followers gave good results, and they usually do not ask for payment. If they do ask, the fee is typically around 100 or less. [L0788.007]
- Best follower range in one tested mix: roughly 30,000 to 300,000, because these accounts have a more targeted and engaged audience. Above about 1 million followers, the audience becomes too broad and conversion drops. [L0790.048]

#### Micro-influencers versus larger publications

- Small micro-influencers with 1,000 to 2,000 followers rarely convert into customers for a new store. Affiliate partnerships are better with larger online publications, such as blogs, digital magazines and companies, that already reach people interested in the product. [L0471.024] *(Source A, 2024.)*
- Micro-influencers with niche authority and smaller but engaged audiences are more accessible and effective than celebrities. A creator with 1,000 followers in your niche who posts regularly can drive trust-based conversions better than a celebrity with no connection to the product. [L0226.001]
- These two statements conflict in the number they name (1,000 followers is effective in L0226.001 and rarely converts in L0471.024). Apply L0226.001 when the creator is in your niche and posts regularly; apply L0471.024 when judging a small account for affiliate sales for a new store. [L0226.001, L0471.024]

#### Tier mix from one tested campaign

- The influencer mix used was 20% micro-influencers, 50% mid-level and 30% high-level. Micro-influencers work for free product, mid-level usually expects payment, and high-level influencers are expensive. [L0790.045]
- Use high-level influencers only after testing and only with a budget that can absorb the risk. Keep the first posts with micro and mid-level creators until you know which ones convert. [L0790.065]
- High-level influencers with very large followings tend to have lower engagement and are less likely to convert. Their posts reach only a fraction of followers, and they are costly and often require a manager or agency. [L0790.049]

### Choosing by Audience Fit, Not Size

#### Demographic match first

- Choose influencers by whether their followers match your customer demographic, not by follower count, because a large following does not guarantee that the audience will buy from you. [L0479.006]
- Assuming that a large follower count means an influencer can sell effectively to your customers is a common error. [L0479.007]
- Partnering with an influencer whose followers match your buyer demographic lets you reach likely customers quickly. Matching demographics matter more than raw audience size. [L0480.002]
- An influencer's audience must match the brand's target customer. For example, a brand selling to middle-aged women should avoid a child toy reviewer whose audience is about 10 years old. [L0505.009]
- Influencers in different niches can have completely different audiences, so an influencer's demographic must be compared with your target customers before any collaboration. A large following in the wrong demographic is not a sales channel for your product. [L0480.027]
- Choosing the wrong influencers can do more harm than good to a brand, so selection matters more than volume. The right creators increase engagement, awareness and conversion rates. [L0505.002]
- An influencer whose audience matches your demographic can be worth working with even if you personally do not align with them. Decide in advance which content you are willing to repost. [L0790.054]
- Very niche creators, such as eyelash or gym-focused influencers, and YouTube creators can deliver loyal audiences at lower cost. The speaker reported about a 10x return on influencer spend when research was done carefully. [L1213.048]

#### Niche and style fit

- Do not assume an influencer successful with one brand will generate results for your product; influencer performance is inconsistent across different brands and products. [L0296.026]
- Study the influencer's content on every platform they use, not just one, and check that their style, tone, theme and brand message align with yours. Misaligned messaging is a reason to skip the collaboration, even when the audience is large. [L0782.002]
- Pet-focused accounts can engage well with their followers and promote products, but some animals or accounts over-promote many brands. Assess the account's posting history before working with one. [L0790.055]
- Read the influencer's past promotions to judge whether the style feels authentic and engaging before partnering. [L0789.005]

#### Audience demographics to check

- Review the audience breakdown by country, gender and age. [L0789.005]
- Compare the demographics (age, location, interests) and audience countries with your product before committing budget. [L0296.025]
- Compare the demographics and engagement rates on the platform before deciding. [L0480.013]
- Platform data allows a data-driven, informed choice of influencers. [L0480.013]

### Evaluating Engagement

#### Engagement rate benchmarks

- Assess influencer quality by evaluating followers count, engagement rate on posts, content relevance to your niche, posting frequency, and audience demographic alignment with your target customers. [L0226.004]
- Use engagement rate, not follower count, as the main selection metric, and require at least 5 percent. Engagement can be faked too, so verify it with a second analytics tool before reaching out. [L0789.002]
- Healthy influencer engagement is about 5% to 10% of followers as likes. Also check that the comments are positive and that followers actually interact with the posts. [L1213.044]
- A high engagement rate (likes, comments and shares relative to the audience) suggests a dedicated, responsive audience and is a positive signal when choosing influencers. Use this metric to judge audience activity, not follower count alone. [L0782.003]
- Judge a creator by engagement and by the conversation under their posts, not by follower count alone. A large following on TikTok, or a celebrity with millions of followers, often comes with lower engagement per follower. [L0505.019]
- Check each partner's engagement before reaching out and skip those with fake engagement or overpriced rates. Not every large audience is worth paying for. [L0528.008]

#### Recent engagement and views

- When hiring influencers or creators on Twitter or other platforms, check engagement in the last three months rather than only follower count. Creators with good recent engagement are a better bet than those with large but inactive audiences. [L0561.062]
- Follower count is a weak predictor of views because TikTok reach is highly volatile. A small account can out-view a much larger one, so judge creators by actual recent views rather than by followers. [L1379.002]
- An account with about 50,000 followers should typically generate at least about 3,000 views per video, so a sponsored post with a steady audience can reach a meaningful number of people. [L1379.037]
- Example: a channel with 100,000 subscribers should have a recent video with at least 20,000 to 30,000 views. If it only gets views from one or two viral videos, the channel is considered dead. [L0788.012]

#### Follower-to-engagement example from a real account

- A genuine creator with about 113,000 followers had likes that varied widely from roughly 6 to 1,500 per post, with specific and relevant comments. Uniform, inflated engagement with generic emoji comments is the warning sign. [L0790.093]

### Detecting Fake Followers and Comments

#### Principles

- Fake or bought followers are common and can make a profile look successful. Verify engagement carefully before sending product, because some fake profiles reach out to brands constantly asking for free product. [L0790.053]
- Follower count alone is not a quality signal, because about 30,000 followers can be bought cheaply on freelance marketplaces. Fake profiles built this way then pitch brands constantly for free product. [L0790.092]
- Many influencers buy fake likes and comments, so judging them by appearance or follower count is unreliable. Evaluate their audience engagement and comment quality instead. [L1213.047]
- Views and likes are easy to fake, so check the comments on an influencer's posts. Real, content-specific comments indicate genuine engagement. [L0671.099, L0671.236]

#### Comment and like check

Red flags:
- Generic emoji-only comments and irrelevant replies usually mean bots or bought followers. [L0790.052]
- Very consistent or inflated like counts can indicate fake engagement. [L0790.052]
- Uniform, inflated engagement with generic emoji comments is the warning sign. [L0790.093]

Green signals:
- Real, content-specific comments indicate genuine engagement. [L0671.099, L0671.236]
- Likes that vary from post to post and comments that are specific and relevant. [L0790.093]
- Comments are positive and followers actually interact with the posts. [L1213.044]

### Growth Curves and Follower Trends

- Check the follower growth curve over recent months. A steady decline in followers, especially after a public controversy, signals lost engagement. A small drop of around 5 percent can be accepted, while larger drops are a red flag. [L0789.004]

### Past Collaborations and Authenticity

#### Reviewing past brand work

- Review past brand collaborations and check that the content looks genuine. [L0782.001]
- Check past collaborations to see whether the influencer's content looks genuine: people should interact with it, and their earlier ads with other brands should show how well they work with brands like yours. This indicates whether their audience will respond to your product. [L0782.004]
- Count how many paid placements a brand has run with an influencer. Three or more previous placements by different brands signal the influencer is profitable, while a single one-off promotion is a warning sign. [L0789.003]
- Look at the posts they made for other brands and judge how well those posts performed. [L0790.052]
- Ask the brands they have worked with about how reliably they executed. [L0790.052]
- Check whether the audiences of the influencer and of similar brands overlap. [L0792.001]

#### Vetting order before outreach

Vet a potential influencer in this order before reaching out:

1. Study their content across all platforms and check their style, tone, theme and brand message for alignment with your brand. [L0792.001, L0782.001]
2. Evaluate engagement rate from likes, comments and shares; high engagement signals a dedicated, responsive audience. [L0792.001, L0782.001]
3. Review past collaborations and authenticity: look at their previous ads, how they worked with other brands, and whether their audience overlaps with the audiences of similar brands. [L0792.001]
4. Contact the influencer only after these checks are done. [L0782.001]

#### Loyalty and trust

- For mid-level creators, a loyal following matters more than raw reach: check whether followers trust the creator and want to be like them. That trust is what turns viewers into buyers. [L0790.097]

### Full Vetting Checklist

Use this checklist in order before offering product or budget. [L0790.052]

1. Confirm the follower count is in the range that fits your budget, for example 30,000 to 300,000 for micro-influencers. [L0790.052]
2. Check the post count and compare it to the follower count; a very low number of posts for a large following is a warning sign. [L0790.052]
3. Read the comments: generic emoji-only comments and irrelevant replies usually mean bots or bought followers. [L0790.052]
4. Check whether likes look organic, because very consistent or inflated like counts can indicate fake engagement. [L0790.052]
5. Look at the posts they made for other brands and judge how well those posts performed. [L0790.052]
6. Ask the brands they have worked with about how reliably they executed. [L0790.052]
7. Confirm that their audience matches your target demographic before offering product. [L0790.052]

### Requesting Analytics and Media Kits

#### Ask before you commit

- Ask influencers to share their platform analytics before a collaboration; most influencers provide these freely when asked. [L0479.030]
- Ask the creator for views from the past week and past month, plus average story views. [L1379.006]
- Ask for a screenshot of the creator's TikTok analytics and do not work with anyone who refuses. [L1379.006]

#### Verifying TikTok analytics

- To verify a TikTok creator's performance, open TikTok Creator Tools and then Analytics. Ask the creator to send a screenshot of this Analytics page covering the past week and the past month. [L1379.053]

#### Media kits

- TikTok has an in-app media kit generator that lets creators build a shareable media kit without leaving the app. It was launched after Instagram's Edits app had introduced a similar feature. [L1338.012]
- The Instagram Edits app can export a one-page PDF of your analytics, covering audience analytics, post analytics for the past 30 days, or analytics for one specific post. Send this PDF to brands when they ask for performance data. [L1338.013]
- When a brand asks for a media kit, send one generated from TikTok or Instagram, because those apps hold the platform's own analytics and are the most accurate source. [L1338.014]

### Building a Shortlist from Creator Research

1. Find creators whose audience matches your potential customers. [L1379.006]
2. Check the creator's recent followers and commenters. [L1379.006]
3. Check which other creators in your niche those followers follow. [L1379.006]
4. Record followers, posting frequency and recent views for each creator in a list. [L1379.006]
5. Ask the creator for views from the past week and past month, plus average story views. [L1379.006]
6. Ask for a screenshot of the creator's TikTok analytics and do not work with anyone who refuses. [L1379.006]
7. Start contacting the creators on the list, most promising first. [L1379.006]

### Red Flags Summary

| Red flag | Threshold or sign | Source ids |
|---|---|---|
| Engagement too low | Below 5% (use as minimum); healthy 5% to 10% of followers as likes | L0789.002, L1213.044 |
| Follower decline | Steady decline; drop above about 5% is a red flag | L0789.004 |
| One-off promotions only | Single one-off placement is a warning sign; three or more by different brands signal profitability | L0789.003 |
| Inactive audience | Little engagement in the last three months | L0561.062 |
| Views from viral spikes only | Only one or two viral videos; channel considered dead | L0788.012 |
| Uniform inflated likes | Very consistent or inflated like counts | L0790.052, L0790.093 |
| Generic comments | Emoji-only or irrelevant replies | L0790.052, L0790.093 |
| Overposting pets or accounts | Many brands promoted; check posting history | L0790.055 |
| Refuses analytics | Do not work with anyone who refuses a TikTok analytics screenshot | L1379.006 |
| Pitching for free product constantly | Typical of fake profiles | L0790.053, L0790.092 |
| Demographic mismatch | Audience does not match target customer | L0479.006, L0505.009, L0480.027 |
| Misaligned messaging | Style, tone or brand message does not fit | L0782.002 |

## Relationship Building Before the Pitch

### Dream 100 Engagement Before Outreach

- **Rule of 10:** Before contacting a Dream 100 prospect directly, aim for at least 10 engagements with their content, such as comments, replies or other interactions. Treat this as a guideline and use judgment rather than a hard rule. If the prospect produces content less often, reduce the requirement proportionally. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0202.002, L0525.019]
- **Reduced threshold for periodic publishers:** The source gives two reduction rules:
  - Use the proportional reduction for any prospect who produces content less often. [L0202.002]
  - For prospects who publish only periodically, about 5 engagements before reaching out is enough. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0525.020]
- **Back catalogue counts:** Engagements on older content count toward the threshold, and working through a prospect's back catalogue of posts speeds up reaching 10. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0525.021]
- **The threshold is a default:** If a prospect replies to your emails and asks about your business, direct contact can start much earlier. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0525.022]
- **Engage only where you add value:** Engage with a Dream 100 prospect only when their audience is one you can genuinely help. If you cannot add real value for that audience, skip the prospect rather than commenting just to be seen. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0453.022]
- **Relationships create opportunities:** In high-ticket dropshipping, building relationships with people in your market uncovers many opportunities that stay hidden if the business stays isolated. Starting conversations makes you known to them, and every business in the space should do it. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0529.002]

### Engagement Routine

1. Interact with each prospect's content in their communities and forums. [L0202.003]
2. Provide helpful responses to community members. [L0202.003]
3. Continue until you reach at least 10 meaningful interactions. [L0202.003]
4. Then proceed to direct outreach. [L0202.003]

*(Older procedure, 2021-22.)*

A simple daily Dream 100 routine, in order: *(Older procedure, 2021-22.)* [L0529.007]

1. Open YouTube and check whether the creators you follow or subscribe to have posted new videos you can watch.
2. Check your inbox for newsletters from the email lists you have joined and reply to any that are relevant.
3. Visit the Facebook groups or forums you belong to and review the day's new posts.
4. Where you have relevant knowledge of the market, products or space, write a short helpful paragraph on a few posts. You do not need to answer every post.

- **Low-effort option:** Leave brief, sincere comments on a creator's new video, such as praising a specific point or asking a follow-up question. These take little focused thinking and still make you visible to the people in your market. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0529.012]
- **Patience:** Dream 100 activity pays off over the long term, not as a quick win. Do not rush it or expect results within days. The only requirement is to keep doing it regularly. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0529.008]

### Public Appreciation and Shout-Outs

- **Praise without strings:** Public appreciation, such as writing about a creator's work, linking to it, or building on it and sharing the result, builds relationships without requiring a reply. Expecting a response creates pressure, so give praise without strings attached. [L1343.020]
- **Shout-outs grow the brand's account:** Influencer shout-outs on a creator's account can grow the brand's own Instagram account. As that account grows, creators may start contacting the brand directly, which becomes an inbound source of partnerships. [L1379.051]
- **Name influencers in your content:** Mention relevant influencers by name in your content, since people like being talked about and praised. A featured influencer is much more likely to share the content than to respond to a cold request. [L0899.015]

Procedure for featured influencers: [L0899.014]

1. Build a Dream 100 list of the most relevant influencers in your niche.
2. When a post mentions one of them, send them a direct message.
3. Praise their account, tell them they were featured in your content, include the link and ask for a share. Do not send the same generic message to all influencers.

Template for the message to a featured influencer: [L0899.016]

```text
Hi [Influencer name], I really love your account and your content about [their topic]. We featured you in our new guide [guide title] on our website, and I wanted to make sure you saw it. Here is the link: [URL]. If you think it's useful for your audience, I would really appreciate a share. Thanks, [Your name]
```

[L0899.016]

### Thanks and Gratitude

- **Thank every creator:** Thank influencers in every case, whether you pay them, send free product or work on a gifted basis. Building a long-term relationship makes creators more willing to help again later, even for free. [L0782.013]
- **Gratitude pays off later:** Expressing gratitude and aiming for a long-term relationship pays off later. A creator who likes working with you may promote your product again, even for free. [L0792.010]

Contributor thank-you email, sent on the day the article goes live: [L0899.018]

```text
Subject: Your article is live

Hi [Contributor name],

Thank you again for contributing to our article [Article title]. It is now live here: [URL]

If it fits your channels, I would really appreciate it if you could share it with your audience, for example on your blog, your Facebook page or group, or your website. Nothing mandatory, just a casual request.

Thanks again,
[Your name]
```

[L0899.018]

### Mentions and Roundups

- **Best of the interwebs procedure:** [L1421.018] *(Older procedure, 2021-22.)*
  1. Publish the collection and name each featured creator or site.
  2. After publishing, contact each featured owner or creator by email, using the outreach template.
  3. Tell them they were featured and that they are welcome to share the piece with their audience, email list or website.
  4. Expect that not all will share, but some will, and use the contact to build relationships in your market.
- **Roundups leverage others' attention:** Best of the interwebs and expert roundups build relationships in the market and leverage other people's attention. This helps before you have earned attention yourself. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L1421.027]
- **Attention matrix before roundups:** Before creating roundup content, prepare a list of the experts in your market (an attention matrix) so you know whom to contact for quotes. Use this list as the source of contributors for expert roundup posts. *(Older step, 2021-22.)* [L1461.027]
- **Tagging brands in trend videos:** Tagging a brand in a trend-based, meme-style video can earn a reply from the brand and free publicity if the video goes viral. Tag only when the content is strong, since brands mostly respond to big views. [L1429.041]

### Community and Seeding Through Relationships

- **Community creates unpaid content:** Build a sense of community and genuine care for creators so they feel close to the brand. Creators with a close connection often post unpaid content for the brand, which adds value beyond the paid deliverables. [L0783.009]
- **Open, ongoing relationships:** The goal of outreach is a friendly, ongoing relationship in which creators feel comfortable sharing their own content ideas and bouncing ideas off the brand. This openness produces the best and most worthwhile content. [L0783.021]
- **Earn product through relationships:** Celebrity wear was earned through relationships, not paid for. Attend artists' events, such as concerts, buy an extra ticket for backstage access where possible, meet their team, and explain your vision, who you are and what makes your designs different. [L1438.040]

### Trust and Transparency Before the Pitch

- **Show numbers first:** Build trust before the pitch by showing numbers. Without your own track record, relevant case studies from other industries can demonstrate that the approach works, but they must not be presented as your own results. [L0789.024]
- **No cold requests:** Influencers rarely accept a deal based on a cold request. Build the relationship first with a call, and bring a prepared promotion script and brief, since influencers do not know how to promote, use scarcity or trigger emotion. [L0789.053]
- **Full transparency from the start:** Be fully transparent about what the collaboration looks like from the beginning to build a solid foundation. Stay flexible in how you work together, especially with larger influencers, and frame the deal as mutually beneficial. [L0792.005]

### The Partnership Call

- **Format:** The call can be a phone call, a Zoom call or a Skype call. The platform matters less than agreeing on a time and having the conversation. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0525.025]
- **Purpose:** The first partnership call is a getting-to-know-you conversation, not a sales call. Because outcomes are hard to predict, no fixed script is needed. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0525.026]
- **Core question:** Ask how you can work together to benefit both businesses. You share an audience, your product is relevant to their customers, and their content is relevant to yours. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0525.027]
- **Preparation:** [L0525.028] *(Older procedure, 2021-22.)*
  1. Review the prospect's content and learn what they do.
  2. Check whether they promote other products, run affiliate deals, or sell their own products.
  3. Use that knowledge to suggest suitable partnership options on the call.
- **Call after following for a while:** Calling after you have followed a prospect's content for some time makes the conversation easier, because you already understand their business and topics. A cold call with little research is much harder. *(Older advice, 2021-22.)* [L0525.029]

## Outreach Messages and Sequences

### Channel: DM or Email

- Send outreach as a direct message where possible, since DMs are faster, get higher response rates, and reach the creator directly instead of a manager who may slow the reply. Use email only when DMs are not possible. [L0782.005, L0792.002]
- Use email as the first contact when the creator lists an email address, and follow up with a DM. Instagram DMs are often buried and rarely read. [L1379.005, L1379.007]
- Use email for influencer outreach because it looks more professional. A DM can work only when the sender has a verified account with a large follower base; otherwise lean toward email. [L0783.002]
- Which rule applies:

| Situation | Rule to follow | Source |
|---|---|---|
| A DM route exists and the email address is not listed | DM first | L0782.005, L0792.002 |
| The creator lists an email address | Email first, then a follow-up DM | L1379.005, L1379.007 |
| The sender has a verified account with a large follower base | DM is acceptable | L0783.002 |
| The sender has no verified large account | Email | L0783.002 |

- Outreach emails should come from a personal-style address on a separate outreach domain. Details are in the sender section below. [L0789.012]

### Platform Choice

- Outreach works best on the platform where a creator is least active or has the fewest followers, because they reply more often there. [L1214.046]
- If you find a creator on one platform, check their other accounts and message the one with the smallest following. [L1214.046]

### Sender Identity and Outreach Domain

- Send outreach from a personal-style address on a separate domain, formatted as firstname.lastname@ followed by a separate outreach domain. [L0789.012]
- Sign with a title such as Marketing Officer and the company name. [L0789.012]
- The source describes this setup as significantly raising open and reply rates. [L0789.012]

### Vetting Before Outreach

1. Build a list of influencers that fit the criteria: one country or language, one niche, follower range, minimum 5 percent engagement rate, and no own product yet. [L0789.015]
2. Verify engagement rate and follower trend with a second analytics tool, and check placement history. [L0789.015]
3. Send the first outreach email from a personal-style address with a marketing-officer signature, using an automated sequence. [L0789.015]
4. Once there is a positive reply, send a due-diligence template asking the influencer for audience countries, age split, gender split, and store reviews, to confirm the analytics data. [L0789.015]
5. Move the conversation to a call, since influencers avoid direct partnership pitches by email. [L0789.015]
6. Agree a deal structure and calculate what you can pay before sending a promotion brief. [L0789.015]

### Personalisation

- Tailor every outreach message to the individual creator. Reference one specific piece of their content they did well. [L0782.007]
- Never send the same copy-pasted message to many influencers. Each outreach should pick out something specific the creator did well and explain why that content fits your brand and campaign. [L0782.007, L0792.004]
- Address each creator by name and mention a specific aspect of their work that matches your brand, because creators can immediately tell a personal message from a mass one. [L0783.003]
- Mass emails with unfilled merge fields in the greeting, such as a placeholder where the creator's name or handle should be, are recognised at once as copy-paste outreach and are sent straight to spam by creators. [L0783.004]
- Each outreach message should name a specific reason the creator fits, such as their style or feed, instead of generic praise. This makes the request look personal and gives the creator a reason to respond. [L0791.003]
- Clearly state how the collaboration fits your brand and also how it helps the influencer reach their own goals. This alignment is a key reason creators accept. [L0792.006]
- A handwritten note from a founder or CEO that refers to a specific recent video of the creator makes a PR package far more persuasive and increases the creator's willingness to work with the brand. The note works because it shows real interest in what the creator makes, not only in the product. [L0783.005]

### Opening Lines

- An opener such as "we would love to work with you" without any details gets an immediate rejection from creators. [L0783.008]
- Opening formula (Source E): the creator's name, one concrete reference to a recent video or post, and the single reason the brand fits their audience. It works because it proves the message was written for that particular person. [L0783.006]
  - Example 1: Hi Maya, the drawer-organization video you posted last week made me rethink how we lay out our product range, and I would love to talk about a collaboration. [L0783.006]
  - Example 2: Hi Jonas, the way you broke down your marathon training plan in your last series is exactly how our running-gear customers think, so I would like to discuss a campaign with you. [L0783.006]

### Core Message Formulas

- Short DM formula (Source C): one sentence introducing yourself and your brand, one specific sentence praising a particular piece of their work, and one sentence explaining why they fit your current campaign and how the collaboration serves both sides. Keep the message brief and clear. [L0782.006]
  - Example A (fitness supplement brand, 2026): Hi Lena, I'm Marco from Northfield Nutrition. Your morning-routine series on creatine timing was the clearest thing I've seen on the topic. Our new electrolyte launch fits your audience of home-workout viewers, and I think a paid collaboration would work well for both of us. [L0782.006]
  - Example B (pet accessories store): Hi Tom, I'm Sara, founder of Pawline. Your slow-motion clips of your rescue dog on the trail are great, especially the one with the harness. We're launching a reflective leash in March that suits your outdoor content, and I'd love to talk terms if you're open to it. [L0782.006]
- Four-part DM formula (Source C): a very short message with (1) a brief introduction of you and your brand, (2) a specific expression of admiration for their work, (3) a clear explanation of why they fit your current campaign, and (4) a simple next step. The influencer can read it in seconds and sees that you actually looked at their content. [L0792.003]
  - Example 1: Hi Lena, I'm Sam from a home-kitchen brand. Your slow-motion knife-skills video made me rethink how we show product texture. We're launching a cookware set for home cooks next month and your audience is a close match, so would you be open to a short call about a paid collaboration? [L0792.003]
  - Example 2: Hey Marco, I run a small outdoor gear shop. Your honest review of a beginner trail pack stood out because you showed what failed too. We're building a spring campaign for first-time hikers and I think your style would carry it well. Can I send you the details? [L0792.003]
- Ask for one clear action per message: ask whether they are interested, or request their media kit after they have shown interest. Several requests in one message make the reply harder. [L0791.004]
- Eight-step structure (Source C):
  1. Find the creator's contact details; an email address in the bio is preferred because it feels more professional. [L0788.005]
  2. Open with praise for a specific piece of their work, in two or three lines. [L0788.005]
  3. Pitch your product and explain how it helps their audience. [L0788.005]
  4. Mention the collaboration and the benefit it gives them. [L0788.005]
  5. Use the headline brand collaboration opportunity so the message feels like a big opportunity to them. [L0788.005]
  6. If there is no reply, follow up by email. [L0788.005]
- Outreach message pattern (2021-2022, older): the first message should be short and personal, not a sales pitch. It should name something specific you admire in their work, state the shared space or audience in one line, mention that you see possible joint opportunities, and ask directly whether they would join a short call. [L0525.024]
  - Example: Hi Sam, I enjoyed your piece on home coffee gear, and our customers overlap a lot. I think there is a good way for us to work together. Would you be open to a 20-minute call next week? [L0525.024]
- Outreach procedure (2021-2022, older):
  1. Reach out in the channel you already use with the prospect, such as email if you have their address, a Facebook message to a group admin, or an Instagram direct message. [L0525.023]
  2. Send a short introduction message that says you like their work, that you are in the same space, that you see possible opportunities to work together, and asks whether they would be open to a call. [L0525.023]
  3. If they agree, agree on a time for the call. [L0525.023]
  4. Hold the call and explore how you can work together. [L0525.023]
- Collaboration discussion steps (2021-2022, older):
  1. Use email templates to reach out when relevant. [L0202.005]
  2. Initiate a discussion about collaboration opportunities. [L0202.005]
  3. Frame it as finding mutual benefit. [L0202.005]
  4. Ask directly: "How can we work together?" [L0202.005]
  5. Identify specific collaboration possibilities during discussion. [L0202.005]

### Full Cold-Outreach Templates

Template: trial offer for paid advertising on blogs, sites, channels, and events. [L0183.006]

```
I recently discovered your [blog/site/channel/event] and am interested in advertising my e-commerce store through your platform. Our approach to partnerships typically begins with a complimentary seven-day trial period. During this week, I monitor how the ads perform and what traffic they generate. Based on these results, I decide whether to proceed with a formal advertising contract. I have run this trial approach with five or six different properties and moved forward with contracts for most of them. You can visit my store at [yourwebsite.com]. Would this trial period align with how you prefer to work with new advertisers? If so, we can get started.
```
[L0183.006]

Template: social activation request with full deliverables and timeline.

```
Hi [CREATOR NAME],

I hope you're doing well. I saw your [SPECIFIC VIDEO OR SERIES] and [ONE SPECIFIC DETAIL THAT FITS THE BRAND]. My name is [YOUR NAME] and I am [YOUR ROLE] at [BRAND OR AGENCY]. I'm reaching out about a social activation we are running for the launch of [PRODUCT NAME]. We want to work with creators to promote it, but the content has to feel authentic and fit naturally into your channel, so we would love to hear your ideas for the content.

Product: [PRODUCT LINK]

If this is of interest, please let us know your fee for the following:

- Territory: Worldwide
- Formats and media: all digital and electronic media, including brand-controlled global social accounts, websites (brand and third-party, including e-commerce product pages), other digital delivery such as email marketing and digital ads, on computer and mobile platforms

Timeline (tight deadline):
- As soon as possible: product shipped and content brief sent
- [DATE]: first edit (pending product arrival)
- [DATE]: client feedback and any changes
- [DATE]: content live

Looking forward to hearing from you.

Thanks,
[YOUR NAME]
[ROLE]
[CONTACT DETAILS]
```

Template: first contact for a collaboration (Source C).

```
Subject: [suggested: Collaboration with [BRAND NAME]]

Hello [name],

I hope things are going well for you!

Your profile caught my eye, especially [SPECIFIC DETAIL: a post, video, or part of their feed style]. In my view, your aesthetic and feed align closely with our brand, and I'd be delighted if you would promote [BRAND NAME] on your social channels.
```

### Comment-Based Openers

- Expect that most influencers will not accept a proposal from the first direct message. Plan to contact a large list, because a low response rate is normal. [L1379.004]
- Comment-based procedure (Source C):
  1. Send an email to the creator if an email address is listed. [L1379.007]
  2. Send a follow-up DM on Instagram or TikTok. [L1379.007]
  3. If there is no email or DM option, comment on the creator's most recent video with a short collaboration message. [L1379.007]
  4. Be among the first commenters, because creators tend to reply to the first 10 to 15 comments and to new messages. [L1379.007]
- Comment opener template:

```
Check your DM, let's work together! (Alternative openers: 'Collaboration?' or 'Do you take sponsors now?')
```
[L1379.008]

- Post this opener as a comment on the creator's newest video so it is among the first comments. [L1379.008]
- Reply template for a creator who commented on your post:

```
Thanks so much for commenting! We would love to send you [PRODUCT] for free if you'd like to promote it on your socials. Reply here if you're interested and I'll send you the details.
```
[L1379.009]

### Offer Messages: Gifting, Affiliate, and Podcasts

- Gifting template (product under a value cap or a specific product):

Should you be open to it, we'd like to ship you [a product under $800 in value, or the specific product I want featured]. In return, you'd produce a video, publish it on your YouTube channel, and give us a shout-out saying you got the item from [brand name] and that [brand name] is a strong place to shop for anyone in your audience who wants [product].
[L0528.031]

- Affiliate template (commission-based, no upfront cost to the creator):

```
Hello, I'm reaching out on behalf of [brand name]. If it interests you, we run an affiliate program: you share a link to our shop and collect [5% or 7%] of the sale for each purchase that comes through it. Payment happens only when clicks convert into orders, so trying it costs you nothing.
```

- Podcast pitch: pitch with specific episode ideas that match what the audience cares about, such as market trends or a new brand, and offer to appear as a guest. Each accepted appearance sends traffic to your store. [L0528.009]

- Influencer outreach agents are inexpensive to hire, and more outreach generally produces more promotions, more posts, and more sales. Even if the owner is better at picking talent, outreach volume still drives deals. [L1129.007]

### Terms and Timing of the Deal Conversation

- Do not negotiate terms in the first outreach message. Start the terms discussion (compensation, content, timelines, contract details) only after the influencer has replied and shown real interest in working with you. [L0782.015]
- State the core terms in the first message: deliverables, timeline, and whether the campaign is paid. Compensation can be left for the negotiation stage, but everything else should be open from the start, since creators receive many emails daily and avoid vague messages that need several exchanges. [L0783.007]
- Both rules apply together: name the deliverables, timeline, and paid status in the first message, and hold the compensation negotiation until the creator has replied. [L0782.015, L0783.007]
- Case: a technology brand launched a wireless mechanical keyboard and mouse set in a special colour edition and wanted creators to promote it as a social activation. [L0783.012]
  - The agency's casting producer emailed a creator with the product link, a description of the campaign, and a request for the creator's content ideas. [L0783.012]
  - The offer listed the deliverables: 1 TikTok post with a paid media push, plus a 6-month usage term across the brand's channels with worldwide territory and all digital formats. [L0783.012]
  - The timeline was: product and content brief sent as soon as possible, first edit on 4 Nov (pending product arrival), client feedback on 5 Nov, and content live on 9 Nov. [L0783.012]
  - Because the email was complete and clearly a legitimate inquiry, the creator responded immediately, and rates were negotiated afterwards. [L0783.012]
  - Knowing the brand beforehand helped but was not required. [L0783.012]

### Follow-Up Sequence and Timing

1. Send the first outreach mail introducing yourself, your brand, and the niche, and asking whether the creator is interested. [L0791.001]
2. If the creator replies positively, send the second mail with the collaboration brief and ask for their media kit. [L0791.001]
3. If there is no reply after 3 days, send the first follow-up. [L0791.001]
4. If there is still no reply 2 days after the first follow-up, send the second follow-up. [L0791.001]
5. The sequence has no step after the second follow-up. [L0791.001]

- Timing: wait 3 days after the first outreach mail before the first follow-up, then wait 2 days after the first follow-up before the second follow-up. [L0791.002]
- Keep the same thread so the creator sees the earlier messages. [L0791.002]

### Response-Rate Expectations

| Measure | Value | Source | When it applies |
|---|---|---|---|
| Typical response rate for influencer outreach | 2% to 3% | L0788.006 | General planning; contact volume must be high |
| Replies from a list of 100 contacts | About 10 reply; 3 to 4 agree to your terms | L1213.045 | Prospecting session with 100 influencers |
| Outreach emails to meetings and partnerships | About 1,000 emails lead to about 8 meetings and 1 profitable partnership | L0789.016 | Full funnel from email to profitable deal |
| Accepted paid influencer offers (cold, general) | From 30 influencers contacted, expect 1 to 2 to accept; plan for rejection as the baseline | L0226.003 | Baseline for cold influencer outreach |
| Trial-offer method for paid advertising | Works 9 out of 10 times | L0183.004 | Standard trial offer method for paid placements (blog, site, channel, event) |

- The figures above measure different steps (replies, agreements, meetings, accepted offers), so read each against its own step. [L788.006, L1213.045, L0789.016, L0226.003, L0183.004]
- Each careful research session takes about two to three hours. [L1213.045]
- Expect that most creators contacted early will not reply, and that roughly the first 20 outreach messages may produce few or no responses. Keep building the list rather than judging the campaign by the first few contacts. [L1379.052]
- Early outreach to creators was manual: the team searched Instagram by category and sent individual emails with short, specific subject lines. Reply rates were higher in the early years and dropped as competition for creators grew. [L0790.099]

### Volume and Split Testing

- Split-test outreach templates because a template that works in one market may fail in another. Keep the first email short and aimed at getting any positive reply, such as a request for more information or a yes. [L0789.013]
- Contact a large list when prospecting, because low response rates are normal and volume drives results. [L1379.004, L1213.045, L1129.007]
- Each message should contain one clear call to action, so split tests should vary one element at a time. [L0791.004, L0789.013]

## Gifting and Seeding Campaigns

### Gifting campaign phases and funnel benchmarks

1. Gift products to a broad list of creators and record their details in a spreadsheet (Google Sheets), starting with 30 to 50 creators. [L0915.016]
2. Expect attrition. From 50 outreach DMs, roughly 30 reply, 20 want the product, and 10 post on Instagram. [L0915.016, L0915.017]
3. Track which creators engage with the brand on their own. These smaller creators are the ones to move into paid partnerships. [L0915.016]

- Funnel benchmark for creator outreach: of 50 DMs sent, about 30 reply, about 20 want the product, and about 10 post on Instagram. [L0915.017]
- Plan for roughly a 60 percent loss from reply to posting, so start with more creators than you need. [L0915.017]
- Arithmetic from the same benchmark: reply to post is a loss of about 67 percent (30 to 10), product request to post about 50 percent (20 to 10), and DM to post about 80 percent (50 to 10). The stated 60 percent does not match the 30-to-10 figure exactly, so keep both and use the stage figures to see where creators drop out. [L0915.017]

Numbered campaign procedure:

1. Gift the product to a broad list of 30 to 50 creators and record each creator's details in a Google Sheets list. [L0915.022]
