Following up manually and sporadically left a large amount of quoted business unclosed, with about $70,000 in open quotes at one point. Quotes were sent once and then forgotten when staff did not remember to call back. A dated follow-up system fixes this, because each card shows its next due date. [L1396.030]

### Prospect sheets and short codes

Record every prospect who does not buy immediately in a prospect sheet, so that no lead slips through. In the notes, use short codes such as PH for phone and EM for email, plus the product sought and the reason for not buying. [L1000.053]

## Calling abandoned checkouts

### Why speed decides the outcome

- Contacting a lead within minutes of abandonment, instead of 30 minutes after, makes contact about 100 times more likely, because memory and task focus degrade quickly. [L0281.001]
- Contacting within 5 minutes, instead of 30 minutes after cart abandonment, makes lead qualification about 21 times more likely. [L0281.002]
- Immediate contact, within minutes, lets the customer assume a legitimate checkout issue. They are less likely to perceive aggressive marketing and more likely to complete the purchase. [L0286.034]

### Catching abandoned checkouts in real time

- **Mistake:** Checking abandoned carts manually in Shopify Admin (Orders > Abandoned Orders) every few hours or days. Compared with immediate real-time notification, this delay cuts contact likelihood by 100 times and qualification likelihood by 21 times. [L0281.013]
- **Principle:** Orders valued at $2,000-$3,000 or higher nearly require a phone conversation to close. Use automation to identify these abandoned carts and send immediate alerts to the sales team. [L0286.017]
- **Slack alert:** A notification goes to the phone team as soon as a new abandoned cart arrives, so calls can start quickly. [L0737.015]
- **Slack alert content:** Customer name, products left in the cart, and phone number. [L1092.086] *(Older: 2022)*
- **Sheet:** The same data also lands in the tracking sheet, where the team logs results. [L0737.015]

### Capturing the phone number at checkout

- Roughly half or more of abandoned checkouts can yield a phone number, so the checkout should ask for one. Capturing it is what makes the follow-up call possible. [L1522.024] *(Older: 2021-22)*
- Handle abandoned checkouts in this order: [L1522.025] *(Older: 2021-22)*
  1. Ask for and capture the shopper's phone number during checkout.
  2. Call every abandoned checkout with a phone number as soon as possible.
  3. Send the abandoned checkout email flow to all abandoned checkouts, including those without a phone number.
- When you have the customer's phone number, combine email follow-up with a call or text. Many carts can still be converted into sales this way. [L1285.066] *(2024)*

### Timing the call

- Contact every abandoned checkout as soon as possible, ideally straight away, by phone. The call aims to find and fix the problem that stopped the sale. [L1522.023] *(Older: 2021-22)*
- Call customers who abandoned checkout to ask why they did not finish the order, except on Sundays. [L1090.139] *(Older: 2021)*

### Working each row (phone team routine)

For each abandoned cart row: [L0737.013]

1. Call the customer and record in the Notes column what happened: whether the person picked up, whether it was a wrong number, whether they bought, and what was said on the call.
2. Set the row color according to the call outcome so that results can be read at a glance.
3. If a paid order later comes in from the same email, the Recovered column is filled automatically with the purchase date.

Alternative call procedure from the 2022 course: [L1092.086] *(Older: 2022)*

1. Receive a Slack notification showing the customer's name, the products left in the cart and the phone number.
2. Call from a business number such as Mighty Call or Google Voice.
3. Say that you saw they were on the store, did not finish the order, and ask whether you can help.

### Call scripts

Phone script for an unfinished checkout. Adjust it to your store, and stay warm and never pushy. [L1522.026] *(Older: 2021-22)*

```
When a customer leaves a checkout unfinished, use this phone script, adjusted to your store, and stay warm and never pushy. Greet the customer by first name, introduce yourself and your store, and say you noticed they started an order but did not complete it. Ask whether anything went wrong during checkout and whether there is something you can fix or help with. Say you would be glad to have them as a customer. If a problem came up, write down exactly what it was, then either fix it or escalate it, and confirm the result back to the customer. If no problem came up, thank them, ask whether they have questions about the product or shipping, and end the call politely. Log the outcome and the reason for the abandonment in your notes.
```

Opening script (2021). Two identical copies in the course; the text is unchanged. [L0671.021, L0671.297] *(Older: 2021)*

```
Hi, this is [your name] from [store name].com. We noticed you were just about to complete your order for [product name] but did not finish checking out. I just wanted to follow up quickly to see if you ran into any trouble or if there is anything I can help you with. If they are ready to buy, offer to send them a direct link back to checkout.
```

Message script (2024). [L1285.065] *(2024)*

```
Hi, this is [Your name], the owner of [Store name]. I noticed you started the checkout for [product name] but did not complete your order. If you have any questions about this product, I am happy to help, so just text me back and I will take care of you.
```

### Voicemail and text follow-up

- Phone calls after abandoned checkouts are often unanswered, so pair each call with a voicemail and a later text. [L0806.096] *(2024)*
- Plan the follow-up over about a week to measure whether it recovers sales. [L0806.096] *(2024)*
- The call comes first. The voicemail and text follow after it, as the second step of the same sequence. [L0806.096, L0737.013] *(2024)*

### Tracking sheet setup

- Color-code the tracking sheet rows by call result so outcomes are visible at a glance. [L0737.014]
- Place the color key at the top of the sheet. [L0737.014]
- Notes column: record pickup, wrong number, purchase, and call content for each row. [L0737.013]
- Recovered column: filled automatically with the purchase date when a paid order arrives from the same email. [L0737.013]

### Using the answers as feedback

- Use customers' answers about why they abandoned as qualitative feedback for fixing the store. [L1090.139] *(Older: 2021)*
- Log the outcome and the reason for the abandonment in the notes, so the reasons can be reviewed later. [L1522.026] *(Older: 2021-22)*

## Post-purchase, confirmation and review calls

### Order confirmation calls

#### When to use an order confirmation call

- Use a confirmation call only for orders that look suspicious or that need verification before shipping. [L0960.015]
- The call checks the shipping destination, billing address, and connection location against each other, then asks the customer to confirm or correct the details. [L0960.015]

#### Order confirmation script (2019, older)

```
Hi, this is [Your name] from [Store name]. We received your order for [product] and want to confirm it is yours before we ship. Our records show it is going to [shipping state or city], the billing address is in [billing state or city], and the connection came from [IP location]. Could you confirm these details and tell me whether anything looks different from what you expected? Thank you, and we will get your order on its way once we have confirmed it.
```
[L0960.015]

### Thank-you and satisfaction calls

#### Purpose and timing of the post-sale call

- The first call is a post-sales support call, not a review request. Opening this way feels natural to the customer, and most businesses do not follow up at all, so the call builds goodwill before the request is made. [L1012.014]
- Schedule a post-purchase call to every customer at the same point the automated review email would go out, typically around 7 to 14 days after the order or after the usual delivery time. For example, if most orders arrive within 7 days, call at day 7; if the review email goes out at 2 weeks, call at 2 weeks. [L1012.010]
- Call new customers after purchase to thank them and confirm the order. Calls cost nothing if done with your own time or on commission, and take about 10 to 20 minutes each. [L1076.046]
- Make an upsell only when a product truly fits the customer's purchase. [L1076.046]

#### Goals of the review call

- A personal thank-you.
- Gauging satisfaction with the business and product.
- Resolving any problems.
- Securing at least a text review.
- Requesting a photo of the customer with the product.
- Requesting a video review via VideoPeel. [L1012.017]

#### Structure of a post-sale call

1. Open by asking a series of questions about whether the customer is getting the value they expected from the product and whether anything is wrong. [L1011.006]
2. Answer any questions the customer has. [L1011.006]
3. At the end of the call, ask the customer to leave a review. [L1011.006]

#### Post-purchase call script (Source A)

Use this post-purchase call script with placeholders filled in:

```
Hello [first name], this is [your name] from [store name]. Thank you for your business. I wanted to let you know that we have your order [order number] confirmed, and it usually ships within 48 hours. Here is what to expect: you will get tracking updates by email as soon as it ships. If you have any questions, you can call us at [phone number], email [email address], or use live chat on our site between 9 and 5. We appreciate you, and we are here to support you.
```
[L1076.047]

- If the customer does not answer, leave a voicemail with the same thank-you message and the same contact details, and do not pitch a product in the voicemail. [L1076.047]

#### Use the script as a guide

- Use a call script as a guide to the content only. Callers should speak in their own natural language rather than reading the script word for word. [L1012.015]

### Review call procedure

#### Step-by-step review call

1. Call the customer at the scheduled point after the order (usually 7 to 14 days). [L1012.013]
2. Open with a personal thank-you for the order and say the call is a check-in to make sure everything arrived fine. [L1012.013]
3. Ask whether the customer is happy with the product. [L1012.013]
4. If the customer is satisfied, explain that reviews help the business serve customers better and ask whether they would leave a quick two-minute review. [L1012.013]
5. If the customer is unhappy, listen and try to resolve the problem on the call, since a resolved issue often produces a stronger review. [L1012.013]
6. Request a text review at minimum. [L1012.013]
7. Offer the option of a video review (via VideoPeel) and/or a photo of the customer with the product. [L1012.013]
8. Close the call and follow up with the email sequence that goes with the script. [L1012.013]

### Finding unhappy customers

- Callers must find out when a customer is unhappy, because customers often will not say so themselves. [L1012.016]
- A problem that gets resolved on the call can turn into a more credible five-star review that mentions the good service. [L1012.016]
- Ask whether the customer is happy with the product before asking for a review, so unhappy customers are identified first. [L1012.013]

### Starting new staff on calls

- Do not start new customer service staff on live calls straight away if the product is complex or technical. [L1012.012]
- Start new staff with outbound scripted calls to existing customers. This lets them learn the product and customer language first. [L1012.012]

## Upselling and cross-selling on calls

### Where phone upselling fits

- Phone upselling and cross-selling can increase store profit substantially, but it is optional and is a different style of selling from the core approach. A store with a net margin of about 30% can run without it. (Older advice, 2021.) [L0834.095]

### Upsell planner for agents

- Give every customer service agent the full upsell planner: the list of core products and their related upsells. This lets agents know which products to offer with which core product. If you handle service alone, the planner applies to you too. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1409.021]

### Answer first, then offer

- Answer the customer's question first, then offer the related upsell product. For example, answer a shipping question and then mention the related product that goes with the item. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1409.022]

### Relevance over frequency

- Offer upsells only where they fit the customer's purchase. Relevance matters more than offering every time, so skip the offer when it does not fit. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1409.026]

### Phone and chat upsell steps

Steps for customer service agents:

1. Answer the customer's question first. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1409.023]
2. Mention the related upsell product that pairs with the core product the customer is buying. [L1409.023]
3. Ask whether the customer wants to add it to the order. [L1409.023]
4. If the customer agrees on the phone, create the checkout for them and send it, or walk them through finding the product on the site, particularly when a deal applies. [L1409.023]
5. If the customer is in online chat, send a direct link to the product page or checkout. [L1409.023]
6. If a discount or special offer applies, give the customer the discount code or apply the offer. [L1409.023]

### Agent scripts and training

- Provide agents with a written script and instructions covering when and how to offer upsells. Build the upsell step into the customer service process or SOPs. Agents need practice before the upsell becomes routine. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1409.024]
- Upsells in customer service fail when agents have not been trained or when the step is not part of the service process. Practice the script with agents and make the upsell step a standard part of their workflow. (Older advice, 2021-22.) [L1409.025]

### Post-purchase calls and offers

- A post-purchase call should add a helpful offer only when a better product or benefit makes sense for the buyer. Calling a customer just to tell them they should have bought something else damages trust. [L1076.048]
- Case: a business owner with a sales background called every buyer after purchase for a few months, after selling the store.
  - The owner offered a different product, extended warranties and faster shipping over the phone. The owner had previously offered these on the site.
  - The owner saw sales climb steadily during that time.
  - The approach needs a team member or owner who is comfortable on the phone, and it takes little time. [L1076.049]

## Preparing for supplier calls

### Why phone beats email

- Phone communication works better than email because people connect through voice, so a call allows real-time discussion and problem-solving that the back-and-forth chains of email cannot provide. (Older: 2021-22.) [L0235.002]
- Call suppliers rather than relying on email, because a phone call gets a clear answer far more often. The lesson reports approval rates above 60% when calling suppliers, and email follow-up alone was less effective. (Older: 2021-22.) [L0458.038]
- Calling gives an immediate yes, no or call-back answer, which speeds up approvals. (Older: 2021.) [L0469.109]
- If a call is not possible, use email and follow up persistently. (Older: 2021.) [L0469.109]
- Use phone calls to supplier contacts as the default approach, because emails are easy to ignore and calls build a stronger connection. (2023.) [L0970.155]
- Call first and email second, because a phone call gets a yes or no faster than email. (Older: 2022.) [L0803.022]
- Call the supplier first and make your case by phone rather than email, because a call cuts through the noise and gets you to the decision maker faster. [L0928.016]
- Calling is faster than emailing for getting approved, especially when you need a direct answer. Pair calls with follow-up emails, since many suppliers only respond after a second contact. (Older: 2021.) [L1090.138]
- Phone calls to suppliers are the most efficient route to approval. (2024.) [L0836.057]

### Vetting suppliers

- Vet a supplier before calling: search the company name for reviews and reputation, and confirm they are sold on competitor sites. The call then only confirms the details. (Older: 2022.) [L0963.079]

### Building the call list

- Keep building the supplier list and collect all contact details during the holiday period. (Older: 2020.) [L0551.020]
- Build a contact list of at least 20 suppliers before you start calling. Not all of them will approve you from the first call. [L0933.031]
- Some suppliers need education about the business model, and approval can take many months. (Older: 2018.) [L1085.091]
- Prepare your own pitch script and expect a dialogue rather than a single call. (Older: 2018.) [L1085.091]
- Suppliers with strong brands are usually the hardest to get approved. (Older: 2018.) [L1085.092]
- Starting with silver-tier suppliers and building traffic and sales makes it easier to return to them later. (Older: 2018.) [L1085.092]

**Holiday-period plan (older: 2020)**

Source procedure, kept complete:

1. Keep building the supplier list and collect all contact details during the holiday period. [L0551.020]
2. Finish the demo store so it looks complete before you start calling. [L0551.020]
3. Start supplier calls on the first Monday after the holidays, when companies return to normal business. [L0551.020]
4. Call with the supplier sheet ready to go. [L0551.020]

Step 3 is tied to the return to normal business after the holidays. Timing for calls outside that window is covered under Timing and time zones below.

### Reviewing the supplier's website

- Before calling a supplier, review the supplier's own website and speak back to what it highlights about its brands, as if preparing for a job interview. (2023.) [L0855.160]

### Timing and time zones

- All supplier calls must occur during the supplier's business hours, even if this requires calling at inconvenient times from your location. (Older: 2021-22.) [L0235.007]
- When calling suppliers, call early on weekdays in the supplier's time zone, for example at 8:30 a.m. (2025.) [L1097.042]
- If no one answers, call back at 9:00 a.m. This was the fastest way to get through. (2025.) [L1097.042]
- Use a phone-based process for supplier contact: call first thing in the morning and follow up by phone or email. (2023.) [L0835.104]
- Contacting suppliers early in the day gives you a better chance of reaching the decision maker. (2023.) [L0835.104]
- Calls to suppliers, especially early in the morning, get through to decision makers more often than emails or calls at busy times of the day. (2023.) [L0970.157]
- If no replies come in, change the timing and test again. (2023.) [L0970.157]

**Where the timing sources differ**

- The 2020 holiday plan starts calls on the first Monday after the holidays. It applies to the post-holiday restart. [L0551.020]
- The 2023 and 2025 rules recommend early weekday morning calls in the supplier's time zone. They apply to routine calling. [L0835.104, L0970.157, L1097.042]
- Where the supplier's business hours and your location conflict, the business-hours rule takes priority. [L0235.007]

### Mindset before the call

- Fear of calling suppliers often comes from treating one deal as make-or-break. [L0701.036]
- Having several options lined up makes each call feel less critical, and the calmer energy that results makes others more willing to work with you without changing your words. [L0701.036]
- Present yourself as a partner who will bring them sales, not as a pestering retailer. Approach the call with the expectation that they are glad to hear from you. (Older: 2022.) [L0665.111]
- Supplier calls are normal conversations, not scripted interviews, so questions should be treated as a discussion and not as objections to overcome. [L0933.029]
- Only some of the questions covered here will come up on any given call. [L0933.029]
- Mistake: do not overthink supplier questions or read them as rejections. [L0933.030]
- Preparing answers in advance is useful, but a call should stay natural and confident. [L0933.030]
- Supplier calls are relaxed, informal conversations rather than hiring interviews, and no salary is offered. (Older: 2021.) [L0968.002]
- Prepare by learning about the company and expect questions about your business, but treat the call as a conversation rather than a test. (Older: 2021.) [L0968.002]
- Many new sellers get stuck calling suppliers. (2023.) [L0804.103]
- Making the calls in a single block, recording notes on each call and starting with the top of the list helps overcome the reluctance. (2023.) [L0804.103]
- Nervousness with senior decision-makers often comes from seeking their approval as if you had to beg for it. [L1206.045]
- Ask whether you would physically behave that way in the same situation. If you would not, the posture is a belief you can test and drop. [L1206.045]

### Nervousness and accent

- Accent or non-native English is not a barrier to getting supplier approvals. Suppliers want business relationships that benefit both sides. (Older: 2021.) [L0962.017]
- When making cold calls to suppliers, a non-native accent or nervousness can be named openly as part of your background, which reduces tension and builds trust. [L0832.057]
- Presenting this trait honestly often works better than hiding it. [L0832.057]

### Rehearsal and coaching practice

- Rehearse hard tasks like supplier cold calls with a coaching call before doing them alone. [L0832.035]
- This reduces nervousness and builds the skill over time. [L0832.035]
- Rehearse the script and practise on less important suppliers first. (2024.) [L0836.057]

**Mental rehearsal procedure (Source C)**

1. Before a sales call, list the questions and objections the prospect is most likely to raise. [L1206.044]
2. For each one, work out a clear, specific answer in your mind. [L1206.044]
3. Rehearse the full conversation in your imagination, including the prospect's objections and your replies. [L1206.044]
4. Repeat the rehearsal, especially for difficult objections, until your replies come easily before using them on real calls. [L1206.044]

## Running the supplier call

### Before the call

- Prepare a short script before the first call. The conversation feels less daunting when you have one. [L0771.054] (older advice, 2021-22)
- Keep the core call simple: pick up the phone, introduce yourself and your business, build a little rapport, and ask whether you can sell their products through your website. [L0771.054] (older advice, 2021-22)
- Plan the framework, not the words. Know the purpose of each part (introduction, planned launch, reason for choosing them, request for the application process) and phrase it in your own words on each call. [L0928.017] 
- Suppliers are busy and receive more requests as e-commerce grows, so the call must be ready before you dial. [L0929.004] (older advice, 2021-22)

### Reaching the right person

- Call the supplier using the phone number on their website to start the approval conversation. [L1085.088] (older advice, 2018)
- Use this first-contact procedure:
  1. Introduce yourself briefly and say you want the person who handles working with online retailers. [L0968.001] (older advice, 2021)
  2. Wait for their reply. [L0968.001] (older advice, 2021)
  3. If they are not that person, ask who you should speak to. In very small companies the owner often answers and is the right contact. [L0968.001] (older advice, 2021)
- When calling a supplier for an account or referral, mention the existing supplier relationship and ask for the specific contact who handles approvals. [L0468.178] (older advice, 2020)
- Use this procedure for account requests (Source B):
  1. Call the supplier's phone line and ask for the person who handles new retail or dealer accounts. [L0458.037] (older advice, 2021-22)
  2. Introduce yourself and your business, and say that you have a website built for their products. [L0458.037] (older advice, 2021-22)
  3. Ask whether you can sell their products through your website and whether they drop-ship to customers. [L0458.037] (older advice, 2021-22)
  4. Ask for the online dealer application or product information, and note the name and direction given. [L0458.037] (older advice, 2021-22)
  5. Send a follow-up email after the call to confirm the conversation, and record the date and outcome in your tracker. [L0458.037] (older advice, 2021-22)
- When you get no decision maker, ask for a sales representative. Keep the call short and make sure your message is clear each time. [L0941.097]
- Handle a gatekeeper this way (older advice, 2021-22) [L0929.013]:
  1. Briefly state that you want to talk about becoming a retailer or reseller for their products. [L0929.013]
  2. Let them direct you to the right person, such as the sales contact who handles new retailer requests. If that person is not available, ask for their mobile number. [L0929.013]
  3. If you reach the right person, let them tell you what they need next and respond to that. [L0929.013]
  4. Do not give a long pitch to a gatekeeper, since they cannot approve you. [L0929.013]
- Supplier approval calls should explain why the niche fits the supplier's brand, ask about their products, and ask who handles approvals. [L1111.166] (older advice, 2020)

### Opening the call

Use this opening script, filling in the placeholders (Source B, older advice, 2021-22):

```
Hi, it's [Your name] calling from [Your company name]. How are you?
[Wait for their reply, then continue:] We are an online retailer of [your niche or product category]. We have looked at your products, we like them, and we would like to talk with you about becoming a retailer for them.
[Stop talking and let them respond. Do not fill the silence.]
```
[L0929.012]

### Explaining the model without the word dropshipping

- Avoid the word dropshipping on calls because some people have negative views of it. Describe the model in plain terms such as direct-to-customer or warehouse-direct-to-customer instead. [L0929.015] (older advice, 2021-22)
- Some suppliers avoid working with dropshippers because of bad experiences. Do not use the term in the first contact. Present yourself as an additional sales channel that brings new customers. [L1085.090] (older advice, 2018)
- Use this model explanation, filling in the placeholders (Source B, older advice, 2021-22):

```
Say: Look, we're an online-only retailer and we work on a direct-to-customer basis. If you are at your computer, you can have a quick look at [your website] while we talk. Here is how it works: we build and maintain our website, upload your products to it, handle all the marketing and customer service, and generate the sales. When we make a sale, we send you an order for that product, we pay for it upfront, and you ship it directly from your warehouse to the customer.
[Stop talking after this and let them respond.]
```
[L0929.014]

- Spelling out the model prevents confusion, shows you will not buy in bulk, and sets the basis for the request. (older advice, 2021-22) [L0929.016]
- Mentioning upfront payment in that explanation lowers the supplier's risk immediately. A zero-risk offer is the easiest way to win agreement. (older advice, 2021-22) [L0929.016]
- The same call approach works in any country; it is not specific to one market. (older advice, 2021-22) [L0929.011]

### Stating the launch date

Sources give slightly different windows. Use the table to choose:

| Source | Recommended window | Upper limit | Note |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source A, pitching a new store [L0928.019] | Roughly two to four weeks away, or up to about one month | Never more than two months | A longer timeline makes the supplier treat the store as not relevant right now |
| Source B, opening call (older advice, 2021-22) [L0929.017] | About one month away | None stated | Launching a few days earlier or later is fine |
| Source A, script guidance [L0928.017] | A few weeks to about one month ahead | Never more than two months | Applies to the window the supplier should expect |

- Use a real launch date, not a vague one. [L0928.019]
- Use the window in the table above; the shorter windows fit most calls, and the two-month ceiling is the hard limit. [L0928.017, L0928.019, L0929.017]
- If the store is almost ready, describe it as being in its final touches before launch, not in beta testing. [L0855.161]
- Present the store's future potential, not its current results. Do not present a store as having sales or achievements it does not yet have. (older advice, 2020) [L1111.167]

### Positioning a store with no business history

- If this is the first store, say so honestly. Then explain the niche opportunity, the search demand, the brand quality, and why you want to sell that supplier's products. [L0855.159]
- Use the pronoun I when you run the business alone, instead of we. Use whatever you are comfortable with, but do not claim a team you do not have. (older advice, 2022) [L0803.091]

### Checking US distribution

Use this script for a supplier with unknown US distribution (Source A, older advice, 2022). Replace the brackets and keep the question about shipping:

```
Hello, my name is [name] from [store name]. I noticed your products are listed on many US websites. Do you have distribution in the United States, a warehouse, or a fulfillment partner, and how does your shipping to US customers work?
```
[L0854.108]

### Building rapport

- Ask casual questions about the brand's history, goals, and best products. These questions build a relationship and give you data for your marketing. (older advice, 2021) [L0801.163]
- Build a relationship rather than pitching only price. (older advice, 2020) [L1111.166]

### Making the first request

- Your only request at this point is the product data: the price list, product images, and any useful technical specifications. Ask how soon they can send it to you. [L0929.018]
- Accept any delivery method for the product data, such as a shared cloud folder link, emailed files, a login to a dealer portal, or downloading images from their website. Confirm you will get access; do not insist on a format. [L0929.019] (older advice, 2021-22)

### Tone

- Sound genuinely excited. A flat or disinterested tone makes the supplier less likely to approve you, but do not overdo it. [L0928.006]
- Stay calm, friendly, and respectful even if the supplier does not say what you hoped. Treat them with the same courtesy you would expect yourself. (older advice, 2021-22) [L0929.005]

### Brevity

- Get to the point quickly and say as little as needed. Long rambling calls and long emails waste the supplier's time and weaken your chances. (older advice, 2021-22) [L0929.004]
- Keep the sales call short, concise, and tight. Follow the framework by introducing yourself and your company, then stating which brand you want to carry. [L0936.007]
- When calling suppliers, keep the call short and make sure your message is clear each time. [L0941.097]

### Using scripts as guides

- Scripts are guidelines, not text to read aloud. Use the same key points on every call, phrased naturally. [L0928.017, L0928.018]
- Reading a supplier script word for word sounds unnatural and makes the call feel scripted. [L0928.018]
- Use the same framework in your own words instead of reading a call script word for word, which sounds unnatural and robotic to suppliers. [L0936.008]
- Use the script as a guide, not word for word, but cover the same key points concisely. Let the supplier do most of the talking, hear what they need, and then respond to it. (older advice, 2021-22) [L0929.033]
- Use the supplier call script as a guide and speak naturally. Keep the questions consistent across calls. (older advice, 2022) [L0963.080]

### After a yes

Follow this procedure (older advice, 2021-22):

1. Thank them and confirm when they will send the product data. [L0929.021]
2. Exchange contact details if not already recorded. [L0929.021]
3. Record the outcome in your supplier sheet. [L0929.021]
4. Follow up if the data does not arrive by the date they promised. [L0929.021]
5. Move on to the next call. [L0929.021]

## Handling supplier questions, objections and negotiation

### Opening supplier calls and pitching your store

- Lead with a benefit to the supplier, not a request. You bring traffic, exposure and sales; they only ship orders and answer emails. Keep every conversation pleasant and avoid negativity. [L0962.016]
- Differentiate with a specific reason. Suppliers choose between many callers, so a general claim about being reliable is weaker than a named product attribute. Use this formula:
  1. Name a specific attribute of the supplier's product that stands out from copies in the market.
  2. Show that you researched the brand.
  3. State how your store will serve their customers with care.
  - Furniture example: "Your outdoor sofas use weather-resistant frames that most competitors copy without the same build quality, and we want to show that quality to buyers who need durable outdoor furniture."
  - Skincare example: "Your formulas avoid the fragrance additives that most shelf brands use, and our store targets shoppers with sensitive skin who are looking for exactly that." [L0933.035]
- Show credibility and make the pitch easy to act on. Some suppliers hold back a large amount of their trust until an account is set up, so offer flexible shipping arrangements to reduce the barrier to working with you. [L1441.032]
- Prepare a short paragraph describing the marketing channels you will use to sell their products, and be ready to read it out when asked how you will market them. [L0929.028]

### Handling hesitation and refusals

- Never accept the first no. Politely ask why, because refusals are often quick exits, a busy moment or a need for more time, and the underlying objection can often be resolved. Hanging up without digging can cost you your best supplier. [L0929.010]
- Do not pressure for approval on the spot. Pushing damages a relationship you want to last for years. Many buyers want a day or so to think, and pressure makes them less likely to agree. Give them an easy way out of the call so they do not feel trapped. [L0929.023]
- Where a supplier is not taking new online retailers right now, follow this procedure:
  1. Politely ask why there is a limit, for example a supply shortage, limited product volume or a temporary issue.
  2. If the reason is temporary, offer to set up now but delay your first sales by about a month, so their current supply flow is not disturbed.
  3. If they still refuse, thank them, say you would like to work together later and leave your contact details.
  4. Ask them to contact you if a retailer spot opens up, and offer to start selling straight away.
  5. Record a callback date in your supplier sheet (for example three months later) and make that call. [L0929.025]
- Look for an arrangement that works for both sides rather than insisting on a rigid setup. Starting small and proving sales lets you ask for better terms later, while a hard line at the start can end the relationship before it begins. [L0929.032]

### Deposits, upfront payment and pre-purchase requests

- When a supplier asks for a deposit or pre-purchase, tell them you need to see sales first and propose a test. This reduces risk and keeps the deal open. [L0801.164]
- Upfront payment removes the supplier's financial risk. With credit terms they could be left chasing an unpaid invoice 30 days later, so zero risk is the most effective way to get a yes. [L0929.009]

### Answering "what's in it for us?"

When a supplier asks what is in it for them, offer these three benefits:

| Benefit for the supplier | What it gives them |
|---|---|
| Payment for each order upfront | Reliable cash flow and no late payments to chase |
| Access to new online customers | Their products reach new buyers and their market share grows |
| Fast route for excess stock | A quick way to move excess or discontinued stock |

- Suppliers often offer up to 40% off excess stock if you promote it actively. [L0929.030]

### Wholesale discounts, MAP and margins

- Do not ask for a discount in the first contact with a new supplier. Ask about pricing tiers and let the supplier name its own volume-based pricing before offering anything. [L1281.044]
- On a first call, after receiving the supplier's price list, follow this sequence:
  1. Thank them and say everything looks fine.
  2. Explain that you always look for the best prices so you can put the most money into advertising for every brand you sell.
  3. Ask whether they offer tiered pricing, such as lower rates above a certain dollar amount or a set number of units per month, and what the pricing would be at those levels.
  4. Stop and let the supplier answer.
  5. If the supplier has no tiers, add: most brands you work with have arrangements like that, so would they be open to discussing terms or incentives for selling more of their products? [L1281.043]
- When asked for a wholesale discount, explain the MAP margin reality and ask whether wholesale can be negotiated so that wholesale is half of MAP, rather than asking only for cheaper pricing. [L0665.115]
- If the gap between wholesale and MAP is too narrow to promote the brand heavily, use this email:

```
Hello [Supplier contact name], while going through all our price sheets, I found that the gap between wholesale and MAP is too narrow for us to promote your [brand name] line heavily. We'd genuinely like to do that, but we need a bigger margin to fund marketing for your products. Is there any kind of incentive pricing available? Do you have volume discounts or tiered pricing, such as a percentage off wholesale once we hit a set sales target?
Thanks,
[Your name]
[Company name]
[Phone number]
```
[L0835.047]

- For a phone version of the same request, use this script:

```
Hi, this is [your name] from [your brand]. We were looking over the price lists you sent us. We really want to put a real ad budget behind these products and become one of your top retailers, but the margins aren't where we need them to be. Do you have any incentive programs where, if retailers reach a certain number of units or a certain sales volume, wholesale prices get discounted? If not, please let me know so we can decide our next steps.
```
[L0970.156]

- When a supplier asks about private label, answer in terms of the products that can be relabeled, not as a unique product. [L0855.162]

### Shipping costs that erase the MAP margin

- If shipping costs wipe out the margin at MAP, use this call script:

```
Hi [supplier contact name], this is [your name] from [your store name]. We are interested in selling [product name] and we are ready to move forward. It costs us about $[shipping cost] to ship one [product name], and if we sell at MAP of $[MAP price] we lose about $[loss per sale] on every sale. I can see that [competitor 1], [competitor 2] and [competitor 3] are all selling at MAP. Do you know which carrier they ship with, or do they have better wholesale pricing? Can you help us find a shipping method or wholesale price that lets us make money at MAP?
```
[L1085.085]

- A supplier usually has all the information about how other sellers ship products. Ask them directly how competitors achieve profitable shipping instead of guessing. [L1085.093]

### Checking MAP compliance and pricing discrepancies

- If you see a product listed below the MAP, ask the supplier to confirm before assuming an error on your side:

```
Hi [Supplier contact name], I am not sure if I am misreading your price list. Your MAP for [product name] is [MAP price], but I see this product listed for [lower price] at [link]. Can you confirm whether I have the MAP wrong, and let me know what is going on?
```
[L1111.169]

### Promotions that conflict with MAP

- Before running a bonus promotion that may conflict with MAP, ask for written approval:

```
Hello [SUPPLIER CONTACT], I'd like to run a promotion on our store. When a customer buys [PRODUCT X], they also receive [BONUS PRODUCT Y] free. I know this may conflict with your MAP policy, so I'm asking for your approval before launching. Could you confirm in writing whether you approve this promotion? Thank you, [YOUR NAME] [STORE NAME].
```
[L0855.157]

- If the supplier declines, look for a similar product to use as the bonus instead. [L0855.157]

### Which other brands you work with

- Do not lie about other brands. If asked, name only the suppliers you are actually in an approval process with, meaning you have already submitted an application or were told one would be sent. [L1085.089]

## Supplier follow-up cadence and record keeping

### Day-by-day contact plan

- Start with a phone call on day one whenever the supplier has a phone number. Calls were the quickest route to a yes compared with waiting for email replies. [L0936.005]
- The day one call has two goals: find out the supplier's application process, and identify the decision maker at the company. [L0936.006]
- Day three of the contact plan is another phone call. [L0936.012]
- The full sequence runs to day seven as a one-week follow-up plan that mixes calls and emails. [L0936.012]
- Keep following up using the plan until you get a clear yes or no. You can stop early if you reach the right person on the first call. [L0936.013]
- Do not stop outreach after one unanswered call or email. Suppliers often respond only after repeated follow-ups, so continue through the full sequence. [L0936.014]

### Call first, then email: sequencing

- Call the phone number listed for the supplier first. [L0929.002]
- Send a follow-up email confirming what you discussed. [L0235.004]
- When a supplier does not answer your emails, call instead, because a phone call is the most reliable way to be heard and to get a point of contact. [L1110.006]
- *Older advice (2019).*
- Procedure for an email that went unanswered:
  1. Call the supplier. [L1110.006]
  2. Mention the earlier email and roughly when you sent it. [L1110.006]
  3. Follow the call script from the course. [L1110.006]
- Keep following up by phone and leave voicemails, because many brands return calls later. [L0857.068]
- If a pitch script gets no results, make it specific by explaining how you will drive sales for the brand and how you will handle its customer service. [L0857.068]

### Repeated calls for unanswered suppliers

- Procedure for a supplier that has not replied:
  1. Keep calling if nobody answers, since a persistent caller usually reaches someone. [L0803.023]
  2. If there is no reply after a few days, send a follow-up in the same email thread so the messages stack. [L0803.023]
  3. If still no response, find supplier relations staff on LinkedIn and contact them there. [L0803.023]
- *Older advice (2022).*
- When suppliers do not answer calls, keep following up. Suppliers with limited stock may later accept new dealers, so approved products should be uploaded while contact continues. [L0963.078]
- *Older advice (2022).*
- Supplier approvals often need repeated calls because companies get busy. Keep following up by phone and log each conversation's notes in a tracking sheet. [L1279.085]
- *Older advice (2021).*

### Follow-up scripts

#### Follow-up call for a supplier that has not replied

```
Hi, this is [your name] from [your store name]. I sent an email yesterday to the dealer contact at [supplier domain] about becoming a retailer for [brand name], and I just wanted to make sure you received it. Would you have a few minutes to talk about how we could work together and what the next steps are for approval?
```

[L0470.020]

#### Follow-up call for a supplier that said it is too busy

```
Hi [Supplier contact name], this is [your name] from [store name]. We spoke [timeframe] ago and you asked me to follow up. Our store launched on [date] and we are now showing up for the main keywords in [niche] on Google Shopping. We are selling for [brand A], [brand B] and [brand C], and business is going well. We would like to add you to our lineup so you get this exposure too. When would be a good time to talk?
```

[L0665.112]

*Older advice (2022).*

#### Follow-up call on an application

```
Hi [supplier contact name], this is [your name] from [store name] calling about your application. I wanted to follow up on [previous step, e.g. the application sent on date]. We have [new progress, e.g. grown traffic and a larger email list] and are excited to list your products. What do I need to do next to move forward, and when can we get started?
```

[L1279.084]

*Older advice (2021).*

### Hesitant suppliers and callback dates

- Procedure for a supplier who is hesitant but has not said no:
  1. Do not push for an immediate decision. [L0929.022]
  2. Ask them to think it over for a few days. [L0929.022]
  3. Agree on a specific callback day and say you will call then. [L0929.022]
  4. Send a follow-up email confirming the conversation and including your contact details. [L0929.022]
  5. Note the callback date in your supplier sheet and in your calendar. [L0929.022]
  6. Call back on that date. If they ask you to end the call, end it respectfully and move on. [L0929.022]
- *Older advice (2021-22).*
- Persistence pays. A supplier who believes you will call back is more likely to decide, and a follow-up email keeps you in front of them. Always make the callback you promised. [L0929.024]
- *Older advice (2021-22).*

### Final offers and follow-up dates

- When a supplier declines, make a polite final offer and ask for a follow-up date. Recording that date in your notes gives you a reason to return with results. [L0801.162]
- *Older advice (2021).*

### Notes and tracking sheets

- Keep notes during or right after every supplier call. You will make many calls and cannot remember what each supplier said, and calling back to ask again makes you look unprofessional. [L0929.003]
- *Older advice (2021-22).*
- Procedure for each supplier call:
  1. Record the date of your request call. [L0929.002]
  2. Record what they said about supplying their products, their pricing and anything else specific to them, during or right after the call. [L0929.002]
  3. Record the name of the person you spoke to; this person becomes your contact. [L0929.002]
  4. Record any direct email, direct line or mobile number they give you for follow-up. [L0929.002]
  5. Mark the supplier as Approved (Yes) or not (No). [L0929.002]
  6. Move on to the next supplier. [L0929.002]
- *Older advice (2021-22).*
- Log each conversation's notes in a tracking sheet. [L1279.085]
- *Older advice (2021).*

## Other supplier channels: forms, email, events and in-person pitches

### Online dealer forms and follow-up

Older advice, 2021-2022 (Source B) and 2022 (Source A). Check against current supplier practice before use.

1. Submit the online form on the supplier's website. [L0235.009]
2. Wait 24 hours. [L0235.009]
3. If you receive no response, make a phone call. [L0235.009]

When following up by phone after a form, use this opening (older source, 2021-2022):

```
I'm John from Oz Off Grid. I submitted your online application form about a day ago and wanted to reach out to follow up and discuss it with your team.
```
[L0235.010]

Start supplier contact with the online dealer application form when it is available, and call during free time. The online form takes less time and can be completed in the evening. (Older source, 2022.) [L0665.113]

### Form or phone first: when each applies

These two sources give different first steps. Both are older (2021-2022). Use the phone when a number is available, and the form when calls are not possible.

| Situation | First step | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Online form available, you can call in free time | Form first, then call after 24 hours if no response | [L0665.113, L0235.009] |
| Phone number available | Call first, because direct conversation is more effective than email | [L0665.114] |
| Calls not possible | Fill out the online form | [L0665.114] |

Call a supplier rather than only submitting an online form. A call lets you explain your store, ask for the dealer application, and get the contact moving quickly. (Older source, 2021.) [L0801.161]

### Introduction emails

When first contacting a supplier by email (older source, 2022), a short introduction is enough to get a referral to the right contact if it:
- names your store,
- says you want to sell their products, and
- asks for the person who opens accounts for internet retailers. [L0969.116]

### Pitching in person or on a call

Older source, 2018. Follow these steps:

1. Think about two things first: what the supplier cares about and how they can trust you. [L1085.086]
2. Be honest about where your store is. You can say you are learning from a training program and are just getting started. [L1085.086]
3. Explain the marketing you will use to bring them sales: Google Product Listing Ads, retargeting, exit-intent capture, a follow-up email sequence, YouTube and industry-specific platforms. [L1085.086]
4. Make clear that customer service is your first priority and that you are building a long-term business. [L1085.086]
5. Keep the focus on how you will bring the supplier more sales, not on the money you expect to make. [L1085.086]

Use this opening for a first meeting, adapted to your situation (older source, 2018):

```
I appreciate you meeting with me. I am [your name] and I am starting an online store focused on [niche]. I am still early in the process and I want to be honest about that. I am learning e-commerce from [training program or mentor name], and I plan to bring you more sales by using [traffic channel 1] and [traffic channel 2] to reach new customers. Customer service is my first priority, and I want to build a business that customers come back to for years.
```
[L1085.087]

### Trade events

Older source, 2020. Follow these steps:

1. Attend supplier trade events and meet the representatives in person. [L1111.168]
2. Explain why your store is a good fit. [L1111.168]
3. Ask questions about their products. [L1111.168]
4. Identify the person who can make approval decisions. [L1111.168]
5. Follow up with a short email after the conversation. [L1111.168]

### Competitor calls

Calling a competitor by phone is a quick way to check whether it has a showroom or store. Ask for the opening hours and whether a visit is possible. (Older source, 2020.) [L0551.021]

## Cold calling local businesses and agency clients

### Niche choice and target selection

- Choose a niche with healthy budgets and no shortage of money, such as dentists. [L1185.036]
- Dentists are an example of a local business type that is often not thinking about ads or growth in business terms, which affects how the first conversation must be led. [L0440.055]

### Cold email first

- Send a cold email before calling, so the business has already seen the agency's name when the call arrives. [L0440.054]
- The email should be short, open with one specific observation about the business's current online presence or ads, and ask for a 10-minute call. [L0440.068]

### Call procedure

1. Send a cold email first to introduce the agency. [L0440.054]
2. Call the business. If they are busy, remind them that the email was sent. [L0440.054]
3. Ask for 5 to 10 minutes to discuss their ads or online presence. [L0440.054]
4. Ask about their goals for the coming year, for example more clients, fewer low-value treatments, or more high-value services. [L0440.054]
5. Present how running ads can help reach those goals. [L0440.054]
6. Propose a meeting, ideally at the business's office, to close the sale. [L0440.054]

### Opening the conversation

- Use a shared-interest opener. For example, note that the business owner and the agency both sell a product that solves a customer problem, and that the agency wants to help the business sell that product online. [L0440.056]
- Local business owners are often not thinking about ads or growth in business terms, so the operator must lead the conversation toward growth and explain why ads and product offers matter. [L0440.055]

### Leading the owner toward growth

- Ask the owner about their goals for the coming year, then link ads to those goals. [L0440.054]
- When the business already has an online shop, show a demo store with an easier checkout, relevant apps and automated customer emails, so the gaps in their shop become visible. [L1017.039]
- Quote a price based on what the client is able to pay. [L1017.039]

### Payment plan offers for expensive treatments

- Offer local businesses a payment plan for expensive treatments, such as Invisalign, so that customers can pay monthly instead of a single large sum. [L0440.057]
- Let a third-party installment provider take over collection of the payments to reduce the risk for the business. [L0440.057]
- Example from a Swiss dentist's competitor: the offer was Invisalign on installments of about 60 francs per month, instead of a single payment of 3,000 to 5,000 francs. The installment provider paid the full amount to the dentist upfront and collected the monthly payments, charging late fees if payments were missed. [L0440.058]

### Cold call and email scripts

Use this prompt to generate the scripts. Replace the bracketed placeholders before use.

```
Write me a cold calling script and a cold calling email script for my [type of agency, e.g. digital marketing agency] that offers [services, e.g. Facebook ad management and website design] to [target business, e.g. dentists] in [city]. The email should be short, open with one specific observation about the business's current online presence or ads, and ask for a 10-minute call. The phone script should be in the order it will be spoken and include: an opening line that introduces the agency and the reason for calling, one question about the business's goal for the next year, one sentence on how ads can help reach that goal, and a request for a 10-minute meeting at the business's office. Use simple, friendly language without jargon, and give me the script and the email as separate sections.
```
[L0440.068]

### Lead magnet and monetisation

- Offer a free sample of an improved website as a lead magnet. [L1185.036]
- Upsell ad management once the website is sold. [L1185.036]
- Charge a referral or per-lead fee for every client introduced. [L1185.036]

### Delegated influencer outreach

- Influencer outreach can be delegated to an assistant, using a cold-calling script and a course in the resources section. [L1432.038]
- In the speaker's case, outreach led to two influencer partnerships. [L1432.038]
- A DM alone rarely gets a response, because creators often do not see DMs. Combine the DM with an email and a comment on their latest video. [L1379.046]

## High Probability prospecting calls

### Where prospecting fits in the approach

- The approach has three phases, in this order: High Probability Prospecting, High Probability Selling, and High Probability Closing. [L0770.074]
  - Prospecting: make a short phone contact with a clearly stated offer, let prospects disqualify themselves, and set a meeting only with someone who wants the offer and intends to buy. [L0770.074]
  - Selling: first build trust and respect in a relationship phase, then ask the discovery and disqualification questions in fixed order, letting the prospect end the process at any point. [L0770.074]
  - Closing: define the prospect's Conditions of Satisfaction, obtain a commitment to buy if they are met, and only then present a proposal or demonstration. [L0770.074]
- There are usually far more prospects than a sales team can visit, but at any given time only a small share are ready to buy. Contact as many prospects as possible, briefly, to find that small group, and spend meeting time only on them. [L0770.076]

### Writing the opening offer

- Keep the offer under 45 words, including greeting and introduction. Write it in your own words so that it makes sense to you. [L0770.013]
- Deliver it in a neutral, unemotional tone, because a convincing tone creates resistance even when the words are right. [L0770.013]
- Benchmarks from practice:
  - One seller's offer went through three rounds of trial calls and settled at 34 words. It was later sharpened further based on prospect responses. [L0770.014]
  - Another seller cut a 59-word offer to 42 words and saw better results. Shorter offers generally perform better. [L0770.014]
- Opening offer template for a cold call, filled in and kept under 45 words:

```
Hello, this is [your name] from [company name]. We [concrete description of what you provide, with one specific benefit or measurable result, e.g. the product type and what it does for the buyer]. Is that something you want for [the prospect's product line, business or situation]?
```

  Deliver it in a neutral tone and take the prospect's answer as it comes. [L0770.015]

- Formula for a cold-call offer:
  1. Name yourself and your company.
  2. State concretely what you provide.
  3. Add one specific benefit, coverage detail, or measurable result.
  4. Ask a yes-or-no question about whether the prospect wants it. [L0770.016]
- The question keeps the prospect in control and makes a clear no easy. [L0770.016]
- Own examples of the formula:
  - *This is Mark from Cleanline Office Services. We clean commercial kitchens after hours, which in our clients' experience cuts grease-related inspection failures roughly in half. Is that something you want for your kitchen?* [L0770.016]
  - *This is Lena from Pressgrid Print. We produce custom labels in runs of 500 to 5,000 with a proof sent the same day. Is that something you want for your product line?* [L0770.016]

### Running the call

- Follow this sequence on a High Probability prospecting call: [L0770.012]
  1. State your offer clearly in no more than 45 words, counting the greeting and your introduction. [L0770.012]
  2. Check whether the prospect wants what you are offering. [L0770.012]
  3. If he says yes, ask whether he would like to set up a meeting aimed at doing business. [L0770.012]
  4. If he is not ready at that point, book a new call for a time he chooses, and get his commitment to move forward then. [L0770.012]
  5. End the call on any negative answer. Arrange a callback only if he states he will be a qualified prospect at a specific later time, and make clear that it is completely fine for him to say no whenever he hesitates. [L0770.012]
  6. Disqualify anyone who does not want your offer or will not buy it from you. [L0770.012]
- Two signs that you have slipped into selling on a prospecting call: you feel stress during the call, or the call runs longer than three to four minutes. When either happens, stop pitching and return to asking questions. [L0770.018]

### Qualifying questions

- Collect the following from the prospect before any appointment, in this order: [L0770.019]
  1. Does he want this product?
  2. Does he want to arrange an appointment?
  3. If not now, when?
  4. If not now, does he want you to check back later?
  5. Why does he want to meet at this time?
  6. What would he like to accomplish at the meeting?
- Add further disqualifying questions when the situation calls for them. [L0770.019]

### Handling vague and negative answers

- If a prospect answers with "that sounds interesting", "maybe", "I don't know", "I don't think so" or "I'll consider it", reply in a flat tone: [L0770.020]

```
Does that mean you want what I'm offering, or not?
```

- Treat a no as a clear answer and close the call politely. Do not argue, add benefits, or sell harder. [L0770.020]
- If a prospect asks a question you cannot answer well yet, such as why he should switch when he is happy with his current supplier, use one of these replies in a flat tone: [L0770.022]

```
I don't have a satisfactory answer to that yet. What answer would make sense to you?
```

```
It doesn't sound like this is a good fit for you. Is my offer something you want, or not?
```

  Choose the reply that fits the situation and let the prospect answer. [L0770.022]

- A statement that does not answer your question, such as "I'm not interested", is noise rather than a real answer. Do not respond with a sales pitch. [L0770.023]
  - Ask a clarifying question he can answer, such as whether he is the person who decides on this, and keep the conversation on your questions. [L0770.023]
  - Disqualify him only when he clearly says he does not need, want, or can afford the offer. [L0770.023]
- Interest has no sales value because it is not a commitment. Enthusiasm and direct, quick answers are better signs of a qualified prospect than polite interest. [L0770.024]
- Ask yes-or-no questions that include the option of no, such as whether something is what he wants or not. A clear option to decline reduces resistance and makes the prospect responsible for his own choice. [L0770.025]

### Information requests and materials

- If a prospect asks you to send information, reply in a neutral tone: [L0770.021]

```
When someone asks for information, it often means the conversation is ending politely. If that is your intention, just tell me and that's fine. If you do want the details, tell me what you would need to decide so I can see whether it makes sense to send them.
```

- Send materials only when the prospect wants the offer, needs the information, and is likely to buy after reviewing it. [L0770.021]
- Do not send unsolicited brochures or samples to cold prospects. Keep unsolicited mail for a mass mailing sent two or three times a year, and send individual material only to prospects who have confirmed interest. [L0770.069]

### Finding the right contact

- When you need the right person at a company, first ask the front desk for whoever handles the product area, such as packaging design. [L0770.067]
  - Many switchboards only release the marketing or sales manager's name. Ask for that person and let them point you to the correct contact. [L0770.067]
  - If you still cannot reach the decision-maker, the sales department is a usable alternative route. [L0770.067]
- In companies with several product lines, each line's product manager often owns packaging or purchasing decisions for that line. Identify the manager of each line separately instead of relying on one central contact. [L0770.068]

### Scheduling the meeting

- Never try to sell the appointment. Ask whether he wants to meet to see if your offer fits his needs. Then let him propose the time, and ask him what he wants to accomplish, since a prospect who does not commit to a meeting has disqualified himself. [L0770.017]
- Scheduling a sales meeting by phone: [L0770.070]
  1. Set a tentative date for the meeting, usually a few weeks ahead if the prospect names that timing. [L0770.070]
  2. Ask what the meeting should accomplish and whether the decision-maker should attend. [L0770.070]
  3. Call the day before to confirm the time and the attendees. [L0770.070]
  4. If the prospect does not confirm, treat the appointment as disqualified and do not chase it. [L0770.070]

### Ending a call with a disqualified prospect

- Close politely and do not argue. Say you will only call again if new developments fit his stated needs, and do not try to convert him. [L0770.081]

## High Probability relationship building and discovery

### Relationship phase: purpose and sequence

- Do not discuss your product during relationship building. Your purpose is to learn who the prospect is, what motivates him and how he reached his current role, so you can decide whether you trust and respect him. If you do not trust him, leave politely, even if you cannot yet say why. [L0770.030]
- The relationship phase usually happens in the first meeting, and there is no fixed script or question list. The point is to let the conversation produce the information you need, so the exact questions depend on what the prospect says. [L0770.035]
- Prospects also judge the salesperson during relationship building, and trust shows through how you behave rather than what you say. A relationship of trust and respect gives you an advantage over competitors, because most buyers prefer to deal with people they trust. [L0770.034]
- Do not go on with a long relationship phase when the prospect has not yet shown trust or respect. Leaving early costs little, while investing time in someone you do not trust wastes the rest of the process. [L0770.045]

### When the prospect wants to skip the relationship phase

Use this in a flat, unemotional tone when a prospect in the relationship phase wants to jump straight into business:

```
Before we talk about my product, I like to learn how my customers operate, because that tells me how to serve them. I also need to find out whether I trust and respect the people I work with, and you have the same chance to judge me. So, are you willing to continue this kind of conversation, or would you rather I leave?
```

If he chooses to leave, end the visit politely and treat him as a low-probability prospect. [L0770.071]

### Opening the relationship

- To open a relationship, make a neutral observation about something visible or known, such as the building, the location or the company, and attach a question to it. Then base each follow-up on the prospect's last answer rather than a fixed list. [L0770.031]
  - Example: The loading area here is unusually wide. Was it built for this kind of product flow? [L0770.031]
  - Example: You mentioned the new site opened last spring. What made you move the team there? [L0770.031]
- Use open-ended questions while building the relationship, such as why, what did you do, how did you handle that, and was that something you wanted to do. Open questions let the prospect explain himself instead of answering yes or no. [L0770.032]
- Prospects tend to answer almost any authentic question truthfully when they sense you genuinely want the answer and are not manipulating them. Sincere interest cannot be faked, and prospects will cut short a conversation if they sense you are only going through the motions. [L0770.033]
- Answering a personal disclosure with an unrelated small-talk question, such as about family or hobbies, signals that you are not really interested and damages trust. Respond with a follow-up on what he just said, such as asking why it happened or how he handled it. [L0770.079]

### Listening and note-taking

- Ask a question, then listen to the full answer before thinking about your next question. If an answer is incomplete, ask a follow-up to clarify it for yourself and sometimes for the prospect. [L0770.027]
- Keep your own talking to about 25 percent of a meeting. If you are talking more than that, the meeting is probably going badly; ask why the prospect is unresponsive, and end the meeting if you cannot fix it, unless he is naturally quiet. [L0770.028]
- Take complete notes at every contact, recording the prospect's facts and opinions in his exact words. Exact wording is valuable later when you define his requirements, and it shows him that you value what he says. Missing details from a first meeting are hard to recover later. [L0770.026]

### Handling negativity

Deal with anger, sarcasm, threats, abuse or any other negativity before anything else. Speak in a flat, neutral tone, without judging and without sympathy.

1. Say neutrally that he seems upset. [L0770.029]
2. If he is still upset after explaining why, repeat the observation in the same flat tone, without stressing any word. [L0770.029]
3. If he is still upset, suggest that you discuss the matter at another time. [L0770.029]
4. If he calms down, continue the conversation. If he becomes upset again, return to step 1 and keep your tone even. [L0770.029]
5. If he stays upset, tell him you are not willing to meet right now because it would not serve either of you, and ask whether he wants to schedule another appointment or not. [L0770.029]

- Do not respond with anger to a low-probability prospect. He is simply not a fit, so recognize it, end the meeting politely and move on to the next prospect. [L0770.044]

### Discovery and disqualification questions

Use the wording below in this fixed order, swapping "this product" for your own product or service, and do not mention your company by name. [L0770.036]

1. **Need:** Why do you need this product? [L0770.036]
2. **Want:** Do you want it? If yes, ask why; if no, end the meeting. [L0770.036]
3. **Financial:** This product will cost about [price]; are you prepared to spend that? [L0770.036]
4. **Time:** If you decide to proceed, when would you want this to start, and what happens if it doesn't start then? [L0770.036]
5. **Decision-makers:** When you make a decision like this, who do you usually talk it over with? Then ask whether he'll let you speak with them before you prepare a proposal. [L0770.036]
6. **Authority:** If you went ahead, who else would have to agree? Handle this the same way as decision-makers. [L0770.036]
7. **Commitments:** What would happen if you don't buy this product? [L0770.036]
8. **Brand preference:** If you had to decide right now, without talking to anyone, which brand would you buy? [L0770.036]
9. **Supplier preference:** Is there someone you'd rather do business with? [L0770.036]
10. **Internal procedure:** What is your process for issuing a purchase order? Have him write it down and read it back before you move on. [L0770.036]
11. **Personal motivation:** What would it mean to you personally if you didn't purchase this product? [L0770.036]
12. **Personal prejudices:** Is there any reason you wouldn't want to do business with me? Anything we haven't covered yet, or any emotional reason? [L0770.036]
13. **Hidden obstacles:** What could be lurking in the background that would prevent this from happening? [L0770.036]
14. **Close:** Once questions 1 to 13 are answered satisfactorily and he hasn't disqualified himself: if I can meet all your criteria for this product, what will you do? [L0770.036]

- Discovery questions are general, not about your brand, so the answers describe the prospect's own needs. Ask each question in the exact same words every time and write down the answers precisely, since the wording and tone of his answers can matter later. [L0770.037]
- The prospect can disqualify himself at any of the fourteen discovery questions. Each answer he gives without disqualifying himself builds the relationship and the mutual commitment, and each problem you handle early prevents a deal-breaker later. [L0770.038]
- Do not disqualify a prospect after an objection such as a price limit without first asking why he holds that position. The reason may be solvable, and asking why is better than guessing at his thinking. [L0770.043]

### Decision-makers and approvers

Request to speak with the decision-maker or approver before preparing a proposal:

```
I need to talk with [name or role] before I prepare a proposal. Are you willing to arrange that?
```

If he refuses, reply in a flat tone:

```
That's not the way I work. I won't prepare a proposal without understanding their concerns and objectives, because I don't want a proposal rejected over something we could have handled up front. What would you like to do?
```

If he still will not arrange it, disqualify him. [L0770.039]

### Unclear, evasive and conflicting answers

When a prospect's answer is unclear or evasive, do not move on until you are fully satisfied.

1. Ask for clarification, for example by saying you do not understand what he meant and asking what he means. [L0770.040]
2. If he is still unclear, state that his answer seems evasive and ask whether there is a problem. [L0770.040]
3. If he still avoids answering, tell him you will not move on until the question is answered. [L0770.040]
4. Carry on only when you have a clear answer, because an unresolved issue usually returns later as a problem. [L0770.040]

- When a prospect gives conflicting timing, such as urgent on the phone and six months away in the meeting, ask him directly about the discrepancy before going further. Then either reach a clear commitment for the timing or set a specific return date that he chooses. [L0770.041]

## High Probability commitment, conditions and closing

### Sequence of the Sale

- Do not present a product, quote, or proposal until the prospect has committed to buy if the product meets his stated conditions. The order is: questions, agreement on conditions, commitment, and only then the demonstration or proposal. [L0770.052]
- Selling in this approach means reaching a series of agreements with prospects who first acknowledge that they need, want, and can afford the product, and who commit to buying at a set time if their conditions are met. It is not about persuading anyone to act. A deal exists only when both sides have agreed. [L0770.075]

### Closing Through Mutual Commitment

- Closing means negotiating mutual commitments, never asking for the order. The prospect chooses yes or no, and you are equally satisfied with either answer, because your commitment is to the process rather than to making a sale. [L0770.050]
- Ask only questions whose answers you need. Avoid rhetorical or trial closes, including small either-or choices meant to push a sale. Prospects recognize these tactics and resent them, and they undermine trust. [L0770.051]
- Traditional selling offers a choice of yes or yes: the seller argues for a sale no matter the prospect's view. High Probability selling offers a choice of yes or no and accepts either answer, which is why it produces commitments that hold. [L0770.066]
- Example of a real decision: "Does a one-week delivery window work for you, or not?" Compare "Shall we get you set up?", which only invites a reluctant yes. (Own illustration.) [L0770.066]

### Defining the Conditions of Satisfaction

Open the conditions phase with this template after discovery is complete:

```
It is time to define your Conditions of Satisfaction. I would like us to write down exactly what you require, every requirement, because that is how I determine whether we can provide it. Are you willing to do that?

After he agrees, read back what he said during discovery and ask whether it is correct and whether he wants to add anything.
```
[L0770.072]

Establish the Conditions of Satisfaction in this order:

1. Confirm that the discovery questions are fully answered and that every decision-maker and approver is involved. [L0770.053]
2. Tell the prospect that you now need to define exactly what he requires, and ask whether he is willing to do that. [L0770.053]
3. Ask what he will do if you return with a proposal that meets his conditions. [L0770.053]
4. If he does not give a clear commitment, tell him that you will only prepare a proposal with a commitment to buy if the conditions are met, and disqualify him if he refuses. [L0770.053]
5. Once he commits, read back what he said during discovery and ask whether it is correct and whether he wants to add anything. [L0770.053]
6. Ask for each condition in his exact words and record them. Raise any conditions he has not mentioned that need addressing. [L0770.053]
7. Specify exactly what he will and will not accept. Agree how each condition will be measured, such as a timed test or a signed sample. [L0770.053]
8. Tell him clearly what you can and cannot provide, and offer alternatives where possible without hiding the negatives. [L0770.053]
9. Negotiate any conditions you cannot meet. If an unmet condition cannot be negotiated, disqualify him. If you agree on conditions you can meet, you have a deal. [L0770.053]
10. At the next meeting, present a proposal that shows you meet all conditions, and complete the transaction. [L0770.053]

### Making Conditions Measurable

- Make each condition measurable so both sides can check it. "Easy to set up" becomes a time limit for a shipping clerk to set up the package, including taping. "Vivid four-color art" becomes a signed sample of the minimum quality the buyer will accept. [L0770.054]

### References

When a prospect wants references from existing customers:

1. Ask how many references he wants. [L0770.073]
2. Ask whether he will call those references while you are present. [L0770.073]
3. Ask what he will do if the references give positive endorsements. [L0770.073]
4. Record the agreed answers in his exact words as a condition to be met. [L0770.073]

### Budgetary Quotes

- When you present a budgetary quote to a prospect who has not committed, ask in the same breath what he will do if the price is acceptable. This ties the estimate to a real commitment instead of sending a free number he can shop around. [L0770.077]

### Testing the Commitment

- After a prospect commits, test that commitment by asking whether he is sure and why he wants to proceed. His reasons often surface, and the answer strengthens his commitment. Testing also brings hidden doubts into the open before you leave. [L0770.057]

### Handling Requests You Cannot Meet

When a prospect asks for something you cannot deliver, such as a finish you do not offer:

1. State plainly that you do not offer it, and give the reason in one sentence. [L0770.042]
2. Offer your available option and ask whether he will accept it. [L0770.042]
3. If he insists on the unavailable option, end the meeting instead of hoping he changes his mind. [L0770.042]

Use this template for follow-up replies to question 14, delivered in a flat tone, depending on his response:

```
Follow-up replies to question 14 are delivered in a flat tone, depending on his response. If he answers 'What do you mean?', reply: What do you think I mean? If he says he will seriously consider it, reply: I'm not willing to prepare a proposal unless I have a commitment that we will do business if I meet your criteria. What would you like to do? Unless he clearly states that he will give you his business if you meet his criteria, disqualify him.
```
[L0770.049]

### Pushback and Disqualification

- Commitments tend to hold when they are freely made. A prospect who says yes will usually honor it, while an order that rests on pressure is likely to be cancelled. [L0770.058]
- A prospect who breaks a commitment should be disqualified in most markets. In markets with few buyers, you may have to keep working with him. [L0770.058]
- When a prospect pushes back hard against being disqualified, still disqualify him if you have real doubts about his commitment. A serious buyer rarely accepts disqualification without a struggle, but the struggle alone does not prove that he is qualified. [L0770.078]

### Common Mistakes

- Do not move from discovery straight to the prospect's requests without first asking for commitment. Otherwise the prospect takes the lead, you end up doing what he asks, and the process loses its structure. [L0770.062]
- If you find yourself answering the prospect's questions instead of asking your own, return to asking questions and asking for commitment. It is harder to regain control once you have lost it, but a commitment request can still restore it. [L0770.063]
- Do not assume the sale is made because discovery went well or the prospect seems friendly. Until he commits in writing or aloud to the conditions, he has not committed, and acting as though he has leads to lost orders. [L0770.064]
- Do not try to convince a prospect to change his mind after he has declined a commitment or set a limit you cannot meet. Ending the meeting saves the effort, and trying to talk him out of his conditions creates resistance. [L0770.065]

### Worked Cases
